budget_items.what_was_said: A member said PAC currently gets a percentage of Comcast revenue and that this is likely the main negotiation point; another said that percentage is set by state law as a ceiling.
Members discussed whether Comcast provides free internet connections to the town and schools, concluding the town and the school each pay for their own internet.

A member said the negotiation's lawyer would be paid from PAC/cable funds rather than town general funds, and asked whether the select board must approve the hiring process.
Members discussed the percentage of Comcast revenue the cable fund receives as likely the main point of negotiation, noting state law sets a ceiling on that percentage.

The meeting closed with a roll-call vote to adjourn; no other votes were taken.

why_it_matters: This negotiation will shape the town's next 10-year cable franchise agreement with Comcast, which funds local public-access programming through the PAC/cable fund rather than general tax dollars.
The revenue-share percentage the committee plans to negotiate is capped by state law and is described as the central lever affecting how much money supports local access TV.
The committee plans a public survey as part of its outreach, so residents may be asked for input before terms are finalized.

meetings.headline: Finance Committee reorganized under new leadership and moved budget previews earlier ahead of a special town meeting
meetings.summary: The Lunenburg Finance Committee reorganized (re-electing Chris Manard as chair, electing Peter Beardmore vice chair and Tom Gray clerk), heard a presentation from the Green Communities Committee on Mass Save incentive programs for municipal and school buildings, and reviewed the FY27 state aid ("cherry sheet") changes and the superintendent's proposed use of the resulting funds plus health insurance savings. meetings.headline: Planning Board drafted zoning changes for minor site plan review, cluster housing, and senior/affordable housing.
meetings.summary: The Lunenburg Planning Board held an off-cycle working session to draft language for four zoning bylaw changes: minor site plan review, inclusionary housing, cluster housing, and a new senior housing bylaw. The board worked through a consultant's draft site plan amendment, discussed how an inclusionary housing bylaw with a payment-in-lieu and affordable housing trust could work alongside a proposed senior housing bylaw, and revised numerous cluster-housing standards (acreage threshold, open space percentage, density, buffers, performance guarantees). No formal votes were taken on the bylaw language itself; the board reached working consensus on several specific provisions and set its next working session for August 10th before adjourning with no public comment offered.

budget_items.topic: ARPA funds toward senior housing land
budget_items.what_was_said: A speaker recalled the town's own contribution to a past senior housing project as land plus ARPA funds. The exact dollar figure is garbled in the captions.

budget_items.topic: Inclusionary housing payment-in-lieu, tiered by units
budget_items.what_was_said: Discussion proposed a ramped payment-in-lieu into an affordable housing trust as unit thresholds rise, with a full unit required or its cash equivalent above the top threshold.

budget_items.topic: Housing trust's own home purchase, as a market comparison
budget_items.what_was_said: A board member cited a recent purchase by a housing trust as an example of how tight the local housing market has become.

budget_items.topic: Local housing market costs, cited during inclusionary bylaw discussion
budget_items.what_was_said: A board member described teardown and new-construction costs in town as context for why affordable inclusionary units are hard to produce without incentives.

budget_items.topic: State grant funding for a past affordable senior housing project
budget_items.what_was_said: A presenter described a prior town in which the state eventually funded affordable senior housing units on town-donated land after a multi-year process.

budget_items.topic: Grant to update the town's housing production plan
budget_items.what_was_said: The board discussed pursuing a state one-stop growth grant, since MRPC's regular funding program could not cover a housing production plan update.

decisions.decision: Drop the proposed C2 provision requiring full site plan review for minor changes near residential abutters, in favor of relying on the more easily amended site plan regulations.
Keep the inclusionary housing bylaw applicable to ANR lots for now, revisiting if a pattern of small estate-lot subdivisions emerges.
Reinstate a payment-in-lieu option and an offsite-unit option for developers triggering inclusionary housing requirements, with amounts to ramp up with the number of units.
Raise the single-family density cap in the cluster bylaw from two to four units per acre.
Keep the cluster housing minimum parcel size at 10 acres rather than lowering it to 5.
Add explicit language requiring the percolation test be completed before site plan review for cluster developments.
Reframe the cluster buffer as a non-disturbed area rather than a cleared buffer, with the planning board able to require landscaping if the area is already bare/grass.
Allow the required buffer area to count toward the cluster open-space percentage.
Remove letters of credit as an allowed performance guarantee for cluster developments, limiting security to cash, a AAA-rated bond, or a covenant.
Treat cluster developments as a single parcel with an exclusive-use area rather than individual lots, removing the need for a frontage standard.

meetings.headline: Sewer Commission questioned whether a Mass Ave two-family property was correctly billed connection and betterment fees
meetings.summary: The Sewer Commission reviewed grease trap permit renewals, then spent most of the meeting on whether the 990 Mass Ave property (and similar multi-unit tie-ins) had been correctly charged residential connection fees and betterment/privilege fees for each unit, deciding to raise wording and process questions with town council. It also discussed the stalled 100 Laurel Lane bid, put the CTE contract out to rebid, and reviewed a problem manhole on Prospect Street that a contractor could not enter due to high gas levels and recommended replacing.

votes.motion: Accept the minutes of the June 30th meeting
Adjourn the meeting

budget_items.what_was_said: Permits for the coming year were mailed out; the business manager was still waiting on most permit holders (roughly a dozen accounts) to return theirs by the due date.

budget_items.topic: 990 Mass Ave connection and betterment fees
budget_items.what_was_said: Members debated whether a property recorded as a two-family should be charged a second residential connection fee under the sewer regulations, which set a minimum charge per dwelling unit. A member also raised that a duplex or subdivided property should owe an additional half-betterment privilege fee.

A member described his own past experience being charged an additional privilege fee (half the prior betterment) plus tie-in fees when a single-family property he owned was subdivided and developed further.
Members clarified that privilege fee and betterment money collected does not go into the everyday operating budget but into the commission's reserves used in its own budget.

The business manager said the one-year contract with a two-year option (the commission's option) has run its course and must go back out to bid, with an opening date expected around August 3rd; a member asked the annual price tag.
A contract for the work was drafted and the bid was going out on the street, with bid opening expected around July 21st; no bid figures existed yet at meeting time.

A contractor fixing manholes could not enter this deep manhole due to high gas levels but found it structurally unsound with heavy infiltration and recommended replacement, which would also require rerouting an active pump; described as a larger future project with no cost given.

decisions.decision: The business manager and director will continue handling individual sewer connection/betterment applications rather than requiring every application to come before the full commission.

The business manager will informally ask licensed drainlayers to check the manhole one section up/down/each way from their tie-in work as a courtesy, to help identify infiltration problems without a full re-survey.
The 100 Laurel Lane item stays on current business until bids come in, with bids possibly available by the next meeting.
The Prospect Street/Laurel Lane manhole replacement is carried over as a project to address in the future.

minutes.headline: Board delayed two large subdivisions over storm-water/wildlife concerns; approved several smaller projects
minutes.summary: The Lunenburg Planning Board approved several smaller land-use requests (a duplex conversion on Reservoir Road, a driveway/storm water modification on Arbor Street, and a storm water permit on Mass Ave), while continuing two larger multi-lot subdivisions (Parmenter/Round Road and 860 New Westminster Road) to July 27 pending engineering follow-up, an HOA/maintenance mechanism, and a fire-system cistern review. minutes.summary: The Zoning Board of Appeals held a public hearing on a special permit request from GCJT Realty LLC (applicant Greg Roy) for a dimensional deviation to place a business sign near a new office building at 1325 Mass Ave closer to the street than the standard 20-ft setback. No members of the public attended to comment; after board questions on lighting hours and sign size, the board voted to approve the permit with the sign set 2 ft from the right-of-way line, subject to standard conditions. The board also elected its chairman and vice chairman for the coming term before adjourning.

what_happened.line: ZBA approved a special permit letting a new office building's sign at 1325 Mass Ave sit closer to the street than the standard setback allows.
The applicant agreed to put the sign's downlighting on a timer rather than lit continuously, addressing a board member's concern about the garage across the street.
The board did not require relief on the secondary sign's size; the applicant will narrow it if the building commissioner finds it exceeds the sign bylaw.
No members of the public attended to comment on the request.
The board elected a chairman and vice chairman for the coming term.

why_it_matters: This sets a dimensional precedent for how close a commercial sign can sit to the street on Mass Ave, a standard other applicants may point to.
Residents near the garage across the street gain a lighting-hours condition tied to this specific approval, not a blanket rule.
The sign's ultimate size still depends on a follow-up check by the building commissioner against the town's sign bylaw.

meetings.headline: The board took the Flatill Road bridge land by eminent domain and tabled the DPW union contract over legal disputes.
meetings.summary: The Lunenburg Select Board ratified a police detective promotion and several routine appointments, heard a lengthy planning-director update and a historical society pitch for a Revolutionary War memorial, and got tangled in a dispute over a stalled Trust Fund Commission appointment. It also acted on several money and process items — adopting the IRS mileage rate, taking an eminent-domain easement for the Flatill Road bridge, designating the Cable Advisory Committee as special municipal employees, choosing police over a constable for three upcoming elections, and approving minutes including newly released executive-session employment agreements — while tabling the DPW union contract, the special election warrant, and the trust fund appointment, and deferring a decision on a special town meeting for additional state education funding.

public_comment.topic: Thanked the Lincoln family for privately sponsoring a town band concert and a jazz concert this summer after the override ended town-sponsored concerts.

Promoted the senior-center reading buddies program, raised concern about low third/fifth grade reading proficiency tied to the loss of phonics instruction since 1990, and urged that any new state funding go toward reducing elementary class sizes.

public_comment.topic: Criticized years of lack of progress on municipal building projects and urged the select board to task the Municipal Building Design Committee with a holistic plan for all town buildings, citing the still-unadopted master plan as an example of the town's aversion to planning.

Disputed the town's process for Richard Howard's Trust Fund Commission application, alleging the assistant town manager failed to notify or process his paperwork; the town manager disputed the characterization.

Ratify the town manager's appointment of Braden Rozer as seasonal cemetery laborer.

Adopt the current IRS standard mileage rate (.725/72.5 cents) as the town's official mileage reimbursement rate, with future IRS rate changes to apply automatically.
Designate the Cable Advisory Committee positions as special municipal employees.
Acquire by eminent domain a temporary easement at 890 Flatill Road for the Flatill Road bridge project, with damages of $600 to the affected owner, authorizing the chair to execute related documents.

budget_items.topic: FY27 state budget — net revenue impact for Lunenburg
budget_items.what_was_said: The town manager reported the legislature passed the FY27 state budget, and based on the conference committee version Lunenburg would net additional revenue across education aid, unrestricted general government aid, veterans/elderly exemptions, state-owned land payments, and increased charter-school assessments.

budget_items.topic: Local earmarks in FY27 state budget
budget_items.what_was_said: The state budget included earmarks for Lunenburg schools' technology upgrades and for the fire department's aging portable radios.

budget_items.topic: FY26 winter Road/Recovery Assistance Program (RAP) funds
budget_items.what_was_said: A fair share supplemental bill funded a statewide winter recovery assistance program split between a formula pool and a hardship pool that Lunenburg did not qualify for; Lunenburg's formula share will offset the town's snow-and-ice deficit.
A camera system installation project funded through the FY2025 capital program will install and replace security cameras at Town Hall, the Ritter Building, Eagle House, and DPW.

The planning director described the cost of a full site plan review, including an engineering plan, for a business making only minor changes, calling the current requirement not business-friendly and part of the reason for a proposed minor site plan provision.

The planning director is working through about 70 outstanding 53G developer review-fee accounts dating back years and refunding unused balances; project review fees typically run in the low thousands depending on scope.
The planning director noted Lunenburg's tax revenue share from commercial and industrial development is below the threshold that keeps a town from being classified a bedroom community.

budget_items.topic: Additional Chapter 70 funding and possible special town meeting
budget_items.what_was_said: The board discussed additional state education funding and whether it would restore staff or fund tutoring/professional development; the town manager said reduced classroom sizes were stated by the school committee not to be the intended use regardless of funding.
The board adopted the current IRS standard mileage rate as the town's reimbursement rate for personal vehicle use on town business, with future IRS changes to apply automatically.

budget_items.topic: Eminent domain easement damages, 890 Flatill Road
budget_items.what_was_said: The board took a new temporary easement for the Flatill Road bridge project after the prior easement expired before construction finished, with damages set by an appraisal of diminished property value.
The board arranged to sign an accounts payable warrant, either via DocuSign or in person.

budget_items.topic: Executive session employment agreements (facilities, HR, Council on Aging, DPW, admin staff)
budget_items.what_was_said: A selectman summarized several employment agreements approved in executive session: a vehicle stipend and added vacation for the facilities director, vacation increases for the HR and Council on Aging directors, a wage step increase, stipends and vacation for the DPW director, and a grade step increase for an administrative employee who absorbed IT/communications duties.
Ratification of a brand-new collective bargaining agreement with Teamsters Local 170 was held pending labor counsel's review of discrepancies.

budget_items.topic: Constable vs. police officer for upcoming elections
budget_items.what_was_said: The board discussed using a constable versus police officers for three upcoming elections, with one member noting the constable would likely be cheaper, but voted to use police for all three.

minutes.headline: The board took the Flatill Road bridge land by eminent domain and tabled the DPW union contract over legal disputes.

what_happened.line: The board tabled ratification of the new DPW union contract after labor counsel flagged discrepancies to resolve.
The board voted to take a temporary easement at 890 Flatill Road by eminent domain to keep the bridge project moving.
A dispute over how the town processed Richard Howard's Trust Fund Commission application went unresolved, with the appointment pushed to a future agenda.
Approval of the August 8 special town election warrant was put off a week so town counsel can review new mailing-notice language.
The board also adopted the current IRS mileage rate, named a new detective and other appointees, and reviewed executive-session employment agreements for several town staff.

why_it_matters: A stalled union contract leaves DPW workers' pay and terms unresolved and keeps a labor cost decision open for the town.
The eminent domain action affects a specific property owner on Flatill Road and clears the way for a town bridge project residents depend on.
The election warrant delay and the mailing-notice review could affect how voters are notified ahead of the August 8 special town election.

meetings.summary: This was the first meeting of Lunenburg's Personnel Committee since it was reactivated after being inactive since 2024; the three appointed members elected officers and then read through the town's salary administration plan bylaw section by section, flagging language they want clarified by town counsel and the HR director. No formal policy changes were voted; the committee set a recurring meeting schedule and agreed to bring a list of questions to its next meeting on the 20th.

attendees.name_as_heard: Tanya Doll (also heard as Tanya Willard Doll)

budget_items.topic: Review of wage and salary schedules
budget_items.what_was_said: The bylaw requires the committee to review wage and salary schedules of all positions at a set interval and recommend action to the select board; members said comparable-town wage data has historically been hard to get accurately.

budget_items.topic: New hire starting pay / step approval
budget_items.what_was_said: New employees are to be hired at the minimum of the job's pay range unless the town manager, after consulting the chair, authorizes a higher step; the committee must formally vote to approve any new-hire pay above a stated step.

figures_as_heard: up to five days of vacation leave
budget_items.what_was_said: The plan lets the town manager offer recruitment incentives such as deposited vacation time or a sign-on bonus when hard-to-fill critical positions can't attract qualified applicants; the committee was unsure whether the town manager needs select board sign-off to use this.

Department heads must include a pay-adjustment section in their annual budget request, and any planned increase within the salary plan needs personnel committee approval before it goes into the budget; a member questioned whether step increases are actually automatic rather than discretionary.
Non-exempt employees get overtime at a stated multiplier of their regular rate for hours worked beyond a 40-hour week, counting paid leave time toward the 40 hours.

budget_items.topic: Compensatory time in lieu of overtime
budget_items.what_was_said: Employees may take compensatory time at the overtime rate instead of cash, but it must be used within a stated number of days.

Full-time employees accrue sick leave monthly up to a stated annual amount, cumulative up to a stated maximum, and it can be donated through a sick leave bank whose current status the committee was unsure of.

Employees who retire in good standing and were hired before a stated cutoff date get a percentage of accumulated unused sick leave paid out, rising with years of service; a member noted this only applies to employees hired before a certain date and few may still qualify.

budget_items.topic: Parental leave use of sick leave
budget_items.what_was_said: New parents may draw on a prorated cap of sick leave hours for parental leave.
Employees receive an annual longevity bonus as a percentage of salary starting after a stated years-of-service threshold, increasing at further milestones, paid each year on the anniversary date.

budget_items.topic: Pay upon transfer to a lower-graded job
budget_items.what_was_said: The committee discussed that an employee transferred to a lower-paying job could actually lose pay under the plan's placement formula, and planned to raise questions about it with counsel.

decisions.decision: Invite town counsel Attorney Terry and the HR director to the committee's next meeting (the 20th) to review bylaw language and roles.
Chair will ask the town's IT/facilities contact (Mason) about a portable meeting device (the 'owl') so meetings could move to other rooms.
Chair will compile a written list of the committee's questions for Attorney Terry and HR, to be sent ahead of the next meeting.
Committee will request copies of the recently finalized union contracts once available.
Committee will ask HR/town manager about the current status of the sick leave bank.
Committee will meet on the first and third Monday of each month going forward, and the chair will look into using the senior center or library as a more accessible meeting space.
Members will send any questions for Attorney Terry and HR to the chair by Monday the 13th so they can be answered in advance.

meetings.headline: Assessors reviewed a lakefront property revaluation plan and weighed raising the veterans' tax exemption.
meetings.summary: The Board of Assessors received a detailed update on a neighborhood-by-neighborhood review of waterfront and lake-adjacent property valuations, aimed at correcting mislabeled parcels while avoiding sudden value drops before recoding takes effect on future tax bills. The board also discussed the principal assessor search (two candidates in a second interview round), planned a senior means-tested exemption presentation for early August, and opened discussion on possibly raising the veterans exemption for a future town meeting article. No formal votes were taken; the meeting ended with informal agreement on next steps and September meeting dates.

assessing office staff (addressed directly re: time slips, office software)
assessing office staff (referenced as currently running the office)

budget_items.what_was_said: The presenter said that without adjusting factors, waterfront parcels inside site index one would have dropped in value by roughly this much per parcel.
The waterfront site index one factor was kept the same to avoid dropping values that have held for three years.
Sales reviewed showed little difference across the seven neighborhoods, so the factor was adjusted only slightly rather than left as before.
A small unbuildable waterfront parcel was found valued far higher than a neighboring home's lake-view land, which the board called unreasonable and possibly a data error.
Treating a property as lake-back rather than a standard neighborhood raised its value by this amount in the presenter's test.
A tentative sub-neighborhood factor was applied for properties near but not on the water, pending confirming sales.
The board target for the assessment ratio is 95%, and current values are at or near that target.
The current veterans exemption is reimbursed by the state at this amount, and it has not been increased while other exemptions were.

budget_items.topic: Veterans exemption comparison / state reimbursement formula
budget_items.what_was_said: Other communities have adopted a higher veterans exemption add-on, funded by the town rather than the state, and the state's own reimbursement formula was cited without certainty.
The office is currently being run by one staff member working a limited weekly schedule while covering the whole department.

budget_items.topic: Senior means-tested exemption utilization, prior year
budget_items.what_was_said: The board recalled a low number of applicants used the senior means-tested exemption in its second year, fewer than they had expected.

budget_items.topic: Combined circuit breaker and exemption benefit
budget_items.what_was_said: Combining the circuit breaker credit with the senior exemption was described as putting a substantial amount back into an eligible senior's spending money, though the specific figures given were garbled.

If the senior means-tested exemption amount is raised, the added cost is supposed to be redistributed across all other tax bills via a tax shift rather than paid from the overlay, and the mechanics still need to be worked out.
The exemption cost is currently being covered through an inflated overlay amount because the town lacks a proper overlay figure, which the assessor said needs to be corrected going forward.

decisions.decision: Keep the waterfront site index one factor and the seven-neighborhoods factor essentially unchanged so parcel values do not drop, rather than following the raw sales-derived factors.
Hold off recoding waterfront parcels' site index/land use codes until around August, after the second round of preliminary tax bills goes out, so the new values first appear on the actual tax bill.
Hold the senior means-tested exemption public presentation the week of August 10th at the senior center.
The assessing office resolved its PDF/Adobe software need directly with vendor staff, so the town does not need to purchase a license.
Tentatively set the board's next two meetings for September 9th and September 23rd.
Discuss increasing the veterans exemption further at a future meeting before deciding whether the board will sponsor it for the November special town meeting.
The assessor will research how a larger senior exemption amount could be redistributed across all tax bills via a tax shift instead of being funded through the overlay.

meetings.headline: Sewer board debates charging an extra connection fee when a home is split into more units
meetings.summary: The Lunenburg Sewer Commission reviewed ongoing manhole and pump station repair work, approved end-of-year billing adjustments after a leak-driven $6,000 outlier bill, and discussed delinquency rates on sewer bills. The bulk of substantive discussion concerned whether the town should charge an additional connection fee when a single-family home is converted into multiple dwelling units, with no bylaw change made but the director directed to draft language for the next meeting; commissioners also voted to keep their current roles unchanged.

Commissioners voted 5-0 to accept end-of-year billing adjustments, including a large one-time bill tied to a prolonged water leak that skewed the quarter's totals.

meetings.summary: The Parks Commission heard a skatepark project update -- after nearly a decade and over $400,000 raised, a new town right-of-entry/escrow agreement is drafted but awaiting review by the group's and the town's attorneys before it returns for a vote. The board also endorsed a new Recreation Department mission statement, planned a dedication ceremony renaming the town beach house for Genevieve Nass with a budget capped around $500, and tabled approval of prior minutes over a SharePoint access problem.

The board discussed creating a way to accept public donations toward beach programming, earmarked for swim-lesson scholarships, to be routed through either the town or the department's own revolving account.
The board agreed a cap on ceremony spending sounded reasonable, covering flowers and incidentals while trying to keep costs to a minimum.

The skatepark right-of-entry/escrow agreement is not ready for a board vote; the group's attorney must first confer with town counsel and the funder before it comes back to the commission.

meetings.headline: The committee voted unanimously to ask the select board for a special town meeting to redirect state aid into the school budget.
meetings.summary: The Lunenburg School Committee heard extensive public comment on middle school athletics funding, booster fundraising, and academic performance following the failed override, then reviewed routine business (minutes, a donation, four line-item transfers, warrants, and encumbrances). The superintendent reported on transportation vans, a facilities earmark, staffing changes, and Title IX/booster-donation guidance; the committee also approved an adult meal price increase, relocated the T-ball program to accommodate the food pantry, accepted a curriculum report describing the loss of all reading interventionists and larger class sizes, accepted a strong FY26 quarterly budget report, accepted a personnel report with numerous departures attributed to budget uncertainty, and voted unanimously to ask the select board to convene a special town meeting to direct additional state chapter 70 and other cherry sheet funds into the school budget.

public_comment.topic: Argues the override failed due to lost public confidence, not messaging; cites accreditation risk and reading proficiency, urges review of support programs, academic prioritization, IEP audit, and accountability.

public_comment.speaker_as_heard: Matt Nzareno (heard also as Matt Ezaro)
public_comment.topic: Presented a by-sport athletics cost/revenue analysis built from FY24 actuals, arguing middle school sports were revenue-positive and questioning the decision to cut them for budget reasons.
Spoke on behalf of the community about restoring middle school athletics, requesting a detailed cost/revenue breakdown by sport and guidance on applying community-raised funds, by mid-July.

Requested permission to purchase five football helmets and to fund one-way transportation to away games using booster funds, and pushed back on the characterization of football boosters as "wealthier" than other programs.

public_comment.stated_role: resident, 389 Mus[?] Road, speaking for the music boosters ("musicators")
public_comment.topic: Raised the fundraising policy's two-fundraiser limit, asked for guidance on donating funds for color guard/marching band uniforms and transportation, requested restoring fifth grade band and sixth grade jazz, and raised concerns about scheduling forcing students to choose between electives and academics.

A member praised last year's surplus as evidence of a change in fiscal management, noting the current estimated return is in line with prior years and other departments.
The chair described additional state cherry sheet funding coming to Lunenburg beyond what the town budget assumed, citing differences between the Senate, House and Governor's budget figures.

The town is receiving additional one-time snow and ice removal money, distinguished from the recurring chapter 70 ask; the school department is typically allowed to run a deficit on snow/ice, covered by free cash.

The chair read total estimated state receipts and estimated charges (assessments) figures from the cherry sheet, noting the charges side includes items like MBTA assessment (described as having doubled) and charter/school choice tuition.

The chair stated that chapter 70 funding covers a large share of the entire Lunenburg school budget.
The high-dosage tutoring program was funded through a supplemental state budget grant; members are uncertain it will be available again.
The superintendent said Lunenburg spends well above its state-calculated foundation budget yet remains near the bottom of the list for per-pupil spending compared to peer districts.
A booster asked whether a small amount of funding could restore the cut fifth grade band program, citing its low cost.

meetings.headline: Commissioners rescinded their prior vote and will proceed with the new billing/accounting software vendor.
meetings.summary: The Water District Commissioners reversed a prior vote to cancel a new billing/accounting software switch, approved several purchases (pipe, materials, hydrants) for a PVC water main replacement on Metal Lane, and discussed ongoing PFAS treatment planning that remains stalled pending state guidance. They also tabled a legal/easement dispute over kayaks stored near the Hickory Hills wellfield, discussed the revenue benefits of selling water to commercial buyers, and set a revised July meeting schedule.

public_comment.topic: Asked whether the easement/deed restricting structures at the Hickory Hills pumping station is a recorded legal document, and whether Hickory Hills residents had sent any letter committing to remove kayaks/canoes stored there.

votes.motion: Approve the minutes of June 10th
Rescind the prior (June 10th) vote that had cancelled/changed the plan to switch billing software, and continue moving forward with the vendor (referred to as the 'beta' company)
Approve the pipe quote from EJP (EJ Prescott) for the Metal Lane water main replacement project
Approve purchase of $14,557.89 of materials (excluding hydrants) from Ferguson for the Metal Lane water main replacement project, funded from the equipment and main account
Approve $7,300 for the purchase of two hydrants for the Metal Lane main from the hydrant vendor (heard as 'FW')
Adjourn the meeting

budget_items.what_was_said: After an additional meeting with the vendor, the board decided to proceed with switching accounting systems effective July 1 to align with the new fiscal year, while the actual resident-billing switch may slip to October 1st or January 1st depending on testing.
Ductile iron pipe pricing was compared to the lowest PVC bid; PVC was chosen as a test run for the Metal Lane project, with the pipe quote awarded to EJP.
Ferguson won the materials quote; removing the hydrants from that quote brought the material cost down, to be paid from the equipment and main account.
Two hydrants were purchased separately from the materials quote to match the M&H brand already used on the rest of the project.

Using PVC instead of ductile iron was said to save enough per street that two streets could be done for the cost of one; a prior project (Rolling Acres) was said to have saved roughly half a million dollars by doing the work in-house.

budget_items.topic: Hydrant maintenance reimbursement from the town
budget_items.what_was_said: The district receives a flat annual reimbursement from the town's fire department budget for hydrant maintenance, unchanged by the number of hydrants; a commissioner raised whether hydrant testing/flushing costs are fully covered and asked it be revisited.

budget_items.topic: Cost and revenue from bulk/commercial water sales
budget_items.what_was_said: The district calculated its cost to pump/treat water per million gallons versus what it charges bulk buyers (mainly one large commercial hauler), estimating roughly the stated annual revenue since sales began, which offsets what would otherwise be charged to the roughly 2,500 users.

budget_items.topic: PFAS/PAS water treatment and SRF funding
budget_items.what_was_said: Voters denied SRF funding for treatment, but the board discussed continuing baseline engineering/survey work for a Keyes-to-Lancaster transmission main, comparing costs to other towns' treatment plants.
Revenue from bulk water sales is folded into the roughly stated operating budget; any surplus beyond covering the budget is used for capital items like equipment purchases.

budget_items.topic: New display TV for AMI meter monitoring
budget_items.what_was_said: The district purchased a large TV, described as inexpensive, to display real-time meter/leak data for staff and the public.

transfers.description: Materials purchase for Metal Lane water main project paid from the equipment and main account

decisions.decision: Proceed with switching accounting/billing software to the new vendor effective July 1st for accounting, with the resident billing switch possibly delayed to October or January depending on readiness.
Run the new billing system in parallel (dry run) alongside the existing NDS system before fully switching over, to check accuracy before sending bills.
Superintendent Fran will speak with a newspaper reporter (from the Ledger) about the sale of water to commercial buyers.
Hold off on any action regarding the zone one easement/kayak issue until the next meeting, pending the chair's input and a possible different approach than sending another letter to legal.
Test each of the four wells feeding the Lancaster source individually for PFAS to determine if a weaker well could be shut off while blending the others.
Cancel the July 8th and July 22nd commissioners' meetings and hold a single meeting on July 15th at 4:00, with a public notice of the schedule change.

Clerk will respond to a resident's inquiry by naming the district's attorney (KP Law, Brian Riley) but direct him to route further questions through the water district rather than contacting counsel directly, and will notify the attorney to confirm with the board before engaging.

meetings.headline: Task force keeps refining property-by-property stormwater fee data and leans toward a utility, not the operating budget
meetings.summary: The Stormwater Task Force spent nearly the entire meeting working line-by-line through a combined assessor/Weston & Sampson spreadsheet, assigning ERUs and fixing missing use codes, missing impervious-area data, and how condo/rental/HOA complexes should be billed. It also compared funding the program through the operating budget versus a stand-alone utility fee, leaning toward the utility option, and set next steps (checking an old CI spreadsheet, sending gaps to the consultant, finishing a bylaw draft) before a possible fall Town Meeting article.

attendees.role: task force member (built the property/ERU spreadsheet and MATLAB data processing)
DPW / task force member (holds assessor data, coordinates with assessor's office)

budget_items.topic: Sum of proposed stormwater fees across all properties
budget_items.what_was_said: The consolidated spreadsheet's fee column was summed across all properties to see what the ERU-based fee schedule would raise in total.
The per-ERU fee used in the spreadsheet was described as changeable depending on the final budget target for the program.
It was suggested the per-ERU fee could come down significantly in a future iteration if the budget requirement is reduced, making it more palatable to residents.
A task force member noted their own household's estimated annual fee under the current model.

budget_items.topic: 1295 Massachusetts Ave storage facility bay sale
budget_items.what_was_said: A member noted one storage bay unit in the facility recently sold, illustrating the property is actively subdivided and sold by unit.

budget_items.topic: Property tax calculator - operating budget scenario
budget_items.what_was_said: A member ran the town's property tax calculator assuming the stormwater program were funded through the operating budget with a given increase, to see the effect on the average single-family tax bill versus shifting cost to commercial/industrial.
Based on the calculator, a member said the average home's increase would be somewhat higher than an earlier estimate.

budget_items.topic: Estimated fee jump for one large gravel/industrial property
budget_items.what_was_said: A member estimated the storm water fee for one large industrial/gravel operation would rise sharply from its current near-zero assessment once properly classified.

budget_items.topic: Lunenburg Crossing tax bill and assessment
budget_items.what_was_said: Members looked up the shopping center's current tax bill and assessed value, noting the assessment had fallen from the prior figure, to gauge how a stormwater utility fee would compare to its existing tax burden.

budget_items.topic: Per-acre tax comparison, Lunenburg Crossing vs. typical home
budget_items.what_was_said: Members compared per-acre tax payments between a large commercial property and a typical one-acre single-family home to argue commercial parcels pay less per acre.
A member gave their own per-acre tax figure to illustrate the gap between residential and commercial per-acre taxation.
Members discussed that administrative overhead for billing (integrating into MUNIS, similar to the sewer billing process) had originally been high and was negotiated down.

decisions.decision: For 400 Lemon(ster) Shirley Road (Mary Coburn/Edal property), the use code will be corrected/forced to code 4101 rather than left blank.
Woodlands condominiums and Stone Farm Estates will keep individual per-unit assessment rather than being billed as one global fee, since prior treatment made sense.
1295 Massachusetts Ave storage facility bays: the fee will be assigned to the overall property owner/manager rather than split among individual bay renters.
Tri-Town Apartments (use code 9960) will be billed as one combined fee to the owning entity rather than split by individual building/unit.
The Emerald Place property's impervious area will be combined with the adjacent Arrive property and billed as a single combined fee to the ownership entity.
Future task force meetings will be held on Microsoft Teams instead of Zoom, since the group already has Teams licensing and had recording trouble on Zoom.

Before asking Weston & Sampson for additional survey data, the task force will first check the town's older CI (commercial/industrial) spreadsheet to see if it already has the missing impervious-area figures.
A member will compile the list of properties needing reassessment/additional impervious-area data and send the questions to Weston & Sampson (via the consultant referred to as "J"/"Jice").

The task force leaned toward pursuing a stand-alone stormwater utility rather than funding the program through the operating budget, given the larger tax-bill impact and lost commercial cost-shifting under the operating-budget option.
Combining the sewer commission and a stormwater commission would require action by the state legislature, so this is not being pursued as a near-term option.
The list of properties lacking impervious-area data will simply be sent on to the consultant rather than reviewed line-by-line by the full task force first.
Next two task force meetings set for Monday, July 13th and Thursday, July 30th.

what_happened.line: The task force leaned toward funding stormwater work through a stand-alone utility fee rather than the operating budget.
Members spent most of the meeting correcting property-by-property use codes and impervious-area data feeding the fee model.
The task force set billing rules combining fees for storage bays, apartments and adjoining lots, while keeping some condos billed per unit.
Combining the sewer and a new stormwater commission would need state legislative action, so it is not being pursued now.
Next task force meetings are set for July 13 and July 30, with a bylaw draft due before a possible fall Town Meeting article.

why_it_matters: Whether stormwater costs land on the tax bill or a separate utility fee changes how much residential versus commercial property owners pay.
The property-by-property review, including exceptions for condos, storage units and mixed-ownership sites, will determine each parcel's individual fee.
A fall Town Meeting article would ask voters to act on the funding mechanism and any bylaw the task force drafts.

meetings.headline: Commission approved five wetlands permits, set FY27 fund budgets, and resolved a driveway wetlands violation without a fine
meetings.summary: The Conservation Commission acted on a full slate of wetlands hearings — approving several driveway, septic and carport projects, continuing others pending planning-board or DEP action — and resolved an unpermitted driveway culvert at 314 Highland Street with remediation (riprap and on-site wetland replication) rather than a fine. The commission also set FY2027 budgets for its Hollis Road, Timber Rights and Wetlands Bylaw Fees accounts, while flagging unresolved confusion over the Mass Trails grant account balance, ARPA matching funds, and a town-manager-held bequest fund with no visibility to the commission.

budget_items.what_was_said: The commission noted the town no longer has a dedicated social media manager after the new budget. Office staff have reportedly been trained to handle social media instead, including for the invasives event.
Commissioners asked for an update on where the Mass Trails grant budget stands, since the volunteer tracking it and town finance had not reported back. No figures were given at this point.
The agent reported the revised fund balance on the year-to-date report appears negative, raising questions about how drawdowns and reimbursements are being recorded.

budget_items.topic: Proposed fine for 314 Highland Street violation
budget_items.what_was_said: The agent floated a possible fine for the unpermitted culvert and driveway work, but most commissioners favored remediation only given it appeared an honest mistake.
A bequest fund held for the commission is tracked by the town manager directly through a bank rather than through MUNIS, so the commission has no visibility into its balance or usage rules.

budget_items.topic: Hollis Road revolving fund FY27 balance
budget_items.what_was_said: The agent presented the prior fund balance, this year's changes, and the current balance to use as the basis for next year's Hollis Road budget.

budget_items.topic: Hollis Road purchase-of-service line, prior year
budget_items.what_was_said: Last year's purchase-of-service sub-account was set at one figure with a chunk left unspent, prompting discussion of whether to keep that split given custodian income has stopped.
The agent proposed putting a fixed amount into purchase of service and the remainder into maintenance of grounds, noting the full balance would be available since custodian income had stopped.
The commission voted to set the Hollis Road sub-account budgets for fiscal year 2027 at the proposed figures.

budget_items.topic: Timber Rights fund, prior year split
budget_items.what_was_said: Last year's Timber Rights budget put a small amount to purchase of service and the rest to supplies, out of a fund with roughly this total balance.
A town official confirmed that anything over a stated dollar threshold in services must go out to bid with prevailing wages, which caps how much can go to the purchase-of-service line.

budget_items.topic: Matching funds for Table Rock/Reno trail grants
budget_items.what_was_said: Commissioners discussed needing matching funds, likely from Timber Rights, if pending grant applications for parking area work at Table Rock and Reno are awarded.
The commission voted to set the FY2027 Timber Rights sub-account budgets between purchase of service and supplies at the proposed figures.
The agent reported the fund's current balance from permitting fees and recommended budgeting about half of it for now, pending a planned guided-hike program and flyers.

budget_items.topic: Wetlands Bylaw Fees FY27 budget vote
budget_items.what_was_said: The commission voted to set the Wetlands Protection Bylaw Fees fund budget at the proposed figure to cover items like flyers and guided-hike materials.

budget_items.topic: Mass Trails grant spending to date
budget_items.what_was_said: The year-to-date report showed spending against the grant's budgeted amount, plus an unexplained encumbrance that commissioners could not immediately identify.
Commissioners tried to reconcile the encumbrance against the total grant request and the matching-fund percentage the commission had committed to.

budget_items.topic: Mass Trails/DCR reimbursement and ARPA match
budget_items.what_was_said: Reading from an old email, commissioners noted a partial reimbursement received from the state and a separate ARPA-funded matching amount the town had allocated.

Only a small amount of ARPA funding was left showing against the grant when the town's ARPA spending deadline passed, and it is unclear whether obligations already contracted for were properly covered before those funds expired.

decisions.decision: Minutes from the June 3, 2026 meeting were tabled to the next meeting because a quorum of members who attended that meeting was not present to vote.

Agreed to arrange a meeting among the agent, the chair, the town's grant volunteer and the finance/grants staffer to sort out the Mass Trails grant account before the fiscal year closes.
Commissioners agreed informally to pursue riprap fill in the culvert plus an on-site wetland replication area at 314 Highland Street rather than requiring removal of the pipe or imposing a fine.
Commission will revisit updating the wetlands bylaw and permitting fee structure once the agent meets with town legal counsel about the process.
Agreed to set up a meeting between the town manager, the chair, and possibly a commissioner regarding a new custodial agreement for the Hollis Road property.
Commission will consider adding a recurring 'commissioner updates' or property-updates subsection to future agendas.
Agent will informally raise with the Select Board the idea of an Eagle Scout project to re-seed and plant natives at the town-owned Zero Reservoir Road parcel where a past encroachment was cleared.

meetings.headline: The board voted to press the state legislature to preserve the Foundation Budget Review Commission and boost school aid in the FY27 budget.
meetings.summary: The Lunenburg Select Board ratified two seasonal appointments, adopted an updated environmentally preferable purchasing policy, and voted to support a legislative letter urging retention of the Foundation Budget Review Commission and higher school aid levels in the FY27 state budget. The town manager reported progress on a temporary food pantry site at the former School Street school, the awarded Flat Hill Road Bridge contract, and a dangerous/nuisance dog complaint headed to a standalone hearing; the board also scheduled a July 14 goals workshop, approved several sets of prior minutes, heard numerous committee reports, and voted to enter executive session on non-union personnel matters.

votes.motion: Ratify the town manager's appointment of Charlotte Chiazzo as seasonal lifeguard and Peter Schmidt as seasonal cemetery laborer.
Adopt the updated environmentally preferable purchasing policy.
Support the letter to the conference committee urging retention of the Foundation Budget Review Commission language in the FY27 budget and additional funding for key areas.

Approve minutes from the January 12, 2026 Tri-Board meeting, January 27, 2026 Tri-Board meeting, March 10, 2026 Tri-Board meeting, May 12, 2026 Select Board meeting, May 12 executive session (not for release), May 20, 2025 Select Board meeting, and June 9, 2025 Select Board meeting.

Enter executive session, not to return to open session, pursuant to Mass. General Laws chapter 30 section 21 A(2), for strategy sessions preparing for negotiations with non-union personnel (facilities director, HR director, director of public works, Lunenburg Council on Aging director, executive assistant to the select board and town manager).

budget_items.topic: Food pantry site septic repair (School Street site)
budget_items.what_was_said: A title five inspection done that day gave the septic system a provisional pass, with a potential repair cost, but was otherwise described as in decent shape.

The finance director asked to postpone fiscal year-end transfers, which move money between departments (e.g., from the health insurance line to a department line running short), until July; such transfers require votes of both the Select Board and Finance Committee by July 15.

budget_items.topic: Flat Hill Road Bridge construction contract
budget_items.what_was_said: The town awarded the construction contract to Kodiak, the second low bidder, after the original awarded contractor could not perform and the apparent low bidder on the rebid was bypassed for a defect.

Lunenburg participates in a state recycling dividends grant program earning points, convertible to grant funds, contingent on annually circulating an environmentally preferable purchasing policy to staff.

budget_items.topic: State minimum school aid per pupil / Foundation Budget Review Commission
budget_items.what_was_said: The letter of support states the House and Senate increased minimum aid per pupil above the Governor's proposed figure, and urges the conference committee to fund the higher of the two proposed levels for special education circuit breaker reimbursement and unrestricted general government aid.
The School Committee's facility staff reported savings achieved through competitive bidding of maintenance contracts, per Brian's committee report.

budget_items.topic: School override defeat and budget concerns
budget_items.what_was_said: The School Committee heard public comment about the recent override defeat, school funding concerns, and athletic and music program concerns, and discussed potential additional state aid and a possible special town meeting ahead of the school year.

budget_items.topic: FY27 tax commitments / neighborhood valuation review
budget_items.what_was_said: The Board of Assessors reported completion of preliminary FY27 tax commitments and described an ongoing neighborhood review project, prompted by Department of Revenue recommendations, focused partly on waterfront property valuations.

transfers.outcome: discussed only; postponed to July per finance director's request

decisions.decision: Group looking at food pantry temporary sites coalesced around the School Street site as preferable to the TC Passios site, contingent on the school committee agreeing to move T-ball to the TC Passios area.
Town manager and superintendent agreed to a regularly scheduled (about monthly) cadence of finance/leadership meetings between town and school staff.
Board indicated it would proceed with a standalone, formal public hearing on the dangerous/nuisance dog complaint rather than closing the matter on the investigative report alone.
The environmentally preferable purchasing policy will be re-circulated/re-voted only when the policy changes, not annually.
Goals workshop for the Select Board and Town Manager scheduled for July 14th.
Dangerous dog hearing tentatively placeholder-planned for July 28th, pending coordination with the parties involved; may slip to August.

meetings.headline: The Select Board reconstituted the Personnel Committee as a five-member body and filled its seats along with most other town board vacancies.
meetings.summary: This Select Board meeting was devoted entirely to annual appointments and reappointments to town boards, committees and commissions, with the board interviewing each applicant briefly before voting. By the end of the meeting the board had filled seats on the APDC, Council on Aging, Americans with Disabilities Committee, Conservation Committee, Cultural Council, Green Communities and a newly reconstituted five-member Personnel Committee, leaving remaining vacancies only on Conservation, Cultural Council, Historical Commission and PAC.

budget_items.what_was_said: The town manager/staff explained that Green Communities is a state program that funds certain efficiency projects for cities and towns, such as mini-splits and building weatherization, provided the project meets ROI/efficiency standards. It was noted the program previously funded HVAC/mini-split work at the primary school.

decisions.decision: Richard Taylor decided to withdraw his interest in the other committees he had listed and focus solely on the Americans with Disabilities Committee.

The board agreed not to appoint Vincent ("Vinnie") to Green Communities tonight; he will submit an application/form and be connected with the committee chair (David Blatt) before a future appointment.
The board agreed to keep Dave Passios as the full Green Communities member and expects an additional full-member vacancy when Dave Blatt leaves the community in the fall.
The board noted the Americans with Disabilities Committee likely cannot meet again until it has a member-at-large and a select board representative assigned, which may not happen until August.

meetings.headline: Space-needs survey shows town departments need far less room than the committee's earlier 14,000-sq-ft plan
meetings.summary: The Building Design Committee spent the meeting reviewing department-by-department responses to its staff space-needs survey (town clerk, treasurer, HR, town manager, conservation, planning, facilities, building department, board of health, recreation), flagging where storage and interaction questions needed to be re-asked in clearer terms (e.g., "file cabinets" instead of square footage). No formal building or budget decision was made; the committee agreed to keep assessing needs independent of current buildings, standardize how storage is measured, and reconvene June 29th, while several members stressed the town currently has little appetite or capital funding for new construction.

budget_items.topic: Cost of new building storage space
budget_items.what_was_said: The chair noted that 500 square feet of storage in a new building translates into a large dollar figure, cautioning the committee that small square-footage numbers become much bigger costs when discussing new construction.

budget_items.topic: Prior building proposal vs. current survey estimate
budget_items.what_was_said: A member noted the space needs identified in the new staff survey come in well below his earlier per-person calculation, and well below the committee's previous proposal that was rejected by the town.
The town clerk's office was estimated at roughly 600 square feet for three staff, with the main gaps being vault space, counter space, and a private area for voting-related business.

The treasurer's office was reported at about 128 square feet for three employees, described as tight, with a need for more storage, a secure area for cash handling, and vault space; a member asked for actual square-footage or filing-cabinet estimates rather than vague terms.
HR's current space was reported at about 129 square feet for one employee, which the committee felt was adequate; a small amount of additional storage was requested.

The town manager's office and storage were estimated at roughly 450 square feet of office plus 120 square feet of storage, described as close to adequate, with a request for a private meeting room for up to six people.
Conservation's office and storage were estimated at about 187 square feet for one employee, with a request for a service counter and space to spread out plans with visitors.

The planning department reported about 750 square feet including a conference room, described as an inefficient layout; digitization was said to be reducing storage needs significantly and older records could move offsite.
Facilities reported about 160 square feet of office space at the Ritter building, with the main unmet need being dedicated shop/storage space, currently borrowed from DPW.

The building department reported about 350 square feet of office and counter space, with storage described in cubic feet rather than square feet, which the committee found hard to compare across departments.

budget_items.topic: Board of Health office and storage
budget_items.what_was_said: The Board of Health and a shared part-time staffer occupy about 179 square feet including fourteen filing cabinets, with digitization identified as a way to reduce future storage needs.

decisions.decision: Laura agreed to draft additional survey questions about how often staff interact with other departments/offices, to be sent through the town manager.

Committee agreed (per Chris's suggestion) to assess each department's space needs independent of whether Town Hall or the Ritter building currently houses them, rather than designing around existing buildings first.
Committee agreed to standardize future storage questions around number of filing cabinets (or filing method) and frequency of access, rather than square footage alone.
Next committee meeting set for June 29th.

budget_items.what_was_said: A member recalled that a capital plan item to add cooling at the primary school lacked enough money, so the School Committee asked to redirect those funds to buy mini-splits, which required Finance Committee and Select Board support.

A member recounted a past request, as Parks Commission chair, to use a revolving fund to increase the recreation director's hours; the Select Board supported it but this committee did not at the time. The Parks Commission has since launched a pilot program along similar lines.
The committee listed policy areas to review going forward: free cash, revenue projections, stabilization accounts, the capital committee's process, and OPEB/retirement fund contributions.

A member noted one stabilization account is for fire trucks, around $2 million, and raised the open question of the policy for when funds should be drawn from stabilization accounts versus only for one-time revenue drops or expenses.
A member said the town changed vacation/overtime and paid-time-off policies to retain employees, which had a financial cost, and that money had to be added to an account this year to cover it.

decisions.decision: Committee will compile and prioritize a list of fiscal policies (free cash, revenue projections, stabilization accounts, capital committee, OPEB) for future review, rather than voting on any now.
No consensus reached on reviving a tri-board committee this meeting; the matter is left for Chair Chris to take the lead on when he returns.
Election of a new vice chair (the prior one was lost) will wait until Chair Chris returns, likely discussed at a future meeting rather than July 9th.
Committee will ask Chris about possibly moving the date of the reorg/election meeting so a member unavailable on July 9th can attend.
Year-end transfers are not yet ready and are deferred to a future meeting.

meetings.headline: Board voted to send the Hickory Hills kayak-rack zone-one violation dispute to legal counsel, KP Law
meetings.summary: The Lunenburg Water District commissioners spent most of the meeting on the long-running dispute over kayak racks stored inside the Hickory Hills wellhead zone one protection area, ultimately voting to install a gated barrier to block vehicle access and to refer the underlying violation to KP Law after commissioners could not agree on seeking a DEP variance instead. The board also reviewed a new sanitary survey, heard a detailed PFAS well-pumping remediation proposal aimed at avoiding a treatment plant, voted to abandon a planned switch to new billing software, and took public comment on PFAS costs and the kayak issue.

public_comment.topic: Urged a separate ledger for PFAS-related costs, raised custody-and-control liability if the Hickory Hills kayaks were damaged, said residents were unprepared for the scale of the treatment-plant cost, and urged pressure on federal legislators for PFAS funding.

Criticized a commissioner's ties to a Hickory Hills resident group over the kayak dispute, urged the district to spend whatever it takes on legal action, and suggested the district simply remove the kayak racks itself.

The decision to stay with the current billing vendor affects how and when residents pay their water bills, including features like paperless billing.

meetings.headline: Assessors overhauling flawed waterfront property valuations while approving FY2027 preliminary tax bills
meetings.summary: The Board of Assessors reorganized with a new member, elected officers, and paid tribute to the outgoing principal assessor for stabilizing the office, fixing chapter-land liens, and recovering missed new growth. Most of the meeting covered signing FY2027 preliminary tax warrants and commitments, ongoing GIS/mapping vendor troubles, and a consultant's report on overhauling the town's inconsistent waterfront property valuation neighborhoods, which the board agreed to continue revising. No members of the public were present or commented, and the board set its next three meeting dates before adjourning.

budget_items.topic: Abatement and motor vehicle excise abatement requests for May
budget_items.what_was_said: The office processed a batch of abatement requests and a large number of motor vehicle excise tax abatements for the month, tied to late payment processing by the tax collector.

budget_items.topic: FY2027 preliminary real estate and personal property tax bills/warrant
budget_items.what_was_said: The board reviewed and prepared to sign preliminary FY2027 real estate and personal property tax billing warrants and commitments; personal property bills were clarified as business/professional taxes, not household property.

budget_items.topic: FY2026 supplemental real estate tax bills
budget_items.what_was_said: The board noted these supplemental bills were already signed/approved the prior month, with no new supplemental bills added this cycle.

Residents can defer property taxes, with the deferred amount accumulating against the property at a stated interest rate; the town currently has no active deferral applicants after one incomplete late application last year.

budget_items.topic: Chapter land lien release recording fee
budget_items.what_was_said: Releasing a chapter-land tax lien when a property leaves agricultural (61A) classification requires paying back taxes and a fee to record the release at the Registry of Deeds.

budget_items.topic: Vision vendor quote to update property record cards
budget_items.what_was_said: The board discussed paying an outside vendor to update yearly property record cards after in-house software/PC issues made the process cumbersome, calling the cost well worth it.

The consultant's report proposed applying a combined waterfront valuation factor derived from recent lake-area sales, split into a base factor plus a per-lake sub-neighborhood adjustment, replacing outdated 'good/average/below average' waterfront ratings.
The board discussed Clause 18, a discretionary one-time tax relief tool for taxpayers in dire financial straits, noting the town has no applicants and has not yet finalized criteria for granting it.

budget_items.topic: Senior means-tested tax exemption / circuit breaker
budget_items.what_was_said: The board discussed Lunenburg's locally adopted senior means-tested exemption, which requires filing a federal tax return and qualifying for the state circuit breaker credit, described as a substantial tax break for eligible seniors.

decisions.decision: Board endorsed dedicating a separate server at town hall for GIS map updates so the principal assessor's laptop is no longer tied up for days during updates.
Board agreed to restore both property record card views on the website, with the more frequently updated one clearly labeled 'in process' to avoid confusing residents.
Board agreed to eliminate the 'average' and 'below average' waterfront quality ratings entirely and instead apply valuation factors based on actual property quality.
Board indicated the town intends to acquire the chapter-land property at issue, pending a letter from the Select Board.
Board set July 1, August 5, and September 2 as tentative dates for its next meetings, planning to meet only monthly over the summer.

meetings.headline: Water District held a special meeting vote on borrowing to fund a PFAS treatment plant; result not confirmed in captions
meetings.summary: The Lunenburg Water District held a special district meeting on a single article: authorizing borrowing to fund a PFAS water treatment plant and related well/transmission-main work, prompted by violations found in the district's 2026 DEP sanitary survey. Numerous residents raised concerns about cost, alternatives (point-of-use filters, a Townsend interconnection), and whether the district's DEP filings accurately described the urgency, before voters cast a clicker vote whose outcome the captions do not state.

budget_items.what_was_said: A resident asked the district to disclose the total project cost, what is included/excluded, and the effect on future water rates before any vote, and questioned whether SRF low-interest financing was driving the solution rather than the reverse.

meetings.headline: Failed town override cuts town concert funding and a town staff position, pushing website work onto PACC volunteers
meetings.summary: The Public Access Cable Committee handled routine business: minutes, a volunteer-applicant referral from the select board, the manager's monthly report, and a discussion clarifying that the failed town override (not the base FY2027 budget) is what cost the town its concerts and a town website/social-media staff position. The bulk of the meeting covered a consolidated policy/bylaw binder Steve compiled for review and eventual posting, an update on staffing the new cable advisory committee, and scheduling the July 6th meeting as an organizational meeting to fill two open PACC seats.

attendees.role: chair (conducted roll call, name not stated)

budget_items.what_was_said: The manager reported there are no town concerts because the override did not pass, so there is no funding for them.

A member clarified the override was meant to add extra funds on top of the base budget, not replace it; the base budget passed at town meeting regardless of the override's failure. Anyone counting on override money will not have it, though department heads may seek other adjustments.
It was noted that ordinary micro-adjustments happen within any budget (a role costs more or less, staff turnover) and these are called adjustments, distinct from the override question.
Line item transfers within the town budget are approved by the town manager; department heads can request them but need the town manager's sign-off, unlike in the past.

budget_items.topic: elimination of a town website/social media position
budget_items.what_was_said: Because the override failed, the town is eliminating a position handling website updates, social media and IT liaison work; PACC will informally take over doing the town website updates as a result.

January-through-March investment and interest was posted to the committee's account; the manager discovered the reported total interest actually combines two different bank sources (Main Street Bank and a second bank/entity) and will separate them going forward in Munis.
The committee had to buy a new eight-input ATEM switcher after the previous one burned out from hot-swapping, plus a new wireless transmitter and receiver after one failed.
The manager reported the purchase order for the Castus system was received; installation is not yet scheduled.
This report was not sent to the chair for the meeting because it was covered at the prior meeting.

Agreed to review the consolidated policy/bylaw sections one or two at a time each month going forward, starting with equipment use and drone policy.
Agreed that Steve (PACC) will take over doing the town website updates for the committee's own page, since the town position that did this is being eliminated.

Cable advisory committee membership set: Brian Leptonen (replacing Amanda, who resigned from the select board), Karen Menard, and Tom Bodkin, pending select board appointment; first meeting to be scheduled by contacting Cathy Herrick after June 16th.

meetings.headline: Committee debated reopening FY27 school budget after new state Senate aid, but leaned toward not disturbing the town-meeting-approved budget
meetings.summary: The Finance Committee spent most of the meeting debating whether newly-added state Senate aid should prompt reconsideration of the FY27 budget just approved at town meeting, with members split between honoring the town-meeting result and revisiting free cash, reserve, and OPEB policies given the tight fiscal situation. No formal budget action was taken; the only votes were procedural approval of past minutes and adjournment, while the committee set its next meeting for June 11th and agreed to revisit financial policy work and the tri-board process ahead of FY28.

public_comment.topic: Asked for feedback during the meeting rather than only at the end; raised concern about a select board member's resignation, whether the roughly $400,000/$465,000 in added state aid is directed to Lunenburg, distress over reading program shortfalls in the lower grades, and the cost of PFAS-contaminated fire department turnout gear.
Reminder of the June 3rd water district election and a Sunday town fair event, plus thanks to outgoing member Jean.

budget_items.what_was_said: The third-quarter financial report could not be finalized because the finance director was out sick; the committee will instead target a report around the fourth quarter close. Members asked that any future report include revenue vs. projections, spending to actuals, capital project status, and an assessment of the finance department's operations.
A member said the state Senate has increased aid to Lunenburg in various lines, money she believes could eventually land in free cash rather than be appropriated to the schools now facing cuts.

budget_items.topic: Finance committee reserve account vs. financial policy minimum
budget_items.what_was_said: A member contrasted how the finance committee reserve account was funded against the financial policy's stated minimum, arguing the town manager could be asked to look at using added state aid to help the school budget.

budget_items.topic: Using added state revenue at a special town meeting
budget_items.what_was_said: The chair noted that if additional state aid is finalized, the town would not spend it all at once and could adjust the budget allocation at a special town meeting.
A member noted that a sum the senator secured for Lunenburg last year likely ended up as part of the free cash built up through conservative budgeting.
The chair said current policy sets a $50k minimum reserve but allows up to roughly a 0.5% cap, giving flexibility for tight-budget years.

A resident asked whether a large sum moving through the state Senate has been specifically directed to Lunenburg; the chair said it is still working through reconciliation and has not been signed into law.
A resident described the cost of replacing PFAS-contaminated firefighter turnout gear as a large, currently unaddressed capital-type need, having discussed it with the fire chief months earlier.

Local receipts have not come in below a certain level for the past decade; this year's estimate was set lower and then adjusted upward slightly by the town manager. A member argued for reconsidering how conservatively local receipts are projected given the current budget strain.
A member asked how much free cash the town has this year and historically; the chair gave a rough figure and acknowledged not having the full ten-year history on hand.
The town currently puts a set percentage into OPEB annually per policy; a member questioned whether that approach should be revisited given current budget pressure.
A resident said he was told banks and bonding companies expect continued OPEB-type contributions, citing a large unaddressed liability, and argued token contributions would not be adequate.
The school committee is expected to bring forward a plan for Turkey Hill that will involve a major rebuild or rehabilitation; the town is currently well positioned financially to handle it.

A resident raised concern about reported structural issues with the school bleachers area, which a member confirmed has been discussed at the capital planning committee as an item exceeding normal capital thresholds.
figures_as_heard: a million or two million bucks

decisions.decision: A member urged that if anyone plans to bring an alternate budget proposal next year, it be presented to the finance committee and tri-board for vetting rather than surfacing at town meeting.
General support expressed for continuing a tri-board process next year, reoriented toward strategic financial conversations rather than department-by-department presentations.
Next Finance Committee meeting set for June 11th (rather than June 25th, which conflicts with a member's daughter's wedding).
Chair agreed to talk with the town's finance staff ("Jen") offline about resuming work on the financial policies document, given the lighter summer schedule.

meetings.headline: District presented a $47 million PFAS water-treatment plan for voters; no vote was taken tonight
meetings.summary: The Lunenburg Water District superintendent gave a lengthy informational presentation to residents and the board on a proposed $47 million project to build a centralized water treatment plant addressing PFAS/PFOA contamination and manganese/iron issues at the district's well sites, financed substantially through a proposed SRF loan. Commissioners questioned SRF eligibility thresholds, litigation over EPA PFAS limits, and how applying for SRF or emerging contaminant grants might open access to other funding, but the meeting was informational only and no vote was taken on the project itself.

budget_items.what_was_said: The district is asking voters at a special meeting to appropriate funding for a $47 million project covering water treatment and distribution improvements.
The district applied for a $41 million SRF loan over 30 years at 2.2% interest, with MassDEP adding an extra 0.15% administrative fee.

budget_items.what_was_said: An additional amount was included in the article to construct the raw water transmission main from Keatings to the new treatment plant.
