budget_items.what_was_said: Minimum users would see a quarterly increase in one range, average households a higher range, and high-end (irrigation) users the highest range, tied to loan and future maintenance costs.
EPA announced roughly $1 billion in additional federal assistance to be spread across about 148,000 public drinking water systems nationally, described as not much per town.
The district applied for the full amount under the emerging contaminant grant program but expects to receive less than the full amount.
During construction of the Keating's well around 2009, a federal stimulus package provided close to $700,000 toward what was roughly a million-dollar project, via the SRF program.

budget_items.topic: Other towns' emerging contaminant grant awards
budget_items.what_was_said: A printout of grant awards by town showed Pepperell receiving around the highest amount seen, cited as an example of what such grants can provide.

decisions.decision: District has already applied for the emerging contaminant grant for the full loan amount and separately applied for SRF funding, positioning itself for other federal/state assistance.

meetings.headline: Conservation Commission held a training workshop on riverfront-area regulations; no votes or business conducted
meetings.summary: A wetland science consultant, addressed as Mike, gave the Conservation Commission an informal training workshop on the Riverfront Act (310 CMR 10.58): how to determine if a watercourse is a stream, whether it is perennial or intermittent, where to draw the inner edge of riverfront area, and how a project is classified as previously developed versus undeveloped riverfront area. Commission members asked questions tied to real cases the board had seen, including a beaver-dam/unidirectional-flow situation, and the group discussed following up on conditioning obligations offline and possibly scheduling further training sessions; no votes or agenda business were conducted.

decisions.decision: The commission agreed to follow up with the presenter offline about the commission's obligation to condition certain requirements under 1058.5.
Informal agreement to consider having the presenter return for a similar training session about once a quarter, and possibly a separate session on bank and land-under-water regulations.

topics.topic: Determining whether a watercourse is legally 'a stream' under the Riverfront Act, including culverts and ponds
Determining whether a stream is perennial or intermittent: USGS maps vs. MassMapper, StreamStats criteria, stratified drift, and the 'competent independent observer' standard
Locating the inner edge of riverfront area (bankfull discharge vs. top of bank), upper vs. lower perennial streams, and real project examples including beaver dam and impoundment situations
How a project fits the regulations: previously developed riverfront area (1058.5) vs. undeveloped riverfront area (1058.4), and performance standards including compensatory flood storage
Commission's appreciation for the training and discussion of scheduling further workshops
topics.resolution: informal agreement to consider follow-up sessions

meetings.headline: Override failed; committee accepts a balanced-budget of cuts and eyes another override attempt next year
meetings.summary: The committee processed the fallout of the failed override, with the superintendent outlining the resulting cuts (class sizes, interventionists, middle school sports and transportation, high school world language) and recommending the district implement the balanced budget and form a community task force rather than return to voters immediately. The committee elected new officers for 2026-2027 -- Laura as chair, Tony as vice chair, Mandy Gilman provisionally as secretary -- adopted several revised policies (cash handling, student data privacy, medication administration, advertising), tabled the fifth-grade bus-release procedure pending community feedback, and voted a composite evaluation of the superintendent's first year.

A stormwater utility fee, still in an early data-gathering stage, could eventually become a new charge tied to a property's paved or built-over area.

meetings.headline: Amanda Moore resigns as vice chair citing health; board reorganizes and plans a special election
meetings.summary: The Select Board acknowledged the resignations of the vice chair (citing health, amid the aftermath of the failed override) and two town staff members, then reorganized its own leadership, electing a new chair, vice chair and clerk. It also voted on an ambulance-billing write-off, a nuisance dog investigation, waivers for a town event and a right of first refusal, discussed possibly calling a special town meeting on the budget while deferring to the School and Finance Committees, and heard a town manager's report on bridge and flooring project bids and a culvert grant.

budget_items.what_was_said: The board was asked to write off uncollectible ambulance receipts and send a separate amount to collections; this had not been done in a year due to finance department staffing issues.
A resident said the water district will hold a special meeting on a proposed water treatment plant that would affect water fees charged to all public buildings, including schools.
The purchase price category was excluded from the RFP evaluation criteria given a recent assessment showing the property's value as negative.
The board reviewed an accounts payable warrant in this amount.

Nine bids were opened for the bridge project; the low bid was rejected for missing a bid bond, making the next lowest bid the apparent low bid, against funding from a state small bridge grant and two capital plan years.

budget_items.topic: Pavement management plan contract (Tie and Bond)
budget_items.what_was_said: The town engaged an engineering firm to update the pavement condition assessment and multi-year pavement management plan, funded through Chapter 90 funds.
The town was awarded a grant toward design work for a culvert replacement on Goodrich Street, a corridor whose loss would cause a long detour.

decisions.decision: The board asked John Bowen Jr. to hold the planned flag-retirement burning as a town-run public event on town property rather than a private event at his home, and he agreed.
The board agreed in principle to hold a special town election to fill the vacant vice chair seat, with the date to be set after consulting the town clerk.

The board decided not to call a special town meeting tonight, choosing instead to wait and hear from the School Committee (meeting the next night) and Finance Committee before deciding, and to consider a Tri-Board meeting.
The town manager will ask Amanda Moore whether she wishes to continue serving on the 925 Mass Ave RFP working group despite her board resignation.
The RFP for 925 Mass Ave will be issued next week with responses due back in July.
The board agreed to remove the "unacceptable" rating tier from the RFP evaluation criteria and have the working group reassign point values among the remaining three tiers.

meetings.headline: Task force is assigning stormwater ERU fees property-by-property, leaning toward per-ERU billing over flat tiers
meetings.summary: The Stormwater Task Force reviewed John's detailed matching of the assessor's full property list against Weston & Samson's impervious-area survey, working through Massachusetts use codes one by one to assign a baseline ERU (equivalent residential unit) and resulting fee to every property in town, including tricky cases like garage-only lots, duplexes, condo complexes, and the Housing Authority. No formal vote was taken on the methodology; the group reached working consensus on several categories, assigned homework to review the rest before the next meeting, and discussed presenting both an operating-budget and a stand-alone-utility funding option to voters at the fall special town meeting.

budget_items.what_was_said: John said his baseline model, based on the proposed budget divided across all assessed ERUs, produces a flat annual fee per ERU. He noted this comes down further once the missing ~1,000 residential parcels found by Weston & Samson are added in.

budget_items.topic: Revenue difference: charging by ERU vs. by tier
budget_items.what_was_said: John said charging every property for its actual number of ERUs, instead of truncating each property to the bottom of its tier, raises more revenue overall.
A member referenced the overall budget figure driving the per-ERU fee calculation.

budget_items.topic: Fee for the highest-ERU property (largest impervious area)
budget_items.what_was_said: John calculated what the town's largest single ERU property (believed to be Walmart) would owe at the per-ERU rate, and flagged that his chart's scale may have cut off the true top ERU value.

budget_items.topic: Carousel Lane / Emerald Place combined ERU total
budget_items.what_was_said: Members worked out that Weston & Samson's total impervious area for the whole Carousel Lane complex, divided by the standard ERU size, comes close to the per-unit estimate the group had built up building by building, and used that to size a single combined bill for the property's roughly 155 line items.

budget_items.topic: Another large multi-unit property's ERU total
budget_items.what_was_said: A member read off the Weston & Samson impervious-area figure and resulting ERU count for another large development, and questioned whether it seemed low for its size.

budget_items.topic: Cost of hiring outside help ('a guy') to review all properties
budget_items.what_was_said: A member speculated that if the task force had funding to hire additional help, the overall program budget and the resulting per-resident assessment would both come down.

budget_items.topic: Operating budget vs. stand-alone utility funding structure
budget_items.what_was_said: The group discussed that if the stormwater fee were folded into the operating budget it would rise each year under the town's annual levy increase, unlike a stand-alone utility fee, and agreed both options need to be presented to voters at the fall special town meeting.

decisions.decision: Use code 106 (accessory lot with an improvement, e.g. a detached garage on a split-off lot) will be assigned one ERU.
A property with multiple houses/units but only one line item and one tax bill in the assessor's spreadsheet will be charged one ERU, matched to the tax bill rather than the number of dwellings.

The Carousel Lane / Emerald Place condominium complex, owned by a single LLC, will be billed as one combined property using Weston & Samson's total-property ERU estimate rather than per individual unit.
The Lunenburg Housing Authority property on White Street is flagged as a likely exception (a government entity that would effectively be taxing itself), pending further review.
Members will each review the mass use code document and John's assigned ERU-per-use-code list, and send back any disagreements before the next meeting so John can revise the model.
Next meeting tentatively set for June 24 (a Wednesday), with June 29 as a fallback if that date does not work for everyone, pending confirmation with Tim and Mark.

The task force agreed it should revisit its own officer and liaison assignments (chair, vice chair, board representatives) now that town elections have occurred, though this was deferred rather than acted on.

minutes.headline: Task force is assigning stormwater ERU fees property-by-property, leaning toward per-ERU billing over flat tiers
minutes.summary: The Stormwater Task Force reviewed John's detailed matching of the assessor's full property list against Weston & Samson's impervious-area survey, working through Massachusetts use codes one by one to assign a baseline ERU (equivalent residential unit) and resulting fee to every property in town, including tricky cases like garage-only lots, duplexes, condo complexes, and the Housing Authority. No formal vote was taken on the methodology; the group reached working consensus on several categories, assigned homework to review the rest before the next meeting, and discussed presenting both an operating-budget and a stand-alone-utility funding option to voters at the fall special town meeting.

what_happened.line: The task force decided to bill the Carousel Lane/Emerald Place condo complex as one combined property rather than unit by unit.
The Lunenburg Housing Authority's White Street property was flagged as a likely exception, since billing it would mean the town taxing itself.

Members discussed presenting voters two funding options at the fall special town meeting: folding the fee into the operating budget, where it would rise with the annual levy, or a stand-alone utility fee.

Owners of shared or multi-unit properties should watch how their property is classified, since billing decisions are being made property-by-property rather than unit-by-unit.

meetings.headline: Assessors rewrite the principal assessor job posting and move to bring inspections in-house as Linda departs
meetings.summary: The Board of Assessors reviewed the principal assessor's monthly activity report (excise commitments, abatements, supplemental bills, GIS/server issues) and discussed how to reconcile the fixed annual Vision property card with a more frequently updated CI-based card. With principal assessor Linda departing at the end of June, the board line-edited a draft job posting and description for her replacement, emphasizing assessing (not just appraisal) experience and technology skills, and discussed pulling contracted services such as cyclical inspections back in-house. The board also received a detailed update on a neighborhood/waterfront reclassification project, recommended against the town purchasing a foreclosed Hollis Road property, and set the next meeting for June 3rd before adjourning to executive session.

budget_items.what_was_said: The assessing office processed a commitment of motor vehicle excise bills for the month; the warrant was signed April 22nd.
One additional bill was issued under this commitment number.
64 motor vehicle excise abatements were received and processed in the past month, awaiting payment by the tax collector.
All FY2026 real estate abatements have been processed; some granted, some denied including personal property/sole company items.
Supplemental real estate bills were prepared for three properties whose building value increased more than 50%, based on occupancy date.

The principal assessor gave an update on progress toward the town's new-growth estimate, noting the commercial/industrial figure so far and the equivalent tax bill value; said they may fall a bit short but remain in range.

budget_items.topic: Vision printing of CAI-style property cards
budget_items.what_was_said: A quote was given for Vision to print updated property cards annually instead of doing it in-house, proposed for next year.
A vendor quote was cited for continuously updating GIS layers such as catch basin data, discussed in context of townwide use of the CI/GIS platform.
The board signed and voted to approve the notice of commitment covering the three supplemental bills discussed earlier.
The chair reminded seniors of the circuit breaker tax credit and means-tested exemption, and noted the interest rate that applies if taxes are deferred.

decisions.decision: Board leaned toward keeping both the fixed annual Vision property card (as of January 1) and a CI-based card updated monthly, clearly labeled as to which is which.
Job posting language to be revised to require experience specifically in the assessing field, not just appraisal, and to add computer/CAMA/Munis/Microsoft Suite skills to qualifications.
Job posting/description to require current MAA designation or achievement of it within two years of hire.
Job description language changed from the assessor 'recommends' the tax rate to something like 'presents/estimates tax rate options,' since the assessor does not set the rate.
Add 'deferrals' alongside abatements and exemptions in the job description's duties list.
Narrow 'maintains the town's official maps' to specifically 'tax maps' in the job description.
Board intends to bring cyclical property inspections in-house going forward rather than continue contracting them out.
Next Board of Assessors meeting set for June 3rd.

minutes.headline: Commissioners reworked the pitch for a ~$47M PFAS treatment plant loan ahead of a town vote
minutes.summary: The Lunenburg Water District Commissioners spent most of this meeting line-editing the PowerPoint that will be used to ask voters to approve roughly $47 million in SRF loan and bond financing for a PFAS/iron-manganese water treatment plant, debating which points were fact versus hypothetical and cutting or adding slides. They also discussed a dispute with the Woodlands over a kayak rack (tabled), fielded a resident's pointed questions about how the SRF grant application was submitted months after the board had voted not to apply, and covered routine water-main leak repairs, a proposed PVC pipe cost-saving trial, and mailer logistics for the special town meeting.

what_happened.line: The town faces a new, unplanned DEP requirement to document operation-and-maintenance plans for privately-owned sewer systems tied into the town system.
The commission approved the FY26 fourth-quarter sewer billing commitment by roll call vote.
Crews using old hand-drawn tie cards have not resolved sewer lateral locations at a Wallace Park-area property or at 100 Laurel Lane.
The commission is weighing a drain layer's proposal to extend an existing line at 100 Laurel Lane instead of renting a locating device.
The commission decided to keep its meeting time at 6:00 p.m. rather than reverting to an alternating 6:00/7:00 p.m. schedule.

why_it_matters: The DEP mandate could require owners of privately-owned sewer systems connected to the town system to produce plans and ordinance information on a tight timeline, and it lands on the town with no advance planning.
The approved quarterly commitment is what sets sewer billing for ratepayers this period.
Two property owners are still without a confirmed sewer lateral location, which affects their connection and any repair or extension costs.

The drain layer's estimate for extending the line to reach 100 Laurel Lane

meetings.headline: Board nominates new chair/vice chair for July as a resident's letter warns the override will hurt homebound seniors
meetings.summary: The Council on Aging board heard a town meeting recap (warrant mailing changes, Kids Kingdom transfer, override appropriations) and a resident's letter warning that the pending override vote would hit disabled and homebound seniors hardest. The board nominated David Lincoln as chair and Lou Franco as vice chair for July, discussed staffing for board minutes, got updates on the parking lot/playground project, lobby furniture, a new outreach coordinator, and made informal plans to thank departing members Helen Bolkum and the outgoing vice chair.

Adopt a case-by-case process (certificate and lunch) for future honorary members.
Adjourn the meeting.

budget_items.what_was_said: The chair thanked a lawyer's office for donating architectural plans for the parking lot project and received a thank-you in return.
A letter read into the record described the override forcing cuts to paid help and grocery delivery for a homebound senior already stretching savings.
The letter's author said a clerical error doubled her property taxes and she had to fight for an abatement, which the assessors and state eventually granted.

budget_items.topic: Override tiers one and two appropriations
budget_items.what_was_said: Town meeting approved the appropriations supporting both tier one and tier two of the proposed override; whether either, both, or neither override is enacted is decided by the ballot question on May 16.
A board member noted seniors could take board minutes through the town's tax work-off program to earn credit against their property taxes.
A board member proposed letting people add a voluntary contribution when signing up for trips to help others who can't afford them; this has not been implemented.
A board member described an unrelated giving circle she belongs to that distributes money multiple times a year, raised to explain why vendor presentations avoid business-card handouts.
The donated design work is at roughly a schematic design level; the town has leftover design money from an earlier capital project to advance it toward a more complete design package before bidding.
Once the design reaches a more complete level and a cost estimate exists, the board will explore funding sources including accessibility funding for seniors.
New lobby furniture has been ordered with no reported delays and is expected to be delivered in June.

decisions.decision: Colleen Roy's board application is accepted to fill one of the two vacancies (Helen Bolkum's and Diana's).
Minute-taking will continue as currently arranged for this meeting and possibly the next, pending further discussion with staff about the front-office job description.
The bylaws subcommittee will propose removing the sentence about clerk appointment and bring the bylaws back in the fall.
Future honorary members will be recognized with a certificate and a lunch, handled case-by-case.
The board will send flowers and a card, signed by members, to Helen Bolkum before she moves at the end of May.
The board will hold an end-of-fiscal-year gathering before the outgoing members' terms end.

meetings.headline: Trust Fund Commission publicly accuses town manager and select board of blocking release of funds to veterans and the poor
meetings.summary: The Trust Fund Commission chair used the meeting's public-comment period and most of the meeting itself to accuse the town manager and select board of stonewalling release of trust-fund money meant for veterans and the poor, and to read and rebut point-by-point a town counsel letter responding to the commission's breach notice on several trust funds (Nathaniel Day Worthy Poor Fund, American Legion Post 283 and Poor Funds, J&M Howard sidewalk fund, gazebo fund, Susan Howard fund). No cy pres filings were approved at this meeting; the commission agreed to request the drafted Nathaniel Day petition from counsel and to take up the school department's non-response to records requests at its next meeting, and it approved its prior meeting minutes before adjourning.

budget_items.topic: Trust fund cy pres money for underserved residents
budget_items.what_was_said: The chair said the select board has refused to authorize the cy pres filings needed to release this money, split mainly between the American Legion Poor Fund, Post 283 Fund and the Worthy Poor Fund, to veterans and poor residents.

budget_items.topic: Susan Howard Fund missing money (1905 gift)
budget_items.what_was_said: The chair said money Susan Howard gave to the town in 1905 no longer appears in the ledger and the town cannot locate it, and he wants it investigated.

budget_items.topic: Proposed override's tax impact on residents
budget_items.what_was_said: The chair argued the proposed override would raise typical tax bills by roughly this much a month, which he said makes trust fund assistance more necessary for seniors on fixed incomes.

budget_items.topic: Historical trailer-park water/sewer spending (context, not current budget)
figures_as_heard: million and a half$2 million dollars
budget_items.what_was_said: Richard recalled a roughly 20-year-old town decision to spend far more than a trailer park's assessed value on water and sewer service there, offering it as precedent for valuing people over a pure cost comparison.

budget_items.topic: Town's legal fees responding to the commission's breach notice
budget_items.what_was_said: The chair estimated the town is spending several thousand dollars on its attorney to answer the commission's 55-page filing rather than releasing the funds.

budget_items.topic: Cost of legal response versus cost of requested investigation
budget_items.what_was_said: The chair said the commission does not need to ask town meeting for this amount, but that the town may spend as much fighting the commission legally as it would cost to fund the requested investigations.

budget_items.topic: Nathaniel Day 1901 Worthy Poor Fund cy pres petition
budget_items.what_was_said: Town counsel's letter states this is the only fund currently requiring action and that a cy pres petition has been drafted for the commission's review and vote.

budget_items.topic: Hypothetical funding for fund investigations from the assistant town manager position
budget_items.what_was_said: The chair said he would take this amount from money requested for a new assistant town manager position to pay for investigating the trust funds instead.
The chair said at this salary level the town manager should not need an assistant and should handle more of the workload herself.

Counsel's letter argues the fund is not obsolete because Lunenburg veterans eligible for Legion membership can still receive funds; the chair called this unworkable given the veterans agent's limited authority.
Counsel's letter states this fund has no found devise and is not eligible for administrative cy pres, and would require costly judicial action instead.

budget_items.topic: Potential litigation/expert costs for American Legion Poor Fund
budget_items.what_was_said: Counsel's letter cites the Woodward School for Girls case to say expert testimony for judicial cy pres litigation could cost this much over the life of a case.

budget_items.topic: J&M Howard sidewalk and grounds fund
budget_items.what_was_said: Counsel's letter cites a 1931 town meeting record showing a devise for this fund and says cy pres is not currently required; the chair said no formal devise document has actually been provided to the commission.
Counsel's letter says the fund's purpose is not obsolete because a gazebo exists on town land, so cy pres is not required; the chair asked why a formal devise has still not been drafted.
Counsel's letter says any 1972 recordkeeping questions are now moot under the statute of limitations and that the town holds no funds under this name requiring action.

decisions.decision: The chair will personally call town counsel to request the cy pres petition document for the Nathaniel Day Worthy Poor Fund before the commission votes on it.
A draft compliance/investigation-request letter concerning the school department's non-response on scholarship and trust records will be reviewed at the next meeting.
Next meeting set for May 21.

meetings.headline: Commission recommended the town not exercise interest in acquiring two tax-title Hollis Road properties.
meetings.summary: A routine but heavy Conservation Commission agenda: the board approved or continued roughly twenty wetlands hearings (mostly the Lake Shirley/Round Road subdivision lots, Pine Grove Road, Flatill Road, Ruth Street, Summer Street), ratified a tree-removal determination, and worked through an enforcement violation at 715 Reservoir Road requiring 11 replacement trees. Ordered replacement trees and erosion stabilization at 715 Reservoir Road over a wetlands violation, with daily fines if not completed.
Began work toward raising the commission's fee schedule, which needs new bylaw language and a fall town meeting warrant article.

Asked the incoming finance director to walk the board through the conservation budget before FY27, after it became hard to follow post-merger with land-use.

why_it_matters: The Hollis Road recommendation feeds a Select Board decision on whether the town keeps or disposes of those tax-title parcels.
A higher conservation fee schedule would shift more of the town's legal and review costs onto permit applicants, but it requires a town meeting vote before taking effect.
The budget-clarity request signals a service whose FY27 costs residents may not be able to track clearly until the finance director explains the current structure.

meetings.headline: Water Commissioners set a June special vote on a large loan to fund PFAS and manganese treatment.
meetings.summary: The Lunenburg Water District board spent most of the meeting with its engineer reviewing how State Revolving Fund financing and bidding works for a combined PFAS and iron/manganese treatment project, and finalizing warrant-article language and cost-to-ratepayer estimates ahead of a June 3rd special district meeting where voters will be asked to fund the project. The board also voted to bar equipment access through the water supply protection zone for a tree removal, discussed an unresolved dispute over a kayak rack sited in that same zone, authorized spending on postcards and social media to publicize the June 3rd vote, and heard public comments criticizing the board's conduct during a heated exchange and a resident's request for a long-pending agenda item.

public_comment.topic: Said he felt personally insulted by comments made by the superintendent during the meeting and criticized the board for allowing it.
Agreed with the prior speaker and said the chair failed to control the meeting when a board member ranted.
Asked for a status update on an agenda item he has requested since March and said his questions keep being deferred.

votes.motion: Approve the minutes of April 22nd, 2026
Set a special meeting for Wednesday, June 3rd at 6:00 p.m. at Lunenburg High School
Send a letter to MassDEP requesting a variance for the kayak rack at The Woodlands
No entry, in, around, or through Zone One is allowed for tree removal at the Willets condo residence
Spend $4,000 with Capital Strategic (Nicole) for postcards/social media publicity about the June 3rd special meeting, plus additional funds for postage
votes.outcome: passed (described as two in favor, with at least one abstention/opposed)

budget_items.topic: SRF loan for PFAS / iron-manganese treatment plant
budget_items.what_was_said: The district discussed moving from a 0% to a 2% SRF financing offer on the same project and the cost of waiting another cycle if the June vote fails.

budget_items.topic: SRF loan interest rate and term
budget_items.what_was_said: Commissioners and the engineer clarified which interest rate applies to which loan term.
The engineer explained SRF allows a contingency line before bidding and a smaller one after the bid is locked in.

budget_items.topic: Keating raw water transmission main add-on
budget_items.what_was_said: The board asked whether leftover bid savings could fund adding the Keating transmission main under the same SRF-approved scope.

budget_items.topic: Iron/manganese removal vs. PFAS treatment construction cost
budget_items.what_was_said: The engineer compared what a standalone iron-and-manganese removal system cost versus adding PFAS treatment to an existing plant.

budget_items.topic: Average annual/monthly cost to water takers
budget_items.what_was_said: The presentation showed a rough average annual and monthly cost per water taker under the SRF loan plus the Keating bond, which the board wants broken out by rate tier before publishing.
The engineer said an independent cost estimator's fee to review a set of near-final drawings runs in that range, depending on project size.

budget_items.topic: Water main break repair bill to a resident's electrical contractor
budget_items.what_was_said: The superintendent proposed reducing the bill for repairing a water service hit while installing electrical ground rods down to just the material/labor cost after board discussion of fault.

budget_items.topic: Capital Strategic postcard/social media spending for June 3rd meeting notice
budget_items.what_was_said: The board discussed and authorized spending with a marketing contractor to mail postcards and post on social media publicizing the special meeting, with the exact scope to be confirmed by quote.

budget_items.topic: State supplemental grant for disadvantaged-community infrastructure
budget_items.what_was_said: A commissioner asked whether the district could pursue a state fund aimed at helping disadvantaged communities pay for old infrastructure; to be researched as a follow-up.

decisions.decision: The board agreed the June 3rd warrant article will ask voters to approve funding for the full project scope (design plus construction) rather than a smaller piece.

The board agreed to keep its existing tiered water rate structure and use the Waterworth billing software to model how the new debt service would be spread across usage tiers before publishing a per-household cost figure.

minutes.headline: Water Commissioners set a June special vote on a large loan to fund PFAS and manganese treatment.
minutes.summary: The Lunenburg Water District board spent most of the meeting with its engineer reviewing how State Revolving Fund financing and bidding works for a combined PFAS and iron/manganese treatment project, and finalizing warrant-article language and cost-to-ratepayer estimates ahead of a June 3rd special district meeting where voters will be asked to fund the project. The board also voted to bar equipment access through the water supply protection zone for a tree removal, discussed an unresolved dispute over a kayak rack sited in that same zone, authorized spending on postcards and social media to publicize the June 3rd vote, and heard public comments criticizing the board's conduct during a heated exchange and a resident's request for a long-pending agenda item.

what_happened.line: Water Commissioners set a special district meeting for June 3rd to ask voters to fund PFAS and manganese treatment.
The board agreed the warrant article will cover the full project scope, design and construction together, not a smaller piece.
Commissioners voted to bar all equipment access through the water supply protection zone for a nearby tree removal.
The board authorized spending with a marketing contractor on postcards and social media to publicize the June 3rd vote.
The board agreed to keep the existing tiered water rate structure and model debt service across usage tiers before publishing a cost estimate.

why_it_matters: Residents will be asked at the June 3rd special district meeting to approve loan funding for PFAS and iron/manganese treatment, which will show up on water bills through the rate tiers.
A per-household or per-tier cost estimate has not yet been published; the board said it wants that worked out on the district's billing software before the vote.
A separate, unresolved dispute over a kayak rack sited in the same water supply protection zone remains open, with a variance letter to the state whose outcome was not clearly recorded.

meetings.headline: PACC began recruiting a citizen committee to renegotiate the town's Comcast cable license.
meetings.summary: This Public Access Cable Committee meeting was largely a manager's monthly report (staff retirement, town meeting recording, studio pack-up ahead of a building closure, and financial/budget figures) followed by discussion of outstanding policy documents and a review of an investment/trust account. The most substantive forward-looking item was launching the process to recruit residents for a separate committee to renegotiate the town's Comcast cable license ahead of its expiration, including engaging an attorney and planning a public survey. No major votes were taken beyond routine approval of amended minutes and adjournment, both without audible counts.

The manager reported the current ending balance, which includes all Comcast-related funds and will not appear on the town's own financial report.
Programming has slowed but the share that is locally produced was reported as up.

budget_items.what_was_said: Projected FY27 revenue was compared against projected salaries and operating expenses, showing expenses exceeding revenue.

budget_items.topic: FY27 budget as approved at Town Meeting - retained earnings
budget_items.what_was_said: The final FY27 budget approved at Town Meeting drew a sum from retained earnings to cover the year; retained earnings must be re-qualified by the state before use.
The committee noted it has no budget to rent a storage unit and separately noted an existing annual charge for outside space.
A committee member reviewed the principal placed in an investment account beginning around FY24, the amount presently in it, and an expected additional payment.

budget_items.topic: Historical annual interest vs. budgeted interest
budget_items.what_was_said: The account has historically earned more in annual interest than the amount budgeted, though future interest cannot be predicted.

decisions.decision: Minutes will be corrected to read 'estimated investment value' rather than 'investment value,' since the committee did not set that figure - the town treasurer did.
No vote needed to remove 'videographer editor' from performance-review documents; the role is already listed only as 'videographer.'
Each committee member will individually reach out to residents to recruit volunteers for the Comcast license renegotiation committee, aiming to have names by June.
The committee will try to meet before the end of June to reconcile the enterprise/investment fund numbers with the finance department's posting.
Next PACC meeting set for June 1st at 6 PM in the same room.

meetings.headline: Town meeting passed the FY27 budget and sent two Prop 2½ overrides to a townwide ballot vote.
meetings.summary: Lunenburg's annual town meeting passed a full slate of warrant articles, most consequentially the FY2027 balanced town/school budget and a two-tier Proposition 2½ override package that, if approved by voters at the ballot in two weeks, would restore cut positions and programs in town departments and schools. Extensive public debate covered the balance budget's cuts to school staffing, the library, recreation, and public safety, a new assistant town manager position, and an alternative permanent-investment-trust proposal, before the body voted to approve article 10 and both override tiers under article 11, along with capital, PEG, salary-schedule and union-contract articles.

minutes.headline: Town meeting passed the FY27 budget and sent two Prop 2½ overrides to a townwide ballot vote.
minutes.summary: Lunenburg's annual town meeting passed a full slate of warrant articles, most consequentially the FY2027 balanced town/school budget and a two-tier Proposition 2½ override package that, if approved by voters at the ballot in two weeks, would restore cut positions and programs in town departments and schools. Extensive public debate covered the balance budget's cuts to school staffing, the library, recreation, and public safety, a new assistant town manager position, and an alternative permanent-investment-trust proposal, before the body voted to approve article 10 and both override tiers under article 11, along with capital, PEG, salary-schedule and union-contract articles.

watch_next: The townwide ballot vote on the two Proposition 2½ override tiers
Outcome of article 24 (TCP building decommissioning / assessor's office funding), not captured on this recording

what_happened.line: Town meeting approved the FY27 town and school budget, then sent two Proposition 2½ override tiers to a townwide ballot.
The override votes followed debate over cuts to school staffing, the library, recreation and public safety in the underlying balance budget.
A proposal to fund town operations through a permanent investment trust instead of recurring overrides was raised but not adopted.
Town meeting also approved capital funding, PEG cable funding, the non-union salary schedule, and first-year contracts for the fire, municipal employees' and DPW unions.
The final article, covering TCP building decommissioning costs and a special assistant position in the assessor's office, was still under discussion when the recording ended with no vote captured.

why_it_matters: The two override tiers now go to a townwide ballot; that vote decides whether cut school and town positions and programs are restored and affects the property tax bill.
The FY27 budget that passed is a balance budget built around the cuts described at the meeting, so its effects take hold unless the ballot overrides pass.
The union contracts and salary schedule approved at the meeting affect town and school staff pay regardless of how the override vote turns out.

minutes.summary: Lunenburg's annual town meeting adopted a level-services FY27 town/school budget requiring deep staff and program cuts, then separately approved (for the ballot) a tier-one $2.4 million and tier-two $3.3 million Proposition 2½ override, each restoring cut positions in town departments and schools if voters approve. what_happened.line: Town meeting adopted a level-services FY27 town and school budget that requires cuts to staff and programs.
Town meeting separately approved two Proposition 2½ override questions, sending both to a townwide ballot; either would restore some of the cut positions if voters approve.
Town meeting approved closing and decommissioning the TC Pacios building, after ruling a floor amendment to fund food-pantry relocation costs outside that article's scope.
A new assistant town manager position was created and the current post retitled HR director, and future town-meeting notices move to a postcard/opt-in system.
Care and custody of part of the Kids Kingdom playground land was transferred from the school committee to the select board.

why_it_matters: Residents will be asked to vote yes or no on the two override questions at the ballot; the outcome decides whether staffing and programs cut from the base budget are restored.
TC Pacios housed the food pantry, the PEG public-access studio and a gym, and the building's closure means those users need a new location before it is decommissioned.
The new administrative position and the switch to a postcard/opt-in mailing change both the cost of town administration and how residents learn about future town meetings.

meetings.headline: Select Board ratified three union contracts (fire, municipal employees, DPW) after executive session.

meetings.headline: Committee missed the spring energy-grant deadline and will apply in the fall instead
meetings.summary: The Green Community Task Force reviewed why it missed the spring grant round (an unfinished refrigeration project and a pending final report) and will instead target the fall round. Most of the meeting was a walkthrough of a free comprehensive building assessment for the public safety building, with a similar assessment planned for Turkey Hill, plus updates on Turkey Hill's renovation plan, a possible Town Hall/Ritter building consolidation, and unresolved questions about who owns and benefits from Turkey Hill's solar panels. No funding was voted; the group agreed on next steps and adjourned.

budget_items.what_was_said: A refrigeration project for the schools was not completed in time, causing the town to miss the deadline for the spring green communities grant round; the group will now apply in the fall.
The chair reported the town hit a 30% threshold under the Green Communities program and hopes to receive a club award for it at the June meeting.
A comprehensive building assessment for the public safety building was completed at no cost to the town through Rise Energy and MassSave.

budget_items.topic: Roof insulation cost, public safety building
budget_items.what_was_said: The CBA flagged roof insulation as a simple efficiency fix but the chair said the cost makes it unlikely to happen soon in this town.
The CBA found the building has a large unused electrical capacity, relevant to a future switch from oil to electric heating.

budget_items.topic: Length of public safety building CBA study
budget_items.what_was_said: The comprehensive building assessment document itself was described as a lengthy study.

budget_items.topic: Full heating/cooling system replacement, public safety building
budget_items.what_was_said: The CBA priced full replacement of the building's heating and cooling systems including chillers and boilers; the chair said that cost makes it unlikely to happen soon.
The chair said the funding available from the upcoming grant round would mainly go toward keeping the schools and the public safety building viable rather than town hall.
The chair said asking to appropriate funds to redo town hall and the Ritter building would be a hard sell, especially given the pending override vote.

budget_items.topic: 1960s Wayland Lake land purchase (planning committee history)
budget_items.what_was_said: A member recalled that decades ago the planning committee looked at buying lakefront land to extend the town beach, which the town passed on over cost.

decisions.decision: Skip the spring grant round and target the fall grant round instead, since the report and paperwork were not ready in time.
Prioritize getting comprehensive building assessments (CBAs) done for Turkey Hill and the public safety building rather than a broader public-buildings PPP review first.
Building design committee's direction is to keep and renovate Turkey Hill rather than replace it, aiming for at least 10 more years of use, and to pursue MSBA funding for the upgrade.

Elections will move from Passios to the school building starting next school year, with the school closed on election day; an override vote, if it reaches the ballot, would likely still be held at Passios.
Town is exploring consolidating town administration into one building (possibly a Ritter renovation), with a presentation planned for fall town meeting.
Plan to hold a joint meeting with the school committee once the Turkey Hill CBA is ready, to explain the assessment and possible state (MSBA) funding routes.
Chair will finalize the grant report, then call the next Green Committee meeting for sometime in May, and will try to add two new members (Tyler and John) to the committee.

meetings.headline: Board can't vote yet on whether the town should keep two tax-foreclosed Hollis Road properties.
meetings.summary: The Lunenburg Planning Board held storm water permit hearings for Zero Reservoir Road, 60 Cross Road/30 Pine Grove/68 Cross Road, and 222 West Townsend Road, approving the Zero Reservoir Road permit and continuing the others to May 11. A board member noted the Capital Planning Committee would meet to make last-minute changes because it has been an unusually challenging budget year; no figures were given.

what_happened.line: The board could not vote on whether the town should keep two tax-foreclosed Hollis Road properties, pushing the decision to May 11.
Storm water permit hearings for two other developments were continued to May 11 pending further review.
The board approved a storm water permit for the Zero Reservoir Road development after adding a requirement for town counsel to review the HOA document.
After residents raised concerns about erosion and incomplete hydroseeding, the board set a cash bond for stabilization work at 7-Eleven Mass Ave, not releasable before November 1, 2026.

The chair noted a change in state tax title law now requires the town to pay a foreclosed owner the difference between what was owed and the property's appraised value, rather than keeping the full property.

why_it_matters: Whether the town keeps or disposes of the Hollis Road properties affects options like municipal or senior housing use, and the new tax title law changes what the town owes a former owner either way.
Residents near the 60 Cross Road and 222 West Townsend Road sites raised drainage and erosion concerns that remain unresolved until the May 11 hearing.
The bond set at 7-Eleven Mass Ave is meant to ensure erosion and hydroseeding work gets finished, with the money held until vegetation is established.

meetings.headline: Committee weighs saving part of TC Pacios vs. town hall/Ritter consolidation, with no decision made
meetings.summary: The Municipal Building Design Committee discussed the fate of the vacated TC Pacios building -- whether any part of it (gym, kitchen, roof) is worth saving versus the committee's charter to consolidate town administrative functions into Ritter/Town Hall -- alongside an update on Turkey Hill Elementary's coming MSBA process. No formal votes were taken on substance; the committee agreed to refine and send out a facilities survey, add TC Pacios-related questions to it, and reconvene May 18th.

budget_items.what_was_said: Adding a needed new boiler (the current one is leaking) to the roof/section repair would bring the cost to roughly this figure to save those parts of the building.

budget_items.what_was_said: A member reiterated this figure for a community-center-type renovation, calling it a nice-to-have rather than a necessity given other town needs.

figures_as_heard: close to or if not over a half million
budget_items.what_was_said: Combining the cost of prior studies for TCP reuse, TCP teardown/rebuild, and an initial Ritter study, a member estimated the town has spent roughly this amount without a resulting project.

A member recalled that the original full renovation plan to modern standards, including seismic and structural work, was estimated at this figure, distinguishing it from a smaller roof-only repair option now being discussed.

budget_items.topic: TC Pacios roof repair appropriation, 2024 special town meeting
budget_items.what_was_said: A member noted town meeting had voted to appropriate this amount to repair a section of the TC Pacios roof, but the funds were never used because of other building issues that made it seem an unwise use of funds.

budget_items.topic: PAC relocation cost within prior $26 million building project
budget_items.what_was_said: A member recalled that a late decision by the select board to put PAC in a new building's basement added a large, costly amount of square footage to that overall project.
Members joked about adding a fourth override tier worth this figure while discussing the town's multi-tier override structure being decided around the same time.

decisions.decision: The chair will meet in person with the town manager next week to finalize and push forward the town hall/facilities survey.
The committee agreed to add a survey question asking residents how they use TC Pacios (storage, functions, voting) and where those uses would go if it closes.
Laura offered to convert the chair's draft survey document into a Google Form so responses can be compiled in a spreadsheet; the chair agreed to send her the document.
The committee set its next meeting for May 18th, keeping the first-and-third-Monday schedule.

The committee reaffirmed that its current charter is to investigate consolidating town administrative functions into one building, not to take on TC Pacios reuse as a new project without changing that charter.

meetings.headline: Commission passed a motion letting one member keep managing trust funds if it loses quorum
meetings.summary: The trust fund commission's chair delivered an extended legal presentation arguing the town, select board, town manager and school department are in breach of fiduciary duty under Massachusetts trust law (MGL 203E) for decades of undistributed trust income, and reported an attorney general breach notice has been filed and is under review. The commission then voted to adopt a formal motion preserving fiduciary oversight and authorizing a lone remaining commissioner to continue ministerial/administrative duties if the board loses quorum; no trust money was distributed at this meeting.

The chair noted the cemetery commission did not put a request for a sum on this year's town meeting warrant after he clarified the cemetery commission is its own trustee body with independent authority to use its own funds.

budget_items.what_was_said: Richard read a statement prepared with other residents arguing the town's balanced budget maintains core operations without an override, that tier one appears to be the intended landing point, and that no department has shown the override is legally necessary.

decisions.decision: The board will maintain the delegation-of-authority framework so that as long as one elected commissioner remains, ministerial duties continue to be administered even without a quorum.
Review of the rewritten risk management policy was pushed off to the following week's meeting.
The upcoming annual town meeting report to the town manager will include a summary of the breach notice and other recent commission actions, not just prior meeting topics.

meetings.headline: Commissioners split over locking in state loan funding for the PFAS treatment plant ahead of a May resident vote
meetings.summary: The Lunenburg Water District board spent most of this meeting refining a joint PowerPoint on funding options (SRF loan and bond) for a combined PFAS/iron-manganese treatment plant and transmission-main project, ahead of a special resident meeting set for late May. Commissioners disagreed sharply over whether to secure the full SRF loan amount now versus waiting for firmer design-stage cost numbers, with no vote taken on that question; the board also voted on a special-meeting date, amended shutoff/collections rules, and directed a letter to MassDEP over a condo association's kayak rack.

budget_items.topic: Baseline cost for PFAS/iron-manganese treatment plant and transmission mains
budget_items.what_was_said: The board set a baseline construction estimate combining the Hickory Hills SRF-funded portion and the Keings project, to be presented as a single combined vote for residents.

budget_items.topic: SRF vs. bond interest rates for the two project components
budget_items.what_was_said: Commissioners discussed borrowing the larger Hickory Hills/Lancaster portion under the SRF at one rate and financing the smaller Keings portion separately at a higher rate.

budget_items.topic: SRF principal forgiveness and possible emerging-contaminant grant
budget_items.what_was_said: The board debated whether a percentage of principal forgiveness applies automatically under the SRF application, and whether a separate emerging-contaminants grant pool might add further funding; they agreed to seek clarity.

budget_items.topic: Engineering design-services line within the SRF application
budget_items.what_was_said: A commissioner calculated that the budgeted design-services fee, at an assumed hourly engineer rate, implied an unreasonably large number of full-time-equivalent engineer-years, arguing the true design cost is much lower; another commissioner noted the figure is the maximum SRF allows, not the actual cost.
The same commissioner compared the budgeted construction-oversight fee to what one engineer working the full construction period at an hourly rate would cost, arguing a large gap between the two.

budget_items.topic: Capital cost per gallon of treatment capacity, compared nationally
budget_items.what_was_said: A commissioner presented national cost data for similar-sized PFAS and iron/manganese treatment plants and argued the district's estimated building cost is several times higher than comparable plants elsewhere.

budget_items.topic: Residential vs. commercial water-use figures behind the cost allocation
budget_items.what_was_said: The clerk/treasurer explained a spreadsheet used for the annual statistical report that breaks down usage by connection type, used to check the numbers behind the funding slides.

budget_items.topic: Cost of the Keings-to-Lancaster transmission main
budget_items.what_was_said: A commissioner noted the transmission-line cost estimate has varied widely across different reports and design assumptions (pipe diameter), and said the true number awaits final design.

budget_items.topic: Total project cost and impact on resident water bills
budget_items.what_was_said: A resident said the plant, financing and operating costs over the loan term would roughly triple a typical household's annual water bill, and warned many customers are already behind on payments.

budget_items.topic: Delinquent accounts and collections behind new shutoff rule
budget_items.what_was_said: The clerk described the number of bills sent, second notices issued, and accounts running behind, used to justify adding formal payment-plan and shutoff language to the rules and regulations.

budget_items.topic: Resident survey response rate on funding options
budget_items.what_was_said: The board noted only a small share of water takers had responded to the survey and decided to extend the deadline and publicize it further before the special meeting vote.

decisions.decision: A commissioner will draft a letter to MassDEP requesting a variance to allow the Woodland Condo Association's kayak rack to remain, to be reviewed by the absent third commissioner and voted on at a future meeting.

The two commissioners agreed to merge their separate PowerPoint drafts into one combined presentation on PFAS/water treatment funding options, using one commissioner's visual diagram and the other's cost detail.
The board agreed to hold a public presentation at town hall, recorded for local TV, ahead of the special meeting vote.
Extend the resident funding-options survey a couple more weeks and promote it via social media before closing it.

Clarified that the planned SRF/bond vote authorizes funding for the Hickory Hills-to-Lancaster plant and transmission main and, separately at a different rate, the Keings transmission main, and either portion could later be declined if not needed.
Agreed to add discussion of the board's own agenda-item process to the next meeting's agenda.

meetings.headline: Board took only routine votes; public comment sharply disputed override claims of fire and police service cuts
meetings.summary: The Select Board handled routine business -- a class 2 motor vehicle license, a one-day liquor license, lifeguard/beach director appointments, a videographer resignation, and setting a July 1 start date for the new sick leave bank policy -- alongside a town manager update on IFBs, recruitments, and town meeting logistics. The most substantive content was extended public comment in which a resident challenged claims that the FY27 balanced budget and override option cut fire and police services, followed by another resident promoting property-tax relief programs; the meeting closed by voting to enter executive session over firefighter and AFSCME collective bargaining strategy.

budget_items.topic: Fire department Sunday shift staffing cost, PDM coverage vs. career firefighters

budget_items.what_was_said: The commenter said a portion of the FY25 override went unspent due to lack of tracking under the former superintendent, which she said hurt students.

budget_items.what_was_said: The commenter said the balanced budget sets aside a reserve amount well above what the town's financial policy calls for.

budget_items.what_was_said: The commenter said new revenue is being used for capital expenses including vehicles rather than drawing from an existing reserve account.
The commenter listed the band concert as a small service being eliminated in the balanced budget.
The commenter cited the town beach's net cost as another small service affected by budget choices.
The commenter framed the eliminated small services as insignificant relative to the total town budget, but said they matter to affected families and seniors.

budget_items.topic: School reserve accounts vs. amount needed for current services
budget_items.what_was_said: The commenter questioned why school reserve accounts exceed what she said is needed to maintain current services, given warnings that schools would be devastated if the override fails.

budget_items.topic: 41A property tax deferral and circuit breaker eligibility thresholds
budget_items.what_was_said: A resident described income and home-value thresholds under the state's 41A deferral and circuit breaker tax credit programs, saying eligibility is broader than residents realize.

budget_items.topic: State income tax circuit breaker credit
budget_items.what_was_said: The same resident said qualifying residents could also get an income tax break under the circuit breaker program.

budget_items.topic: Lunenburg Crossing stormwater fee vs. tax bill
budget_items.what_was_said: The group discussed that a large commercial property's tax bill was much larger than its estimated stormwater utility fee would be, estimating the fee at roughly 15% of that tax bill as a comparison point.

budget_items.topic: Junior engineer position and utility overhead
budget_items.what_was_said: Members discussed that if a proposed junior engineer position is funded in the town's override budget, its salary would be removed from the storm water utility's overhead calculation.
The group discussed a roughly 30% overhead figure on Bill's stormwater budget, questioning what indirect costs (accounting, treasury, legal) made up that share.
A member walked through a spreadsheet formula summing indirect cost lines to produce the overhead total being debated.

budget_items.topic: Full stormwater funding in override budget
budget_items.what_was_said: It was noted that full funding of storm water almost made it into a tier-one override budget this year but did not, which a member called a disappointment.

budget_items.topic: Cap on fee relative to assessed value
budget_items.what_was_said: A member suggested flagging or capping the stormwater fee for small businesses if it exceeded some threshold share of their assessed property value.

budget_items.topic: Residential vs. business share of cost under utility vs. tax funding
budget_items.what_was_said: A member estimated that under a utility approach residents would bear a much smaller share of storm water cost than under the current property-tax-funded approach.

decisions.decision: One member will enter the new impervious-area data into the broader fee spreadsheet and calculate a proposed fee for each property using the task force's current tier structure.
The group agreed to build the overhead comparison as three columns: operating-budget cost, utility cost, and the difference (net overhead) between them, for the next presentation.
The task force agreed its next public/Finance Committee presentation should center on the financial impact and cost comparison to residents, rather than general storm water education.
The task force set its next meeting for May 14th.

topics.topic: Planning the comparison presentation of operating-budget vs. utility funding costs to residents and businesses
Timing of the new stormwater discharge permit and shifting presentation focus to financial impact on residents

what_happened.line: No decision was made on funding stormwater through a new utility fee versus the town's tax-funded operating budget, after debate over utility overhead.
The group agreed to build a comparison of operating-budget cost, utility cost, and the difference between them for a future presentation.
That presentation will focus on the financial impact and cost comparison to residents, not general stormwater education.
A property-fee model is being built from GIS impervious-surface data for roughly 700 properties, with a fee to be calculated for each.
The next meeting is set for May 14.

why_it_matters: This decides whether stormwater work shows up as a new separate fee on a resident's bill or stays folded into the property tax rate.
How overhead and cost are split between a stand-alone utility and the operating budget could shift how much of the cost businesses versus homeowners pay.
No funding method has been chosen yet; the task force is still building the cost comparison that would inform that choice.

what_happened.line: The commission approved a private water main extension along Round/Parmenter/Ruth Streets while explicitly declining to certify the wetland flags shown on the applicant's own plan.
A resident had told the commission wetlands near his Ruth Street home were not flagged like others on that same project, given its size and proximity to Lake Shirley.
A disputed house reconstruction at 18 Oakridge Road stalled over the project's encroachment into the 50-foot wetland no-build zone and was continued to May 6.
The commission voted not to exercise the town's right of first refusal on a Lemonster/Lancaster Road property.
Hickory Hills' accessible parking and rain garden plan was approved on the condition of an asphalt surface and an agent-approved maintenance plan.

why_it_matters: The water main approval lets private construction proceed near Lake Shirley without the commission certifying where the wetlands actually are, a gap a resident raised directly at the hearing.
The town is passing on a chance to acquire the Lemonster/Lancaster Road parcel, which leaves its future use to whatever private sale follows.
A homeowner on Oakridge Road remains unable to finish a reconstruction project until the setback dispute is resolved at the May 6 hearing.

meetings.headline: Schools urged town unity ahead of the override vote; routine grants and policy readings were approved
meetings.summary: The meeting was dominated by the superintendent and chair urging the town to approach the upcoming Proposition 2½ override and town meeting collaboratively rather than divisively, describing this year's tri-board budget process as unusually transparent. The committee also heard a LEAF Foundation fundraising update, approved two state grant submissions and a farm-to-school grant, discussed a scholarship trust/EIN dispute with the town's Trust Commission, revisited unified sports options, reviewed the quarterly budget and personnel reports, assigned negotiating teams for two union contracts, set a process for the superintendent's evaluation, and waived first readings on four policies.

what_happened.line: The superintendent and chair urged residents to approach the coming override vote and town meeting collaboratively, calling this year's budget process unusually transparent.
The committee voted to submit two Prism grant applications and a Farm to Table grant to bring in state funding for staff training and curriculum.
A dispute over a scholarship trust fund's EIN with the town's Trust Commission was sent to legal counsel rather than resolved tonight.
First readings were waived on four policies, including student data privacy and security rules that address AI use.
Negotiating teams were assigned for the custodians' and cafeteria workers' union contracts, and a fee increase for the extended day program was pushed to a future agenda.

why_it_matters: The override and town meeting the superintendent referenced would set the tax bill residents vote on, and the meeting framed this year's budget process as more transparent than past years.
watch_next: Superintendent evaluation rubric scores due around May 13, with compilation and discussion at the May 20 meeting
A future agenda item on an extended day program fee increase

meetings.headline: Public comment turned into a pitched fight over the FY27 override, staffing cuts, and a disputed Ledger story.
meetings.summary: The bulk of this meeting was public comment: the fire chief, both police and fire union presidents, a school committee member speaking as a parent, and residents disputed a local newspaper's coverage of the FY27 balanced budget, override, and staffing cuts, followed by lengthy rebuttals from board members and the Town Manager. The board also handled routine license and event-permit hearings, a town manager's report, tax-title property and cover-photo votes, committee reports, and voted to enter executive session over opioid-litigation settlement strategy; no vote was taken on the override itself.

what_happened.line: The Council on Aging director reported the 41A property tax deferral program has disappeared from the town website's exemptions listing, weeks before the override vote.
The board urged seniors to attend the upcoming special town meeting and discussed what an override would mean for residents on fixed incomes.
Members voted to have a board member and a resident explore next steps and funding for a donated playground and parking-lot redesign.
The board voted to set case-by-case criteria for honorary Council on Aging membership, then voted to award one to Pete Lincoln.
The board decided to get the 41A deferral program corrected on the town website and produce handout material ahead of the override vote.

why_it_matters: The 41A deferral lets eligible seniors put off paying part of their property tax bill, and its disappearance from the town's own listing could leave residents facing a higher override bill unaware the option exists.
Seniors on fixed incomes are the group most exposed to an override's effect on the tax bill, which is why the board is pressing attendance at the special town meeting where the override is decided.

The playground and parking-lot redesign draws on funds already set aside at a prior town meeting, so its progress depends on a design estimate and possible added grant funding, not a new appropriation.

meetings.headline: Assessors voted to shift $27,500 from the overlay reserve to fund the neighborhood review project position.
meetings.summary: The Board of Assessors approved backlogged minutes, reviewed a status report covering excise and real estate abatements, veterans'/Hero Act exemption reimbursements, and progress on the townwide neighborhood review project. The board voted not to exercise the town's right of first refusal on a Chapter 61 parcel at 35 Leominster Road, signed roll-back tax paperwork for that property, and voted to transfer $27,500 from the overlay reserve to fund the neighborhood review position for FY2027 rather than rely on an override. The board scheduled meetings for April 22 and May 13 and then entered executive session to discuss pending abatement/exemption applications, including a resident's property tax question.

minutes.headline: Board approved a Round Road water main extension and scheduled a workshop on the $41 million SRF loan due by June 30
minutes.summary: The Lunenburg Water Commissioners reorganized (electing Matthew Woodward chair), approved a new water main extension plan for a 25-lot Round Road development and authorized exploring a state growth grant for it, and voted to purchase a used Volvo excavator near the previously appropriated amount. A resident challenged the superintendent over a large SRF loan application submitted in 2023/2026 without board approval, and the board deferred answering until next meeting; it also scheduled a dedicated workshop to decide how to present the district's SRF financing options to voters ahead of a June 30 deadline.

what_happened.line: The board scheduled a dedicated workshop on how to present water financing options to voters ahead of a June 30 deadline.
Commissioners approved a water main extension plan for a new Round Road-area development and voted to explore a state growth grant toward it.
A resident challenged the superintendent over a large loan application submitted without board approval; the board deferred answering until next meeting.
The board voted to buy a used excavator, trimming which attachments to include to stay near the amount previously approved.
The board reorganized for the year, electing Matthew Woodward as chair.

what_happened.line: The Select Board voted unanimously to recommend the FY27 balanced budget for town meeting.
The board recommended the override's second tier by a 3-1 vote; the first tier's vote outcome was not audible on the recording.
Public commenters objected to proposed cuts to the library, senior center and beach program alongside new spending on an assistant town manager and a fourth fire shift.
The board also recommended the PAC/PEG, solid waste, water and sewer enterprise fund articles, all unanimously.
The board scheduled a budget public information meeting for the evening of April 28 at the Adult Activity Center.

why_it_matters: Both the balanced budget and the override now go to town meeting, where the choice is between a level-services budget with cuts to programs like the library, senior center and beach program, or an override that funds the assistant town manager position and a fourth fire shift.
A resident weighing the override should note the split board vote on its second tier, which signals the choice was not unanimous even among the officials recommending it.
The April 28 public information meeting is the town's forum for residents to ask about the budget and override before voting.

meetings.headline: Finance Committee voted to recommend both Prop 2½ override tiers for town meeting, 4-2 each
meetings.summary: The Finance Committee re-voted a batch of previously split or 5-member warrant-article recommendations so the chair's vote could be added, and worked through remaining deferred articles for the May town meeting warrant, most consequentially the FY27 omnibus balanced budget and the two-tier Proposition 2½ override. One member repeatedly argued the balanced budget under-documents new positions (an assistant town manager and HR director) and cuts services in a way designed to pressure voters toward the override, while other members defended the process and voted to recommend both override tiers. The committee also approved its FY27 annual report for inclusion in the mailed warrant and set its next meeting for April 23.

The committee voted 4-2 to add the assistant town manager and HR director positions to the salary grid, which a member said bypassed the town's normal job-description process.

meetings.headline: PACC will ask town meeting to tap retained earnings to close a budget gap and replace its aging broadcast system.
meetings.summary: The Public Access Cable Committee reviewed the manager's report, a FY26 salary shortfall covered by line-item transfers, and the FY27 budget, then spent most of the meeting going through a vendor quote to replace its aging Castis broadcast system. No formal budget or purchase vote was taken; both the FY27 PEG operating budget shortfall and the Castis system replacement will go to town meeting as warrant articles funded partly from retained earnings. A pending PACC policy vote was tabled because a member was absent.

The quoted Castis unit itself was the first line item on the vendor's quote.

decisions.decision: Agreed that if the Castis system isn't fully installed by June 30, that is fine because it is budgeted and committed in FY26.

Enterprise fund investment status will be reported at the next meeting once the town's figures are available.

Spending limits were read for ambulance billing, timber rights, school custodial special details, Green Thumb, library, Council on Aging, storm water task force, electric/gas/plumbing inspector, technology, wetlands protection fees, COA meal site, and parks programming revolving funds.

budget_items.what_was_said: The current estimated operating deficit, driven mostly by snow and ice removal, was given; transfers will cover part of it and up to a stated amount was earmarked from free cash pending final snow and ice bills.
Two override tiers would go to voters as separate ballot questions, with only the highest approved amount implemented; the Finance Committee deferred taking a position pending the full board.

An accounting error had moved the same unspent FY23 capital funds through two prior votes (TCP roof repair, then FY26 capital); this article unwinds both so the money returns to the FY26 capital plan cleanly.

Individual capital items were read out including DPW bridge completion, a police cruiser, a fire engine/brush truck, primary school entry/driveway and playground design, public safety building roof and boiler work, door security intercoms at Turkey Hill and the primary school, and a DPW front-end loader.
The planned motion would transfer this amount from solid waste enterprise revenue to operate the program for FY2027; the fund does not cover recycling costs.
The fund would use enterprise revenue to pay Fitchburg for water and recoup a percentage under an intermunicipal agreement; figures were based on usage estimates.

what_happened.line: The committee put off recommending a position on the FY27 Proposition 2½ override until the full five-member board can meet.
It also deferred the FY27 omnibus town and school operating budget because final transfer figures were not yet ready.
A new special-purpose health insurance stabilization fund transfer passed its recommendation on a 4-1 vote.
A proposed Assistant Town Manager/HR Director grade change was pushed to the next meeting after members said it needed further discussion.
Most routine warrant articles -- revolving funds, the FY27 capital budget, and the water and solid waste enterprise funds -- were recommended for approval.

why_it_matters: The override recommendation touches what residents are asked to approve at town meeting or the ballot, and the committee is not yet on record with a position.
The FY27 omnibus budget funds town and school operations for the coming year; its numbers were not final at this meeting.
The health insurance stabilization fund is a new savings mechanism for a cost that affects both town and school budgets, and it did not pass without dissent.
watch_next: The next Finance Committee meeting, when the full board is expected to take up the override recommendation.
A future vote on the FY27 omnibus town/school budget article, once closeout and transfer figures are final.

meetings.headline: Commission approved DPW's Northville Crossing culvert replacement after a years-long right-of-entry delay was resolved.
meetings.summary: This was a long hearing-heavy Conservation Commission meeting covering two certificates of compliance, several continued wetlands permit hearings for a multi-lot subdivision on Parmenter/Round Road, a proposed multi-year herbicide/vegetation management plan for Marshall Pond, and approval of a long-delayed DPW culvert replacement at Northville Crossing. The commission also worked through several enforcement/violation matters (48 Meadow Lane, a drainage-area violation, 715 Reservoir Road, 314 Highland Street), agreeing on remediation plantings and signage rather than formal violation filings in most cases, and discussed longer-term administrative matters including the conservation budget, a possible riverfront-regulations training session, and future plans for the Hollis Road property.
