meetings.headline: Committee voted to keep charging the student bus fee despite members calling it unfair, citing budget desperation.
meetings.summary: The Lunenburg School Committee heard public comment on an override, a student proposal to credit after-school sports as PE, and updates on capital projects and grant-seeking, then worked through a long list of votes: continuing the bus fee, discontinuing the lifelong learning program, approving a $300,000 federal earmark request, and endorsing a letter to legislators on Chapter 70 funding. Facilities updates covered an energy-efficiency program at the high school, relocating a generator from the Pacios building, solar array repairs, and Turkey Hill bathroom renovations, alongside several retirement and new-hire announcements including a new Turkey Hill principal.

public_comment.topic: Advocated that participation in after-school sports count as PE/gym credit for high schoolers, citing a student survey and studies on mental health benefits.
Raised concerns about the override not being a permanent fix, wanted long-range financial projections, and described rising need at the local food pantry and community mutual aid.
Reminded residents that the override must pass at both the May 2nd town meeting and the May 16th ballot, and urged attendance at both.
Raised concern that unified sports/arts opportunities for students with disabilities are shrinking and asked for a fuller committee conversation on options.

budget_items.what_was_said: The town manager approved three capital requests: two feasibility studies for the primary school (playground and drive/playground) and camera systems for building entrances. Other requested items were deferred for later in the year due to funding and the Pacios building situation.

The district is seeking one-time federal earmark funding to build a district-wide instructional framework and offset a projected cut to Title One funding; the district would not have to make up any shortfall if the full amount isn't awarded.
Funds previously voted to be accepted from the scholarship fund were not actually transferred from the estate to students due to a legal/executor issue; the district will bring it back once resolved.
As of month-end the district was at 66.1% of budget expended, rising to 68.6% once a payroll posted; last year the district was at 67% at the same point, having spent less overall.
The collaborative tuition line is overspent because circuit breaker reimbursement money has not yet been posted back into it; this is described as a normally hard line to budget.

Electrical spending is running over budget due to a colder winter and last year's underbudgeting; gas/heating has money remaining, and next year's electrical budget was adjusted based on recent actuals.
Legal expenses are running hot this year and the FY27 budget has been adjusted upward as a result.

The district described fee revenue collected over two periods and the fee schedule by family size and reduced-fee eligibility, and members debated the fairness of the fee against the roughly $70,000 it raises given the district's financial situation.

Chapter 70 does not include transportation costs at all, and regional districts get 75% of transportation reimbursed while Lunenburg does not, which a member said could be worth a large additional sum if reimbursed similarly.

The adult men's basketball program generated minimal revenue per player and relies on unpaid volunteer facilitators; the adult health and fitness program is a pass-through to a private vendor with the district retaining no financial benefit, supporting the recommendation to discontinue the district-run program.

A draft letter to legislators notes Lunenburg ranks near the bottom statewide for per-pupil spending while spending well above the state-required minimum, which members attribute to flaws in how Chapter 70 categorizes districts.
A building-controls efficiency study at the high school may be covered up to 100% by the program, addressing malfunctioning thermostats and actuators causing temperature problems.
The existing landscaping contract for the district's three athletic fields has expired and is going out to bid; costs under the prior contract were described as escalating over the years.
The PTO reported raising a significant amount at a recent dance fundraiser, plus a separate Great Wolf Lodge fundraiser.

decisions.decision: Bring Eden Fry's proposal on counting after-school sports as PE credit to the appropriate staff member (Mr. Sanders) and put it on a future agenda.

If the larger override passes and the town hires a full-time recreation director, the committee will coordinate with that person on facility scheduling and possible partnership on adult/community programs.
Invite Shannina to a future meeting to discuss why unified spring sports had low participation and what other successful districts do, before deciding on any changes.
Begin discussing the superintendent's evaluation at the next meeting.

Committee will split up and pair experienced with new members to begin the contract negotiation process starting next week.
Business manager will provide an HR report to the committee, expected to cover the full year.

why_it_matters: The bus fee stays in place for families who use it, separate from and regardless of the outcome of the townwide override vote in May.
Ending the lifelong learning program removes a district-run adult offering, though students already enrolled will finish the current session before it closes.
The letter to legislators is an ask, not a change in funding -- any shift in how Chapter 70 treats transportation or per-pupil spending depends on action in Boston, not this committee.

meetings.headline: Board set the FY27 town meeting warrant and voted a two-tier override question onto the town election ballot
meetings.summary: The Select Board worked through the annual town meeting warrant article by article with town counsel, deferring several items (prior-year invoices, FY26 budget adjustments, the snow-and-ice closeout, and union contract funding) to town meeting itself, and declining -- after individual members stated concerns -- to include a Trust Fund Commission legal-fees article or a quorum bylaw article that counsel flagged as legally uncertain. The board voted to place a two-tier Proposition 2½ override question on the annual town election ballot, rounding the tiers to clean dollar figures and choosing a "Question 1/Question 2" ballot format, while one member stated ongoing concerns about the override's affordability. It also discussed but did not finalize where the override and other articles should sit in the warrant order and consent agenda.

public_comment.topic: Asked the board to randomize/lottery the order of non-fixed warrant articles at town meeting to stop "vote stacking" around the override.

Clarified the "rule of necessity" legal doctrine behind the trust fund quorum article and said the commission has filed a breach-of-fiduciary-duty notice against the town with a 30-day response request.

minutes.headline: Board set the FY27 town meeting warrant and voted a two-tier override question onto the town election ballot
minutes.summary: The Select Board worked through the annual town meeting warrant article by article with town counsel, deferring several items (prior-year invoices, FY26 budget adjustments, the snow-and-ice closeout, and union contract funding) to town meeting itself, and declining -- after individual members stated concerns -- to include a Trust Fund Commission legal-fees article or a quorum bylaw article that counsel flagged as legally uncertain. The board voted to place a two-tier Proposition 2½ override question on the annual town election ballot, rounding the tiers to clean dollar figures and choosing a "Question 1/Question 2" ballot format, while one member stated ongoing concerns about the override's affordability. It also discussed but did not finalize where the override and other articles should sit in the warrant order and consent agenda.

what_happened.line: Board voted 5-0 to place a two-tier Proposition 2½ override question on the annual town election ballot, pending town counsel's final edits.
Board members individually declined to put two Trust Fund Commission articles, on legal fees and a quorum bylaw, on the town meeting warrant.
The board deferred several FY27 warrant items, including prior-year invoices and union contract funding, to town meeting itself.
A Trust Fund Commission representative told the board the commission has filed a notice of breach of fiduciary duty against the town.

why_it_matters: The override question, if it proceeds as set, will ask voters at the annual town election to approve additional property tax collection above the state cap, split into two tiers residents can vote on separately.

Sending prior-year invoices, FY26 budget adjustments, and union contract funding to town meeting itself means those costs will be settled by the voters present rather than decided in advance by the board.
The declined Trust Fund Commission articles and the fiduciary-duty notice point to an unresolved dispute between that commission and the town that may surface again at town meeting.

meetings.headline: Sewer board finds major manhole water infiltration on Laurel Lane but can't fund a wider search this year
meetings.summary: The Lunenburg Sewer Commission reviewed ongoing manhole-lining repairs, heard that a commissioner discovered a discontinued pump line pouring significant groundwater into the system on Laurel Lane, and discussed possibly requiring developers to offset added sewer capacity by fixing leaking pipes elsewhere. The FY27 budget and rate increase, already approved at a prior meeting, is moving to town meeting, and no further study of infiltration hotspots will happen this fiscal year due to tight funds.

votes.motion: Accept the minutes from the March 10, 2026 meeting
Adjourn the meeting

budget_items.topic: Manhole repair IFB / In Situ Technologies contract
budget_items.what_was_said: The DPW director said the contractor still has roughly 10 to 15 manholes to line and about 15 more needing frame-and-cover replacement, expected to finish within about a month once cold weather breaks.
The business manager gave a ballpark cost per manhole for the cementitious liner used to seal them.
A commissioner estimated a discontinued 1.25-inch pump line was leaking roughly that much water per day into the sewer system, discovered while investigating an unrelated job.
The business manager said the commission is tight on funds at the end of the fiscal year, so a wider survey of manholes flagged in past studies cannot be done right now.

budget_items.topic: FY26 third quarter demands / delinquency rate
budget_items.what_was_said: Demands were sent out March 16 and people are starting to pay; the combined delinquency rate was described as around that figure, under 20%.

The board noted it already voted to approve the FY27 budget and an associated rate increase at a prior meeting; the town manager had follow-up questions but nothing changed, and it moves forward to town meeting.

budget_items.topic: Pawn Street sewer district connection request
budget_items.what_was_said: A resident/owner interested in joining the sewer district would need to pay for engineering plans before the board can vote on anything, and it is unclear if the owner wants to proceed given the cost.

budget_items.topic: Developer betterment for added sewer capacity (I&I offset)
budget_items.what_was_said: A commissioner described a practice used by other towns where a developer adding gallonage to the district must locate and fix an equivalent amount of leaking pipe capacity at their own expense.
The business manager said existing regulations already require developments above a certain size to eliminate I&I or pay a fee that goes into the district's I&I account.

decisions.decision: The DPW director will give the manhole-lining contractor the go-ahead to resume work once nighttime temperatures rise above freezing this week.

what_happened.line: The Finance Committee closed its public hearing on the FY27 school and town budgets without voting on the budget, an override, or any warrant article.

The superintendent laid out a level-funded budget with cuts to teaching positions, music, and athletics, against two override scenarios that would restore and add staff across schools, police, fire, DPW, and the library.
Draft warrant articles, including the override article itself, were walked through but not voted on.
The committee scheduled an additional virtual meeting for April 6 to vote on the warrant articles and finalize its report before the town meeting deadline.

why_it_matters: Whether voters pass a tier-1 or tier-2 override in May decides whether class sizes rise and positions such as teachers, a custodian, and an occupational therapy assistant go unfilled.
The warrant articles still being drafted will set exactly what residents are asked to vote on at town meeting and on the override ballot.
Town departments including police, fire, DPW, and the library face the same level-funded-versus-override choice as the schools.

meetings.headline: Trust Fund board voted to notify the Attorney General of a 50-year town breach managing charitable trusts
meetings.summary: The Board of Trust Fund Commissioners (two members, John Bowen and Richard Howard) spent nearly the entire meeting on a detailed breach notice alleging the Town of Lunenburg has failed for over 50 years to properly administer, document, and distribute numerous charitable trust funds, including missing donor declarations, an entirely missing fund, and unresolved American Legion fund eligibility requirements. The board voted to send a letter and submission packet to the Attorney General's Division of Public Charities and to the Town Manager and Select Board, giving the town 30 days to act, and also voted to amend the operating policy for the American Legion funds and adopt signature-page documents to formalize the filings. Chair Bowen also raised in commission comment concerns about the town's proposed override and his own re-election filing for the board.

budget_items.what_was_said: The chair said the trust funds have taken in a substantial amount of income, citing a total figure with a portion of it available to distribute out of that total.
The chair said he had proposed a smaller tax increase two years ago than what is now being sought, arguing the town wasted two years of investment income by not acting sooner.

budget_items.topic: Warrant article request for trust investigation funding
budget_items.what_was_said: The chair said the commission should not have had to request funding via warrant article for the town to investigate and administer the trust funds, arguing the town already has a fiduciary duty to fund this.

budget_items.topic: Repayment of improperly dispersed trust funds
budget_items.what_was_said: The chair said a past dispersement from the Worthy Poor fund to a landlord needs to be repaid to the board by the town, not by the individual who received it.

budget_items.topic: Woodward School for Girls v. Quincy case liability
budget_items.what_was_said: The chair cited a Massachusetts case where a town was held liable for failing to manage a charitable trust, used as precedent for the town's liability here.

budget_items.topic: 1901 Nathaniel Day trust gift, present-day value
budget_items.what_was_said: The chair displayed a 1901 donation receipt and said the amount would be worth much more today, illustrating funds that currently cannot be distributed.
The letter to the Attorney General states the town has allowed a sum in earnings to accumulate without lawful distribution across the charitable trust funds.

meetings.headline: Back-lot cemetery expansion cost estimate came in far above the $50,000 budgeted, forcing redesign before bidding.
meetings.summary: The Cemetery Commission approved routine minutes, Memorial Day flowers, a $20,000 transfer from sale-of-lots funds, a Fish Street plaque design, and a lot exchange recognizing a donor family. Most of the meeting was spent on the DPW director's report that the engineering estimate for the South Cemetery back-lot expansion came back far higher than the $50,000 placeholder budgeted, prompting discussion of cost-cutting (reusing town millings, cheaper gravel, dropping engineering-during-construction costs) and funding options (sale-of-lots balance, rate increases, possible non-resident burials) before the project can go out to bid.

budget_items.what_was_said: The commission listed already-committed costs: gravestone straightening and repair, the Fish Street Cemetery wall, and plaque/stonework.
Members recalled last year's flower cost and discussed capping this year's purchase, unsure of exact prior figure amid inflation.

The commission discussed whether a $20,000 warrant article was still needed for town meeting, and learned the town manager said it was not required going forward; a written authorization to the treasurer suffices instead.

budget_items.topic: South Cemetery / Fish Street project funding need
budget_items.what_was_said: The chair reviewed the outstanding commitment for South Cemetery and Fish Street work against the current balance to determine how much more was needed before the $20,000 transfer.

budget_items.topic: Remaining balance after transfer and flowers
budget_items.what_was_said: After applying the planned $20,000 transfer and assumed $600 flower cost, the commission worked out roughly how much would remain for the rest of the year.

The DPW director presented a new engineering cost estimate for the back-lot cemetery expansion that came in far above the original placeholder figure, calling it a shock, and outlined ways to bring it down.
The director proposed eliminating this line since he could answer bidder questions himself, paying an engineer hourly only if needed.
A line for moving contractor equipment onto site was discussed as an area that might be trimmed or folded into unit prices.

budget_items.topic: Sale of lots and perpetual care account balances
budget_items.what_was_said: Members discussed the sale-of-lots balance after the planned transfer and a separate, larger perpetual care account whose interest only can be used.
It was suggested that allowing non-residents to be buried in the cemetery, as some other towns do, could bring in additional revenue toward the expansion.
A per-stump estimate was called unrealistically low given hauling and documentation requirements, with a revised total suggested to be much higher.
The department is rehiring two part-time seasonal helpers from last year, within a limited budget that must last through the end of the fiscal year.

transfers.description: $20,000 from the sale-of-lots account to fund cemetery care, improvement and expansion

decisions.decision: Going forward, the commission will submit written authorization to the town treasurer/accountant to transfer sale-of-lots funds rather than seeking a town meeting warrant article each year.
The commission agreed it does not want to drain the sale-of-lots account to a low balance and will revise the expansion cost estimate before deciding how much of the project to bid.
The commission cannot solicit donations from town residents directly since it is a town body, though it could accept unsolicited gifts or support a resident-formed 501(c)3.
The commission will not go out to bid until the funding amount is confirmed; the DPW director will first revise the cost estimate and reduce scope where possible.
Board members will take home the revised cemetery rules and regulations document to review before discussing changes at the next meeting.
Next meeting set for April 23rd.

meetings.headline: Board defended SRF/PFAS funding against a resident group's bid to block it; a 29-year commissioner's last meeting
meetings.summary: The Lunenburg Water District heard a developer's petition to expand the district for a 17-lot Birch Street subdivision, headed to a vote at Saturday's special district meeting, and discussed hiring Tighe & Bond to pursue a state grant for a Lancaster Shirley Road water main extension. Much of the meeting centered on a dispute with a resident group, described as opposing SRF/PFAS treatment-plant funding, which had lobbied MassDEP to pull the district's funding; the superintendent defended the funding and warned of much higher bond-financing costs if it is lost, and outlined plans for a May special meeting to seek borrowing authorization. The meeting closed with tributes to and a lengthy, contentious farewell from Commissioner John Esposito, who is retiring after 29 years.

A resident asked whether the commission had analyzed how much revenue the proposed district expansion would generate, and pressed the board to state a position on the petition.
A resident thanked John Esposito personally for bringing him onto the board/work years ago and recalled their first meeting.

Questioned whether the board actually voted in December to approve pursuing SRF funding, noting the May minutes show a prior vote not to pursue funding and that the superintendent submitted before any approving vote.
Said this round of SRF funding again left out one of the three well fields (the district's main well), unlike what had been discussed, and expressed frustration.

Article 4B (a candidate speaking opportunity) was deferred because one of the two candidates, Mr. Emkey, could not attend; the other candidate's invitation was withdrawn/deferred for equal treatment.

If the district vote passes, the board will also bring forward a boundary cleanup amendment to align the existing district line with the new proposed district boundary along the affected property lines.
The superintendent plans to call a special district meeting in May to seek authorization to borrow for the SRF-funded project, with a possible second attempt in June if the first vote fails.
Residents with questions should call the water district or ask to be placed on a meeting agenda; the district will not respond to questions or accusations posted on social media.
Public comment going forward will be limited to about three minutes per speaker and kept as one-way comment rather than a back-and-forth with commissioners.

meetings.summary: The Select Board, Finance Committee and School Committee met jointly to finalize the structure and dollar figures of a Proposition 2½ override for the May town meeting and ballot, after months of separate budget work. They voted to pursue a two-tier override rather than one number, agreed to pull a stormwater utility request out of the override for now, and the School Committee raised its lower-tier ask to 1.6 million; officials could not guarantee the higher tier would prevent another override request next year, and the boards turned to planning joint public messaging before adjourning.

meetings.headline: School Committee locked in its override request; without it, elementary classes grow and sports/band busing are cut.
meetings.summary: The School Committee heard extensive public comment on proposed cuts to athletic and band transportation, middle school sports, and primary school staffing ahead of the next night's tri-board override meeting. The superintendent presented a revised balanced budget with both new positions (English learner teacher, restored assistant principals, special education teacher) and cuts (athletic trainer hours, several sports, transportation, custodial and technology lines), and the committee voted to accept that fallback budget while reaffirming its lowest override request as the one it will bring to town meeting.

reconciliation.summary: The three substantive votes (waive comment limit, drop MASC dues, accept the balanced budget) agree in both records, and the meeting's few concrete dollar figures that survive into the official text (the $2,400/$3,300/$4,200/$9,976/$14,415/$4,439 middle-school-sports set, the $6,500 MASC dues, and the $1.6M override figure) match. meetings.headline: Commission found unpermitted tree removals at several properties and continued four hearings to April
meetings.summary: The Lunenburg Conservation Commission opened with a resident's storm-water complaint that led into review of a related unpermitted tree-cutting and driveway violation at his property, then heard several notices of intent (Hickory Hills ADA dock/ramp, a new home on Flat Hill Road, an addition at Hemlock Drive, a DPW culvert replacement, and a floodplain-fill project), most of which were continued to April pending storm-water calculations, revised plans, or site walks. Along the way the commission discovered unpermitted tree removals at two more properties, ratified an administrative tree-removal determination at 100 Hemlock Road, discussed outstanding violations at Highland Street and Middle Lane, and planned an Earth Day event for April 22.

budget_items.what_was_said: The chair explained the storm water task force's goal is establishing a storm water utility, collected separately like the sewer commission, to fund storm water infrastructure improvements town-wide. No figures were given.

budget_items.topic: Tree removal fine, 922 Flat Hill Road
budget_items.what_was_said: The agent recommended the commission issue a fine for removing trees without a permit; a member suggested replacement plantings could be used in lieu of the fee.
The agent said it would be her recommendation to issue a formal violation fine if the property owner does not resolve the matter by the next meeting.
The agent asked the commission for about a month before providing concrete budget figures, citing unresolved issues with fund allocation since the office combined with land use.

decisions.decision: No vote needed on the 1147 Massachusetts Avenue violation; the agent will arrange a site inspection with the property owner and advise on required filings for the removed tree.
Applicant at 922 Flat Hill Road to tabulate and plot the removed trees on an updated plan rather than an immediate fine being issued.
Required plan revisions set for the Catales project at 189 Hemlock Drive: no enclosed porch, no new retaining wall, removal of the carport, and additional plantings, ahead of a site walk.

The four dead trees at 100 Hemlock Road may be cut with stumps left in place to preserve slope stability; no replacement plantings required given existing canopy, though understory plantings were encouraged.
The agent will continue bringing administrative determinations before the full commission while she becomes familiar with local regulations, rather than deciding them independently.
Commission will hold off on any formal violation or fine for 314 Highland Street until the property owner appears at the April 1 meeting.
Commission agreed to give the agent about a month before presenting concrete budget figures.

meetings.headline: Committee picked one override number (core "Scenario C") and, if it fails, will cut athletic transportation to save a teacher and a therapy aide
meetings.summary: The School Committee spent most of a long meeting building two FY27 budgets: an override ask (core "scenario C," roughly $1.5-1.6 million) that it voted to send to the Select Board as a single number, and a "balanced" no-override budget that cuts classroom teachers, an assistant principal, a custodian, an occupational therapy assistant, and other positions through attrition. After extended debate over cutting athletics versus classroom staff, the committee voted to accept the balanced budget minus the athletic transportation line, directing the superintendent's team to decide how to reallocate that cut to restore a teacher and an occupational therapy assistant. Members also voted to formalize the town's PEC health-insurance opt-out enhancement, approved a scholarship payout, an international trip, and childcare-program handbook changes.

Accept the balanced (no-override) budget as proposed, except cut the athletic transportation line, with the superintendent's team to decide how to use that cut to restore one classroom teacher position and the certified occupational therapy assistant position, and report back.
Revisit the PEC health-insurance opt-out agreement roughly every three years, aligned with the PEC's contract term.

what_happened.line: The committee voted to send the Select Board one override number, built from a "core" budget option, instead of asking for two tiers.

It also voted to accept a no-override "balanced" budget but cut athletic transportation instead of a teacher, and told staff to find a way to restore that teacher and an occupational therapy aide position.
Members added back a small music-teacher position to the override budget to preserve fifth-grade band.
The committee voted to move forward on a richer health-insurance opt-out incentive for employees who decline coverage.
A resident in public comment asked, without answer in the minutes, what happened to money left over from a prior override.

why_it_matters: Town meeting voters will be asked to approve a single override figure built from this "core" budget, so this is the number that reaches the ballot.

If the override fails, whether a classroom teacher and an occupational therapy aide keep their positions now depends on how the district reallocates the athletic-transportation cut, a decision still pending from the superintendent's team.
The health-insurance opt-out change affects what the town and school pay employees who decline coverage, on both the town and school side of the budget.

meetings.headline: Board included nearly all FY27 warrant articles; TC Passios' safety issues leave the food pantry's future unresolved.
meetings.summary: The Select Board worked through most of the draft FY2027 annual town meeting warrant, voting to include (and in some cases recommend) dozens of articles covering capital cleanup items, union contract funding, an OPEB trust appropriation, a vacation-buyout liability reduction, and several bylaw changes, while holding off on the override placeholder, trust fund commission articles, a stormwater bylaw, and the Central Mass Mosquito Control article pending more information. The board also heard an extended, unresolved presentation from the Lunenburg Community Food Pantry about the deteriorating TC Passios building, where the food pantry currently operates, and closed a public hearing on opting out of mail-in early voting before entering executive session to discuss a collective bargaining agreement.

The food pantry's future home is unresolved: the board said it will not fund TC Passios roof or heating repairs without a broader plan for the building.
A handful of warrant articles -- a stormwater bylaw, mosquito control participation, and trust fund commission bylaws -- are still open and could return changed before town meeting.

meetings.headline: Planning Board sets its FY27 zoning-amendment priorities and continues two housing hearings pending fire/engineering review
meetings.summary: The Lunenburg Planning Board acted on several site-plan and ANR matters, including continuing a 20-unit townhome project on New West Townsend Road pending fire department and peer-engineering review, approving de minimis changes for a solar array and a garage rebuild, and declining the town's first right of refusal on Chapter land. The bulk of the meeting was spent giving detailed feedback on the draft master plan and agreeing on the town planner's 2026 work program, settling on four zoning amendments (inclusionary zoning, senior housing, minor site plan review, and a cluster-development bylaw) to pursue before the next annual town meeting.

budget_items.topic: 925 Mass Ave gas station RFP / brownfields cleanup
budget_items.what_was_said: The director reported MRPC brownfield funding paid for a consultant to develop a recommended cleanup option, a cost estimate, a timeframe, and a list of funding sources ahead of the town's RFP for the property.
The board wants a cash bond rather than a surety bond to cover remaining loam and seeding work, with a contingency escalator built into the bond up front.
The applicant's engineer said there may be no money left in the 53G account funding peer review, and the account will likely need to be replenished for further lots.

budget_items.topic: 860 New West Townsend Road 53G peer-review account
budget_items.what_was_said: The applicant proactively set up a 53G account to fund a peer-review consultant given the timing of the conservation commission filing.

budget_items.topic: Town budget deficit and commercial development
budget_items.what_was_said: A board member argued the town can't afford to reject chain businesses given the town's budget deficit and limited commercial land.
The town planner called the current fee schedule overly complicated and said he would bring a simplified version to the board.

budget_items.topic: Housing production plan / one-stop growth grant
budget_items.what_was_said: The town planner is updating the expired housing production plan, which extends safe-harbor status by creating units, while MRPC applies for a one-stop growth grant after an earlier DTA application went unfunded.

budget_items.topic: District Local Technical Assistance grant - buildout analysis
budget_items.what_was_said: A DLTA grant from MRPC will fund a review of remaining developable commercial and industrial land against the town's older buildout maps, expected by end of summer.

budget_items.topic: Master plan consultant contract - final presentation
budget_items.what_was_said: The board discussed whether to require a formal final presentation from the master plan consultant, noting one is already included in the existing contract.

The Capital Planning Committee could not meet to finalize capital numbers because the town budget wasn't ready, amid what was described as a severe budget challenge and a past shortage of budgeting staff.
Montachusett Regional Planning Commission business included approving member travel and allocating money to hire another planner.

decisions.decision: 10 Parmentor Road applicant's counsel agreed to discuss with the client whether to split the 25-lot storm water/driveway permits into fewer, phased applications rather than filing them lot-by-lot.

For 10 Parmentor Road, the board indicated it would accept a plan note stating Lot 1 is to be conveyed to the abutting Perkins Revocable Trust property (rather than standing as a separate buildable lot) to resolve the frontage/cul-de-sac issue.
For 860 New West Townsend Road, the applicant agreed to set up a meeting with the fire chief to review the common driveway/fire-truck turnaround concerns before the continued hearing.
Staff will obtain a copy of the ZBA decision approving the townhome use at 860 New West Townsend Road and add it to the project file.
The board will forward Adam's and Amanda's written comments on the draft master plan to the consultant (Over&Under) to finish the document, rather than have every comment individually re-debated.
The board decided it does not need a formal ceremonial presentation from the master plan consultant once the plan is finalized.

The board settled on four zoning amendments to pursue before the next annual town meeting: rewriting inclusionary zoning, a senior housing bylaw, minor site plan review, and a cluster-development-by-right bylaw.
The scenic road bylaw and a town signage bylaw were pushed off to a second year of zoning work rather than pursued this year.

what_happened.line: The board settled on four zoning amendments to bring to the next annual town meeting: inclusionary zoning, senior housing, minor site plan review, and cluster development.
The 20-unit townhome project on New West Townsend Road was continued to mid-April pending fire department review of the driveway and engineering review.
The board advised the select board to decline the town's first right of refusal on Chapter land at Northfield Road.
De minimis site plan changes were approved for a rooftop solar/battery project and for a garage rebuild.

why_it_matters: The zoning amendments, if brought to town meeting, would change rules for housing density, senior housing, and small-project review townwide.
The continued hearing means the townhome project's fire-access and engineering questions are unresolved and will return for another public hearing.
Declining the right of first refusal clears the way for the Northfield Road land to be sold or developed privately rather than held or acquired by the town.

meetings.headline: Select Board leaned toward a two-tier (core + restoration) joint town/school override, no vote taken
meetings.summary: The Select Board spent a line-by-line workshop walking through every department's FY27 budget changes since the February 19 preliminary budget, flagging cuts (police clerk, second SRO, fire per diem, recreation director, communications/IT, animal control, town clerk staffing) as candidates to restore if an override passes. By the end the board leaned toward a tiered override structure (a core/level-service budget plus a separate restoration ask, for both town and school) but took no formal vote on it, and set a deadline of Thursday for the town's restoration number and Wednesday for the school committee's numbers.

reconciliation.what: Our minutes against the minutes the town published. caption_error = the same fact the captions rendered badly, resolved by the official reading shown beside the as-heard one; discrepancy = a substantive difference, flagged and not resolved. Neither record is treated as the referee.
reconciliation.summary: The two records agree closely on substance — nearly every dollar figure, department-by-department cut, and forward-looking decision in our minutes has a matching sentence in the official minutes, and the official version is considerably more detailed (full names, added narrative context, several figures we didn't catch). The main things worth checking: our minutes only captured two board members by first name and invented a "Melissa" who doesn't appear in the official roster at all; a few figures (the fire per-diem hours, the snow-and-ice "2.5% increase," a Wednesday vs. Thursday deadline, and whether fire needed *additional* restoration funding or none) point in different directions between the two records and should be checked against the recording rather than assumed resolved.

what_happened.line: The Select Board leaned toward a two-tier override structure -- a core budget plus a separate restoration ask -- for both town and school, without taking a formal vote.

Board members worked line by line through department cuts made since the February 19 preliminary budget, flagging items such as a police clerk position, a second school resource officer, fire department per diem coverage, the recreation director post, communications/IT staffing and animal control funding as candidates to restore if an override passes.

The town manager was asked to produce the town's restoration budget number by Thursday, and Thursday's planned Tri-Board meeting was flagged for cancellation or reconsideration so the school committee's core and restoration figures could come in by Wednesday instead.

The board also settled smaller line items along the way, including pursuing a town engineer position in the restoration budget regardless of storm water compliance funding and leaving the snow and ice budget unchanged rather than risk a later cut.

why_it_matters: This is the shape of the override question residents may eventually vote on -- a base town/school budget plus a separate restoration ask, rather than one combined number.
The restoration list touches police staffing, a school resource officer, fire coverage, recreation programming and animal control -- services that stay cut if no override passes.

meetings.headline: Finance Committee reviewed FY27 department budgets amid a large town-school funding gap, with an override now expected.
meetings.summary: The Finance Committee heard FY27 budget presentations from DPW/sewer, land use, and general government departments, plus a trust fund commissioners' warrant article seeking money to legally investigate several neglected municipal trust funds, which the committee suggested moving to a special town meeting for a firmer estimate. No budget votes were taken; the committee recapped a prior tri-board session where all members agreed an override belongs on the ballot, split on whether it should be one or two amounts, and rescheduled its public hearing and a tri-board meeting for the following weeks.

budget_items.what_was_said: The general fund free cash was certified this week; Karen Brochu was thanked for putting together the free cash submission to the state.
Bill Bernard presented an overall DPW budget higher than previous years, covering mandatory work, a new part-time clerk, restored pavement management, and MS4 storm water compliance money.

Bernard's budget restores pavement management to $650,000 'where it should be,' while the town manager's preliminary budget shows only $279,000; a committee member said they will not support the restoration in the final budget.
Street light electricity costs were estimated at $30,000 originally, came in just over $30,500, then rose further; the line moved into DPW's budget after conversion to LED lighting.
Bernard requested a $340,000 increase in the storm water line item to get closer to MS4 permit compliance, covering catch basin cleaning and street sweeping.

budget_items.topic: Catch basin cleaning and sweeping performance
budget_items.what_was_said: In-house work over the last three years has completed about 30% of catch basin cleaning and 22% of street sweeping, well short of what is mandated.
Bernard estimated it would cost about $100,000 less per year to contract out catch basin cleaning and sweeping than to hire three additional staff.
Bernard modeled a 3% annual increase for DPW, clerical union, and himself across FY25-27 to estimate roughly $52,000 in added salary cost, pending ongoing CBA negotiations.
The snow and ice budget is being increased 2.5% per year to close the gap between budget and actual spending, currently around $800,000.
Vehicle repair costs sent out to contractors exceeded the budgeted line significantly last year, prompting a requested increase.
The recycling budget was reduced after a closer look at actual spending; last year's budget was much higher than what is actually being spent.
The trash program is described as roughly self-funding at about $500,000 per year.
DPW cited a small bridge grant for the Flaill road bridge, a storm water asset management grant from the Mass Clean Water Trust, and a pending Mass Community Cover grant for engineering on a culvert.
Bernard plans to apply for a Complete Streets grant and has a cost estimate of about a million dollars for sidewalk construction and repair between the high school and Marshall Park.
Chapter 90 funding for FY27 is expected at a higher level than the typical amount; continuing at the higher level over several years would add nearly $1.7 million versus normal funding.
The sewer enterprise fund budget is just under $2 million, with expenses and revenues nearly balanced showing an estimated small surplus.
The town pays Leominster and Fitchburg to treat sewage since Lunenburg has no treatment plant of its own; this is the largest driver of the sewer budget.
The engineering line was budgeted at $30,000 last year but actual cost was $80,000 after DEP required additional engineering work; the line is being increased again.
Money is set aside to replace aging pumps, controllers, and pipe as the sewer system approaches the end of its design life.

Without a rate increase, user charge revenue was estimated to leave a large deficit; with the proposed rate increase the budget shows only a small surplus, avoiding further draws on retained earnings.
The proposed sewer rate increase is about 16%, driven by Leominster and Fitchburg raising their own disposal charges.

The per-unit user rate would rise from its current level to a higher figure (about 16% increase), while the minimum charge rises only about 5%, intended to soften the impact on lower-usage households.

budget_items.topic: Sewer grant indirect cost line (health insurance)
budget_items.what_was_said: This line, which covers the sewer enterprise's share of health insurance and treasurer/collector office costs, was questioned for how it compares to prior years' actuals and budgets amid an 8% health insurance increase.
Total sewer expenses were compared across FY25 actual, FY26 budget, and FY27 request.
The combined conservation, building, and planning/economic development budget request represents a modest increase, driven mainly by step and cost-of-living increases.

budget_items.topic: Land use mapping purchase of services line
budget_items.what_was_said: A new line item funds mapping for zoning changes and proposals that previously had no dedicated funding mechanism.
About 16% of land use funding comes from the general fund, roughly 75% from building permit fees, and about 4% from specialty permits.
Some shovel-ready projects have not yet pulled permits; the building department has roughly this much in expected but uncollected permit fee receivables.

budget_items.topic: Trust funds legal investigation warrant article
budget_items.what_was_said: The trust fund commissioners requested this appropriation to fund roughly 40 hours of professional legal investigation into several long-neglected municipal trust funds.
The requested amount was calculated as approximately 40 hours of investigation at $350 per hour, covering all five flagged trust funds.

budget_items.topic: Total trust fund dollars at stake
budget_items.what_was_said: John Bowen said the funds under dispute total in this range, currently unable to be distributed to Lunenburg residents and veterans without a legal investigation.

budget_items.topic: Nathaniel Day worthy poor fund original gift
budget_items.what_was_said: The 1901 donation establishing the worthy poor fund is estimated to be worth this much in today's dollars.
The town manager cited the school budget figure under full restoration as part of the overall FY27 budget update.
The presenter stated an overall projected budget deficit split between town and school portions.

budget_items.topic: Property tax levy and revenue estimates
budget_items.what_was_said: Property tax levy and total revenue estimates were cited, along with adjustments to motor vehicle excise and investment income revenue lines.
The overall general government budget changed slightly from the preliminary figure to the current figure presented tonight.

budget_items.topic: Town manager's office budget / assistant town manager position
budget_items.what_was_said: The town manager's budget rose substantially to fund a new assistant town manager position for a full year; restructuring by eliminating the communications/IT director position reduced the net new cost from $120,000 to $60,000.
Audit costs are rising because the town's former auditing firm was absorbed into a larger firm (CBIZ) at greater cost, and a competing firm lacked capacity to take on the town.
Small reductions were made to the treasurer and collector office budgets based on actual spending, including contracted services covering the deputy tax collector and Unibank services.
The assessor's budget is nearly level; a temporary special assistant position is being moved out of the operating budget to one-time funding; abatement counts have declined from a 2023 spike.
FY26 and FY25 real estate exemption counts and total dollar amounts were compared; the senior means-tested exemption was not approved for FY2025.
The town clerk's overall budget is roughly level, but the elections line rises sharply because 2026 is an election year with a September primary and November general election.
The APDC physicals budget was increased due to under-budgeting, and a new economic development committee line funds an annual town official meet-and-greet event.
The town report/printing line rose sharply because it had not been properly budgeted, covering the annual report, town meeting booklet, and special town meeting warrant printing and mailing.
The reserve fund is level funded; the town manager raised the idea of increasing it given department budgets are being tightened, citing prior years' transfer amounts.
The salary reserve has not been adjusted for FY27 pending outcomes of ongoing DPW, clerical, and firefighter contract negotiations; an anticipated 3% COLA for non-union (SAP) employees is assumed.
Central purchasing, which now includes consolidated postage costs, is level funded.
The veterans budget is largely driven by Chapter 115 benefit payments currently serving seven residents; the town receives trailing state reimbursement the following fiscal year.
This line rose almost entirely due to the non-discretionary Worcester County retirement assessment.
The unclassified budget, covering liability, workers comp, health, life insurance, unemployment and Medicare, increased from the preliminary figure due to a correction in Medicare supplement counts.
Liability insurance covers property/casualty with a rate guarantee through FY27, plus a separate injured-on-duty policy for police and fire and a small risk-management training line.
Workers compensation was reduced based on conversations with the town's insurance representative, applying available credits.
Group health insurance, the largest piece of the unclassified budget, increased; a separate line funds employees who opt out of coverage.
Retiree health insurance covers town and school retirees at estimated Medicare Blue and Medex rates, plus a Medicare supplement paid twice yearly.

reconciliation.coverage: official minutes are a summary only
reconciliation.summary: The two records agree closely on the headline figures the town chose to write down — free cash, the deficit, the school restoration number, the DPW and sewer budget totals, the land use budget, the trust fund warrant amount — and several of the "differences" are just caption garbling of the same digits (e.g. $3,25,5124 for $3,205,051.24). meetings.headline: Commission votes it and the Select Board lack the expertise to decide Legion trust fund eligibility questions
meetings.summary: The Lunenburg Trust Fund Commission discussed a warrant article to fund roughly 40 hours of outside legal investigation into trust fund donor intent (particularly the American Legion fund, whose eligibility language proved unworkable on close reading), and a bylaw to let the Select Board temporarily manage trust distributions if the commission lacks a quorum. The commission adopted a citizenship/residency verification policy and passed a motion declaring that neither it nor the Select Board has the professional expertise to decide these trust-fund legal questions without hiring outside investigators.

meetings.headline: Sewer Commission weighed extending sewer service for a proposed duplex development via town meeting warrant article
meetings.summary: The Sewer Commission spent most of the meeting on a developer's request to extend sewer service up Pond Street to serve a planned duplex subdivision, discussing a possible town meeting warrant article and whether the commission would support it once engineered plans are ready. The commission also reviewed FY27 user rate and budget updates, ongoing infiltration/inflow and manhole repair work, a minor sewer bylaw wording change tied to the new ADU bylaw, and the pending storm water utility warrant article, approving prior minutes and adjourning by roll call.

public_comment.topic: Proposed extending the sewer line up Pond Street to serve a planned duplex development (an ANR subdivision) near the old driving range on Wham, asking whether the commission would extend the sewer district and eventually give its blessing before a town meeting warrant article.

votes.motion: Approve the minutes of 2/24 and the joint select board meeting minutes of 3/3
Adjourn the meeting

budget_items.what_was_said: The commission reviewed the proposed FY27 rate, keeping the minimum charge increase at 5% while raising the regular usage charge more (about 16%), shifting more of the burden to higher water users. Staff said the rate is driven by what Leominster and Fitchburg charge Lunenburg for sewer treatment.
Demand fee notices will be mailed the week of March 16th; residents who have not paid their sewer bill were asked to pay before Friday, in person or online.

The commission recapped that it had already voted the FY27 budget in at a prior meeting so it could go out with the town warrants; a budget presentation was scheduled for Thursday night before FinCom. The budget avoids using retained earnings this year, with capital gains funding slightly reduced.

Members noted betterment revenue is slowing down as fewer new betterments come in, which is part of what is pushing the rate increases; the goal was described as trying to keep rates level rather than see dramatic swings.

budget_items.topic: Capital projects - Pump 2 and manhole covers
budget_items.what_was_said: Upcoming capital work includes work at Pump 2 and resetting manhole covers; the wrong size covers had been ordered but the correct size is in the warehouse and ready to install, targeted around April 15th.

An existing manhole repair contract is targeting manholes previously inspected and suspected of having inflow and infiltration (I&I); a member pushed for a more proactive approach to find and fix leaks rather than just tracking rising charges from Fitchburg/Leominster.

If a storm water utility is established, residents would be billed separately, similar to a sewer bill, with revenue used to fund street sweeping, storm drain cleaning and other work needed for federal storm water permit compliance.

budget_items.topic: Cost of special permit / engineering for duplex proposal
budget_items.what_was_said: The developer said he did not want to spend roughly two years and about $100,000 pursuing a special permit, preferring an as-of-right ANR approach; he said he is open to spending tens of thousands of dollars on engineered plans and to commission review of them.

decisions.decision: Recommended the developer file a citizen's petition warrant article by March 16th to make the May 2nd town meeting deadline.
Developer asked to return to the March 31st commission meeting so the commission could consider giving its "blessing" to the sewer extension plan ahead of town meeting.
Demand fee notices to go out the week of March 16th.
Sewer bylaw wording amendment (two words changed for consistency with the new ADU bylaw), already reviewed by town counsel, to proceed to town meeting for a vote.
Set upcoming meeting dates: March 31, 2026 (Zoom); April 14, 2026 (in-person/hybrid); April 28, 2026 (Zoom); May 12, 2026 (in-person/hybrid).

meetings.headline: TriBoard split near evenly on one FY27 override vs. two tiers, but agreed unanimously to put one on the ballot.
meetings.summary: The Select Board, Finance Committee and School Committee met jointly to debate how to structure a Proposition 2½ override for next year's budget, weighing a single combined ask against tiered options. Every member present favored putting some override on the ballot, but the group was closely divided over one number versus two, and no final figure was set that night. meetings.headline: Select Board leans toward letting town meeting voters decide on continued mosquito-control funding.
meetings.summary: The select board approved a one-day liquor license, then held a joint meeting with the board of health for an extensive educational presentation by Central Mass Mosquito Control Project on its surveillance, ditch-maintenance, larval and adult mosquito control work, amid a town budget shortfall that has put the district's assessment on the table. No vote was taken on the mosquito control funding; the chair said it should go to town meeting voters. The board also acknowledged a Conservation Commission resignation, heard a brief town manager report on a building leak, and reviewed (without voting on) draft warrant articles for the 2026 annual town meeting before recessing into a tri-board meeting.

The board approved a one-day liquor license for the Lunenburg Diner for a March 19 event.

The board reviewed, but did not vote on, draft 2026 town meeting warrant articles covering a new Economic Development revolving fund, a technology revolving fund renaming, an FY26 capital cleanup item, and vacation buyout transition language.
The board acknowledged a resignation from the Conservation Commission.

why_it_matters: If mosquito control funding goes to town meeting, residents will be asked to vote directly on whether to keep paying into that regional assessment, which a board member said the state sets using a land-mass and valuation formula rather than local choice.

The draft warrant articles reviewed -- a new revolving fund, a capital reallocation, and a policy change to vacation buyouts -- are early-stage and not yet committed to the warrant, but they preview what voters may see at the 2026 annual town meeting.
A public commenter raised a concern about pesticide safety to bees, which residents may want addressed before any funding vote.

meetings.headline: Task force outlined a proposed stormwater utility fee; bylaw goes to spring town meeting, fees start later.
meetings.summary: An engineering consultant presented the Stormwater Task Force's plan for a stormwater utility to fund MS4 federal permit compliance, explaining how fees would be based on impervious surface area rather than property value. No fee, budget, or bylaw vote was taken at this meeting; the plan calls for the enabling legislation and bylaw to go before spring town meeting and the storm water budget before fall town meeting, with residents raising questions about state roads, tax-exempt and agricultural properties, and credit caps.

Why the credit for commercial properties that already have stormwater management systems installed would cap at 50% rather than 100%
Comment that open farm fields are pervious area and would generate little or no impervious-surface fee
Suggestion to distribute hard copies of the FAQ document at the library, town hall, Ritter building, and adult activity center

votes.outcome: passed 5-0 (John, Jenny, Mark, Renee, and the chair each voted "I")

A rough estimate of the replacement value of the town's stormwater system (over 1,300 catch basins, ~550 outfalls, 50 miles of roadway infrastructure) was given.
A worked example showed how a commercial property with two equivalent residential units (ERUs) would be billed if the rate were set at a given amount per ERU.

budget_items.topic: Example fee structures in other Massachusetts towns
budget_items.what_was_said: Rutland was described as charging a flat fee for any property with impervious area; Chelmsford charges a flat fee for single/two-family homes and a tiered fee for other properties, with the largest payer cited.

Example properties in a neighboring community with a stormwater utility were shown, including a very large commercial property, a medium commercial property, and a small commercial property, to illustrate the range of fees under an ERU-based system.

budget_items.topic: Proposed small residential stormwater fee for Lunenburg
budget_items.what_was_said: The task force has been looking at a flat fee for small (one-to-two family) residential properties that would not exceed a stated cap, at least initially, with the fee possibly needing adjustment down the road as a new MS4 permit is issued.
The task force is considering a credit of up to a stated share of the assessed fee for properties managing their own stormwater on site, based on other Massachusetts communities' practice.

decisions.decision: Task force plans to bring the stormwater utility enabling legislation and bylaw to spring town meeting for approval, with the stormwater budget to follow at fall town meeting.
Fee collection under the proposed utility would not begin until a target future date, contingent on fall town meeting approving the storm water budget.
Task force agreed to make the FAQ document available in hard copy at locations such as the library, town hall, the Ritter building, and the adult activity center, in addition to the town website.

meetings.headline: Finance Committee warns a large school 'restoration' override could fail, as one did in 2012.
meetings.summary: The committee heard FY27 budget presentations from the Council on Aging (level-funded), the Library (a modest increase plus a push for above-level programming funding), and Public Access Cable, which described a widening deficit from declining Comcast franchise fees and a forced studio relocation. The bulk of the meeting was a debate over the upcoming Proposition 2½ override: members worried that bundling the town's mostly level-service requests with the school committee's much larger 'restoration' budget into a single ask risks a failure like the town's 2012 override, which passed by roughly two-to-one against and led to a decade of cuts.

public_comment.topic: Criticized the library presentation as too general with no itemized spending, and argued PAC should pursue nonprofit status and grants rather than seek town funding, citing pending state legislation he says is unlikely to pass soon.

The library expects to receive state aid this fiscal year for meeting state certification standards.

The library anticipates receiving outside grant funding this fiscal year, separate from town appropriation and state aid.
A grant from Emerson Hospital's community benefit fund will support a memory-kit partnership with the Adult Activity Center.
The Cultural Council awarded funding for cultural programming, described as notably less than in recent years.

PAC's proposed budget exceeds anticipated Comcast franchise revenue, leaving a deficit the department proposes covering with retained earnings.
The amount of retained earnings PAC used last year versus proposed for FY27 was discussed, with the manager citing differing figures for the prior year during the exchange.
An aging program server needs replacement at a cost described as over $52,000 plus installation, bringing new equipment costs up.
The capital equipment line rises year over year, driven mainly by the one-time server replacement, which includes cloud services, closed captioning, and app features.
With PAC's current facility (TCP) closing, the manager built a contingency budget including a new studio lease cost, still being finalized among a few options.
Contracted services funding increases to cover staff training on new studio equipment/software if PAC has to relocate.
A large jump in the PEG access operations line was questioned; after discussion the committee identified the FY26 comparison column had not been summed correctly.

budget_items.topic: PAC funding sources: investment income and franchise fees
budget_items.what_was_said: PAC funding comes mostly from Comcast franchise fees, supplemented by investment income from bond funds; franchise revenue has been declining.
Quarterly Comcast franchise payments have fallen below $40,000 for the first time, and FY27 revenue was projected on a reduced quarterly estimate.

A committee member described the school department's level-service budget as substantially above what was funded at town meeting, with an additional 'restoration' budget adding roughly another million dollars on top.
A member recalled a prior override request failing by roughly two-to-one, leading to a decade of service cuts including reduced library hours and a town employee hours reduction.

Confirmed the tri-board meeting on the FY27 budget and a possible Proposition 2½ override is scheduled for March 10 at 7:30pm at town hall (or via Zoom if weather requires).

Review of minutes from two prior meetings was deferred to the following week.
Noted an upcoming Municipal Building Committee meeting on Monday at 5:30pm via Zoom.

meetings.summary: This was a routine Conservation Commission hearing night: the board worked through several new and continued wetlands filings, including a large proposed townhouse subdivision off New Westminster Road, a deck replacement, a rooftop-solar/battery storage project, and a lakefront cottage rebuild, most resolved with negative determinations, approvals with conditions, or continuances for site walks once snow clears. The commission also declined to exercise its right of first refusal on a chapter 61 forestry property that is being sold, had an applicant withdraw an improperly-noticed amended order request, discussed updating its fee schedule and the future of the town-owned Hollis Road residence, and appointed a new liaison to the Open Space Committee.

budget_items.topic: Right of first refusal - 1083 Northfield Road
budget_items.what_was_said: The chair reported the sale offer on the chapter 61 forestry parcel subject to the town's right of first refusal.

The agent said the fee schedule sits in both the town charter and the bylaw so the commission cannot change it without going through the select board and town meeting, and proposed moving it into the bylaw alone; she noted fees are currently collected only on notices of intent, not on administrative approvals, amendments, certificates of compliance or extensions.
Mary recalled a prior cost estimate for printing the wetlands buffer-zone flyer for inclusion in a town tax mailing.
Andrea and Mike discussed the license fee to screen the documentary for a community audience versus an individual ticket, reading a figure off the distributor's website.

budget_items.topic: Grant match requirement / conservation land funding
budget_items.what_was_said: Mary said grants the commission applies for require a match, historically covered partly by tree-harvesting revenue on conservation land, and cautioned that revenue source needs a replacement plan before it is reduced.

budget_items.topic: Hollis Road residence upkeep and renovation
budget_items.what_was_said: The chair said ongoing heating and electricity costs are being incurred to maintain the currently-unused Hollis Road residence, and she is checking with the town manager on the prevailing-wage threshold for work to make it habitable.

budget_items.topic: 50 Pine Grove Road amended order filing fee
budget_items.what_was_said: There was uncertainty on the call whether an application fee had already been paid for the amended order request, given the applicant will have to refile.

decisions.decision: The applicant for the 50 Pine Grove Road amended order agreed to withdraw the request and refile it with proper abutter and DEP notification rather than continue without a duly noticed public hearing.

The commission agreed by informal poll to let the applicant file for a full certificate of compliance on the FRA portion of 260 Fitchburg Road, while withholding a certificate for the Tango Construction portion until its restoration work is finished.
The commission decided to take no formal action on reported off-trail snowmobile use near the Lane property for now, and to monitor and coordinate with the snowmobile club if it recurs.

The conservation agent will meet with town counsel about moving the commission's fee schedule out of the town charter and into its own bylaw, and about charging fees for administrative items not currently billed.
The agent will proceed with planning a small Earth Day event on April 22 at TC Pacios with local environmental organizations despite the short notice.
The stormwater committee set a public information session with Weston and Samson at the library the next evening and plans to reduce meeting frequency afterward, ahead of town meeting.

what_happened.line: Commission voted not to exercise the town's right of first refusal on a chapter 61 forestry parcel at 1083 Northfield Road, letting the pending sale proceed.
An applicant withdrew a request to amend wetlands conditions at 50 Pine Grove Road after the hearing was found improperly noticed, and will refile with proper notice.
The conservation agent will consult town counsel about moving the fee schedule out of the town charter and into a commission bylaw, and about billing for items not currently charged.
A proposed 20-unit townhouse subdivision's common driveway on New Westminster Road was continued to April 1 while other wetlands filings were approved with conditions or continued for site walks.
Members noted that grants requiring a local match have relied on tree-harvesting revenue from conservation land, and said a replacement funding source needs planning if that revenue drops.

why_it_matters: Declining the right of first refusal means the town gives up its option to buy or steer the future use of the chapter 61 land before it changes private hands.
Moving the fee schedule into a standalone bylaw and billing for administrative approvals, amendments, and certificates could raise the cost of routine wetlands filings for residents.
The revenue the commission uses to match conservation grants comes from harvesting on town conservation land, a source members flagged as needing a backup plan.

meetings.headline: Parks Commission voted to raise Town Beach and swim-lesson fees for 2026 to cut the town's subsidy.

what_happened.line: The Parks Commission voted to raise 2026 Town Beach season and day pass rates, aiming to shrink the town's subsidy of the beach program.
The Commission also voted, 3-0, to raise 2026 swim lesson rates, with a per-family cap for both residents and non-residents.
Staff said the new rates are still projected to fall short of covering the beach's costs, with the Parks revolving account as a possible backstop for the gap.
The Commission adopted an amended park facilities signage policy that removes the Commission itself from sign-approval authority, shifting it to staff.
Field-use rules and a proposed vendor-fair partnership were held off until a recreation director is hired, a position still vacant.

why_it_matters: This sets what residents and non-residents pay for beach passes and swim lessons in 2026, and it comes up in the context of a possible town override vote on covering town costs.
The rate increase is presented as narrowing, not closing, the gap between beach revenue and beach costs, so the shortfall may still draw on other town funds.
Sign approval at town park facilities now rests with staff rather than the elected Commission, changing who signs off on that kind of decision going forward.

minutes.headline: Task force fine-tuned its draft public presentation on a proposed town-wide stormwater utility fee; no fee was set.
minutes.summary: The Stormwater Task Force spent the meeting line-by-line reviewing a draft slide presentation and a separate FAQ document to be shown at an upcoming public meeting on a proposed stormwater utility fee. Members discussed sample fee tables for residential and commercial properties, comparisons to peer towns, the case for a dedicated stormwater program manager, and the approval process, but took no vote other than to adjourn.

budget_items.topic: Average single-family home value used in fee illustration
budget_items.what_was_said: The average home value in Lunenburg was cited to anchor the middle tier of an illustrative residential fee table.

budget_items.topic: Storm water budget figure used in fee-impact example
budget_items.what_was_said: A member noted the example used an older, smaller total storm water budget figure rather than the newer, larger one, which changes the resulting fee percentages.

budget_items.topic: Property-tax-based method for illustrating fee equivalents (residential A/B/C)
budget_items.what_was_said: A member proposed showing what residents already pay toward stormwater through property taxes, using the town's tax rate and the storm water budget's share of the total tax levy.

budget_items.topic: Old vs. new storm water budget total used in percentage calculations
budget_items.what_was_said: Members compared results from dividing the old, smaller budget figure versus the new, larger figure by the town's total tax levy.
A calculation for a small residential property showed it would pay more under the flat utility fee than it currently contributes through taxes, raising concern about that message.

budget_items.topic: Upper-tier cap for large commercial properties
budget_items.what_was_said: The consultant's original proposal had capped large commercial parcel fees at one level; the task force previously rejected that cap and discussed extrapolating tiers upward instead, to preserve revenue and room for partial abatements.
A tax-exempt church property, currently paying nothing, would owe a new fee under the proposed structure, illustrating a new revenue source the utility would capture.

budget_items.topic: Large commercial fee example from a peer town (Dennis)
budget_items.what_was_said: A shopping complex in Dennis, MA was cited as paying a very high storm water fee under that town's tiered structure, used as a comparison point.

budget_items.topic: Estimated total impervious area and revenue-share correlation
budget_items.what_was_said: Members recalculated the number of parcels times average impervious area, producing updated percentages for the table showing how revenue share compares to impervious-area share.

budget_items.topic: Cap on stormwater credit/abatement for good housekeeping practices
budget_items.what_was_said: The task force discussed capping credits/abatements at a percentage of the fee, based on what other Massachusetts communities with utilities offer.

budget_items.topic: Assumed revenue loss from abatement program
budget_items.what_was_said: A rule of thumb from other communities assumes a portion of revenue will be lost to abatements once the credit program is in place, and some towns budget higher in year one to compensate.

budget_items.topic: Estimated replacement value of town storm water infrastructure
budget_items.what_was_said: A wide range was initially used to estimate the value of the town's storm drainage network; the task force agreed to use the higher end on the slide.

budget_items.topic: Estimated miles of storm drain pipe and roads with storm infrastructure
budget_items.what_was_said: Rough estimates of pipe and road mileage were used to size the infrastructure-value slide; a member said these need to be verified with the DPW's own figures.

budget_items.topic: Infrastructure valuation framed as a park comparison
budget_items.what_was_said: The estimated value of the storm water network was compared to a large capital asset to make the scale tangible to residents.

budget_items.topic: Number of properties and parcels in the fee dataset
budget_items.what_was_said: The rate-structure analysis covers a defined subset of properties out of the town's full assessor's parcel list, with impervious area to be entered for each.

budget_items.topic: DPW operating budget request for storm water items ahead of the utility
budget_items.what_was_said: Bill said an extra amount was added to the DPW operational budget this cycle in case the utility fee is not approved in time, though he expects it may not survive budget cuts.

Using the state's override calculator, the group modeled what an increase to the general tax levy (covering basin cleaning, sweeping, and added engineering needs) would cost an average homeowner, as an alternative to the flat utility fee.

decisions.decision: Bill agreed to bring hard copies of the FAQ document to hand out at the public meeting.
Keep the residential/commercial fee-impact comparison slide (with the added revenue column), to be refined once real numbers are added.
Add a caveat to the presentation noting the fee is not guaranteed to stay flat, given uncertainty from a pending new EPA stormwater permit.
Keep the 50% cap on credits/abatements in the presentation, consistent with other Massachusetts communities.
Leave fee-structure governance with the select board for now rather than pursuing a combined sewer/storm commission, since that would require a multi-year legislative process.
Remove the 'drainage improvement projects' line item from the funding-use slide since it is not currently budgeted through the utility.
Bill's GIS team will go back and delineate impervious area for previously miscoded properties (e.g., Jaclyn Drive) that lacked a proper land-use code.
John will independently build his own spreadsheet model from the impervious-area data to test rate-structure trade-offs, in parallel with the consultant's team.
Someone will contact the library the next day to confirm the room and whether a screen/projector will be available for the presentation.
Hold audience questions until after the full slideshow is presented, given the likely larger turnout for this meeting.
The FAQ document will not be further revised for now; Jarice will send a final revised slide deck by end of day the next day.
Meeting adjourned at 8:26 p.m. on March 3, 2026.
