budget_items.what_was_said: The Town Manager said the select board budget is largely driven by staff covering the assistant town manager, HR/procurement director, executive assistant and minute clerks.

budget_items.topic: Select Board / Town Manager budget increase
budget_items.what_was_said: A modest select board increase was described as mostly expense-driven, while the town manager budget rises substantially due to the new assistant town manager position and a higher legal line.
The Town Manager proposed creating a standalone assistant town manager position, funded for half the year starting January 1, estimated near full-time cost if annualized.
A contracted services line created last year for staff appreciation is proposed to increase to give room for unforeseen contracted needs.
The FY26 accountant budget required a large special town meeting supplement due to transition costs, consultants and hiring, which the Town Manager said should not recur in FY27.
The finance department total was cited while discussing staffing changes including a retirement that offset new hires.
The audit line was said to have been underbudgeted; the actual FY27 audit cost is now expected to be much higher, partly because only two municipal auditors remain in Massachusetts.
Tax title is moving into the operating budget with no change in level funding; a request to restore treasurer/collector staff hours to 40 (from 36) drives a salary increase.

The FY26 IT budget was described as half a million dollars, and the preliminary FY27 IT budget increases further, driven mostly by Munis software costs and a reclassified communications/IT staff position.
The telephone budget line was raised to match actual cell phone and phone system bills, which had been historically underbudgeted.
A large increase to purchase of service is almost entirely Munis-driven; last year's upgrade cost was offset by ARPA which is not available this year, plus a contractual increase.
The on-site IT contractor line reflects five-days-a-week service; the Town Manager has already reduced to four days as of January and hopes to reduce further to three in FY27.
A line covers all townwide phone and cell phone bills across multiple carriers.
The FY27 budget is an election year and salary-driven, with an increase attributed mainly to election costs.
The finance committee's own budget was decreased slightly, while its training/reserve line was kept level from last year.
The salary reserve figure was called premature and not a real number, pending outcomes of active DPW, fire and clerical union negotiations and COLA decisions.

budget_items.topic: Town report / annual meeting booklet printing
budget_items.what_was_said: A large increase in the town report line was explained as covering both the report and the printing of annual/special town meeting booklets, not just the report itself.
Postage was consolidated into one line for the first time last year; it is currently running under budget and may be reduced if the trend holds.
The physicals budget for new hires, including heightened police/fire pre-employment screening, is being raised to align with actual year-to-date spending.
Total debt service is decreasing again in FY27 though by a smaller amount than the prior year's larger drop.
The Worcester County Regional retirement assessment is the main driver in intergovernmental costs and is a non-discretionary increase.

budget_items.topic: Land Use / building department permit revenue
budget_items.what_was_said: Building department fee revenue is projected roughly at recent average levels across permits, plumbing, electrical and gas.
Preliminary total FY27 revenue was presented, described as heavily reliant on property taxes.

budget_items.topic: Levy limit build-up (2.5%, new growth, excluded debt)
budget_items.what_was_said: The levy limit calculation adds the automatic Proposition 2½ increase, estimated new growth, and excluded debt on top before subtracting it back out on the expenditure side.
New growth for FY27 is estimated by the assessors, compared against last year's estimate versus higher actual new growth received.

State aid was presented at the current FY26 actual cherry sheet figure, covering Chapter 70, unrestricted government aid, library funding, school choice and veterans funding, held level pending the Governor's budget.
Local receipts (motor vehicle excise, meals tax, fees, fines, licensing) are being held level pending FY25 closeout, though investment income came in well above projection last year.
State assessments, school choice/library aid pass-throughs and the overlay reserve are subtracted off the top of revenue as non-appropriated, along with a pay-as-you-go capital contribution.

budget_items.topic: New revenue for FY27 and apportionment
budget_items.what_was_said: The remaining new revenue after FY26 appropriations was apportioned traditionally between school, town and Monty Tech by percentage share.

budget_items.topic: Health insurance impact on new revenue
budget_items.what_was_said: Subtracting projected non-discretionary health insurance increases for school and town from new revenue leaves only a small amount for all raises and new costs combined.
The town has been told to budget health insurance at a set percentage increase, which is what was used to reach the small remaining new-revenue figure.
A vehicle stabilization fund exists and part of the FY27 capital plan, including a needed ladder truck, is planned to draw from it.
A fire department budget request for an additional shift was described as not yet included in the presented numbers, at a stated additional cost.
Separate cost figures were cited for funding cost-of-living increases across the town's employee unions.
A finance committee member questioned why the town pays a large annual amount for recycling and suggested it as a possible operational efficiency.
The shared building referred to as TCP/TCPasios was said to cost more annually than the town currently has available in its operating budget.
The Town Manager's working figure for the outer bound of a potential override, before further cuts and efficiencies, was cited from the presentation.

No vote was taken at this joint Select Board, Finance Committee, and School Committee session.

why_it_matters: A property tax override would go to voters and would raise bills beyond the state's normal levy cap, and officials here signaled they see it as likely for FY27.
Rising fixed costs -- health insurance, an audit line, IT/Munis software -- absorb new town revenue before it reaches raises, staffing, or school and town services.
A new assistant town manager position is a town-side staffing addition, separate from the school budget rule 11 governs.

meetings.headline: Task force plans to bring a stormwater utility bylaw (not yet the fee) to May 2026 town meeting
meetings.summary: The Stormwater Task Force met with its consultant (Weston and Sampson) to review contract progress on impervious surface data, rate structure, and public engagement materials, and spent most of the meeting building a detailed calendar of Finance Committee, Select Board and public information session dates leading up to the March 16 warrant closing and May town meeting. The group decided to bring forward only the enabling bylaw establishing the utility framework this spring, holding the fee/rate structure and budget vote for a later town meeting, and reviewed a draft stormwater budget with the DPW representative covering Chapter 90 and residential/commercial funding splits. No members of the public were present or commented, and the only votes taken were procedural approvals of prior minutes and adjournment.

budget_items.what_was_said: The task force discussed the contract with Weston and Sampson covering impervious surface delineation, rate structure review, and community engagement materials.
The consultant, who lives in Reading, described that town's remote utility fee as a comparison point for what a small residential fee might look like.
A member estimated what a typical home might pay annually under the new utility, noting it would be a small fee relative to mitigation costs.
A member described spending on water mitigation during a personal home renovation as an example of what residents already invest in their own properties.
The consultant recalled that Concord, MA was fined under the 2003 MS4 permit, offered as an example of enforcement risk for non-compliance.

budget_items.what_was_said: The consultant estimated how many Massachusetts communities currently have a stormwater utility in place.
Members discussed the high cost of specialized catch-basin and street-sweeping vehicles and whether sharing with neighboring towns made sense.

budget_items.what_was_said: The consultant described Shrewsbury's experience billing even parcels with no impervious area a flat fee, which proved administratively burdensome for little revenue.
The DPW representative's draft budget for the utility was reviewed line by line, with discussion of which costs are one-time versus recurring.

budget_items.what_was_said: The spreadsheet showed a Chapter 90 funding component within the stormwater budget, prompting questions about which projects it could legally support.

budget_items.topic: Existing operating budget storm water mitigation line
budget_items.what_was_said: A member noted the town's current operating budget carries a stormwater mitigation line that would largely be replaced by utility fee revenue, freeing that money for other town uses.

budget_items.topic: Net impact on resident tax bill
budget_items.what_was_said: A member explained that the new fee would look like an increase to residents but actually reflects money shifting out of the general tax budget rather than a wholly new cost.
Members discussed the overhead of a separate mailed bill for the utility fee versus combining it with an existing bill.

decisions.decision: Move forward with a standalone bylaw establishing the stormwater utility framework at the May 2026 town meeting, without setting the fee/rate structure yet.

Timeline set: task force meeting January 28, Finance Committee presentation January 29, Select Board presentation February 10, task force meeting February 19, public information session March 5 (evening, hybrid via Zoom).
Plan to hold only one public information session before the March 16 warrant closing, keeping a second session in reserve for the fall town meeting if needed.

meetings.headline: FinCom says FY27 leaves almost no room after health insurance; a school override looms and deep cuts are floated
meetings.summary: The Finance Committee heard that the finance/accounting office is in crisis (a departed finance director, an unclosed FY25, a retired accountant filling in part-time) and got an early FY27 revenue estimate that leaves very little after health insurance. Members debated whether to support another Proposition 2½ override, with one member insisting the town do "hard work" on cuts (recycling, the TCP building, ambulance receipts, capital funding sources) before any override is considered, while the town manager warned that a no-override budget likely means real staffing/service cuts. The committee also adjusted its budget-season calendar to bring Monty Tech and the schools in earlier, reviewed the capital plan ranking, water billing/enterprise fund problems, and approved its prior minutes and adjournment by roll call.

what_happened.line: The Board of Assessors set the FY27 overlay reserve target, the account that funds abatements and exemptions, in a unanimous vote.
The board voted to keep the FY27 new-growth estimate flat with the prior two years, citing no known large new projects.
Staff described ongoing "bridge" errors between the CAMA valuation system and the town's financial system affecting tax billing.

After an update on the track/turf field project, the committee agreed to ask the superintendent to request a placeholder warrant article for the engineering funding.
A member was tasked with drafting a framework for deciding between rebuilding Turkey Hill or building new under MSBA before that choice comes back for a vote.

why_it_matters: Returning Kids Kingdom shifts upkeep and liability for that playground from the school district to the town.
A placeholder warrant article for the track/field project, and a coming decision on rebuilding versus replacing Turkey Hill, are steps toward items that could appear on a town ballot.
The push for one shared override number across the three boards signals that residents may be asked to vote on a single town-wide tax increase rather than separate asks.

meetings.headline: Chair flags a possible large historic shortfall in old trust funds, pushing a bylaw for no-quorum releases
meetings.summary: The Trust Fund Commission (chair John Bowen and vice chair Richard Howard, the only two present) spent most of the meeting reviewing decades of historic trust fund records ahead of drafting a bylaw that would let the select board release trust fund money when the commission lacks a quorum. In the process the chair identified an unresolved 2017 loan redetermination, a fund from 2017 with no discoverable records, and a large apparent gap between what a 1931 sidewalk/memorial fund should be worth today and its current balance, all of which he committed to investigate further. No formal votes were taken except the roll-call vote to adjourn.

budget_items.what_was_said: The chair reviewed a 2017 dispersement from the worthy poor fund's earnings to a resident, structured as a loan with a six-month redetermination that was never followed up on. He said this board will now have to take up that redetermination.
Reading a 1966 record at the Worcester Savings Institute, the chair cited the fund's total, its original principal, and interest recorded as of a 1965 date.

budget_items.topic: Nathaniel Day fund and missing Treasury bond
budget_items.what_was_said: The chair read the Nathaniel Day fund's savings balance and noted a 90-day Treasury bond in that fund that he cannot locate; he wants to find where it is and whether it was cashed.

The chair said Susan Howard's separate fund (distinct from the sidewalk fund) held Treasury bonds, and estimated informally what decades of compounding might now be worth if the bonds were never cashed.

budget_items.topic: Sidewalk (John and Mary Caldwell Howard) fund, 1931
budget_items.what_was_said: The chair read the 1931 warrant article establishing the fund with a stated principal and annual interest amount, to be spent on sidewalks and public grounds within one mile of town center in perpetuity.

A commissioner asked why the fund shows a much lower current balance than what decades of interest at the stated rate should have produced; the chair said he has to find where the money went and will pursue it.
The chair read two 1931 warrant articles accepting sums for perpetual care of specific cemetery lots in the North Cemetery.

A 2013 letter setting up the fund specified that only annual interest could be dispersed, capped at a share of that year's interest, until the fund passed a threshold at which principal above that amount could also be used for veterans' benefits.

decisions.decision: Chair and vice chair will brainstorm a bylaw allowing the select board to release trust fund money in the absence of a quorum, to be drafted by the chair as a hard copy for the next meeting.
The commission wants a public comment period built into the process before finalizing bylaw changes and any cy pres filing, even though it is not legally required.
The chair will personally contact individuals named in the 2017 meeting minutes to recover missing trust fund records rather than wait for them to come forward.
The chair will investigate the unexplained 'Lind Saxon' fund from 2017 with the accounting department, since no records or dispersements for it can be found.
A cy pres court filing to update the American Legion veterans fund's restrictions will wait until after the next election cycle due to the town attorney's town meeting workload.
The chair will contact the U.S. Treasury to try to locate the Nathaniel Day fund's Treasury bond and determine its status.
The chair will investigate why the sidewalk (Howard) fund's current balance is far below what decades of stated interest should have produced.
Interns will not be used this year due to lack of a prepared curriculum; it may be revisited next year.
The commission has an open vacancy and is inviting interested residents to come forward.

meetings.headline: Capital Planning Committee unanimously adopted a tentative order-of-merit ranking of 22 FY27 capital requests
meetings.summary: The Capital Planning Committee reviewed members' individual rankings of 22 FY27 capital requests, resolved several ranking ties (including flipping the order of a DPW dump truck and an IT network upgrade), and discussed funding constraints given roughly $3.3 million in requests against a typical $1-1.5 million annual funding capacity. The committee voted unanimously to adopt the resulting order-of-merit list as a tentative recommendation, to be revisited once the town manager's financial picture is clearer, and tentatively scheduled its next meeting for January 28; it also discussed unused ClearGov budgeting software costing about $20,000 a year and outyear capital request planning.

budget_items.topic: Total FY27 capital requests vs. likely funding
budget_items.what_was_said: The chair noted requests total roughly $3.3 million while the town typically funds between $1 million and $1.5 million a year from raise-and-appropriate, non-expended capital, or free cash.

A member described a DPW business case showing savings from buying a six-wheel dump truck versus contracting the work, at a cost noted in captions; the town currently has six of seven trucks of that class after recent ARPA investment.

budget_items.topic: Relative sizes of dump truck vs. IT/network items
budget_items.what_was_said: The chair contrasted a large dump truck cost against a much smaller IT activity center network upgrade and school items to illustrate how a funding cutline could reorder priorities.
A member said the network upgrade items seemed cobbled together just to clear a stated capital threshold and said he didn't want to reward that.

A member argued that funding design money alone, rather than full projects, could let the town scope larger items before committing, citing a small design spend as an example of avoiding a bigger unnecessary project.
The town manager said the ClearGov software, currently unused, costs about the figure heard annually and she has not yet decided whether to pause or terminate it.
The town manager said a ballpark free cash number should be available roughly a week before the January 31st closing, accurate to within the figure heard.

budget_items.topic: Prior year outyear request example (stone fence)
budget_items.what_was_said: A member noted relief that this year had far fewer extreme outyear requests, citing as an example a prior year's request for a cemetery stone fence at roughly the figure heard, which did not recur this year.
figures_as_heard: a third or almost a half million dollars

decisions.decision: The committee will submit a tentative/provisional order-of-merit ranking tonight to meet the year-end charter deadline, and revisit it in late January or February once the town manager is closer to a formal capital plan recommendation.
The committee agreed to flip the order of the DPW six-wheel dump truck and the IT/Activity Center network upgrade in the ranking.
The committee kept the supervisor cruiser replacement ranked above the public safety building roof repair, despite one member preferring the reverse.
The committee tentatively set its next meeting for Wednesday, January 28, pending confirmation once free cash figures are closer to being known.

Members resolved several ranking ties by discussion, including flipping the order of a DPW dump truck and an IT network upgrade.
The committee plans to revisit the ranking once the town manager's financial picture is clearer.
The next meeting was tentatively set for January 28, pending confirmation once free cash figures are known.

why_it_matters: This ranking shapes which capital purchases -- vehicles, IT upgrades, building repairs -- the town manager and town meeting are likely to fund first next year.
Because requests exceed what the town typically funds in a year, items near the bottom of this list may wait, get scaled to design-only funding, or be cut.
The order is explicitly tentative and tied to the free cash certification, so it can still change before it reaches a town meeting warrant.
watch_next: Next Capital Planning Committee meeting, tentatively January 28
Town manager's free cash estimate, expected about a week before the January 31 closing

meetings.headline: Parks Commission tables the roughly $14 million Marshall Park project until town finances are clearer.
meetings.summary: The Lunenburg Parks Commission, meeting with only three of its members present, decided to replace the storm-damaged Fitzgerald Field sign and handed the long-stalled beach house dedication sign project to a newer member. Most of the meeting concerned deferring a decision on the large Marshall Park project until the town's overall financial picture is clearer, along with ongoing struggles to fill the vacant recreation director position and a plan to draft written field-use policies and forms, with no change to youth sports field fees this year.

budget_items.what_was_said: The storm-damaged Fitzgerald Field sign will be replaced using parks funds; the chair said she asked Chris Ruth the cost but he had not given her a figure.

A local company (Dillis) had agreed roughly two years ago to cover the cost of a new sign naming the beach house after Genevieve Nass; the chair said the project stalled and is handing it to Maryanne.

Dillis and Roy produced a prevailing-wage estimate for the skate park that came in around figures_as_heard, but it omitted town administrative/bid costs that were part of the original ballpark figure; final decisions expected in January.
The chair said she thought about figures_as_heard remained but it turned out closer to a lower figure; remaining money comes from ARPA (a smaller amount) and from town-meeting-approved capital funds.
A board member said the town needs to understand its finances before pushing a project of that scale forward again at town meeting.

The vacant rec director position is a 19-hour-a-week job with no benefits; a member said covering the paperwork duties falls outside the volunteer commission's purview and suggested a stipend for whoever takes it on.

budget_items.topic: Youth sports per-player field use fee
budget_items.what_was_said: The commission charges youth leagues a flat per-player fee for a season rather than an hourly rate like the school uses; figures were recalled for comparison but the board confirmed no fee change this spring.

decisions.decision: Chair will tell Chris Ruth to go ahead and replace the Fitzgerald Field sign as long as the price is reasonable, aiming for a more permanent design.
Maryanne will take over the beach house sign and dedication project from the chair, who will forward prior graphics and pricing information.
No decision on Marshall Park tonight; the chair will bring information back to the town manager in January rather than deciding in December.
The board will table further discussion of recruiting/electing new commission members and the Marshall Park path forward until closer to January.
Chair will bring a formal vote to the January agenda seeking permission to personally process field-use paperwork if the recreation director position remains unfilled.
No change to youth sports per-player field use fees this spring season.
Chair will draft revised field-use forms and bring them to an upcoming meeting in January or February.
Next meeting set for January 28th (the fourth Wednesday).

meetings.headline: Committee says it won't choose between a full-time athletic director and reading interventionists in FY27.

A paraprofessional undercount already found in the FY26 budget is a data gap worth watching for whether it recurs or grows in the FY27 numbers that underlie any override ask.

meetings.headline: Select Board rehired retired town accountant Karen Brochu as interim finance director amid a stalled recruitment.
meetings.summary: The Lunenburg Select Board ratified Stephen Wallace as the new planning and economic development director, heard a clean FY24 audit from CBIZ that flagged behind-schedule cash and receivable reconciliations and an unresolved ~$90,000 Fitchburg water-billing issue, and approved bringing retired accountant Karen Brochu back part-time as interim finance director after the posted position drew no viable candidates. The board also approved several license renewals, an interim finance director's contract, and a letter to the Governor urging significantly more state local aid (citing a $351 million statewide UGGA ask) ahead of the FY2027 budget process, and opened discussion on the future redevelopment of 925 Mass Ave, appointment policy revisions, and opioid settlement fund planning.

attendees.role: director of planning and economic development (newly appointed), presenter

public_comment.topic: Asked whether the audit and Wallace introduction were public hearings, pressed for a public hearing on the $90,000 owed related to the Fitchburg water billing issue and on school department financial concerns, and criticized lack of interaction during public comment.
Asked what an 'intermittent heavy equipment operator' position is, and suggested the letter to the Governor should also press the state to fund unfunded state mandates.

votes.motion: Ratify the town manager's appointment of Steven Wallace as director of planning and economic development.
Ratify the town manager's appointment of Brandy Oul as meal site manager.
Ratify the town manager's appointment of Joseph Davis as intermittent heavy equipment operator.
Approve the annual license renewals as printed on the agenda, with contingent votes for the applicants with outstanding items (excepting Smokestack, addressed separately).
Approve an additional annual common victualler license renewal that had been omitted from the agenda.
Approve the employment agreement for Karen Brochu as interim finance director/town accountant.
Approve the letter to Governor Healey on local aid and the FY2027 budget, and send copies to the Governor, legislators, the school committee and the finance committee.
Adjourn.

budget_items.what_was_said: The auditor reported the total general fund balance, with portions set aside for encumbrances and free cash used for the FY25 budget, leaving an unassigned balance that rose from the prior year.
The auditor listed balances in the general, zoning, vehicle and equipment, health insurance, and opioid stabilization funds, noting the general stabilization fund has grown steadily since 2013.
The auditor said real estate and personal property tax collections remained strong.
The auditor described a revenue surplus and underspending across departments, offset by use of free cash to balance the FY24 budget.
The town's OPEB trust contribution and investment income grew the fund, while the net OPEB liability fell, tied partly to a higher blended discount rate.

budget_items.topic: Net pension liability, Worcester Regional Retirement System
budget_items.what_was_said: The auditor reported the town's net pension liability rose slightly while the system's funded ratio improved.
Capital asset additions for general government, mainly road paving and equipment, were reported; none for the sewer enterprise.
Short-term debt outstanding funded the capital plan and a land purchase; required long-term debt payments for governmental and sewer funds were noted.
The town exceeded the federal expenditure threshold requiring a single audit, with the education stabilization fund selected for testing and no findings.
A resident and board members discussed money owed related to the town not raising water rates or billing timely when Fitchburg raised its rates; described as an FY25/26 issue outside the FY24 audit.
The town manager reported the MMA is calling for a statewide increase to UGGA to restore pre-recession local aid levels.

budget_items.topic: Finance director recruitment / recruiting agency fee
budget_items.what_was_said: The town manager said Robert Half would be engaged to help recruit a finance director and payroll/benefits administrator, with a fee only if a hire results.
The board approved contingent votes for several license applicants with outstanding paperwork, inspections, or landlord issues.

budget_items.topic: Employment agreement, interim finance director Karen Brochu
budget_items.what_was_said: A retired former town accountant/finance director agreed to return on an hourly, part-time basis with no additional benefits, capped by retiree earnings limits.
A board member found the MMA's report basis for its ask, benchmarking UGGA against historical local tax share, yielding a similar but not identical figure to what was cited.
A board member reported a one-time reimbursement grant amount for Lunenburg from a fund tied to a regional hospital closure, based on a base amount plus a call-volume formula.
The planning board report noted a completed lot posted a performance guarantee bond, after which the certificate of occupancy could be issued.

decisions.decision: The town will engage CBIZ again for the FY25 audit once FY25 is closed, targeted for around January 31st, with a contract signed before work begins.
When engaging the auditor for FY25, the town manager will request special attention to issues including the Fitchburg water billing matter.
Board members indicated comfort proceeding with contingent votes on pending license renewals, including Lunenburg Gas, rather than delaying or calling a special meeting.
Board members will review the prior Mass Development presentation video (June 11) on 925 Mass Ave before the next discussion.
If any board member wants Mass Development's representative to give a follow-up presentation, they should tell the town manager before the following week.
The board's focus at the next 925 Mass Ave discussion will be the evaluation criteria on pages 16-17 of the draft RFP.
Board flagged for further consideration in January whether/how to structure a subcommittee to screen or interview appointment applicants, given open meeting law implications.
The appointment policy's key dates section will read simply 'June' rather than 'first and second Tuesday in June.'
A future agenda item will be scheduled to decide how the town will approach expenditure of opioid settlement funds.
Board members will coordinate signing the letter to the Governor via DocuSign or in person on another day, since it was not yet printed and a board member was absent.

minutes.headline: Select Board rehired retired town accountant Karen Brochu as interim finance director amid a stalled recruitment.
minutes.summary: The Lunenburg Select Board ratified Stephen Wallace as the new planning and economic development director, heard a clean FY24 audit from CBIZ that flagged behind-schedule cash and receivable reconciliations and an unresolved ~$90,000 Fitchburg water-billing issue, and approved bringing retired accountant Karen Brochu back part-time as interim finance director after the posted position drew no viable candidates. The board also approved several license renewals, an interim finance director's contract, and a letter to the Governor urging significantly more state local aid (citing a $351 million statewide UGGA ask) ahead of the FY2027 budget process, and opened discussion on the future redevelopment of 925 Mass Ave, appointment policy revisions, and opioid settlement fund planning.

meetings.headline: Committee met its energy-reduction goal but remains stalled awaiting building energy audits needed for Turkey Hill decisions.
meetings.summary: The Green Community Task Force reviewed its FY26 annual energy report, which showed the town hit its energy-reduction goal, with Turkey Hill and the old elementary building flagged as the largest energy users. Most of the meeting covered stalled progress: a National Grid building-energy audit and analysis six months overdue, no reserve fund for future LED streetlight maintenance, an unsuccessful styrofoam-recycling grant push, and broader town indecision on Turkey Hill, Town Hall and other building needs. No substantive votes were taken beyond routine approval of minutes and adjournment; the group discussed renaming itself an energy/sustainability committee and pursuing Tyler's appointment to a soon-open seat.

Adjourn the meeting

budget_items.what_was_said: The committee reported total municipal energy consumption fell versus the baseline, meeting the green-communities reduction goal, with the largest drop in buildings.
The annual report narrative stated total municipal, building and vehicle energy use all decreased while water and sewer energy use increased.
The chair reported the November streetlight bill was high but far below what the town paid before it owned its own streetlights.

budget_items.topic: Streetlight savings and a proposed maintenance reserve fund
budget_items.what_was_said: Members said savings from lower streetlight bills have just been absorbed into the general budget with nothing set aside for future LED maintenance, and discussed creating a reserve or special revolving fund instead.
A member said the town badly needs an experienced grant writer, and noted a budgeted grant-writer line had gone unspent before.

budget_items.topic: PPP energy audit and comprehensive building analysis (CBA)
budget_items.what_was_said: National Grid was to provide a free preliminary audit and a comprehensive building analysis of all twelve town buildings, but the committee said it has waited months with no result.

budget_items.topic: Capital outlay override for building projects
budget_items.what_was_said: A member described how the town of Ashby used a one-time capital outlay override to fund and pay off building projects in a single year, and suggested Lunenburg consider it for its aging buildings.
A member said current incentives make an electric riding mower roughly half the price of an equivalent gas model, but the town would need duplicate equipment for separate departments.

budget_items.topic: Capital planning equipment list / mower purchase
budget_items.what_was_said: A member said the school department's capital plan includes buying a new zero-turn mower and the group discussed pushing for an electric model.

A member relayed that capital planning discussed a perceived risk that hybrid police vehicle batteries could be costly once out of warranty, and that gas vehicle quotes may be sought for the next replacement round.

decisions.decision: Committee agreed to consider renaming itself from a Green Community committee toward something like an Energy or Energy and Sustainability Committee.
A member agreed to update the committee's Facebook page with the annual energy report the chair would send.
Chair agreed to push for Tyler's official appointment to an upcoming open committee seat.
Next meeting set for roughly mid-January, once the PPP building audit results are available.

minutes.summary: The Green Community Task Force reviewed its FY26 annual energy report, which showed the town hit its energy-reduction goal, with Turkey Hill and the old elementary building flagged as the largest energy users. Most of the meeting covered stalled progress: a National Grid building-energy audit and analysis six months overdue, no reserve fund for future LED streetlight maintenance, an unsuccessful styrofoam-recycling grant push, and broader town indecision on Turkey Hill, Town Hall and other building needs. what_happened.line: The town met its green-communities energy-reduction goal for FY26, with buildings driving most of the drop.
A promised National Grid audit and building-by-building analysis, needed before any Turkey Hill decision, is months overdue with no date given.
Streetlight bill savings are going into the general budget with no reserve set aside for future LED maintenance.
The committee took no votes on policy; it discussed renaming itself an energy/sustainability committee and backing Tyler for an open seat.

why_it_matters: Turkey Hill and Town Hall building decisions, and any capital ask tied to them, are on hold until the overdue energy audit comes back.
Streetlight savings with no maintenance reserve means a future LED repair cost would compete with other budget lines rather than draw on savings already realized.
A committee name change and a pending appointment are procedural and do not commit the town to any spending.

meetings.headline: Town hires a new planning/economic development director as the three-year master plan process wraps up.
meetings.summary: The Lunenburg Planning Board met to announce the hiring of a new planning and economic development director and the completion of the three-year master plan steering committee process, then handled routine land-use business: an ANR endorsement, a storm water permit hearing for a proposed 4-lot subdivision on Reservoir Road with significant board concern about a common driveway's safety near a road curve, and a bond/performance guarantee for a completed home on Townsend Harbor Road. No public comment was offered at either public hearing, and all votes taken were unanimous 3-0 roll calls among the three members present.

meetings.headline: APDC voted to press the Select Board to act on town meeting's directive to sell or lease the Brooks House.
meetings.summary: The Architectural Preservation District Commission (three members present, no public) received updates on 50 Main Street's office condo, the Lunenburg Municipal Building Design Committee's plan to consolidate town offices in the Ritter building using GSA space standards and an elevator rather than the existing chairlift, and the nearly-finished 10-year master plan covering housing pressure from state law, excluded debt, and priority facility projects (Town Hall, Ritter, Turkey Hill, Marshall Park). The commission voted to have a member raise the long-unaddressed Brooks House sell-or-lease town meeting vote with the Select Board, and deferred approval of prior meeting minutes to January.

budget_items.topic: Master plan steering committee consultant work
budget_items.what_was_said: The chair said that had Kim Duffy not taken over managing the master plan steering committee's work after it had gone unmet for almost a year, the process would have been a waste of the town's money. He cited the cost as a figure in the captions.

budget_items.topic: 2004 town meeting Ritter addition project (May town meeting project)
budget_items.what_was_said: The chair described a prior, larger proposed addition to the Ritter building that the design committee has now decided not to pursue, in favor of modifying the existing 1963 addition instead.
The design committee is adopting GSA space guidelines to size staff offices in a consolidated Ritter building, with different footage for managers versus staff.

The master plan will include an analysis of the town's excluded debt, showing it is declining as older capital projects from 2004 are paid down, which the chair argued creates capacity to take on new debt for facility needs.
The chair noted a prior town meeting vote directed the town to sell or lease the Brooks House, that this has not been acted on, and that he intends to raise it with the Select Board.

decisions.decision: Vote on approval of the October and November meeting minutes will be deferred to the January meeting since not all members had reviewed the November minutes.
Confirmed the next APDC meeting is January 8, correcting an earlier stated date of January 18.
Nathan will draft and send a letter to the owner of the 50 Main Street office condo over the holidays, a task carried over from the November meeting.
The chair will bring the Brooks House issue back up at the January APDC meeting regardless of the Select Board outcome.

what_happened.line: The commission voted 3-0 to have its chair press the Select Board to finally act on a town meeting vote to sell or lease the Brooks House.
A near-final town facilities master plan recommends consolidating town offices into the Ritter building, replacing the existing chairlift with an elevator.
The chair said the master plan will show the town's excluded debt declining, which he argued creates room to borrow for facility projects at Town Hall, Ritter, Turkey Hill, and Marshall Park.
Approval of the October and November meeting minutes was pushed to January because not all members had reviewed them.
A letter to the owner of the 50 Main Street office condo, first raised in November, is still unsent going into the holidays.

why_it_matters: A town meeting directive to sell or lease the Brooks House has sat unacted on; this vote is a push to get the Select Board to move on a decision residents already made.

The facilities master plan under discussion could shape future borrowing and building projects -- Town Hall, Ritter, Turkey Hill, Marshall Park -- that would eventually come back to voters as debt exclusions or town meeting articles.
None of tonight's items were town meeting or ballot votes; they are groundwork -- a letter, a plan, and a request to another board -- that could turn into one later.

meetings.headline: Committee finalized its ~22-item FY27 capital request list for members to rank, amid free-cash funding uncertainty
meetings.summary: The Capital Planning Committee heard its final FY27 department presentation, from IT, on a roughly $20,000 network upgrade for the Adult Activity Center (Eagle House), and discussed a longer-range five-year network/licensing plan and a possible community compact grant for a larger FY32 upgrade. The bulk of the meeting concerned assembling and validating a rolled-up list of about 22-23 FY27 capital requests, assigning members homework to rank them by the following Tuesday, and discussing how uncertain free cash certification timing (not expected until around February) will complicate finalizing a funding plan before town meeting.

what_happened.line: Members began ranking a rolled-up list of roughly two dozen FY27 capital requests, due to the chair by end of day the following Tuesday.
The town manager said the free cash figure needed to fund the capital plan will not even be estimated until January, clouding the timeline before town meeting.
The committee dropped the public safety garage heater request from the list because no cost estimate was ever submitted.
IT presented its only FY27 capital request, a network upgrade for the Adult Activity Center (Eagle House), alongside a longer-range five-year network plan carried in the operating budget instead.
The chair will have department heads and the town manager validate the rollup spreadsheet's figures before it goes back out to members.

why_it_matters: This rolled-up list is the slate of capital projects -- from a bridge repair to town network equipment to vehicles -- that will compete for funding recommendations going to town meeting, so how members rank them shapes what advances.

Not knowing the free cash figure until January means the committee may have to set priorities before it knows how much money is actually available, which could force re-ranking or cuts closer to town meeting.
A resident with a stake in a specific item, like the dropped heater request or the bridge project, should check whether it stays on the validated list once it comes back from department heads.

meetings.headline: Committee finished editing its draft master-plan recommendations before sending them to the planning board
meetings.summary: In what was billed as its final meeting, the Master Plan Steering Committee went line-by-line through a spreadsheet of draft recommendations with consultants Ramy and Tristan, softening or consolidating wording on housing, farmland, school facilities, Lake Shirley access, town-owned parcels, business development and recreation. No formal votes were taken on the edits; the chair will compile outstanding meeting minutes and a list of past members, and the draft plan is expected to go to the planning board around mid-to-late January.

budget_items.what_was_said: A member said the town's current consultant contract, described as $42,000, is to help build the process for charging residents and businesses a stormwater utility fee.
It was said the task force may set a flat annual fee for all residences in a range described, while commercial/industrial fees would be based on impervious surface.
A member recalled that a grant used to fund half the cost of building dog parks, and that dog parks are described as wildly expensive at a figure given.

decisions.decision: Remove committees from the recommendations list that said the work doesn't fall in their purview, and combine remaining committee names into the 'required resources' column instead of a separate volunteers note.
Change the first-time homebuyer program recommendation to 'promote' rather than 'advertise,' and list only the Lunenburg Housing Authority as an owner, dropping other agencies.
Remove reference to TC Pacios from the town-center events-programming recommendation so it covers the town center more broadly.
Update Turkey Hill and other school-related recommendations to 'three-year' language per the school committee's request.
Reword the STEM recommendation to 'explore funding options for additional steam programs as part of school budget,' with STEAM defined in the text.
Change 'create a trades program' to 'explore options for creating greater opportunities for Lunenburg students to engage with trades programs,' since Monty Tech precludes a separate district program.
Reword the green-community recommendation to 'strive to maintain status as a green community' and specify it refers to the Massachusetts program.
Consolidate the Turkey Hill renovation and school-accessibility recommendations into one line about evaluating renovations to meet accessibility standards, removing the duplicate.
Leave the Brooks House out of the recommendations document, as it did not rank in the top building priorities.
Reword the Lake Shirley recommendation to 'maintain access to Lake Shirley for [Lunenburg] residents,' reflecting the resolved Shady Point agreement.

Simplify the 30 School Street recommendation to 'develop options for [the] parcel,' removing references to parking and green space, since it's covered by the broader town-property inventory recommendation.

Add the library to the list of components (with TC Pacios and Adult Activity Center) in the town-green/fire-lane recommendation, and fold the geogrid fire-lane detail into that recommendation's description rather than as a separate line.

Remove the duplicate community-garden line and the separate 'assess allowing public use of the greenhouse' line, keeping one recommendation to continue school gardening with a note that public use could follow if the school program ends.
Reword the assisted-living recommendation to 'assess the conditions that would allow for the development of' assisted living.
Reword the low-income senior housing recommendation similarly to 'assess the conditions that would allow the development of low-income senior housing.'
Consolidate two similar business-investment/zoning-barrier recommendations into one: 'assess existing bylaws and processes to reduce barriers to business development.'
Add wildlife-connectivity and native-landscaping/climate-resilience language into the recommendation guiding new development, rather than creating a new recommendation.
Limit the uniform town-signage recommendation to municipal buildings only, not private property.
Chair will send the draft recommendations spreadsheet to committee members and, once the plan draft is ready (expected mid-to-late January), circulate it before it goes to the planning board.

what_happened.line: The steering committee went line-by-line through its draft master-plan recommendations, softening or combining wording across housing, schools, farmland, Lake Shirley, town parcels, business and recreation, without taking a formal vote on any edit.

School-related recommendations were changed to match school committee feedback, including three-year language for Turkey Hill and folding a separate accessibility line into one renovation recommendation.
The Lake Shirley recommendation was reworded to say the town will maintain resident access, reflecting a resolved Shady Point agreement.
Housing recommendations were softened to say the town will 'assess the conditions' for assisted living and low-income senior housing rather than commit to developing them.
The committee treated this as its final working meeting; the chair will compile outstanding minutes and a list of members before the draft goes to the planning board.

why_it_matters: This is the wording the planning board will receive and act on for the town's next master plan, covering housing, schools, farmland, recreation and business development.
None of the edits were put to a formal vote, so the record of what changed rests on this meeting rather than on a roll call.
Recommendations on Turkey Hill, Lake Shirley access and senior/affordable housing options set the direction future boards will be asked to fund or zone for.

what_happened.line: The Commission will bring a proposed rule to the spring special town meeting requiring new sewer hookups to tie into the line on the street the property is actually addressed to.

meetings.headline: Chamber of Commerce briefed EDC on business resources; no town decisions were voted.
meetings.summary: The Economic Development Committee spent most of its meeting hosting a presentation from the North Central Massachusetts Chamber of Commerce and its development corporation, covering tourism, small-business loan programs, and advocacy work relevant to Lunenburg. The committee also heard planning-department and downtown-business updates, approved its October minutes, and agreed to form a small subcommittee to draft a business-friendly bylaw ahead of the next meeting, without taking any other formal votes.

attendees.role: presenter, director of public affairs, North Central Massachusetts Chamber of Commerce
presenter, manager of economic development, chamber's development corporation

votes.motion: Approve the October 14, 2025 minutes
Adjourn at 6:56

budget_items.what_was_said: A workshop gave away a marketing package as a raffle prize.
The chamber described its annual scholarship program for students, including trade-school and non-college pathways.
The development corporation's microloan program lends to small businesses that cannot get bank financing, covering leasehold improvements, equipment, inventory, refinancing and gap financing.
The presenter said the corporation has lent a large sum over more than 30 years, at a typical loan size, creating or retaining many jobs.
A newer fund offers low- or no-cost financing for development projects, with extra incentive in low-to-moderate income areas; requires a town letter of support and a job-creation ratio.
A quick-turnaround loan for equipment/vehicle repairs requires a minimum credit score, unlike the corporation's other products.
The presenter cited an approximate figure for tourism dollars coming into the region but said she would confirm it rather than misquote it.
A member raised concern that a stormwater utility fee under consideration by the town could be an excessive burden on local businesses; the chamber said it would advocate if asked.

Participants noted state (MassDOT) grant funding exists for sidewalk and Complete Streets projects, but design requirements make such projects expensive and land-intensive on state roads.

The group agreed to pause and relocate to the community room at 8:00 when the current meeting space closed for the evening.

meetings.headline: Board will push legal action against Woodlands condo trust over kayak racks in the well's protected zone
meetings.summary: The Lunenburg Water District Commissioners reviewed the in-house cost of the Roland Acres water main replacement versus hiring it out, discussed a near-final draft of a community engagement survey on water source options, and spent significant time on the Woodlands condo trust's refusal to remove kayak racks from the well's Zone One protection area, concluding they will pursue legal action if the racks are not voluntarily moved. The meeting also covered SRF grant funding status, a possible new hire and equipment purchase for future in-house projects, a proposal to explore alternative voting methods for ratepayers, and recognized the superintendent's 40th work anniversary, closing with extended public comment challenging the survey's cost estimates.

budget_items.topic: Roland Acres water main replacement — cost review
budget_items.what_was_said: The board reviewed two cost figures for the in-house replacement job: the materials-only cost and a figure that adds the value of crew labor, comparing both to an estimate of what it would have cost to hire the job out at current 2023-era bids.
A commissioner proposed reinvesting the savings from doing the water main job in-house into a rubber-tire excavator and tandem-wheeler to allow the district to keep doing similar projects itself.

budget_items.topic: Possible new hire for in-house main work
budget_items.what_was_said: Commissioners discussed bringing on another employee in late winter/early spring to continue in-house main replacement work, and agreed to start putting together the annual expense estimate for staffing and equipment to present at a future meeting.
A commissioner said pursuing the zero-percent-interest SRF loan option was estimated to save a large sum compared to conventional financing.

budget_items.topic: O&M cost differential between water source options (survey)
budget_items.what_was_said: A resident presented his own analysis arguing the operations-and-maintenance cost difference between two water-source combination options was understated in the district's consultant figures, using a baseline and a variable-cost percentage split; the district said its consultants (Tighe & Bond) were confident in their numbers but did not have them itemized as a line item.

budget_items.topic: Capital cost of the three-well treatment option
budget_items.what_was_said: A resident questioned why moving from a two-source to a three-source treatment configuration added several million dollars in capital cost; the superintendent explained it required a larger treatment plant and a raw water transmission main.

decisions.decision: Staff will begin putting together annual expense projections for hiring an additional employee and for equipment, to bring to a future meeting as part of a three-to-five-year plan.
The community engagement survey draft will be finalized and brought back to the board for approval before release, alongside a draft postcard mailer and website.

The district will continue pursuing removal of the Woodlands condo trust's kayak racks from the Zone One well protection area, through its attorney if necessary, and will seek to recover costs from the Woodlands if legal action becomes necessary.

The clerk/president will look into whether the district's bylaws allow shutting off a ratepayer for non-compliance with district regulations (not just non-payment), and report back at the next meeting.
The board will ask town counsel whether an alternative voting method (e.g., a paper ballot period before the meeting) could legally be offered to increase ratepayer participation.

meetings.summary: The Conservation Commission held several wetlands permit hearings: it approved a restoration project at 199 Massachusetts Ave (twice, after rescinding to drop an erosion-control requirement), issued a positive determination against a proposed three-season porch at 13 Birch Island Way for sitting inside the 50-foot no-structure zone, and continued three other hearings to December 17th over unresolved landowner permission and boundary-measurement issues. It also reviewed the newly reclassified conservation agent job posting, voted a budget split for the Hollis property (Haw) fund, and got updates on the conservation trust fund and a recreational trails grant reimbursement and extension.

meetings.headline: Select Board voted unanimously to let the town manager sign a low-income community solar discount deal.
meetings.summary: The Select Board heard a presentation from the new LEAF education nonprofit and voted unanimously to authorize the town manager to sign onto a Colonial Power Group low-income solar (SMART) discount program. The board also reviewed a draft tri-board communication letter ahead of a budget season expected to be difficult, discussed the finance department's ongoing staffing transition, license renewals, and heard committee reports including the school committee's plan to build three FY27 budget scenarios, before voting to enter executive session on firefighter union bargaining.

Active bargaining with three unions and an executive session on firefighter contract talks touch town payroll costs that eventually show up in the budget residents vote on.

meetings.headline: Committee floats putting all town offices into the Ritter building, forms subcommittee to survey department heads
meetings.summary: The Building Design Committee reviewed the chair's rough sketch for consolidating nearly all town office functions into the Ritter building, with the old Town Hall becoming a meeting house/PACC studio space. what_happened.line: The Sewer Commission voted down a sewer easement waiver for the 763 Massachusetts Ave duplex conversion project.
All members present voted against the waiver, denying the developer's request to use an easement instead of a direct street tie-in.
The commission adopted a new one-time connection charge policy for accessory dwelling units, based on Title 5 flow.
Members agreed to draft a future regulation requiring sewer connections to run to a property's own street rather than through an easement.
The commission granted the manhole-replacement contractor an extension to June 30, 2026, since roads cannot be reopened after mid-November.

why_it_matters: The denied waiver means the 763 Massachusetts Ave duplex project cannot proceed with an easement-based sewer connection and would need a different, likely costlier, tie-in approach.
A future regulation requiring direct street tie-ins instead of easements could affect how other properties near shared sewer mains are allowed to connect going forward.
Owners adding accessory dwelling units will now face a one-time sewer connection charge calculated per gallon under Title 5 flow standards.

meetings.headline: District previews FY27-29 outlook, asking to restore staff cut in FY26; no vote was taken.
meetings.summary: The select board, finance committee and school committee met jointly to hear a preliminary, forward-looking FY27-29 school budget outlook, explicitly deferring any FY25 questions to a later public forum. The superintendent and business manager walked through contractual assumptions (salaries, health insurance, utilities, transportation) and a series of requested staff restorations -- interventionists, a kindergarten paraprofessional, a world-language teacher, a music teacher, a bridge/TLC program, an ELL teacher, and a debated full-time athletic director/assistant principal split -- framed as restoring FY26 cuts rather than new expansion. No formal votes were taken on any budget item; the boards adjourned after discussion, with several follow-up items assigned to the administration for the next budget cycle.

budget_items.what_was_said: The district assumed a 20% annual health insurance increase for FY27 through FY29, projecting a large rise from FY23 actuals.
Electricity costs were shown rising from FY23 to a much higher FY29 projection, tied to a locked-in per-kWh rate with the district's provider.
Heating costs were projected lower than electricity and are currently under review for possible savings.
The transportation contract is described as effectively uncompetitive since no other vendor has bid in years, making the cost locked in regardless of market forces.
The general education transportation line was under-budgeted for FY26 despite being under contract, which will require a line-item transfer.
A requested 1.0 interventionist position to address early literacy and math gaps, costed at a master's-with-experience salary step.
A new kindergarten paraprofessional position was proposed, to be funded by the primary school through reductions in general supplies.
A board member asked what the paraprofessional salary works out to hourly, comparing it unfavorably to retail wages.
A new world language teacher is requested to avoid delaying language instruction or cutting the Latin program for a large incoming class.
The Turkey Hill interventionist restoration carries an associated insurance cost figure discussed alongside the high school positions.
Of the two new high school positions, only one carries a health insurance cost since the other is already part-time with insurance.
Adding one van with a monitor to a transportation route that can't be regionalized for two students was cited as a striking cost example.
A guesstimated salary range was given for making the athletic director position full-time again.
The athletic director was previously paid as a stipend rather than a full position, cited to contrast with the current full-time ask.

Eliminating the reading coach and converting the math coach to a partly direct-service instructional specialist role was costed as a small net add, since the individual would move to the teachers' contract.

budget_items.topic: Data reporting manager / assistant business manager restructuring
budget_items.what_was_said: Reducing the data reporting manager to half-time while adding a new assistant business manager position was presented as a net savings.
The net effect of the central office restructuring was summarized as roughly breakeven once insurance costs were included.
The estimated total cost of all proposed restorations and restructuring, assuming highest-tier insurance for all new hires, was presented as the headline ask.
The remaining available FY25 budget and percent used were reported as the year wrapped up.

budget_items.topic: FY26 total budget with free cash
budget_items.what_was_said: The FY26 total budget including one-time free cash was broken into salaries and expenses.
Level-service FY27 salaries and expenses were projected without any of the new requested positions included.
FY28 projections show expenses rising notably, driven largely by health insurance and special education cost growth.
FY29 projections were given as the final year of the three-year outlook.
Excluding the one-time free cash, the level-service FY27 budget represents a percentage increase over FY26.

budget_items.topic: FY26 free cash split between salaries and expenses
budget_items.what_was_said: Of the $500,000 in free cash used in FY26, most but not all was applied to salaries.
Combining the level-service budget with the cost of restored positions produced the total needs-based FY27 figure.

budget_items.topic: Health insurance estimate vs. actual (override context)
budget_items.what_was_said: During the override discussion, the health insurance increase was initially estimated much higher than what it actually came in at, prompting a request to isolate that line going forward.
A count of district staff currently enrolled in some form of health insurance was given as roughly half to sixty percent of staff.

budget_items.what_was_said: Incoming school-choice tuition revenue on the cherry sheet has fallen sharply over five to six years, shifting cost onto the town budget.

budget_items.topic: School choice per-pupil funding vs. cost
budget_items.what_was_said: The district receives a set amount per accepted school-choice student but the district's own per-pupil cost is much higher.

Psychologist services spending also rose from FY24 to FY25.
A running total of fee revenue collected this year from bus and athletic fees was reported as higher than expected.

minutes.headline: Town meeting reversed a failed vote to pay Fitchburg the water bills Lunenburg forgot to send for over a year
minutes.summary: This special town meeting worked through 17+ warrant articles, most contentiously a near-failed then reconsidered vote to pay Fitchburg for water bills the town had failed to send to 11 accounts for over a year, plus a $195,790.97 FY26 budget amendment driven by heavy finance-department staff turnover. Town meeting also funded a storm water utility consultant and a capital cost-estimating fund, created a special education out-of-district reserve fund, raised the senior tax-deferral income limit, adopted an MBTA Communities Act zoning overlay at Tritown, revised SAP personnel/benefit rules, passed over a Kids Kingdom playground transfer and a warrant-mailing change amid public pushback, and narrowly voted down eliminating the town's volunteer personnel committee.

what_happened.line: Town meeting rejected, then reconsidered and passed, paying Fitchburg for water bills the town failed to send to 11 accounts for over a year.
Town meeting approved a mid-year FY26 budget amendment driven by turnover of the finance director, assistant accountant, and payroll coordinator.
Town meeting created a special education out-of-district reserve fund over the finance committee's own recommendation against it.
Town meeting adopted a zoning overlay at Tritown to comply with the state's MBTA Communities Act.
Town meeting narrowly voted to keep the volunteer personnel committee rather than dissolve it.

why_it_matters: The Fitchburg billing lapse left the water enterprise fund short of budgeted revenue, which the finance director said could complicate setting the tax rate, and it is the reason a related capital-fund transfer needed town meeting approval at all.

The new special education reserve fund is a standing account town meeting still controls dollar by dollar, meant to absorb the swings in out-of-district placement costs that have come up in three straight budget seasons.
The MBTA Communities zoning overlay is a compliance vote, not a building proposal by itself, but it sets the multifamily density allowed at Tritown going forward.
watch_next: The storm water task force said it plans to bring a storm water utility article to the spring 2026 annual town meeting.

meetings.headline: Committee leans toward expanding the Ritter/annex building for offices, leaving Town Hall as meeting space
meetings.summary:
The Design Committee reviewed a prior architect's concept for reusing Town Hall as meeting space with PAC on the second floor, then heard PAC's current and future space/technology needs from PAC chair Steve Walker, including its Comcast contract renewal and a pending state streaming bill. The bulk of the meeting was a working discussion of department adjacencies and square footage using Chris Ruth's spreadsheet, concluding that effort should focus on sizing a two- or three-story addition to the Ritter building/annex rather than reconfiguring Town Hall, with a rough schematic to be drawn before the December 1st meeting.</parameter>
</invoke>

budget_items.what_was_said: Steve Walker said PAC is budgeting for a new server next financial year expected to last about 8 to 10 years.
Steve Walker said PAC has money set aside for a new studio but is starting to dip into it to cover basic operating expenses because Comcast-linked income is declining.
Steve Walker confirmed the cable contract is up for renewal, expiring February 28, 2028, with construction timing possibly overlapping negotiations.

budget_items.topic: PAC income from Comcast / franchise fee cap
budget_items.what_was_said: Steve Walker said PAC's income is down from just over $200,000 after doubling under the last contract at the legal maximum of 5%, and a pending streaming bill could restore lost revenue via a state-collected fee on streaming services.
A member used an industry-standard figure of square footage per employee, including common area allocation, to estimate space needed for assessors, treasurer, and town clerk staff (about 17 people).
Members estimated the current 65 annex is roughly 30 by 60 feet, with about 700-800 square feet actually used as planning office space.

budget_items.topic: Total office space needed if consolidating at Ritter/annex
budget_items.what_was_said: A member estimated town hall's first floor footprint plus the town manager's office at roughly 4,000 square feet that would need to be accommodated at the Ritter building if town hall is repurposed entirely for meeting space.

A member calculated that replacing the 1965 annex with a two-story addition to house about 5,000 square feet of combined office space would need roughly a 2,500 square foot footprint, an increase of several hundred square feet over the current annex footprint.
A member said the town clerk had estimated the vault needs to be about twice its current size, an additional square footage requirement not yet counted in the space analysis.
A member calculated that a three-story replacement of the 1965 annex in the same footprint would yield significantly more space than the current arrangement, versus a two-story option.

A member cited the zoning ordinance section limiting non-residential/mixed-use building height in the town center to a maximum and to no more than three stories, confirming a three-story addition would be allowed.
A member sketched a rough floor sized for about 10 people to illustrate an addex layout, replicated on a second floor with a conference room of comparable size.

decisions.decision: Committee agreed the group needs to develop true adjacency requirements and dial in square footage needs before finalizing a layout, rather than relying on Chris Ruth's first-pass spreadsheet alone.

Committee agreed public-facing staff (e.g., town manager, tax collector) need a buffer/controlled access from the public in any layout, distinct from non-public staff who can be placed further inside the building.

Committee agreed future-proofing for town growth is necessary rather than designing only to current staffing levels, citing Lunenburg's population and growth relative to average Massachusetts town size.

Committee agreed to focus the next round of work on sizing a Ritter/annex addition rather than reworking old space-use assumptions, and to produce a rough floor-plan schematic (Tony to sketch, Greg to render in AutoCAD) before showing anything to the town manager.

Committee agreed to concentrate initial design efforts on the Town Hall/Ritter (annex) expansion rather than the town hall/meeting house reconfiguration, since no new square footage is being added to town hall itself, only internal partitioning.
Next meeting set for December 1st.

what_happened.line: The board found a long-standing failure to properly bill City of Fitchburg water customers, leaving an accrued balance with interest, and put off a recommendation on paying it.
The board unanimously recommended approval of an amendment to the FY2026 town budget covering town accountant transition costs, audit costs, and contracted services.
Officials raised switching Fitchburg water billing from quarterly to monthly to cut down on interest charges, without a formal vote.
The board will take up a water rate adjustment at a future meeting.
A tri-board meeting was confirmed for November 24th.

why_it_matters: Residents served by City of Fitchburg water may face a bill reflecting years of under-billing plus interest, and a possible shift to monthly billing.
The budget amendment funds town accountant, audit, and finance-office costs and goes to special town meeting for a vote.
A future water rate adjustment could change what water customers pay going forward.

meetings.headline: Finance Committee splits on scrapping the Personnel Committee; defers most Nov. 18 warrant articles to Town Meeting
meetings.summary: The Finance Committee held its public hearing on the warrant for the November 18 special town meeting, going article by article. It approved several routine transfers, deferred a number of contested or under-documented articles (a stormwater consulting appropriation, a special education reserve fund, a senior tax deferral expansion, and two salary-plan articles) so the town manager could present more detail at Town Meeting, and split its votes on a proposal to change how warrants are distributed and on a proposal to eliminate the Personnel Committee.

meetings.headline: Trust Fund chair disputes school committee's control over scholarship funds, citing state trust law
meetings.summary: The Trust Fund Commission chair gave an extended report on his research into which of roughly 51 school-held scholarship funds legally qualify as trusts subject to the commission's oversight, disputing the school committee chair's position that the school committee could withhold fund declarations. The board also reviewed confusing and possibly inconsistent investment-return figures from its Bartholomew-managed trust account, tabled a risk management policy with only minor edits, and reset its next meeting date around Thanksgiving.

A member said an earlier discussion had floated a large cost for a PFAS treatment plant serving town water takers, plus ongoing annual maintenance, calling these affordability concerns comparable to building projects.

decisions.decision: Committee agreed it is identifying priority capital projects, not formally ranking them numerically.
Consultant and committee converged on treating Town Hall/Ritter as one linked project, plus Marshall Park and the elementary school (Turkey Hill), as three priority project groupings.
Noted possible headroom for a third debt-exclusion project since older debt-excluded projects will be paid off before the new master plan's 10-year horizon, pending finance committee input.
Agreed to remove the recommendation to reduce minimum lot size for agricultural preservation, since the 5-acre threshold is set by the state and the town has no local authority to change it.
Agreed to revise the senior tax relief recommendation to focus on reviewing whether existing eligibility thresholds are set appropriately, rather than creating new relief.

Agreed to soften recommendation language from the town 'providing' marketing/space-advertising for businesses to 'establishing and maintaining a relationship with the Lunenburg Business Association' to support small business marketing.

Agreed to change recommendation language away from 'establish a town fund' for stormwater infrastructure to more neutral wording (e.g., 'managing'), since the town has not decided between a stormwater utility fund or traditional taxation.
Agreed to repeat/reference Turkey Hill specifically under the schools section even though it's already listed under municipal buildings, given it is the top facilities priority.
Set December 10th as the deadline for the committee's last round of comments/feedback to the consultant on the recommendations and implementation table.
Consultant indicated a realistic target of a draft final report by the end of January.
Committee members encouraged each other to attend the Marshall Park facility tour on Saturday, November 15th at 10:30am.

minutes.headline: Committee narrows to three priority capital projects and sets a Dec. 10 deadline for board feedback
minutes.summary: The Master Plan Steering Committee spent most of the meeting reviewing October facility tours of Town Hall, Ritter, and Turkey Hill, then debated how to present capital priorities without formally ranking them, converging on Town Hall/Ritter, Turkey Hill, and Marshall Park as the priority groupings. what_happened.line: Committee converged on three priority capital project groupings -- Town Hall/Ritter, Turkey Hill, and Marshall Park -- rather than a formal ranking.
Set December 10 as the deadline for boards to send final feedback on the draft recommendations and implementation table.
Consultant targeted a draft final master plan report for late January.

what_happened.line: The committee agreed to a staged, multi-meeting process for deciding whether to renovate or replace Turkey Hill Elementary, starting with building needs before cost or funding options.
Rather than have the facilities director attend the next meeting, the committee will first collect written feedback from Turkey Hill staff on what the building needs.

The committee took first readings on four policies -- advertising in schools, a Monty Tech pathway program, cashless payment at events, and competency determination -- and sent each to a second reading.

The Trust Fund Commission's chairman told the committee that school-related gifts and trusts are town property under statute and asked that scholarship and donor records be turned over to the treasurer's office for review.
The committee approved routine items: two line-item transfers, four donations, and a new scholarship named for James J. Larkin.

why_it_matters: The renovate-versus-rebuild choice for Turkey Hill will eventually come before residents as a building project and a tax question, and how much the state's MSBA program reimburses depends on which path the committee picks.

The four policies now headed to a second reading -- including cashless payment at school events -- will return for further debate before they take effect, and could change how families pay for or access school activities.
A request to catalog school-related trusts and scholarships touches funds set aside for student scholarships and could affect who has authority to approve them.
