meetings.headline: Fire and DPW presented decade-long capital plans; committee weighed using the $2.5M stabilization fund for big vehicles
meetings.summary: The Capital Planning Committee heard detailed FY27-FY37 capital plans from the Fire Chief (apparatus, ambulances) and the DPW director (trucks, drainage, bridge, salt barn), including grant prospects and financing tradeoffs. No formal votes were taken on funding besides procedural adjournment; the committee agreed to submit written follow-up questions on the DPW plan and discussed how to weigh the special purpose stabilization fund, possible debt exclusions, and a new state zero-emission vehicle mandate against future requests.

votes.motion: Motion to adjourn

budget_items.what_was_said: Chief proposed replacing the 36-year-old light/medium brush truck, which has had repeated breakdowns; an assistance-to-firefighters federal grant was applied for but is almost certainly not awarded due to the federal shutdown.

budget_items.topic: AFG grant match figures for engine 2 and squad/brush truck
budget_items.what_was_said: Chief described the 80/20 federal match structure and what the town's share would have been for engine 2 versus the larger brush truck grant that was not pursued this cycle.
Chief proposed replacing the 2019 ambulance based on 5%-per-year escalation off the 2023 purchase price, with the retired unit kept as a mechanical spare rather than adding a vehicle to the fleet.

budget_items.topic: Fire: Car One (chief's vehicle), pushed to FY28/FY30
budget_items.what_was_said: Chief recommended delaying replacement of his own vehicle a year, noting good mileage and leaving the decision on vehicle type to his successor.

budget_items.topic: Fire: Squad 3 / heavy rescue pumper, moved to FY29
budget_items.what_was_said: Chief moved this big-ticket heavy rescue/pumper replacement out because engine 2 was the higher priority this year; a rough quote was given based on the vehicle as currently equipped, though new lighter equipment (battery tools) may lower the eventual cost.
Chief proposed spacing replacement of the first paramedic-era cardiac monitors over two fiscal years as they reach the 10-year mark, based on 5%-per-year pricing.
Planned replacement continuing the three-vehicle ambulance rotation, cost estimated on a 5%-per-year escalation from the prior purchase.

budget_items.topic: Fire: Heavy-duty brush truck replacement, FY33
budget_items.what_was_said: This AFG-grant-funded truck would be about 30 years old at replacement; chief suggested a possible future swap to a small tanker given town areas without hydrants.
Mutual-aid engine planned for replacement at a 20-year lifespan, cost based on 5%-per-year escalation from the prior engine purchase.
Another planned ambulance replacement on the 5%-per-year escalation model; committee members remarked on how high the projected price has become.

budget_items.topic: Storm water utility consultant work, warrant article
budget_items.what_was_said: A special town meeting warrant article would transfer old capital funds to finish consultant work needed before a storm water utility option could be presented to voters at town meeting.

DPW requested funds to complete the bridge project after the original contractor failed to follow through; existing grant and FY22 capital funds cover part of the anticipated construction cost, with more needed for engineering and construction.
DPW compared the cost of renting a loader for the winter versus purchasing, finding purchase cheaper over a 15-year life; last winter's four-month rental was costly.

budget_items.topic: DPW: six-wheel dump truck / salt spreader replacements
budget_items.what_was_said: DPW described replacing aging snow/salt trucks, noting the chassis is a fraction of the cost and the upfitting (plow, dump, spreader) is the larger expense; goal is seven trucks for seven snow routes.

budget_items.topic: DPW: one-ton dump truck replacement schedule
budget_items.what_was_said: DPW obtained multiple quotes for routine one-ton truck replacements and requested funding on the high end of the quoted range to buffer against future price increases.

budget_items.topic: DPW: New West Townsend Road drainage design consultant
budget_items.what_was_said: DPW requested funds to design fixes for roughly eleven undocumented, deteriorating drainage pipe locations along the road; design costs would let construction be phased.
A failing 72-inch pipe under Goodridge Street needs replacement; because of the stream width the project may effectively become a small bridge, raising the cost.

DPW requested design funds to replace the aging, damaged salt shed with a fabric-style structure, also enabling anti-icing liquid infrastructure and reduced salt spillage near the municipal water supply.
Two consultants gave rough cost estimates for engineering an anti-icing liquid system (storage tanks, saddle tanks, spray bars) to reduce salt use.
A member reported the fund balance as of annual town meeting, noting the town cannot expect to add to it soon and asking the committee to weigh which size of project should draw on it.
A member flagged that the track and field project would likely require regular borrowing with a debt service on the order described, over a term no longer than the turf's expected life.

meetings.headline: Town manager says finance-department transition is causing substantial, monthslong operational and financial disruption
meetings.summary: The Select Board heard a Lunenburg Snow Riders equipment gift, ratified three town-hire appointments, and voted to sign a Massachusetts Teachers Association-linked advocacy letter to the state legislature on FY27 school funding over one member's objection about scope and a resident's objection about partisanship. The board worked through special-town-meeting warrant articles (voting recommendations on two planning board articles), heard the town manager describe a difficult and costly finance-department staffing transition and a corrected new-growth figure, and set up scheduling for a pre-town-meeting session and a tri-board meeting with the schools before entering executive session on a non-union personnel matter.

budget_items.what_was_said: The Lunenburg Snow Riders donated a portable chainsaw for police/fire use; no vote was needed because it falls under the gift-acceptance policy threshold.
The Snow Riders said they have brought over $200,000 in RTP grants to the community over 15 years, an 80/20 grant with roughly $60,000 representing the club's volunteer match.
The town manager reported actual new growth over the estimated $400,000 as approximately $180,000, correcting a rumor it was over a million.
MassDOT agreed to extend the $600,000 small bridge grant through December 31, 2027, so the town will not lose the funding; construction is now expected to run October 2026 to June 2027.

The town manager listed open positions including a new library assistant hire at 19 hours/week, and vacancies for payroll and benefits (36 hrs/week), dietary aide (9 hrs/week), heavy equipment operator, land use director (40 hrs/week) and recreation director (19 hrs/week).
The town manager corrected the earlier new-growth figure, saying it is actually $118,000, not $180,000.
The town manager is working with the finance director toward roughly $150,000 in FY26 budget adjustments, mostly consultant costs and vacation buyouts tied to the finance department transition.
Retiree health insurance came in about $100,000 higher than budgeted; the town manager hopes to absorb it using contingency positions already parked in the active budget.
About $140,000 remains in the health insurance stabilization fund, which the town manager would propose using if the retiree health insurance increase cannot otherwise be absorbed.

The town manager plans to bring the salary reserve transfer funding the first year of the new police contract to town meeting as a matter of tradition, with other salary reserve transfers handled directly at town meeting.

Members debated where to put a new elevator and whether to rebuild the 1965 Ritter annex to fix the two buildings' split-level access, reaching no decision.
One member raised abandoning Ritter for a new or purchased building; others pushed back on cost and on moving town government out of downtown.
The committee set aside the Brooks House as outside its scope and suggested a separate committee study non-town uses for it and 925 Mass. Ave.

meetings.headline: Assessors accepted the LA4 report and corrected the FY26 new-growth figure used to set the tax rate.
meetings.summary: The Board of Assessors reviewed the FY2026 interim year-end adjustments, accepted the LA4 assessment-to-sales-ratio report, and clarified that the new growth figure for the LA13 growth report had been corrected downward after duplicate entries were found in the state's Gateway system. The board also discussed methodology still needed for the new senior means-tested exemption tax shift, planning for the November 25th tax classification hearing, a possible GIS vendor change, the neighborhood/site-index restructuring effort ahead of town meeting, and scheduling a joint meeting with the select board to consider appointing a new assessor member.

budget_items.topic: Motor vehicle excise tax abatements processed
budget_items.what_was_said: The principal assessor reported a number of motor vehicle excise abatements processed in the past month, awaiting payment processing by the tax collector.
The board approved a batch of exemptions totaling a dollar figure at the prior meeting; approval and denial letters were mailed to residents on the 30th.

budget_items.topic: Single family sale price / LA4 assessment ratio
budget_items.what_was_said: The assessor reported the average single-family sale price for fiscal 2026 versus last year, an increase used in the LA4 assessment-to-sales ratio analysis.

The originally reported new growth figure was corrected downward after duplicates were found in the Gateway upload; a member clarified this was not several hundred thousand dollars more than expected.
The town had budgeted for new growth around a lower figure and came in roughly a quarter higher, though not the large jump some had assumed.
A member recalled prior year's new growth being much higher due to a large commercial building coming online, giving an approximate recollected figure.

budget_items.topic: New growth versus budget, net difference
budget_items.what_was_said: The new growth total was said to be only a modest amount higher than what was budgeted for the tax rate.
A line item figure for personal property assessments was mentioned as part of what makes the growth numbers confusing to reconcile.

Shifting the tax burden removed from approved senior means-tested exemption applicants onto all other taxpayers was described as amounting to only a small addition per bill, funded this year from the overlay account.
Of the applicants for the new senior means-tested exemption, some were approved, some needed new signatures, and some were denied, totaling six.

budget_items.topic: GIS/CI vendor invoices and possible new vendor cost
budget_items.what_was_said: The assessor noted receiving invoices from the current GIS vendor (CI) despite map updates not being completed, and mentioned a price increase; a competing vendor discussed offering a free transition period before a possible fiscal 2027 switch.

decisions.decision: Principal assessor to research and bring back a methodology for calculating the adjusted tax rate needed to redistribute the senior means-tested exemption shift onto other taxpayers.
Consensus to keep the neighborhood/site-index review process in-house rather than contracting it out, pending the seasonal position being funded at town meeting.

Board to arrange a joint meeting with the select board to consider appointing a new assessor board member, proposing Monday the 17th at 5:30pm or Thursday the 20th at 7:00pm, subject to the applicant's and town manager's availability.
Keep the senior exemption tax methodology item on the November 19th agenda.
Move discussion of Clause 18 and the GIS/CI vendor decision from November 19th to the December 3rd meeting.

why_it_matters: The LA4 report and the corrected new-growth figure are inputs to how the FY26 tax rate gets set, which affects every property tax bill in town.

The senior means-tested exemption removes tax burden from approved applicants and shifts it onto everyone else; how that shift is calculated is still being worked out and returns to the board on November 19.
The November 25 classification hearing is where the select board decides whether residential and commercial property are taxed at the same or different rates.

meetings.headline: Commission tabled a 763 Mass Ave sewer easement to weigh extending service down Chestnut Street
meetings.summary: The Sewer Commission held two public hearings on Massachusetts Avenue sewer easement waivers. The larger of the two, a request to consolidate three new house lots into one easement/tie-in near Chestnut Street, was continued to the next meeting so the applicant can locate an existing sewer stub and determine pipe size, after members debated whether granting it would foreclose ever extending sewer service down Chestnut Street; a second, smaller easement waiver for 830/832 Massachusetts Avenue was voted and passed. The commission also heard that town counsel reviewed proposed waiver-bylaw wording and recommended replacing "emergency" with "unusual and extraordinary," and got an update that a manhole repair is delayed because replacement frames arrived the wrong size.

meetings.headline: Board votes to recommend MBTA Communities compliance via a density bump at Tritown, not new sites
meetings.summary: The Lunenburg Planning Board endorsed a routine ANR lot-line adjustment for a Unitil substation expansion, then continued a contested storm water permit for 255 Sunny Hill Road to November 10 after abutters raised unresolved drainage-pipe and lawsuit concerns and outstanding taxes on the property surfaced. The board then closed public hearings and voted to recommend to town meeting both an MBTA Communities compliance bylaw (achieving compliance by raising the density cap at the existing Tritown development rather than opening new land) and a minor amendment removing a paving requirement from the common driveways bylaw, alongside routine committee reports and administrative votes.

In discussing development pressure, a board member cited the current median home assessment as an example of why builders want to build wherever they can.

The chair reported that Richard Harris is again being retained by the town as interim consultant/land use manager, after a prior gap caused by limits on his allowed hours, not any problem with the working relationship.
The chair noted the Capital Planning Committee begins hearing department requests this week and expects to function more as a ranking committee again this year given competing priorities.

Board agreed not to schedule a meeting three days before Christmas.

Chair will draft written material for the next meeting laying out why the zoning bylaw needs a full rewrite, to support future funding requests for a consultant.
Board directed the storm water applicant and the abutter to try to work out details of the pipe/culvert plan before the November 10 meeting.

The board also walked through a draft investment/operating policy line by line without voting on it, and ratified minutes from two prior meetings before adjourning.

meetings.headline: Task force voted to approve a scaled-back, roughly half-cost stormwater utility study proposal from Weston and Sampson.
meetings.summary: The Lunenburg Stormwater Task Force reviewed a revised, scaled-back proposal from consultant Weston and Sampson for a stormwater utility feasibility study, after members had met with the firm to cut scope items including background data collection, a DPW capabilities assessment, and an ArcGIS online tool, in order to roughly halve the cost. The task force voted to approve the revised proposal dated October 10, 2025, discussed funding it via reappropriation of unspent old capital project money through a November town meeting warrant article, and received an update that earthwork on their demonstration BMP project is complete with a kiosk and drainage grates still to be installed.

budget_items.what_was_said: The number of parcels to be covered by the impervious-cover GIS layer was discussed with several conflicting figures read off different copies of the proposal; the group settled that around 700 parcels, covering commercial and non-single-family properties, would be included.

budget_items.topic: Minimum square footage threshold for GIS parcel review
budget_items.what_was_said: The minimum square footage a property must have to be looked at was raised from the original Concord-based proposal figure to a higher figure in the new proposal.

The task force discussed removing most of the fee-structure work since they feel comfortable with what was already proposed for the town's own tiers, leaving Weston and Sampson to do a smaller review/advisory pass.

budget_items.topic: Task 2 cost - fee structure review, town vs. Concord comparison
budget_items.what_was_said: The cost for this task was compared to what Weston and Sampson charged Concord for similar work, and the new town figure was read out.
This task's cost was reported to have stayed the same as the prior proposal; printing and distribution costs are not included in the scope.

budget_items.topic: Meetings and project management scope and cost
budget_items.what_was_said: The number of small-group, public, and monthly progress meetings was cut roughly in half to a third, and the associated cost was reduced.

budget_items.topic: Total revised Weston and Sampson proposal cost
budget_items.what_was_said: The task force said the overall proposal cost was brought down substantially from the original figure after asking the consultant what budget they were targeting.

budget_items.topic: Task force's own budget vs. proposal cost
budget_items.what_was_said: A member said their current budget does not cover the new proposal cost and described a worst-case shortfall, noting the town manager has it covered but more money is still needed.

budget_items.what_was_said: Funding for the stormwater work is proposed to come from previously allocated but unspent capital project money, to be reappropriated via a town meeting warrant article.

meetings.headline: Consultants presented Lunenburg's draft master plan -- 8 goals, ~80 recommendations -- ahead of a December report; no votes held.
meetings.summary: This was the sixth and final public information session on Lunenburg's master plan, led by the steering committee chair, planning board chair Matt Brener, and consultants from OverUnder. The consultants walked through eight community-derived goals (housing options, farmland protection, small business support, open space/recreation, community gathering spaces, municipal building prioritization, school facilities, and resilient infrastructure) and roughly 80 supporting recommendations, then described a three-part implementation strategy (an implementation committee, a filter checklist, and an implementation table) before residents asked about the adequacy of public input and how town government might respond; the session then moved into hands-on breakout activities with no formal votes taken.

public_comment.stated_role: a resident who has participated in the master plan steering committee process

budget_items.topic: cost-tier framework for master plan recommendations (low/medium/high cost)
budget_items.what_was_said: The consultant proposed working cost categories for recommendations -- low, medium, and high -- to be tweaked with town staff feedback. Low and medium cost items were described as coverable within an operational budget, high cost typically not.

budget_items.topic: possible tax relief for senior citizens
budget_items.what_was_said: As property values and tax rates rise it becomes a greater burden for those on fixed incomes, so the plan may recommend the town consider tax relief for seniors. No figures were given.
A recommendation to establish an affordable housing trust was described as a clearinghouse to help identify funding opportunities for new homeowners, not a funding source itself.

A recommendation to create a fund to help preserve farmland when land goes up for sale, possibly giving the town a right of first refusal, so it stays open space rather than becoming developable land.
A recommendation to establish a town fund dedicated to stormwater infrastructure and maintenance.

decisions.decision: The consultants plan to hand the completed master plan report to the town in December.
The group agreed to move from Q&A directly into the breakout activity sessions, with further questions to be handled there.

The consultants walked through eight community-derived goals (housing options, farmland protection, small business support, open space/recreation, community gathering spaces, municipal building prioritization, school facilities, and resilient infrastructure) and roughly 80 supporting recommendations, then described a three-part implementation strategy (an implementation committee, a filter checklist, and an implementation table) before residents asked about the adequacy of public input and how town government might respond; the session then moved into hands-on breakout activities with no formal votes taken.

what_happened.line: Consultants presented Lunenburg's draft master plan -- eight goals and roughly 80 recommendations -- with a final report due in December.
The plan's implementation strategy pairs a new committee with a filter checklist and a table to prioritize recommendations.
Recommendations include a possible affordable housing trust, a farmland preservation fund, and a stormwater infrastructure fund, none funded yet.
A resident asked whether outreach for the plan reached enough residents, given low turnout at this final session.
No votes were taken; the session moved into breakout activities for further discussion.

why_it_matters: Any adopted housing trust, farmland fund, or stormwater fund would need its own town funding mechanism, which could reach a future town meeting warrant.
The plan's goals for schools, housing, and infrastructure could shape capital requests and budget priorities over the next decade.
watch_next: The completed master plan report, due to the town in December 2025.
How the proposed implementation committee and filter/priority table are set up to act on the recommendations.

meetings.headline: Commissioners move to fine and force removal of kayak racks illegally stored in the water supply protection zone
meetings.summary: The Board of Water Commissioners voted to move ahead with fines and possible forced removal to make the Woodlands take kayak racks out of the water supply protection zone, after months of the association's lawyer stalling. Commissioners also reviewed quotes for a new excavator to replace aging equipment, heard how much the district saved doing the Rolling Acres water main project in-house, and approved upgrading the district's billing software to better track backflow testing.

meetings.headline: ZBA approved a special permit for a used-car lot at 149 Summer Street, capping it at 12 display cars.
meetings.summary: The Lunenburg Zoning Board of Appeals held a public hearing on an application by Philip S. Smith to operate a used/secondhand motor vehicle sales lot at 149 Summer Street, a site currently used as a gas-station-turned-repair-garage. After lengthy questioning about the number of vehicles currently on the lot, environmental concerns from a former kerosene pump, lighting, hours, grandfathered repair-garage use, and parking layout, the board approved a special permit limiting the lot to 12 vehicles for sale plus five customer and four repair/employee parking spaces, with conditions including inside-only repair work and periodic compliance review, noting the applicant will still need planning board site plan approval.

budget_items.what_was_said: The applicant's written submission stated the proposed used-car business would not have any negative financial effect to the town and is fully compliant with the zoning ordinance.

decisions.decision: Board decided not to continue the hearing to wait for planning board action, choosing instead to act on the special permit now, noting planning board site plan approval would still be required afterward.

Board set the approved plan's parking layout (12 display cars, 5 customer spaces, 4 repair/employee spaces in back) as the fixed configuration the building inspector will enforce, rather than adding a separate 'not to exceed' numeric stipulation.
Board put on the record that all repair work must be conducted inside the building.

what_happened.line: Select Board voted 3-2 to pull the APDC/Historical Commission merger article from the special town meeting warrant.
The vote followed extended public opposition and a town counsel review of legal questions the merger raised.

The 41A article, if approved by voters at the November 18 special town meeting, would let more senior homeowners qualify to defer their property tax bills.
The special education reserve fund article changes how the town could set aside money for special-ed costs; it carries no budget impact yet, but a member noted it could down the road.

meetings.headline: Assessors pressed vendor Vision over late FY26 valuation data, pushing the classification hearing to late Nov/Dec
meetings.summary: The Board of Assessors reviewed a lengthy, repeatedly late set of FY26 interim property valuation adjustments from vendor Vision, expressing frustration over years of missed deadlines and unclear report formatting while working to finalize sales data (LA-3/LA-15) ahead of a tentative late-November classification hearing. The board also discussed a prospective new board member applicant, a warrant article raising the senior tax deferral income limit to the circuit breaker cap, a chapter-land property under a pending sale, a possible GIS mapping software upgrade, and drafted a response to the town's master plan committee, before entering executive session to review FY26 exemption applications.

budget_items.what_was_said: The principal assessor reported growth figures received from RRC for personal property, given as an assessed value and the corresponding tax dollars, described as growth only, not a new total.
A separate growth figure was given for the other property classes, described as being in valuation.
Combined growth in valuation was said to be roughly a figure that far exceeded an earlier estimate, credited partly to fieldwork finding previously unrecorded property.
The board signed the warrant for motor vehicle excise commitment number five, covering a stated number of bills and a total tax amount, for both the tax collector's and accountant's copies.

budget_items.topic: Interim value adjustments by property class (FY26)
budget_items.what_was_said: Vision's late interim adjustment figures were summarized: increases for single families, condos, two-families, three-families and the land curve, based on prior-year to current-year interim values and excluding growth.
The per-acre value used for excess or residual land beyond the prime site acreage was stated as unchanged from the prior year.

budget_items.topic: Seasonal temporary employee for neighborhood directive project
budget_items.what_was_said: Because no bids were received for the neighborhood directive project, the board discussed hiring a temporary/seasonal employee instead, to be added as a personnel item on the special town meeting warrant.

budget_items.topic: Clause 41A senior tax deferral income limit
budget_items.what_was_said: A warrant article for town meeting would raise the income limit for the senior tax deferral program from a fixed figure to one tied to the state circuit breaker credit's income cap, with some uncertainty about how the cap applies to married/head-of-household filers.

budget_items.topic: Chapter 61 rollback taxes / lien on land taken out of chapter land
budget_items.what_was_said: A property removed from chapter land after failing to file an application was returned to full value, and the owner remains liable for a period of back rollback taxes because a lien had been recorded.

budget_items.topic: Cost to record a chapter-land lien with the Registry of Deeds
budget_items.what_was_said: Recording a chapter-land lien costs a fee paid by check to the Registry of Deeds, not out of the assessors' office budget.

An estimate for a mapping software upgrade was described as a modest increase over current cost, but could not be pursued until fiscal 2027; the board wants more detail on field-mapping functionality and possibly other vendors before committing.

decisions.decision: Put establishing hardship criteria for Clause 18 tax relief on the agenda for the next meeting, before any application is reviewed.
Revise the executive session minutes language to read "the first two of a total of eight" applications reviewed, rather than implying all eight were reviewed.
Try to schedule an additional meeting the following week, tentatively Wednesday October 22 at 6:30pm, focused on reviewing interim adjustments.
Hold the tentative classification hearing on November 25 or December 2, pending approval of the LA-3/LA-15 submission.
Send the board's drafted response to the master planning committee covering exemptions and chapter land programs.

The board will hold off on any action regarding the chapter-land property under a purchase-and-sale agreement until the Select Board's first-right-of-refusal process and open space committee review progress further.
Add a code-of-conduct document (modeled on one from Littleton) to a future agenda for discussion.
Have the principal assessor ask the town's IT/records contact whether board members can be granted access to a shared file system without each creating a separate account.
Prioritize meeting with any new applicants for the vacant board seat at the next meeting if scheduling allows.

meetings.headline: Commission will refer unauthorized trail-building in town conservation land to the town attorney.
meetings.summary: The Lunenburg Conservation Commission held a routine hearing session: it approved a notice of intent for a septic system replacement at 23 Tilton Avenue, continued a DPW culvert-replacement hearing at Northfield crossing to November 5, approved an administrative determination for a dock replacement at 135 Flynn Road with an erosion-control condition, and granted a partial certificate of compliance for 155 Reservoir Road. It also voted to move funds into its trail-maintenance account, discussed a chapter 61 forest cutting plan on Flat Hill Road on which it has no regulatory authority, and flagged unauthorized trail-building on town conservation land for referral to the town attorney.

budget_items.what_was_said: A commission member relayed a request from an absent member, hospitalized, that $2,000 be added to the MACPO trail/bridge fund to cover cost overruns from a United Way Caring Day boardwalk and bridge project.
Volunteers estimated the remaining material cost needed to finish proposed catwalks near the Mulpus Brook bridge.
After covering the overage and new material, a member estimated funds would remain in the MACPO for upcoming winter/spring bridge and walkway repairs.

decisions.decision: Consultant engineer will send a formal letter outlining next steps, and the chair will request an extension from the grant administrator for the wildlife-viewing-platform access road project.
Chair will contact the town manager and the town's attorney, Adam Costa, about unauthorized trail-building in the Lane and Largetown Forest conservation area.
Chair will follow up with a commission member (Mike) about the agenda PDF's hyperlink not working when converted/uploaded.

meetings.headline: Committee reversed itself, voting to let soccer teams wear the new uniforms already purchased
meetings.summary: The School Committee accepted PTO donations, a state legislative earmark for primary-school touch screens and restoring I-Ready, and reversed a prior vote to release new soccer uniforms to players this season. The bulk of the meeting covered an assessment/accountability report showing concerning third-grade reading and special-education scores linked partly to prior budget cuts, followed by the superintendent's FY28 budget priorities, her first-year evaluation goals, and a discussion setting draft committee goals around Turkey Hill's future, capital planning, and a more reasoned budget-decision process.

budget_items.what_was_said: The parent-teacher organization donated funds to each school, left to each principal's discretion, and the committee voted to accept three such donations.
The superintendent described a one-time, non-recurring earmark from state legislators that cannot be added to the base budget; the captions gave inconsistent figures for the total and its two pieces.
The superintendent proposed spending part of the earmark on touch screens for every primary school classroom, the only school without them, replacing projectors.
The superintendent proposed restoring I-Ready diagnostic and instructional access for at least one more year; asked the cost, she said it was about 47.

The district considered using the earmark for smaller transportation vans instead, but determined the cost would exceed the available money and require driver stipends and special licenses, so it was not pursued.
Members noted the athletic fee was previously increased and is intended to partially cover uniform costs, though it does not cover the full cost.

The district previously cut a single dedicated Wilson reading position at Turkey Hill and instead used training funds to certify multiple inclusion teachers district-wide in the Wilson reading system.

Members discussed that compensation, especially for paraprofessionals, is weak compared to other districts, making positions hard to fill, though the superintendent cited staff loyalty to Lunenburg as a mitigating factor.

budget_items.topic: Teacher and instructional staff retention rate
budget_items.what_was_said: The superintendent set a goal of 90% or higher staff retention; last year's rate, which included layoffs, was described as concerningly low.
A member asked about anticipated multi-year budget impacts as union contracts, capped at three-year terms, come up for renewal; the business manager is building this into the long-term forecast.
The superintendent said she is conservatively forecasting entitlement grant funding to come in lower next year given uncertainty at the federal level.

budget_items.topic: Turkey Hill Elementary renovation cost estimate
budget_items.what_was_said: A member cited a prior renovation estimate for Turkey Hill, calling it likely too low, while pushing the committee to commit to a renovate-or-rebuild direction.
A warrant article is expected proposing the school committee give up budget responsibility for Kids Kingdom; a member said this would make the school budget more realistic.

The superintendent's first-year evaluation goals will be a formal action item at next month's meeting.

Rather than a strict numeric formula, the committee leaned toward a small set of guiding questions/rubric, building on the superintendent's five budget-priority questions, to weigh competing budget requests.
A member will draft written testimony on the statewide K-2 (Chapter 70) school finance formula for the committee to review, to potentially submit to the state working group.
The committee will talk with the facilities director about Turkey Hill as a next step.

meetings.headline: Finance Committee pushed back on rushing Personnel Committee/APDC bylaw changes to November Town Meeting
meetings.summary: The Finance Committee spent most of the meeting reviewing two Special Town Meeting warrant articles proposed by the Town Manager -- eliminating the Personnel Committee and merging the APDC into the Historical Commission -- with a member arguing both need more public process before going to voters, and the committee agreeing to vote on the full warrant at its next meeting (Oct. 23) ahead of the Nov. 18 Special Town Meeting. Members also discussed FY26 school budget growth compared to FY25 actuals, long-term facilities/capital planning (Turkey Hill, Ritter/Town Hall building costs), separation of the town accountant and finance director roles, and approved prior tri-board meeting minutes.

budget_items.topic: Special Town Meeting warrant: eliminate Personnel Committee
budget_items.what_was_said: A member argued eliminating the Personnel Committee is too big a change to make without more public input and comparison to other towns' experience.

budget_items.what_was_said: A member raised concerns about folding the Architectural/Preservation Design Commission's function into the Historical Commission without a public process.

budget_items.topic: FY26 school budget vs FY25 actuals
budget_items.what_was_said: A member said the schools' FY26 budget is well above FY25 actual spending, calling it a large one-year increase on a roughly $25 million budget.

budget_items.topic: FY25 override plus increase, two-year total
budget_items.what_was_said: The same member noted FY25 included the override plus an additional increase, adding up to a large combined increase over two years.

budget_items.topic: Ritter/Town Hall building cost estimating approach
budget_items.what_was_said: A member suggested using a rough-order-of-magnitude cost-per-square-foot estimate rather than paying for full architectural design work upfront.
Members worried that redesign costs on town building projects have been paid multiple times over and cautioned against spending heavily on plans that go unused.
A member recalled the earlier building project estimate was set deliberately high so the town would not later be asked for significantly more money.

budget_items.topic: Possible solar panel revenue on parking lot
budget_items.what_was_said: If extra money were available from the building project, the committee had discussed adding solar panels on a parking lot to generate revenue.

budget_items.topic: Special Town Meeting hearing timing requirement
budget_items.what_was_said: Members discussed whether a finance committee hearing on money articles must be posted a set number of days before the Special Town Meeting.

decisions.decision: Committee agreed it does not need to vote on the Special Town Meeting warrant articles at this meeting; a vote will happen at a later meeting before the November Town Meeting.
Several members agreed the Personnel Committee and APDC warrant articles are premature for the November Special Town Meeting and should wait, possibly until the May Annual Town Meeting.
Committee agreed to ask the tri-board presenters to send budget presentation materials about a week ahead of the meeting rather than the day of.

Committee decided not to align itself with other committees' individual bylaws/policies when responding to the master plan steering committee questionnaire, since Finance only reviews financial impact.
Committee determined the next meeting, October 23rd, will serve as the vote/hearing on the Special Town Meeting warrant, to meet the 14-day requirement before the November 18th Town Meeting.

meetings.headline: Commission voted to give its chairman broad authority to investigate town land sales and trust-fund handling.
meetings.summary: The Trust Fund Commission chair delivered an extended report on the commission's research into its fiduciary duties over gifted real estate, scholarships, cemetery funds and historical assets, citing case law (Woodward School for Girls v. Quincy, Cohen v. Lynn, Carol v. Select Board of Norwell) to argue the town may owe proceeds from sold trust land back to designated purposes. meetings.headline: Water Commission delays a vote on a roughly $90,000 PFAS pilot study, awaiting DEP input before a special town meeting

The board reviewed but did not vote on a broad rewrite of the town's personnel bylaw that would dissolve the Personnel Committee and change vacation, sick leave and grievance rules.
The town manager said free cash may not be certified before the warrant prints but is expected by mid-November, which would determine whether some capital items rely on older appropriations instead.

why_it_matters: The special-education reserve fund would let the town cover unanticipated out-of-district placement costs without a town meeting vote, though a board member raised whether it could mask underfunding of the special-education line rather than fix it.

The Architectural Preservation District article affects any resident in that district doing exterior repairs, and a resident's objection that it bypassed the normal zoning-change process could shape whether it comes back for a public hearing before Town Meeting votes on it.

The personnel bylaw rewrite would change how town employees accrue leave and file grievances and who has authority over those decisions, which affects the workforce providing town services even though it is not a resident-facing vote.

meetings.headline: Board can't fund new means-tested tax exemptions in Munis; approved contingent on fixing that.
meetings.summary: The Board of Assessors reviewed routine assessing operations -- exemption and abatement processing, chapter land applications, removal of unsupported functional/economic obsolescence discounts, and pending vendor-supplied interim property valuations -- and worked through several minutes approvals. The most substantive discussion was that the town has no established mechanism to fund newly-authorized means-tested property tax exemptions, so the board planned to approve the current applicants contingent on resolving how the cost will be spread across taxpayers; the board also reviewed a GIS/mapping software proposal and discussed staffing and office-hours pressures. The meeting closed by entering executive session to discuss abatement/exemption applications under the statutory exemption for such proceedings.

budget_items.what_was_said: The office reported four abatement requests and 43 motor vehicle excise tax abatements processed in Munis for September, awaiting payment processing by the tax collector.
FY2026 real estate exemption applications were mailed September 1st with an April 1 deadline; applications received by mid-November will still be applied to the next tax bill.
The 41D exemption amount was increased with a cost-of-living adjustment, and income/asset limits were adjusted at town meeting for both 41D and 17E/F.

budget_items.topic: Social security income deduction for 41D eligibility
budget_items.what_was_said: After consulting DLS, the assessor confirmed a social security income deduction can be applied to 41D applications, which brings some previously-excluded applicants back into eligibility.
Chapter land applications for fiscal year 2027 are due December 1st, and the office is now requiring all supporting paperwork before processing.

budget_items.topic: Roll-back tax invoice, 222 West Townsend Road
budget_items.what_was_said: A roll-back tax invoice was prepared after a chapter land property lost its exemption; the select board reportedly declined right of first refusal.
The FY2026 smart-growth cost report covering motor vehicle excise and additional property tax revenue, largely tied to Tri Town Drive, was submitted to DLS and the state; growth funding is expected.

New growth in tax dollars for residential, commercial, industrial and chapter land was reported, with personal property growth from a vendor still pending and expected to exceed the town's original estimate.

budget_items.topic: DLS request to accelerate free cash reporting
budget_items.what_was_said: The board noted a DLS request to accelerate free cash certification and said it needs to check with the town accountant on timing.
Discounts removed after inspections or non-response totaled a stated tax-assessed value and tax-dollar impact, following a Department of Revenue order to remove unexplained discounts.
A separate set of economic obsolescence discounts (excluding commercial items handled by the vendor) was removed, with a stated assessed-value and tax-dollar impact.
The board noted the 41A income limit had been unchanged for exactly two decades at a stated figure, which had caused at least one prior applicant to be rejected.

budget_items.topic: 41A adoption/interest rate proposal from Council on Aging
budget_items.what_was_said: A warrant article submitted via the Council on Aging proposed adopting 41A (already state-mandated and previously adopted) and lowering its interest rate; the assessor called it unnecessary and duplicative.

budget_items.topic: Roll-back taxes, chapter land release (six lots)
budget_items.what_was_said: A chapter land parcel is being released from chapter status, generating roll-back taxes with interest, with the property expected to become six new house lots.

budget_items.topic: GIS/mapping software ("One Map"/Data Scout) proposal cost
budget_items.what_was_said: A proposed GIS mapping and field-data platform was compared against the town's existing CI/CAI mapping contract, with a net annual cost increase discussed for switching or adding the new service.

Eight applications for a means-tested exemption were reported as qualifying, representing a small share of the tax levy, but there is no method in Munis to implement the burden-shift the statute requires.

budget_items.topic: Overlay account as possible funding source for means-tested exemptions
budget_items.what_was_said: The board discussed whether the overlay reserve account could absorb the cost of the means-tested exemptions, noting that is not the account's intended purpose.
The board discussed wanting to increase the part-time inspector/assistant's hours, citing a backlog of roughly 500 needed inspections, ahead of the May town meeting.

decisions.decision: Assessor will apply the DLS-confirmed social security income deduction to 41D applications, restoring eligibility for some applicants close to the income limit.
Assessor asked the Town Manager's office to document the Select Board's declination of first refusal on 222 West Townsend Road in a letter for the file.
Board asked the assessor to have future sales reports sorted by percent change rather than by ratio, and broken out by neighborhood/site index.
Board agreed to hold off requesting a new sales report from the vendor until the Department of Revenue submission process is complete.
Revised 41A warrant article draft (with added income explanation) to be submitted to the Town Manager ahead of tomorrow's deadline.
No action needed on the Council on Aging's proposed 41A adoption/interest-rate warrant article, since 41A is already state-mandated and previously adopted; feedback given to the Town Manager.
Board will approve the eight qualifying means-tested exemption applications tonight contingent on later resolving how they will actually be funded/implemented in Munis.
Assessor will forward Westford's disabled-persons exemption criteria for the board to consider drafting a comparable local-option exemption.
Room reservation for the October 15th meeting will stand for now, to be cancelled if the date changes.

The assessor confirmed with the Department of Revenue that a social security income deduction can be applied to 41D applications, restoring eligibility for some applicants near the income limit.
The board asked the Town Manager's office to put in writing that the Select Board declined the town's right of first refusal on a property at 222 West Townsend Road.

meetings.headline: Committee backed a special-ed reserve-fund warrant article but withdrew a separate bid for extra Chapter 70 money
meetings.summary: The committee voted to put a special reserve fund for unbudgeted out-of-district special education and transportation costs on the November town meeting warrant, approved two new paraprofessional positions and restoring a full-time IT support position, and heard quarterly budget, athletics, and facilities reports. After extended debate, a second proposed warrant article to immediately appropriate roughly $22,185 in additional Chapter 70 funding was withdrawn in favor of seeking it through the regular FY27 budget process, and a proposal for an outside comprehensive/forensic audit of FY25 finances was deferred pending further talks with the town manager; the committee also discussed what to do about football and soccer uniforms that had been purchased without proper authorization.

what_happened.line: The committee voted to place a special reserve fund for unbudgeted out-of-district special education and transportation costs on the November town meeting warrant.
A separate warrant article seeking additional Chapter 70 funding, an amount as heard, was withdrawn in favor of pursuing it through the regular FY27 budget process.
The committee approved two new paraprofessional positions and restoring a full-time IT support position, both drawn from the salary reserve line.
A proposal for an outside comprehensive audit of FY25 finances, funded from returned free cash, was deferred pending talks with the town manager.
Football and soccer uniforms bought without required purchase-order approval will not be penalized retroactively; undistributed soccer uniforms will be held for next year's replacement rotation.

why_it_matters: The reserve fund is a warrant article residents will vote on at November town meeting; it would let year-end school budget surplus automatically cover special education placement and transportation costs that come in over budget.
Withdrawing the Chapter 70 warrant article means any additional state aid this year would not be spent immediately but would instead be weighed against other priorities in the FY27 budget process.

The unauthorized uniform purchases and the salary-reserve-funded hires prompted the committee to signal it will develop a policy requiring pre-approval before staff spend outside the certified budget.

Policy subcommittee's proposed pre-approval policy for spending outside the certified budget

budget_items.topic: MART Council on Aging agreement - insurance language
budget_items.what_was_said: The agreement's insurance clause for MART was holdover language never actually charged; town staff said it was a cleanup, not a substantive change.

budget_items.topic: DPW snow/ice: own equipment vs. hiring out
budget_items.what_was_said: Bill Bernard said an analysis showed it is cheaper to use town equipment and operators than to hire private vendors, based on the cost of the highest-paid heavy equipment operator.
The DPW director plans to request a new CDL-class dump truck in this year's capital request, noting the price has risen sharply since he first priced the same truck in 2022.
The DPW director said the department has run a deficit in the snow and ice budget over the last five years and plans a 2.5% annual increase to reduce, but not eliminate, it.
Failure to comply with the federal MS4 stormwater permit could carry penalties, though the director does not expect the town would actually be fined that amount.
The DPW director said the plan is a flat annual fee for residential properties, with a sliding scale for businesses based on impervious surface.

budget_items.topic: Storm water utility revenue target vs. current spending
budget_items.what_was_said: The DPW director said the target is to collect roughly a set amount annually through the new utility, well above what the current storm water/drainage budget spends.
The DPW director gave a preliminary multi-year capital outlook covering equipment replacement and drainage/bridge engineering and construction.

budget_items.topic: Cost difference if storm water utility is not enacted
budget_items.what_was_said: The director said drainage and storm water line items would need to be higher in FY28 and FY29 if the utility is not approved, compared with if it is.
The DPW director said he assumed the typical annual Chapter 90 amount going forward, not the doubled amount received this year, because it is uncertain whether the increase continues.
A board member asked whether fair share money promised when voters supported the tax would continue; the DPW director said that was uncertain.

budget_items.topic: TCP building revolving account deficit closeout
budget_items.what_was_said: Officials recalled a one-time payment made at special town meeting to zero out a negative TCP revolving fund balance that had built up because the building had no real operating budget.
The facilities director said TCP's gas bill has historically run around a certain amount and he is projecting roughly half that as the building is partially decommissioned.
The facilities director restored the cleaning contract budget to its FY25 level after issues with the cleaning contractor.

budget_items.topic: TCP expense line / lost rent offset
budget_items.what_was_said: A line was added back to the facilities budget to cover the loss of rent revenue after the extended day program left the TCP building.

budget_items.topic: Food pantry electricity use at TCP
budget_items.what_was_said: The facilities director estimated the food pantry's refrigeration equipment accounts for a large share of TCP's electric cost, with an equipment-rated estimate versus a measured range.

The facilities director said he has not fully estimated the abatement cost for the decommissioned half of the TCP building but would not be surprised if it reached a certain figure; this would be requested as a capital item.
The facilities director noted the building now carries a commercial internet cost, mainly for the public access studio, higher than he expected.

budget_items.topic: Fire Dept. FY27 salary increase for 4th shift
budget_items.what_was_said: The fire chief said the salary increase reflects three step-two firefighter paramedics and one promotion to lieutenant, based on the current collective bargaining agreement.
The chief said overtime would rise due to additional time off accrued by new staff and a higher overtime rate under the new work-week schedule.
Holiday pay would increase to cover three additional staff and a higher average overtime rate.
The chief summarized the combined increase across hiring and overtime lines needed to fund a fourth shift.

budget_items.topic: Fire Dept. benefits (OPEB) cost of new hires
budget_items.what_was_said: The chief said the benefits estimate for the new positions, developed with HR and finance, assumes a worst-case top-end family health plan.

budget_items.topic: Fire Dept. total requested budget increase
budget_items.what_was_said: The chief gave the combined total increase across salary and benefits needed to add the fourth shift.

budget_items.topic: Fire Dept. EMS supplies and equipment maintenance
budget_items.what_was_said: The chief requested an increase to cover rising costs of medication, oxygen, disposable supplies and required annual servicing of paramedic-level equipment.

budget_items.topic: Fire Dept. vehicle maintenance / prior reserve fund transfer
budget_items.what_was_said: The chief noted he had requested a reserve fund transfer this past fiscal year to cover an ambulance repair, part of a broader increase needed in vehicle maintenance.

budget_items.topic: Fire Dept. total requested expense-line increase
budget_items.what_was_said: The chief gave the total requested increase across the department's expense lines.

budget_items.topic: Police lockup costs / Worcester County Sheriff program
budget_items.what_was_said: The police chief said housing male prisoners through the Worcester County Sheriff's program sharply cut the lockup budget from what it used to run.
The police chief said the town's share of regional dispatch costs stays roughly steady regardless of call volume, split evenly among member towns by formula.

budget_items.topic: Police vehicle maintenance - hybrid battery failures
budget_items.what_was_said: The chief said three hybrid cruiser batteries failed this year around the same mileage, each costing roughly the same amount to replace, though covered by warranty this time.

budget_items.topic: Police collective bargaining agreement, next three years
budget_items.what_was_said: The chief said the new contract calls for salary increases over the next three years, with expenses otherwise level-funded.

meetings.headline: Superintendent signals schools want to keep the ACE program and central offices at Turkey Hill, shrinking the town hall project.
meetings.summary: The Lunenburg Municipal Building Design Committee interviewed new Superintendent Dr. Fortuna, who said the ACE program must stay collocated with the director of special services and that the superintendent's office does not need to be collocated with the town manager — a reversal of the prior superintendent's stated need that had driven significant square footage into the Ritter/town hall renovation plan. The committee treated this as a major finding that could shrink its project scope, discussed reduced need for a single consolidated town hall given growing online town services, set two Brooks House tour dates with the facilities director, and scheduled its next meeting for October 20th to get the town manager's input on collocation needs.

The committee treated this as a major finding that could shrink its project scope, discussed reduced need for a single consolidated town hall given growing online town services, set two Brooks House tour dates with the facilities director, and scheduled its next meeting for October 20th to get the town manager's input on collocation needs.

meetings.headline: Commission voted to draw an extra $10,000 from the sale-of-lots fund to cover hedge and grounds work.
meetings.summary: The Lunenburg Cemetery Commission approved three sets of prior meeting minutes, reviewed cemetery fund expenditures and balances, and voted to draw an additional $10,000 from the sale-of-lots fund to cover hedge trimming and grounds work. The board also received updates on the North Cemetery backlot expansion engineering survey, South Cemetery stone wall repairs, burial and niche-wall activity, grant options, and historical headstone repairs, and set its meeting schedule through the winter before adjourning.

budget_items.what_was_said: The board reviewed a spreadsheet listing recent expenditures already approved by motion, including flower plantings, a file cabinet, SIMS software maintenance, and North Cemetery hedge and stone wall work.

budget_items.topic: Remaining amount owed on approved projects
budget_items.what_was_said: After the backlot expansion (funded from the capital plan) was set aside, a remaining balance was calculated for the other approved but unpaid expenditures.

budget_items.topic: Perpetual care and capital transfer fund allocation
budget_items.what_was_said: The chair allocated last year's expenditures between the perpetual care fund and the capital transfer fund.
After subtracting the allocated amounts, remaining balances were calculated in both the perpetual care fund and the capital transfer fund.
The board worked through what total funds remained after the committed expenditures were subtracted, concluding they did not yet have enough for the remaining hedge trimming work.
The sale of lots fund was identified as an available source to draw additional money from.

budget_items.topic: Additional draw from sale of lots fund
budget_items.what_was_said: The board voted to request an additional amount from the sale of lots fund to cover the shortfall for hedge trimming and related work.

budget_items.topic: Engineering cost for backlot expansion survey
budget_items.what_was_said: The engineer's fee for the site survey and plan phase of the North Cemetery backlot expansion was discussed, funded from the capital plan allocation.
After the engineering cost, the board discussed how much of the capital plan allocation for the backlot expansion remained.

budget_items.topic: Hedge trimming and hedge planting expenditures
budget_items.what_was_said: The board distinguished between an already-approved amount for purchasing and installing new hedges and a separate, not-yet-approved amount for trimming existing hedges.

budget_items.topic: South Cemetery stone wall repair cost
budget_items.what_was_said: The board confirmed it had agreed to pay a set amount for a contractor to begin rebuilding a collapsed section of the South Cemetery stone wall, to be reassessed once that amount is used.
The board discussed pursuing a Massachusetts preservation projects grant but noted this cycle's deadline was too close to prepare an application in time.
The board agreed to get a price to repair damaged half-headstones for a historical family plot, using salvaged stone rather than new monuments.

budget_items.topic: Children's grave marker and plaque cost
budget_items.what_was_said: The board discussed getting a price from a monument company for a granite marker and bronze plaque to mark several unmarked children's graves, using stone Bill already has on hand.

decisions.decision: Backlot expansion bid work will be scheduled for summer rather than winter.
Hedge trimming will be done on a two-year cycle going forward.
South Cemetery stone wall repair will be completed before starting similar work at North Cemetery, done one section at a time.
Next meetings set for October 30th and November 19th, with a target of meeting again in the second week of December rather than skipping to February.
A SIMS software training session will be scheduled separately and will not be publicized or recorded as a regular open meeting.

meetings.headline: Task force to slash Weston & Sampson stormwater fee-study scope to fit budget, then bring it to the Town Manager
meetings.summary: The Stormwater Task Force reviewed a new, expensive scope-of-work proposal from consultant Weston & Sampson for a stormwater utility fee study and worked through cutting it down task by task -- excluding residential parcels from impervious-area assessment, dropping two tasks entirely, and reducing the number of public and progress meetings -- to bring a smaller cost figure back to the Town Manager. They also approved prior minutes by roll call, discussed funding the study via a Chapter 90 transfer instead of a special town meeting, gave input to the master plan steering committee, and set the next meeting for October 16.

budget_items.topic: Weston & Sampson stormwater utility feasibility study proposal
budget_items.what_was_said: The task force reviewed a new cost estimate from Weston and Sampson (successor to prior consultant CI) and said it "breaks the bank," prompting discussion of reducing the scope of work.
A member asked how much is left to spend on the storm water initiative; Bill said the demonstration BMP would draw further from that same pool, leaving little remaining.

Members questioned where CI's parcel counts came from, since the GIS database was updated more recently than CI's report; they discussed narrowing the number of parcels needing individual impervious-area review by excluding residential codes.
A member estimated that excluding residential parcels and other scope cuts to Task 3/Task 4 would save a meaningful amount.
Members discussed a target figure they are trying to reach for the overall consultant scope, referencing a number below what was originally proposed.
Members discussed whether bills should go out quarterly or twice a year to save printing/mailing cost, noting the per-bill amount would simply be larger if billed less often.

budget_items.topic: Revised total scope-of-work cost after cuts
budget_items.what_was_said: A member did quick math on cutting Task 6 meetings in half and eliminating Tasks 2 and 4, arriving at a reduced total to bring back to the Town Manager.

budget_items.topic: Comparison to prior consultant CI's pricing
budget_items.what_was_said: Members compared the new reduced estimate to what CI had charged for a comparable scope including BMP and storm water utility work.

budget_items.topic: Chapter 90 funds as possible funding source
budget_items.what_was_said: Rather than a special town meeting request, a member suggested transferring available Chapter 90 highway funds into the storm water study, noting the town may receive a larger Chapter 90 allocation this year that has not yet arrived.

budget_items.topic: Town budget capacity for the study
budget_items.what_was_said: A member noted the town's contact (Jen) does not have funds on hand to cover the study's cost either, reinforcing the need to reduce scope before returning to her.

decisions.decision: Modify Task 3 of the Weston & Sampson scope to exclude residential parcels (and related codes such as condos) from individual impervious-area review.
Remove Task 2 and Task 4 from the proposed scope of work, and reduce Task 6 to one small-group meeting, two public presentations, and five monthly progress meetings.
Take the reduced scope-of-work cost figure to the Town Manager before proceeding.
Explore transferring available Chapter 90 highway funds to cover the study cost rather than seeking money at a special town meeting.
Set up a call/Zoom with Weston & Sampson, with one or two task force members participating, to discuss reducing the scope of work.

Respond to the master plan steering committee's questionnaire identifying the storm water infrastructure fund item, and taking the position that storm water infrastructure also counts as a resiliency strategy for conservation land.
Produce a durable (tin/aluminum) sign for the storm water BMP kiosk describing what the demonstration BMP is and how it works, then hand the design off to be fabricated.
Set the next meeting date for October 16.

meetings.headline: Entire town finance department is turning over at once; a new finance director starts October 20
meetings.summary: The Lunenburg Finance Committee heard that the town's entire finance department is turning over — the finance director, the payroll/benefits administrator, and the assistant accountant are all leaving, with a new finance director, Katie McKenna, hired to start October 20 and interim coverage in place. The committee also reviewed a master planning committee questionnaire (voted to send it), previewed the upcoming tri-board meeting and the town meeting warrant (including dropping a TC Pacios roof repair article and possible personnel board and pay-plan changes), and discussed ongoing efforts to reconcile school budget data, without resolving the underlying discrepancies.

budget_items.topic: Line-item budget review approach for tri-board departments
budget_items.what_was_said: A member said the committee should not scrutinize small line items like a name-tag purchase and should instead focus on major changes, and that departments should vet ideas with their own boards before bringing budget requests to finance committee.

budget_items.topic: TC Pacios roof warrant article / FY23 capital appropriation
budget_items.what_was_said: The town manager recommended not moving forward with a partial roof repair warrant article; the prior FY23 appropriation would stay attached to that year's capital projects and be reappropriated through the normal capital planning process rather than returned to free cash.

budget_items.topic: School budget $600k underrun / current fiscal year baseline
budget_items.what_was_said: The chair described ongoing questions to the superintendent and new business manager about a reported underrun and where money went relative to the current fiscal year's budget baseline.

budget_items.topic: School department purchase orders and encumbrances
budget_items.what_was_said: A member described how duplicate or unclosed purchase orders inflate apparent spending, citing figures that moved as POs were closed and money was freed up as encumbrances were resolved.

decisions.decision: Chair's completed master planning committee questionnaire responses would be sent to the master plan steering committee as filled in.

The partial TC Pacios roof repair will not proceed as a warrant article; the roof project will instead go through the normal capital planning process, with the prior FY23 appropriation left in place for reappropriation.
Finance committee will aim to review the Q1 FY26 Munis report at its October 23rd meeting.
Town finance policies review will be brought back onto the agenda in November rather than waiting until the end of the calendar year.

The town manager recommended dropping a partial roof repair project from the town meeting warrant, routing it through the normal capital planning process instead.

meetings.headline: Board delays costly Kedings PFAS pilot study pushed by state, awaits Tighe & Bond's price first
meetings.summary: The Lunenburg Water District Commissioners reviewed and signed the warrant, approved prior minutes, and discussed a proposal from Verdantis/a hydrogeologist to investigate potential bedrock well sites near 361 Mass Path, deciding to get test-well pricing before signing any agreement. They also voted on a policy formalizing employee use of district vehicles for on-call response, received an update on the Rolling Acres water main replacement project (including a failed-then-repeated bacteria test and future equipment needs like a skid steer, sweeper and trailer), discussed a poorly-executed private trench dig on Harbor Road that had to be redone to proper depth, and heard extended public comment from a resident challenging the necessity and cost of an additional DEP-driven pilot study on treating water from the Kedings well.

budget_items.topic: Verdantis fracture-trace/drilling-site study near 361 Mass Path
budget_items.what_was_said: A hydrogeologist proposed redoing a fracture-trace analysis and staking test sites for a potential bedrock well behind Walmart. The commission discussed the cost of this first step before any decision on drilling.

budget_items.topic: Cost to drill a bedrock test well
budget_items.what_was_said: After the site study, drilling and testing an actual bedrock test well was estimated as a further cost, separate from the site study.
Commissioners compared recent residential well-drilling prices as a reference point for what a test well might cost, disagreeing on what a fair price should be.

budget_items.topic: Casing cost for a test well
budget_items.what_was_said: A commissioner estimated the added cost of casing a well hole, on top of the drilling cost, as a hypothetical total.

budget_items.topic: Pressure-test pump for water main work
budget_items.what_was_said: The superintendent said a pump to pressure-test and chlorinate mains in-house was more expensive than expected, but was not asking for a vote, only flagging it for future purchase.
Commissioners discussed buying a trailer to haul a trench box and other equipment, comparing a flat trailer against a tilt-deck model.
A commissioner said a price quote for equipment (discussed in context of a skid steer) came in higher than expected just before the meeting.

budget_items.topic: Rolling Acres water main: in-house labor vs. contracted cost comparison
budget_items.what_was_said: The superintendent plans to track costs of doing the Rolling Acres work with district crews versus what a contracted/budgeted price would have been, to justify future equipment purchases.

budget_items.topic: Tighe & Bond additional Kedings pH/precipitation pilot study cost
budget_items.what_was_said: A resident and commissioners discussed the cost of an additional pilot study DEP is requiring related to Kedings well water treatment, with the superintendent saying the true cost was not yet known but guessing at a lower figure than initially feared.

budget_items.topic: PFAS treatment bed-volume figures used in Tighe & Bond's cost analysis
budget_items.what_was_said: The resident argued the engineering firm used an incorrect, much higher bed-volume figure in their cost analysis table for treating Kedings water, which would overstate operating costs.

decisions.decision: Hold off signing the Verdantis fracture-trace/site-study agreement and first get pricing for actual test wells before proceeding.
Superintendent will compile a cost comparison of in-house vs. contracted water main work (using the Rolling Acres job) to help decide on future equipment purchases.
A private contractor doing a water tap/trench near Harbor Road was ordered to redig and redo the trench to the required depth after it was found too shallow.
Wait to see Tighe & Bond's cost proposal for the additional Kedings pH pilot study before deciding whether to push back on the DEP requirement.

meetings.headline: Committee found the master plan has no prioritized list of town capital projects and began building one from GIS records
meetings.summary: The Master Plan Steering Committee reviewed feedback received so far from other town boards and committees (Open Space Committee, EDC, Council on Aging, Capital Planning, Architectural Preservation District Commission) on draft master plan recommendations, and discussed a newly obtained list from the town manager of statutory plans the town is required to maintain, several of which (hazard mitigation, comprehensive emergency management, ADA transition) are out of date or unfinished. A member reported on the reorganized Building Design Committee and argued the master plan is missing a prioritized list of town capital construction projects, and presented a GIS-derived inventory of town-owned facilities as a starting point; no formal votes were taken.

budget_items.what_was_said: The select board told the rebuilt Building Design Committee not to bring back a project of the prior scale and to look at using more of existing town buildings.

budget_items.what_was_said: A town meeting vote (cited as November 2023) approved spending on repairing the road for TCP, described as an example of a town-meeting-funded item rather than an excluded-debt project.

October 22 will not be a regular committee meeting; the committee will instead do a presentation at a "Smoke Stacks" event at 6pm that date.
No meeting will be held on the 19th (or the following week), to be revisited depending on how far the draft plan has progressed.
Outstanding meeting minutes will be recirculated by email and revisited at the next meeting rather than approved tonight.

The town manager's list of statutory/required town plans (open space & recreation, ADA self-evaluation, hazard mitigation, housing production, comprehensive emergency management) will be shared with the consultant (Ramy) and referenced in the master plan, though responsibility for keeping each current still needs to be assigned.

The committee will ask the consultant (Ramy) at their Tuesday working meeting whether items already listed as goals in the Open Space and Recreation Plan have actually been completed, before carrying them forward as master plan goals.

A member compiled a memo/inventory of town-owned facilities and buildings from GIS records and sent it to Chris Ruth for review, intending it to seed a prioritized capital-projects list for the master plan.

meetings.headline: ZBA granted a special permit shrinking the minimum lot size for a new house at 32 Spring Street

what_happened.line: The Zoning Board of Appeals voted to grant a special permit reducing the minimum lot size at 32 Spring Street so a new single-family house can be built.
The lot-size problem surfaced after a zoning district split between RA and RB was found on the property, following an earlier ANR plan that had already been endorsed.
The board left the boundary of the septic-system area where the plan showed it, though the applicant's engineer said its exact placement had some flexibility.
No members of the public attended or commented on the petition.
The chair read the standard conditions and appeal rights attached to the special permit after the vote.

why_it_matters: The permit allows a smaller lot than the bylaw normally requires so a new house can be built, based on a septic system serving the neighboring house at 31 Spring Street sitting partly on this lot.

The case shows how a zoning district boundary running through a property can create a lot-size problem even after an earlier plan for the same land was already approved, which matters to anyone splitting or building on property near a district line.

meetings.headline: Parks Commission voted a $50 fine against a resident for repeated unleashed dogs at McNiff Park despite an ADA claim
meetings.summary: The Parks Commission approved a beach-use request from a community club, set capital plan priorities (Fitzgerald Field regrading topping the list, Northfield Park kept on the list), and uncovered a $30,000 error in the Marshall Park project's remaining budget that it referred to the town accountant and manager. After lengthy public comment from baseball program members, it voted to issue a $50 fine to one of two residents for repeatedly bringing unleashed dogs onto McNiff Park's ball field despite their claim the dogs were ADA service animals. The commission also reviewed master plan committee feedback, got an update on hiring a new recreation director, and set upcoming meeting dates.

meetings.headline: Committee tentatively ranks Turkey Hill/schools, Town Hall, and Ritter as the town's top three capital priorities.
meetings.summary: The Master Plan Steering Committee reviewed feedback trickling in from town boards (Open Space, APDC, EDC, Council on Aging, Capital Planning) and heard that the town lacks several statutory plans, including an unfinished emergency management plan. Most of the meeting was spent working through a member's memo inventorying every town-owned building, out of which the committee tentatively settled on school facilities, Town Hall, and the Ritter building as its top three capital priorities, deferring Brooks House, Eagle House, Teen Club, and Marshall Park for later ranking pending input from the superintendent. The committee set plans for a final public feedback session on October 22 and a short presentation to a special town meeting on November 18, and discussed how to advertise the session and how candidly to describe the plan's troubled two-year process.

what_happened.line: The board closed the hearing and approved, with conditions, a special permit and site plan for a home ground-mount solar array at 390 Goodrich Street.
Conditions include posting a decommissioning bond before occupancy, sized to the array's removal cost, plus documentation of wiring and the utility interconnection agreement.
Board members said the town's solar bylaw is outdated and raised hiring a planner to update it.
The board agreed that MBTA Communities zoning language from its consultants should go on the town meeting warrant, ahead of an October 2 submission deadline.
The board put off responding to the Master Plan Steering Committee's request for feedback on the town's master plan.

why_it_matters: This sets the bonding and documentation conditions a homeowner installing a ground-mount solar array in Lunenburg can expect to meet.
The solar bylaw is described as outdated, so residents proposing solar projects may see zoning terms change before their own applications are heard.
MBTA Communities zoning language is headed for a town meeting warrant article, meaning residents will be asked to vote on it.
