meetings.headline: PACC drafted its written input to the town's master plan, adding studio-space and building-use goals
meetings.summary: This was a special PACC meeting devoted entirely to filling out the town's master-plan feedback form, since no public was present. meetings.headline: Commission may lose unused recreational-trails grant money if a Dec. 31 deadline isn't extended
meetings.summary: The Conservation Commission approved six sets of back-dated minutes, then heard four wetlands permit matters -- two continued (a Northfield Road culvert replacement and a four-lot common driveway) pending property-owner permission and peer-review sign-off, one solar array approved with conditions on erosion control and pipe size, and one driveway/septic project approved as proposed. It also approved removal of 20 dead trees at a private Hemlock Terrace property without required replanting, and heard that the commission's recreational-trails grant is running out of runway before its December 31 close with two of three funded projects still stalled.

budget_items.what_was_said: The applicant's engineer said DEP's alternatives-analysis form asks for cost information even though the commission itself does not consider cost a factor in permitting. He said the wider alternatives would only increase cost with no offsetting habitat benefit.

No replacement planting or replication is required for the 20 dead trees removed at 44 Hemlock Terrace, given the density of remaining mature trees and understory shown in Mary Wilson's site photos.
The chair/grant contact will ask the state grant administrator whether an extension can be requested on the recreational trails grant before its December 31 close.

The no-replanting decision on the tree removal sets a precedent for how the commission treats vegetation loss on land it regulates.

meetings.headline: FY25 school budget surplus of roughly $600K traced largely to a grant line double-budgeted, unspent
meetings.summary: The School Committee reviewed a reconciled FY25 budget surplus, with the business manager and superintendent explaining it stemmed mainly from a paraprofessional line double-budgeted against a grant plus general underspending on maintenance, custodial and instructional lines, none of which affected the separate cuts made for FY26. Extensive public and committee questioning pressed on accountability, Munis reporting reliability, and the need for regular budget-to-actual reporting and backup support for the business manager going forward. The committee also worked through a draft FY27 capital plan, debating how to finance a needed turf field/track replacement alongside a possible solar revenue project, and took votes on line-item transfers, a music program donation, a grant application, new legal counsel, and added secretarial hours at the high school.

what_happened.line: The business manager reported a reconciled FY25 school budget surplus, attributed mainly to a paraprofessional line double-budgeted against a grant plus underspending on maintenance, custodial and instructional lines.
Officials said the surplus did not affect the separate cuts already made to the FY26 budget.
The committee replaced a generator with the turf field/track project on the draft FY27 capital plan priority list, to be sent to the capital planning committee by October 1.
The business office agreed to start monthly budget-to-actual reporting to the committee after residents said prior requests for such reports had gone unanswered.
The committee also passed routine items: four line-item transfers, a music-boosters donation, a state arts grant application, new legal counsel, and added secretarial hours at the high school.

why_it_matters: The surplus explanation and the new monthly budget-to-actual reports speak to how closely residents can track whether school spending matches what was voted, not to who was at fault for the earlier mismatch.

The turf field/track project's move onto the capital plan, financed through borrowing, is a future debt-service item that would show up in the town's capital budget and tax bills once financing is worked out.
The added secretarial hours and legal counsel change are funded from existing lines and do not appear to require new town money.

meetings.headline: Committee elects new chair, narrows scope to town hall/Ritter/Brooks House, and pushes for a town-wide capital priority list
meetings.summary: A reconstituted Municipal Building Design Committee elected a chair and vice chair, then reset its charter after a prior building project failed at the ballot: the plan now focuses on renovating Ritter/town hall and rehousing PAC and ACE (in the Brooks House) rather than building new space in town hall. Members agreed to interview town departments directly, tour other town halls, and pressed the select board/master plan process for a town-wide capital project priority list before returning to voters, setting the next meeting for September 29th.

what_happened.line: DEP is expected to require Woodlands move kayak racks out of the Zone One wellhead protection area; the board agreed to wait for DEP's official letter before replying further.
The board agreed its message to Woodlands should be that the racks need to move immediately, not on an extended timeline.
The superintendent reported the Rolling Acres water main replacement is nearly complete and on schedule, and the board backed continued work on a multi-year capital plan for main replacement.
The district's hydrogeologist was given the go-ahead to proceed with the next design step for PFAS testing near Keyes, which will require a future warrant article to fund.

why_it_matters: Zone One is the town's wellhead protection area for drinking water, so the kayak-rack dispute touches the safeguards around the water supply.
Any response to PFAS testing at Keyes, and any equipment replacement, would come to residents as a future warrant article -- a vote at town meeting -- rather than being decided by the board alone.
A multi-year capital plan for water main replacement could shape future water rates and the district's borrowing or budget requests.

A board member proposed waiving building permit fees for seniors on small jobs and will bring a presentation back to the board before seeking select board approval.

why_it_matters: The unspent-funds comment raises a question about how override money approved by voters for the schools was actually used in FY25 -- the school budget vs. actual spending is a separate accounting question this board did not itself resolve.

The 41A vote keeps alive a path toward property tax relief for qualifying seniors, and the proposed permit fee waiver would touch town permit revenue and senior services if it advances to the select board.
The push for assisted-living to count as a "must have" in the master plan, and the seasonal cut to senior center hours, both affect what services and facilities seniors in town can expect.

The town manager said the superintendent sent a memo on September 3rd about a budget surplus, formally shared with the community September 4th.

budget_items.topic: Free cash process for FY25 surplus

The town manager said she asked directly whether override-funded positions were restored and Chromebooks purchased in FY25, and was told yes to both.

budget_items.topic: Chapter 90 funds for Flat Hill Road project

A board member reported the Capital Planning Committee urged prompt action on budget requests due by October 1st.
A board member reported the assessors' figures for residential, commercial, industrial and chapter land growth and the expected tax value derived from it.
A board member reminded that the warrant for special town meeting is open and closes October 2nd.

decisions.decision: The board agreed to ratify the three town manager appointments in a single motion, with a legal-review caveat noted for Melissa Richard.

meetings.headline: Sewer Commission drafted proposed ADU sewer connection fees and tie-in rules but took no final vote on them.
meetings.summary: The Sewer Commission spent most of the meeting workshopping a proposed regulation and fee structure for Accessory Dwelling Unit (ADU) sewer connections, comparing draft language from a commissioner and from staff, and discussing tie-in methods, easements, metering, and billing scenarios without taking a formal vote on the policy. meetings.headline: No quorum was reached; members informally discussed heat pump, solar and geothermal grant projects
meetings.summary: The Green Community Task Force never reached a quorum, so no official business or votes occurred; present members had an informal conversation about past and possible energy projects. They discussed the mini-split heat pump project at the schools (framed as both AC and heat, which unlocked grant funding), geothermal well drilling at another school, frustration over losing track of Turkey Hill's solar panel savings after the installer went out of business, predatory solar sales tactics, whether the town's ground-mount solar bylaw needs updating, and the group's ongoing push to get town departments to seek grant money before requesting town meeting funds. The meeting ended without a quorum and without any votes.

budget_items.topic: Mini-split heat pumps as a heat source
budget_items.what_was_said: A member said using mini-splits as a heat source, not just AC, was what enabled the project to qualify for free (grant) money. Getting the school administration to see the heating benefit, not just cooling, was described as a struggle.

budget_items.topic: Comparing mini-split cost to fossil fuel heating
budget_items.what_was_said: A member argued that when a building considers full electrification, the town should also be shown a traditional fossil-fuel cost comparison so voters can make an informed choice.

budget_items.topic: Geothermal wells at a school (state-pushed option)
budget_items.what_was_said: The state was said to be pushing geothermal; a school the size of the middle-high school reportedly drilled a large number of wells, and a member questioned what the return on investment would be.

A member said solar credits from Turkey Hill's panels are going somewhere and could fund the building's electricity so taxes don't rise as much, but the group has lost access to records of what the panels have actually saved since the installer went out of business.

The group discussed whether the town's ground-mount solar bylaw, which capped systems at a certain size, needs updating since panel efficiency has risen and the old cap now limits how much of a home's usage can be offset. They agreed it was worth looking into but did not resolve it.

budget_items.topic: Grant money vs. town-meeting funding requests
budget_items.what_was_said: A member described the task force's ongoing push to get the new town manager, select board, schools, and other town facilities to check with them for available grant/free money before putting funding requests on a town meeting warrant.

budget_items.topic: Next Green Communities grant round projects
budget_items.what_was_said: The task force said it is struggling to identify projects for the next spring grant round, after the mini-split project.

decisions.decision: Members agreed the town's ground-mount solar system size bylaw likely needs to be reviewed, without settling on a change.

meetings.headline: Assessors are stripping undocumented tax discounts from dozens of properties and setting written standards.
meetings.summary: The Board of Assessors reviewed cleanup of long-standing, undocumented functional and economic obsolescence adjustments on residential and commercial properties, removing unexplained discounts and adopting written standard percentages going forward. The board also discussed FY growth figures, the senior means-tested exemption applicant count, a possible move to GIS mapping software and field tablets to reduce paper-based inspections, and software/billing transition issues with Vision and Munis, without taking formal votes on any of these except approving prior minutes and adjournment.

The board wants the 41A income limit indexed to something like the circuit breaker rather than a fixed number, since the current limit is described as very low; the assessor will draft a proposal and research what other towns do.
A presenter gave the annual cost for an online GIS subscription with the tools discussed, plus a per-user add-on fee.
A board member asked what this year's contract cost was for the outside vendor; a figure was given but not clearly attributed to which contract.

budget_items.topic: Tablets and field equipment for inspections
budget_items.what_was_said: The board discussed investigating the cost of tablets with GPS for field inspections to replace paper data collection and transcription, and better measuring tools, without settling a figure.

decisions.decision: Chapter land grading was corrected from 'above average' back to 'average' for consistency.
The office adopted standard functional-obsolescence adjustment percentages (e.g., basement access, structural issues, shared-lot situations) to replace ad hoc, undocumented discounts.
A property owner with a mold-related adjustment will be asked for a 'cost to cure' and given roughly a year to address it before the adjustment is reconsidered.
Properties whose owners did not respond by the August 15 deadline about functional/economic obsolescence adjustments will have those adjustments removed.

For the classification hearing, the board will focus on an old-versus-new value comparison (rather than a straight tax-percentage comparison) to flag the largest tax changes.
Next Board of Assessors meeting set for October 1st, including an executive session for senior means-tested exemption review.
Before committing to new GIS software, the assessor will check what mapping/data access CAI (the town's current vendor) and MassGIS can offer, and get cost comparisons from Data Scout and others.

New standard percentages for obsolescence adjustments mean future requests for discounts (for structural issues, limited access, and similar conditions) will be judged against a written rule rather than case by case.

meetings.headline: Capital Planning re-elected its officers and began FY27 planning, tabling fiscal-policy threshold changes.
meetings.summary: The Capital Planning Committee reorganized for the year, re-electing its chair, vice chair, and clerk, then laid out its FY27 capital planning timeline: department submissions due by end of September, committee review meetings in October and November, and a final ranked list to the town manager by early December. Members reviewed a draft fiscal-policy document (proposed changes to the capital-item dollar threshold and useful-life standard), discussed grant funding uncertainty, gave initial feedback to the master plan steering committee's questionnaire, and approved prior minutes; no capital-plan figures were finalized at this meeting.

Approve the March 20th meeting minutes
Adjourn the meeting

budget_items.what_was_said: A member noted last year's plan funded a large number of smaller projects, an approach the committee will not have the luxury of repeating.
A member warned that a modest early-year capital list can balloon by year five as departments add speculative items.
A member argued Brooks House projects should be purged from the multi-year plan, calling a large expenditure there unwise.
A member suggested plugging estimated placeholder numbers for known-but-undesigned future work like bridge repairs, even without a specific project identified.

budget_items.topic: Capital item dollar threshold and useful life
budget_items.what_was_said: The town manager reviewed a DLS best-practice recommendation to raise the small-capital-item dollar threshold and questioned whether minimum useful life should move from three to five years.
A member recalled the committee last raised the threshold a couple of years ago somewhat arbitrarily rather than through rigorous analysis.
A member said that aside from a federal grant for fire apparatus, departments generally have little grant funding available for routine, recurring capital needs.
A member said state grant funding is increasingly available for culverts, stormwater and hazard mitigation work, even as federal grant money for the same purposes disappears.
The town manager explained the draft fiscal policy document originated from a community-compact best-practices grant the prior town manager obtained with the state Division of Local Services.
The town manager said the town is already paying for the Clear Gov platform and wants to use it, but does not want it to become a burden on department heads.
A member cited a rough total figure discussed for a Turkey Hill renovation project, noting any significant work there would trigger major building-code thresholds.
A member noted the committee spent ARPA money last year on a consultant study comparing rebuilding versus renovating Turkey Hill, and said he disagreed with the consultants' conclusions.
The town manager said the draft fiscal policy would add a requirement that the committee make a financing recommendation in certain borrowing situations.
A member argued the capital plan should weigh projects against available funding sources, borrowing capacity and free cash, not simply present a ranked list of projects.

decisions.decision: The committee will pursue both its annual prioritized capital list for the town manager and a longer-term five-year plan with a financial-planning component this year.
Department heads' capital submissions are due before the end of September, with committee vetting to begin in October.
The committee will plan for roughly five meeting nights in October and November to review capital proposals.
Final capital-plan rankings are expected to be finalized and voted at meetings in the first or second week of December.
The committee agreed it is wise to hold additional capital planning meetings during the town's budget process, as done last year.

The committee will take as homework whether to raise the small-capital-item dollar threshold and lengthen the minimum useful-life standard, possibly carving out police cruisers, ahead of the next meeting.
The committee will not require department heads to complete Clear Gov/Collins scoring this year, leaving evaluation criteria to the committee's own discretion.
The committee agreed to consider holding an additional meeting in late September to finish the fiscal-policy discussion and answer the master plan steering committee's questions.
Members expressed general openness to moving the committee's meeting start time earlier, to accommodate town staff schedules.

Members reviewed a draft fiscal-policy document (proposed changes to the capital-item dollar threshold and useful-life standard), discussed grant funding uncertainty, gave initial feedback to the master plan steering committee's questionnaire, and approved prior minutes; no capital-plan figures were finalized at this meeting.

what_happened.line: Capital Planning set its FY27 timeline: department capital requests are due by the end of September, with review meetings in October and November.
The committee re-elected its chair, vice chair and clerk for the coming year.

meetings.headline: District disclosed a roughly $582,000 unspent FY25 school surplus that went unnoticed and unbudgeted for.
meetings.summary: The School Committee's meeting centered on a newly discovered FY25 budget surplus of roughly $582,000 (about 2% of the budget), far above the district's normal cushion, which the chair and later the business manager attributed to poor financial oversight rather than known wrongdoing. The committee approved FY25 line-item transfers and a warrant, heard the superintendent's and building principals' start-of-year reports (including the first-day fire at the middle/high school), reviewed an FY27 budget timeline, and discussed a possible best-practices/forensic audit, a stabilization fund for out-of-district special education placements, and extra Chapter 70 money for a fall town meeting warrant article; several residents used public comment to press for accountability and clearer FY25-vs-FY26 budget transparency.

Members discussed the idea of a town stabilization fund, funded by annual school surplus remittances, to absorb the cost shock of new out-of-district special education placements moving into town.
The business manager gave the available/unspent budget balances remaining at year end for FY22 through FY24 to show this year's remittance was unusually large by comparison.

The business manager cited a large rise in health insurance costs as another driver identified in the cost comparison.

minutes.headline: Board leans toward a special meeting to fund a pilot study on adding Keating wells to PFAS treatment
minutes.summary: The Water District Commissioners reviewed the ongoing Rolling Acres water main project, discussed doing future main replacement in-house versus hiring it out and a possible multi-year warrant article for equipment and staff, and heard a clerk's report on PFAS settlement checks and legal limits on spending them. A lengthy public comment period featured a resident pressing the board to add a combined Keating-well/Lancaster treatment option to its public survey, which the board said would require a DEP-mandated pilot study and likely its own warrant article at a special meeting; no formal vote was taken on that question.

meetings.headline: Health insurance costs projected to rise about $1 million over three years, pushing talk of opt-out and GIC alternatives
meetings.summary: This joint select board/finance committee/school committee session was a night of preliminary FY27 budget presentations rather than votes: Council on Aging, the library, health insurance, board of health, veteran services, band concerts, and the historic commission each presented before the boards. The heaviest discussion was health insurance, where a three-year projection showed costs climbing sharply, prompting debate over the PEC's opt-out program, plan design, and whether to explore the state's GIC plan; smaller line items (band concerts, veteran services reimbursement) drew pointed questions about oversight and financial reporting that were left for follow-up rather than resolved.

minutes.headline: Health insurance costs projected to rise about $1 million over three years, pushing talk of opt-out and GIC alternatives
minutes.summary: This joint select board/finance committee/school committee session was a night of preliminary FY27 budget presentations rather than votes: Council on Aging, the library, health insurance, board of health, veteran services, band concerts, and the historic commission each presented before the boards. The heaviest discussion was health insurance, where a three-year projection showed costs climbing sharply, prompting debate over the PEC's opt-out program, plan design, and whether to explore the state's GIC plan; smaller line items (band concerts, veteran services reimbursement) drew pointed questions about oversight and financial reporting that were left for follow-up rather than resolved.

meetings.headline: Sewer Commission began drafting new sewer regulations for accessory dwelling units after meeting with town counsel

budget_items.what_was_said: A meter mix-up between two addresses meant the customer at 17 Renny was billed for the wrong usage for several quarters and is owed a credit. The business manager brought the adjustment to the commission for a vote.
A commissioner proposed setting a flat tie-in fee and standard piping requirements for ADU sewer connections rather than deciding case by case.
Leominster reportedly charges an added one-bedroom fee when a bedroom is added to a house rather than a distinct ADU fee; Harvard reportedly has no policy at all.
A commissioner suggested homeowners could rent an ADU for a monthly figure as heard, which he thought would make ADUs increasingly popular.

decisions.decision: Asked staff (Andrew) to start keeping written notes/headings from the ADU discussion (meters, fees, etc.) to build toward a regulation.

Each commissioner agreed to draft their own notes/ideas for ADU sewer regulations and send them to Andrew rather than one person drafting alone.
Agreed on the process for adopting ADU regulations: draft internally, send to town counsel for review, then hold a public hearing before voting the regulation in.

meetings.headline: Board approved a cat shelter's expansion and set a Sept. 22 hearing on MBTA Communities zoning
meetings.summary: The Planning Board approved a site plan for an addition to the Pat Brody shelter for cats at 499 Northfield Road and extended the review period on an ANR lot-line application at 830 Massachusetts Ave to clarify a dimensional-regulations question. The chair reported progress toward a September 22 public hearing on MBTA Communities zoning, a coming land use director/planner job posting, and warned the public about fraudulent invoices sent on town letterhead; the board also fixed a paperwork error on a performance guarantee account and nominated a new member to the Municipal Building Design Committee.

minutes.headline: Board approved a cat shelter's expansion and set a Sept. 22 hearing on MBTA Communities zoning
minutes.summary: The Planning Board approved a site plan for an addition to the Pat Brody shelter for cats at 499 Northfield Road and extended the review period on an ANR lot-line application at 830 Massachusetts Ave to clarify a dimensional-regulations question. The chair reported progress toward a September 22 public hearing on MBTA Communities zoning, a coming land use director/planner job posting, and warned the public about fraudulent invoices sent on town letterhead; the board also fixed a paperwork error on a performance guarantee account and nominated a new member to the Municipal Building Design Committee.

votes.motion: Nominate Matt Brener as the planning board's designator to the Municipal Building Design Committee

Approve the site plan for 499 Northfield Road with all standard conditions plus a special condition requiring submission of an operation and maintenance plan for the storm water drip edge
Close out the current performance guarantee account for 430 Mulpus Road, turn funds over to the town treasurer, and open a new correctly-formatted performance guarantee account
Approve the minutes from the July 14 meeting
Adjourn

budget_items.what_was_said: The chair said the job posting is being changed to focus exclusively on planning and economic development, with the building-management component split into a separate stipend position, to make the role more competitive.

The applicant's engineer said recording an 81X plan currently costs a fee at the registry, which some property owners may consider worthwhile in the long run even though it is not required for this project.

The board voted to close an old performance guarantee (surety) account opened under outdated bank paperwork and have the town treasurer open a correctly formatted replacement account; no dollar amount was stated in the captions.
The chair noted the select board modified the committee's charge after years of the project not moving forward, and the planning board needed to name a new designee.
The chair reported the Capital Planning Committee is just beginning its annual process of getting meetings scheduled again, with nothing yet to report.
A board member urged submitting a warrant article placeholder soon so a deadline for the fall town meeting is not missed while the town lacks a full-time planner.

transfers.description: Close out the old 430 Mulpus Road Performance Guarantee account (opened under an outdated bank account format) and transfer its funds to the town treasurer to establish a new, correctly formatted performance guarantee account for the same surety deposit

decisions.decision: Applicant for the 830 Massachusetts Ave ANR agreed to extend the board's 21-day statutory review period to the September 8 meeting so a dimensional lot-width/lot-area question could be clarified, rather than the board denying and requiring refiling.
The board agreed to carry review of the Master Plan Steering Committee's draft goals/recommendations relevant to the planning board to the first meeting in September, to give members time to read it.
The master plan review item will also be placed on the following meeting's discussion agenda, giving the board two meetings to review it before the end-of-September deadline.
The board will not re-discuss the previously-declined West Townsend Road-area open space parcel unless time allows at a future meeting, since other committees had already said no to picking it up.
The chair's goal is to hold the MBTA Communities zoning public hearing at the September 22 meeting, contingent on the consultant delivering the finalized bylaw language in time.

meetings.headline: Commission approved a 5-year plan to hand-harvest and chemically treat invasive weeds at Lake Wham's town beach.
meetings.summary: The Conservation Commission heard several wetlands notices of intent and requests for determination, approving driveway, septic, deck, wall and tree-removal projects in buffer zones, and continuing two hearings (68A Laurel Lane for a missing NOI number, and a Tanner Cole common driveway pending peer review) to September 3rd. The most significant action was approval of a five-year order of conditions for the town's Lake Wham aquatic plant and algae management program using hand/diver-assisted harvesting and herbicides near the public beach, conditioned on an annual report. Two certificates of compliance and one tree-removal request were left unresolved pending agent follow-up or a site visit.

budget_items.topic: Lake Wham aquatic plant management costs
budget_items.what_was_said: The applicant said diver-assisted suction harvesting is significantly more expensive than plain hand harvesting, so the plan is to hand-harvest first and use herbicides only as needed to control costs to taxpayers.

budget_items.topic: Lake Wham 5-year order of conditions request
budget_items.what_was_said: The applicant said requesting a five-year order (instead of the usual three) was mainly to avoid repeatedly paying a consultant to appear before the commission.

budget_items.what_was_said: The applicant said mailing a certified abutters list would add another cost each time, and preferred relying on the town website and social media instead.
The chair said Massachusetts Association of Conservation Commissions classes and the fall convention are covered under the commission's existing budget and encouraged members to attend.
The chair said the committee is moving to a different consultant to move the stormwater utility program forward, hoping to present something in the fall.

The certificate of compliance for 701 Reservoir Road was held pending the conservation agent's response; the chair will message the administrator and follow up with the applicant.
The certificate of compliance for 155 Reservoir Road will be added to the next meeting's agenda since neither the applicant nor the agent's notes were available.
The tree-removal request for 44 Hemlock Terrace will go on the September 3rd agenda after a site visit is completed beforehand.
Commission members were invited to sign up for a September 19th half-day trail work event at the Cry Nature Center as part of the United Way Day of Caring.

The commission will set aside dedicated time on a future agenda, rather than discuss informally, to go over the master plan steering committee feedback spreadsheet since a quorum discussing it would require an open meeting.
The chair will add a 6:30 p.m. executive session to the September 3rd agenda to discuss the Hollis Road property.

what_happened.line: The Commission approved a five-year order of conditions for the town's Lake Wham aquatic plant and algae management program, hand-harvesting and using herbicides near the public beach, with an annual report required.
The plan favors hand-harvesting over costlier diver-assisted suction and relies on the town website and social media rather than mailed abutter notice ahead of herbicide treatments.
Two hearings were continued to September 3: Ashley Owens's 68A Laurel Lane project, missing its NOI number, and Tanner Cole's common driveway, pending peer review.
The Commission also approved several driveway, septic, wall, deck and tree-removal projects in wetland buffer zones, and issued negative determinations for a well and a deck project.
Two certificates of compliance and one tree-removal request were left unresolved, pending agent follow-up or a site visit before the next meeting.

why_it_matters: The Lake Wham approval sets a five-year plan for herbicide use near the town beach, with notice to residents handled through the town website and social media rather than a mailed abutter list.
Wetland buffer-zone approvals for driveways, septic systems, walls and tree removal show how the Commission conditions rather than blocks routine residential projects near water.
Two properties (68A Laurel Lane, Tanner Cole's driveway) and two certificates of compliance remain undecided, affecting those owners' pending work.

meetings.headline: Select Board set the fall Special Town Meeting for Nov. 18, 2025, with the warrant opening Aug. 20 and closing Oct. 2.
meetings.summary: The Lunenburg Select Board ratified a new police lieutenant and several other appointments, heard a lengthy update from the assessor's office on reforms since the 2023 lakefront tax crisis, and set the fall Special Town Meeting for November 18, 2025 with its warrant timeline. The board also worked through a list of possible warrant articles, declined to pursue a BYOB alcohol policy change for now, authorized a stormwater grant application, sent a legislative support letter for the Nashoba Associated Boards of Health pension issue, and chose not to vote on accepting an unfinished prior tax investigation report.

attendees.role: acting lieutenant, appointee, Lunenburg Police Department
chair, master plan steering committee, presenter

budget_items.what_was_said: The town manager thanked the legislative delegation for securing regional funding for fire and EMS services after the Nashoba Valley Medical Center closure, but said the town would not rely on it for ongoing operations since distribution details are unknown.
The town manager reported Lunenburg Public Schools is receiving a state cyber grant to upgrade three end-of-support network switches.
The town manager reported the final FY26 Chapter 90 apportionment came in well above what was assumed at town meeting, leaving additional funds available for road work.
The town manager relayed rough cost estimates for continuing with the current design firm on Town Hall/Ritter plus Brooks House, versus starting over with a new firm.
The town received one bid for the court resurfacing project that came in under the budgeted amount and is finalizing a contract.

budget_items.topic: Town meeting warrant postcard mailing cost
budget_items.what_was_said: A board member estimated the cost of mailing a full warrant booklet to every registered voter, part of the case for switching to a postcard notice.
A board member noted the state provided additional Chapter 70 funding and suggested coordinating with the school department on a warrant article to appropriate it.

budget_items.topic: Clean Water SRF grant - asset management inventory
budget_items.what_was_said: The town manager described a stormwater asset-mapping project mostly funded by a state grant with the remainder from town funds, requiring board authorization to file the application.
The board accepted a monetary gift from the Lunenburg Friendly Seniors to the Council on Aging.
Two accounts payable warrants were presented to the board without discussion.
The board of assessors liaison reported FY26 growth in assessed value and noted personal property assessed values were lower than the prior year.
The principal assessor cited declining abatement counts as evidence of improved assessing practices compared to the volume issued during the fiscal 2023 lakefront valuation crisis.

decisions.decision: Board agreed in principle to move to a postcard-format town meeting warrant notice with hard copies available on request, and directed that drafting begin; a formal vote will follow when finalized.
Board directed that any warrant article moving additional Chapter 70 state funding to the schools be drafted as an additional appropriation article, with communication to the school department first.

Board declined to commit further resources to researching a BYOB policy change at this time, but was open to the town manager informally asking the requesting business about pursuing a wine/malt pouring license instead.

Board decided not to vote to accept the tax investigation report as submitted and to remove it from the agenda, since none of the current members were involved in the original investigation and the board of assessors has its own corrections pending.
Confirmed a quorum is expected for the August 26 tri-board meeting.
Identified that the board will lack a quorum for the week of September 16 due to two members' absences and will work around it.

meetings.summary: The Economic Development Committee reorganized, electing Josie Gilchrist as chair and Anna Lockwood as vice chair after discussion of the committee's chronic scheduling and structural problems. Members debated at length whether to postpone the annual town official meet-and-greet given the planning office's vacant land use director and conservation agent positions, ultimately deciding to proceed in early October at Smoke Stack Coffee Roasters via a small subgroup. The committee also deferred a broader rewrite of its charge/mission until after a land use director is hired, agreed to survey members on future meeting times, and arranged for minutes going forward to be produced by Danielle from meeting recordings.

what_happened.line: The committee reorganized, electing Josie Gilchrist chair and Anna Lockwood vice chair by roll-call vote.
Members chose to hold the annual town official meet-and-greet as planned in early October, despite two vacant planning office positions.
A subgroup, not the full committee, was authorized to make on-the-ground decisions for that event.
A rewrite of the committee's own charge and mission was postponed until a land use director is hired.
Minutes for future meetings will be produced by Danielle from recordings, addressing a backlog of unapproved past minutes.

meetings.headline: Commission says pooled trust funds sat effectively uninvested for two years despite a signed advisor contract
meetings.summary: The Trust Fund Commission (two members present, one vacancy) spent most of the meeting reviewing the town's contract with private trust company Bartholomew, raising concern that pooled trust funds have gone roughly two years without being actively invested despite fees being charged, and that fee/trading-volume transparency is inadequate. Members also reviewed the terms of several individual trusts (the Worthy Poor Fund, American Legion Post 283, a workers' compensation insurance fund under MGL c.40 §13A), discussed the commission's belief that its statutory advisory authority extends beyond its five named funds to other pooled trusts (e.g., cemetery, conservation), and began a read-through of a draft investment-procedure policy. The only votes taken were procedural: approving prior meeting minutes and adjourning, both said to pass unanimously.

budget_items.topic: Investment advisor and trading fees vs. net return
budget_items.what_was_said: A member said the fees charged relative to the net return the funds are getting are very disproportionate, calling it a split. He said trading fees on top of the management fee are unclear because trade volume/churn is unknown.
The chair initially read the contract's annual management fee as 20% before correcting himself, with Richard's help, to 2%; both said even 2% of the pool is a large sum for the town.
The chair read per-trade charges from the contract's Schedule A for stocks, ETFs and closed-end funds, plus additional fees if e-delivery is not used.
The chair described a handwritten 1901 declaration by a man named Nathaniel Day giving money to Lunenburg (and Shirley) for the benefit of the worthy poor.

budget_items.topic: Worthy Poor Fund and American Legion Post 283 balances
budget_items.what_was_said: Members compared recent fund balances, with some confusion between the figures for the Legion's Post 283 fund and the separate worthy-poor-type Legion fund, settling that the Lunenburg Post 283 fund and the worthy poor fund each held roughly this amount a few months earlier.

The 2013 trust declaration allows dispersements up to a set amount per year to veterans, and once the fund exceeds a threshold, up to a share of that year's interest can be dispersed to grow the fund.

The chair read the statute governing a town-established workers' compensation insurance fund, capping the annual appropriation as a fraction of equalized valuation and capping the fund itself once it reaches a stated share of that valuation.

budget_items.topic: Cemetery Commission withdrawal from the pooled trust fund
budget_items.what_was_said: Reviewing a fund report, members noted the cemetery fund had a transfer/withdrawal during the period while no other funds in the pool had any, which the chair cited as an example of spending he considers excessive.

budget_items.topic: Overall size and return of the commission's pooled funds
budget_items.what_was_said: A member noted the trust fund commission's own funds are comparatively small and asked what protects them if larger funds in the same pool incur fees from frequent withdrawals; another cited this fund total and a return rate to argue the pool is otherwise performing reasonably well net of unknown fees.

decisions.decision: The commission will continue operating with two members and a quorum while seeking a third member to fill its vacancy.
The commission will arrange a meeting with the private trust company, Bartholomew, to ask about fee levels and how many trades are executed on the pooled funds.
The chair will meet with town counsel Adam Costa around the 26th to discuss comparable towns' trust fund commission practices and next legal steps, including the cy pres doctrine question.
Rather than debate the draft investment procedure policy line by line tonight, the commission will do a read-through first and take up detailed discussion/amendments at this and a following meeting.

meetings.headline: FinCom reviewed draft town financial policies (audit, budget, capital, debt) line by line; no policy votes yet
meetings.summary: The Lunenburg Finance Committee heard public and member concerns about an unexplained ~$200,000 in unspent school funds and a school athletics revolving-fund deficit, and about how the school's new business manager was hired without town finance staff involvement. Most of the meeting was spent going section-by-section through a draft town financial policies document (based on a DLS/GFOA template merged with the chair and finance director's own best-practices draft), covering audit selection, budget process, capital planning, and debt management, with the committee raising numerous edits but taking no formal vote on the policies. The committee also planned upcoming tri-board topics (health insurance analysis, culture/recreation programming) and discussed whether to hire a full-time parks and recreation director before resolving open staffing and facilities questions, then approved prior minutes and adjourned.

budget_items.what_was_said: A resident asked the committee to address a report that money was found unspent in the school budget.
A member noted the town passed an override last year and that the unspent school money is part of that override amount.
Beyond the override, the town gave the schools additional money this year toward their budget.
The school athletic revolving account went negative and the school used other unspent budget money to offset it.
A member added the figures together to argue a large sum did not go toward items presented at town meeting.
Additional Chapter 90 road funds came through this year, raising the town's allocation.
The town manager reported a net increase in state aid across various sources, with no plan yet on distribution.
A state fund is being split among 13 communities via a state agency, with rules on use still undetermined.
The town still holds a large unspent Chapter 90 reserve that could fund a big project.
Achieving a GFOA distinguished budget presentation typically requires hiring a consultant.
Draft policy language would have the town strive to appropriate a target share of the general fund budget to capital, net of debt.
Draft debt policy cites a statutory debt limit tied to the town's equalized valuation.

decisions.decision: The town manager will merge her DLS-based draft financial policies with the chair's and finance director's separate best-practices document, gather Finance Committee feedback section by section, then bring the combined document to a Finance Committee vote before sending it to the Select Board.
The committee will pause further detailed review of the capital planning and debt management policy sections until the Capital Plan Committee has weighed in, then circle back.
The town manager will bring the town's health insurance benefit package details and replay the relevant Select Board segment on procurement difficulty to the upcoming tri-board meeting.
The town manager will request comparative health-insurance rate data for similarly sized communities from the Maya rep ahead of the tri-board meeting.
The committee will skip its next regularly scheduled meeting (falling near Labor Day) and instead meet next around September 11.
Detailed parks-and-recreation staffing/maintenance questions will be worked out in an offline meeting with the parks chair and facilities director rather than at the full tri-board meeting.

meetings.headline: Assessors are uncovering decades-old, undocumented property valuation discounts of roughly 10-60%.
meetings.summary: The Lunenburg Board of Assessors received a lengthy status report from the principal assessor covering motor vehicle excise processing in the new Munis system, chapter land rollback taxes and applications, and a systematic finding of long-undocumented functional and economic obsolescence discounts on commercial and residential properties that the board is now reviewing property by property. The board also discussed FY2026 senior exemptions and the new circuit-breaker-linked senior means-tested exemption, updated statewide chapter land value tables, approved several sets of amended executive-session minutes, voted to decline purchasing a parcel on West Townsend Road, and set a plan to respond to a town master-plan feedback survey.

budget_items.what_was_said: The principal assessor reported abutters list requests and motor vehicle excise tax abatements processed in Munis this month, awaiting payment processing by the tax collector.
Four chapter land rollback tax invoices were sent to former chapter landowners in June; one has paid, one status unknown, two have not responded.

budget_items.topic: Functional/economic obsolescence discounts on chapter land, commercial and residential properties
budget_items.what_was_said: Inspections found undocumented obsolescence discounts on many properties dating back years, averaging around 60% with a range starting near 10%; the board asked for a spreadsheet to see the scope.

budget_items.topic: Chapter land (agricultural) use-value cost table update
budget_items.what_was_said: The principal assessor updated statewide chapter land cost/value figures, moving crop/vegetable/tobacco/soil/nursery land to an 'above average' rating; the board questioned whether reclassification was justified given the size of the increase.

budget_items.topic: FY2026 senior real estate exemption COLA
budget_items.what_was_said: The cost-of-living adjustment for the FY2026 senior real estate tax exemptions was confirmed and added to the updated exemption sheet.

Residential/commercial/industrial new growth for FY2026 was estimated, with personal property and utility appraisals still pending; last year's and this year's earlier estimates were recalled for comparison.

The principal assessor explained that seniors who did not qualify for the state circuit breaker cannot qualify for the new local senior means-tested exemption, and the circuit breaker can be claimed retroactively three years by the filer but not administratively by the assessors this first year.

budget_items.topic: 41 warrant article for income limitation increase
budget_items.what_was_said: The board needs to confirm the town meeting date so a warrant article raising the income limitation for exemptions can be prepared in time.

decisions.decision: Put the property obsolescence/abatement review (with correlation to prior abatements and recommendations) on the September 3rd agenda for a possible vote.
Until told otherwise, a person receiving a veteran exemption who also becomes eligible for the new senior means-tested exemption should be allowed to receive both.
Defer deciding the frequency/timing of senior-center outreach sessions to the September 3rd meeting.
Postpone DOR's request to limit land condition factors until neighborhood value corrections are further along; add to a future goals list.
Keep the updated 'above average' chapter land agricultural values as already entered for this year and research the history of the rating in the meantime.
If called for jury duty on the day of a future meeting, the board member will try to participate by phone rather than in person.
The principal assessor will draft a proposed response to the master-plan feedback questionnaire for the board to review before September 3rd.
Cancel the September 24th meeting (a member cannot attend) and set the next September date as TBD.

meetings.headline: Committee unanimously recommends the town not exercise right of first refusal on a 222 West Towns Road parcel
meetings.summary: The Open Space Committee welcomed two new members (from the Parks Commission and Planning Board), approved minutes from a prior joint meeting, and unanimously voted to recommend the Select Board not exercise the town's right of first refusal on a 13-acre Chapter 61 parcel at 222 West Towns Road, finding it did not meet the committee's open-space criteria. The committee also noted its open space plan was extended by the state to 2029, took on a homework assignment from the town's master-plan steering committee, and rescheduled its next meeting to September 3rd.

budget_items.topic: Open space plan extension / grant eligibility
budget_items.what_was_said: The chair reported the state approved extending the open space plan from a seven-year to a 10-year plan, valid through fiscal year 2029, which lets the committee keep applying for open space grants through June 2029 without redoing a plan update next year.

budget_items.topic: Chapter 61/61A/61B tax status on 222 West Towns Road
budget_items.what_was_said: The chair explained that landowners in chapter 61 (forestry), 61A (agriculture) or 61B (conservation/recreation) get a lower tax rate, and if they sell for development they exit chapter status, pay back taxes, and the town gets a right of first refusal to match a sale price.

meetings.headline: Committee sets fall timeline: Oct 1 committee feedback, Oct 22 public forum, plan to Nov town meeting
meetings.summary: The Master Plan Steering Committee reviewed a proposed report structure and the plan's eight community goals with its consultant, discussed how to format and prioritize roughly 100 recommendations, and spent significant time on implementation strategy, town technology/digitization needs, and getting the town's other boards to submit feedback by October 1. No funding was voted; the committee set a schedule of an October public information session, a November town-meeting presentation of the draft plan, and a subsequent Planning Board vote, and approved several sets of past meeting minutes.

budget_items.topic: Recommendation card format: funding sources and rough cost magnitude
budget_items.what_was_said: The consultant proposed that each master-plan recommendation note its funding sources and a rough order-of-magnitude cost (small vs. large) alongside a short/medium/long time frame. The committee discussed adding a simple cost-tier legend so readers can gauge scale.
Members discussed indexing recommendations with dollar-sign symbols to signal rough cost, giving examples of small, medium and large project sizes.
A member noted the town had applied for a competitive state IT grant due earlier in the year and hoped it would be offered again next year to fund technology upgrades.

budget_items.topic: Marshall Park and municipal building articles
budget_items.what_was_said: Members said two capital articles -- Marshall Park improvements and a municipal building project -- failed at town meeting this year, attributing it largely to cost concerns and competition with school budget pressures.

decisions.decision: Hold the next committee meeting on the fourth Wednesday of August to review which committees have responded to the feedback request and assign follow-up on the select board, planning board and school committee as priority laggards.
Hold a public information/input session in October, before the town-meeting presentation, to gather citizen feedback on the draft plan.
Move the committee's own working meeting to October 8th and hold the public info session on October 22nd.
The committee chair, not multiple members, will be the one to present the draft plan at town meeting, with consultant support on slides.
Chair will contact the town manager and Tim Murphy about scheduling the draft plan presentation at the fall special town meeting.

meetings.headline: Sewer Commission weighed letting a developer easement across town land for a new subdivision, decided nothing yet
meetings.summary: The Lunenburg Sewer Commission heard a developer's request for a sewer-line easement to serve a planned common-driveway subdivision on Sunny Hill Drive, and spent much of the meeting debating the precedent such an easement could set for future development and accessory dwelling units. Members also approved the FY29 minutes and the FY2026 billing commitment, discussed a billing-system glitch, an upcoming Town Council meeting on ADU sewer bylaws, a DPW school-supply fundraiser, and got an update on the manhole repair project, without making any final decision on the easement itself.

public_comment.topic: Asked the commission's permission for a sewer line easement across his own land off Sunny Hill Drive/West Street to connect a planned four-house common-driveway subdivision to town sewer, citing a recent bylaw change allowing common driveways and a similar project he had built in Ashburnham.

votes.motion: Approve the minutes of July 29, 2025
Accept the notice of commitment for FY2026 sewer billing
Adjourn for the evening

budget_items.what_was_said: The quarterly bill run went out but took six days due to a software/system upgrade with the billing vendor that caused printing errors, including old 2023 bills reappearing. The issue reportedly affected other municipalities using the same vendor, not just Lunenburg.

budget_items.topic: FY2026 notice of commitment / billing amounts
budget_items.what_was_said: The commission needed to review and sign off on the FY2026 billing commitment amounts and the percentage of past-due accounts; the percent-past-due figure could not be updated until the next demand notice run. A member agreed to stop by the DPW office to sign it.

The commission recalled having discussed a possible flat-rate connection fee for accessory dwelling units of two bedrooms or fewer, with additional-bedroom scaling similar to regular connections, but noted the bylaw currently requires a separate connection to the street for every dwelling.

The commission discussed possibly spending a small amount from its budget on popcorn or cotton candy for the DPW's Touch a Truck/school-supply fundraiser, with one figure mentioned as an upper limit before a commissioner offered to donate his own cotton candy machine instead.

decisions.decision: Ed McWeeny was asked to assemble a full package/presentation, including potential problems avoided by the easement, before bringing the Sunny Hill Drive easement request to a formal hearing.
Two commission members agreed to attend the August 21 Town Council meeting on the ADU sewer bylaw question, since a quorum of the commission itself could not attend.

The commission will accept school-supply donations for the Touch a Truck event at the DPW office, and a commissioner will bring a table and a personal cotton candy machine rather than the commission purchasing supplies.
The manhole repair project is expected to be completed before the first frost, once a subcontractor is scheduled to replace framing and covers.
A formal request for the Sunny Hill Drive easement/extension will require a noticed public hearing, with at least five days' newspaper notice.

meetings.headline: Senior center elevator project ruled out as infeasible; committee to seek input on 10-year senior needs plan
meetings.summary: This Council on Aging meeting was mostly informational: reports on caregiver support programming, a heavily booked September activity calendar, a Unitil solar-interconnection cost complaint, and an update that installing an elevator (Lula Lift) at the senior center is not feasible due to space, code and cost constraints, with porch screening floated as a cheaper alternative. The board also discussed the town's master plan (including a push to make assisted living a formal goal rather than a "nice to have"), agreed to draft a warrant article to get the town to formally approve the 41A tax deferral program, and adjourned after routine reports on kiosk completion, sand-for-seniors delivery, and kitchen staffing.

budget_items.what_was_said: Tickets for the tea party fundraiser go on sale on the 19th.
A resident described Unitil charging a steep fee to expand a solar interconnection, making the return on investment take about 10 years and effectively killing the project.
Governor Healey signed legislation sending state funds to regional fire departments to stabilize emergency response after the Nashoba Valley Medical Center ER closure.
The parking lot remains in next year's budget; an extension was described as a separate, much larger project not currently funded.
A required annual state inspection fee for an elevator was cited as an additional ongoing cost weighing against installing one.

budget_items.topic: Property tax means-testing program eligibility limits
budget_items.what_was_said: The means-testing tax relief program's eligibility limits were described, covering home value and household income.
A resident reportedly lost the ability to defer a sum this year because the town has not formally approved the 41A deferral program, prompting a plan to draft a warrant article.

meetings.headline: Task force stalled on a stormwater utility fee because the underlying impervious-area data is a decade out of date
meetings.summary:
The Stormwater Task Force reviewed a consultant's answers to prior questions and discovered the state's impervious-area GIS data underlying its proposed fee structure has not been updated since 2016, undercounting many developed and expanded properties. The group discussed revising ERU fee tiers, weighed funding the work through a dedicated utility versus the DPW's operating budget, and decided to seek updated parcel data from the assessor's office before setting any fee, with the next meeting tentatively set for September 25th.</parameter>
</invoke>

attendees.role: presenter, Comprehensive Environmental (storm water utility fee consultant)

votes.motion: End/adjourn the meeting

budget_items.what_was_said: The task force asked why the most recent data showed 17 large-area properties subject to the fee versus 21 in earlier data; the consultant said some properties turned out not to be subject to the ERU fee.

budget_items.topic: Parcels subject to the ERU fee
budget_items.what_was_said: The consultant said about 543 parcels have been identified as subject to an ERU-based fee, excluding residential, town-owned, and no-impervious-area parcels.

budget_items.topic: Original memo property count vs. new count
budget_items.what_was_said: A member noted the original memo cited roughly 4,800 properties, which the consultant clarified excludes residential and town-owned parcels.

budget_items.topic: Proposed ERU tier and fee structure
budget_items.what_was_said: The consultant proposed expanding ERU tiers so tier one pays $60 per equivalent unit and a new top tier covers 200 or more units, to reduce the revenue gap.
One equivalent residential unit was defined as 4,200 square feet of impervious area, the basis for all tier calculations.

The DPW director's draft budget for the program, after removing Chapter 90 and one-time purchases, was cited at several figures before the group settled on roughly 873 as the revenue target for fee-setting.

budget_items.topic: Capital project money within the draft budget
budget_items.what_was_said: The draft budget included $300,000 a year for stormwater projects, though the DPW director said current annual project spending is less than $100,000 due to staff and funding limits.

budget_items.topic: Indirect costs in the utility budget
budget_items.what_was_said: The DPW director modeled about $10,000 in indirect/administrative costs into the utility budget, patterned on the sewer enterprise fund.

budget_items.topic: New staff positions funded by the utility
budget_items.what_was_said: The DPW director confirmed the plan involves three new hires, including a dedicated stormwater equipment operator and a GIS engineer, funded through the proposed utility rather than the operating budget.

The consultant suggested a cutoff (e.g. 100 square feet) below which small residential impervious areas would not be billed, which would remove about 80 properties and roughly $4,800 from the fee schedule.
A property near Lunenburg/Shirley previously listed with minimal impervious area was found to have close to 19 acres (roughly 800,000 square feet), prompting talk of adding higher fee tiers.

budget_items.topic: Correction to the large-property ERU estimate
budget_items.what_was_said: The consultant corrected her earlier figure, saying the large property is closer to 197-199 equivalent residential units, just under the proposed 200-unit top tier.

The consultant's data showed about 580 acres of right-of-way parcels, mostly one large parcel, while the DPW director's own pavement survey put town-owned roads at 238 acres, differing from an earlier-cited figure of 383 acres.
A member noted potential fines of up to $50,000 per day for MS4 noncompliance, though nobody could confirm any town had actually been fined.

budget_items.topic: Estimated ERU fee for the Walmart/Mass Ave property
budget_items.what_was_said: The consultant's spreadsheet showed the Walmart-area commercial parcel at roughly 202 equivalent residential units, which a member questioned as seeming low for the size of the property.

decisions.decision: Task force will ask the assessor's office (Linda McQuade) for a list of parcels newly built or occupied since 2016 to help cross-reference impervious-area changes.
Task force will pursue expanding ERU fee tiers beyond the current tier 10 to capture very large properties like the ~19-acre site.
Sarah Dewal (Comprehensive Environmental) will send the task force an updated parcel spreadsheet and the presentation slides by the next day.
Next meeting set for September 25th rather than the usual third Thursday, due to a member's unavailability.
Task force will try to set up a conversation with 'Jen' about the cost of hiring a dedicated consultant for the utility rollout.

minutes.headline: Task force stalled on a stormwater utility fee because the underlying impervious-area data is a decade out of date
minutes.summary:
The Stormwater Task Force reviewed a consultant's answers to prior questions and discovered the state's impervious-area GIS data underlying its proposed fee structure has not been updated since 2016, undercounting many developed and expanded properties. The group discussed revising ERU fee tiers, weighed funding the work through a dedicated utility versus the DPW's operating budget, and decided to seek updated parcel data from the assessor's office before setting any fee, with the next meeting tentatively set for September 25th.</parameter>
</invoke>

what_happened.line: The task force found the state's impervious-area GIS data behind its proposed stormwater fee has not been updated since 2016, undercounting developed properties.
Members agreed to ask the assessor's office for parcels built or occupied since 2016 before any fee is set.
The consultant proposed adding higher ERU fee tiers after a roughly 19-acre property was found to have far more impervious area than earlier data showed.
The group weighed funding the stormwater program through a dedicated utility fee versus the DPW's operating budget, citing exposure to state MS4 fines if funding lapses.
The next meeting was moved to September 25th instead of the usual third Thursday.

why_it_matters: A new stormwater utility fee, billed by impervious surface area, is still under design and has not been set; any property owner could eventually see a line item tied to how much pavement or roof area they have.
The fee structure depends on parcel data the task force says is out of date, so which properties and how much they would owe is not yet settled.
How the stormwater program is funded -- a dedicated fee versus the town's existing operating budget -- will affect whether it appears as a new charge or as part of general tax-funded services.

Updated parcel spreadsheet and revised ERU tier memo from the consultant

meetings.headline: Committee approved business administrator's contract; then trained with MASC on evaluating the new superintendent.
meetings.summary: This was a workshop meeting: the committee welcomed and approved a contract for newly hired business administrator Chris McNamera, accepted a $895 memorial-scholarship gift to athletics, then spent most of the meeting in a MASC-led training on the division between school committee and superintendent roles and on how to structure the new superintendent's annual evaluation under state regulation. No budget votes or major policy decisions were made beyond the personnel and donation items; the committee agreed to hold a follow-up discussion to set a calendar for the superintendent evaluation process.

Adjourn the meeting

budget_items.what_was_said: A gift from the Kevin T. Zozek Memorial Scholarship for Financial Trust was presented to Lunenburg athletics, intended for the middle school athletic department; Zozek was a student athlete who died on 9/11.
The committee moved to formally approve the employment contract for newly hired business administrator Chris McNamera, following discussion in executive session.

The presenter described the committee's fiscal policy role over the year, including optional quarterly budget reporting, approving transfers between cost centers, and signing warrants, as part of a broader financial check-and-balance system.

A member asked whether consolidating facilities with the town would mean losing budget authority while the school budget still pays maintenance salaries; the presenter said such mergers rarely save money unless a whole administrator position is eliminated.

decisions.decision: The committee announced it had already decided to hire Chris McNamera as the district's business administrator.
The committee tentatively agreed to target June for the superintendent's evaluation cycle this year.
The committee agreed to hold a follow-up discussion at a future meeting to plan the calendar and process for the superintendent's evaluation.

The FY25 June financial page was reported as incomplete, missing June interest, but now includes the Comcast payment for May, which was up a few hundred dollars from the prior payment.
The end of FY25 balance was reported, though the manager noted the figure will change once carried over into July.
Money was parked in an investment fund two years ago (July 2023) to pay for a new studio; the balance has grown since then and could help offset streaming-bill related costs.
The current balance in the studio investment fund was reported, representing growth over the original deposit, some of which may cover inflation or streaming-bill impacts.
The cable contract expires February 28, 2028; a figure was mentioned in this context but was not audible clearly.
A payable/OPEB-type advisory item that the town manager had been enthusiastic about stalled; specialized legal advice is needed and this will become a budget item for FY27.

meetings.headline: Commission will keep funding Marshall Park design but delay the next town-meeting vote about a year
meetings.summary: The Parks Commission spent most of the meeting deciding what to do with remaining ARPA and capital design money for Marshall Park, concluding it will keep funding the design but will not bring the project back to town meeting this November, instead waiting roughly a year given the town's broader financial uncertainty. It also heard a skate park funding/construction update, discussed a capital-planning wish list, and reviewed how little park user fees cover of actual maintenance and school-field rental costs compared with other towns, without changing fees.

budget_items.what_was_said: Bids for resurfacing the Wallace tennis/basketball courts were due Monday after the original contractor lost his state-contract status and had to rebid.

The insurance company approved the claim for a vehicle that crashed through the fence and into the toddler play structure at Wallace Park; the structure was removed and mulch replaced as a precaution.
The chair has a list of cultural council grant opportunities, due in September or October, to pass along to Angela, including possible replacements for a vendor who is not returning.

budget_items.topic: Marshall Park ARPA and capital design funds
budget_items.what_was_said: About $13,000 in ARPA funds remains and must be used by year end or lost back to the federal government; a separate total of $97,000 remains from capital funds for the design/engineering process.

budget_items.topic: Design draw percentage reached before town meeting
budget_items.what_was_said: Members tried to recall what percentage draw on the design contract had been reached before annual town meeting, with figures of 60%, 75%, and 34% all mentioned and not resolved.
The skate park presenter reported the project is roughly 91% funded (later restated around 330-ish), with an overall project total described as about 372, including in-kind donations.
About 98% of contract terms with the builder have been negotiated, with only the bonding structure still outstanding; the goal is a signed contract by Labor Day.
An initial amount, heard as 'the initial 50,' was allocated to start a weeds treatment pilot program; no further capital request will be added until that work begins.
The chair said she is sticking with a request to add $10,000 a year to the parks operating budget, which could help fund smaller maintenance projects.

budget_items.topic: Field maintenance contract vs. actual mowing costs
budget_items.what_was_said: The current mowing contract is written for 17 mowings per season, but actual mowing far exceeds that number, so real costs are higher than the contract price shown.

The current parks fee is $20 per resident participant and $30 per non-resident; youth baseball reported 148 participants this spring for a total of $2,960 to reserve five fields from April 3 to June 30.
The school district charges $15 an hour for grass fields and $35 an hour for turf, and is raising those rates by roughly 50%.

budget_items.topic: Comparative cost of turf vs. town fields
budget_items.what_was_said: A summer-league high school soccer program pays about $1,500 to use the turf ten times a season, compared with Little League's roughly $2,960-$3,000 for a full spring season on town fields.

budget_items.topic: Lunenburg Youth Soccer field costs elsewhere
budget_items.what_was_said: Lunenburg Youth Soccer reportedly spends over $10,000, possibly closer to $15,000, to rent turf fields outside town.
A Groton soccer treasurer said her program pays between $13,000 and $14,000 a year across two seasons to lease fields, and that user groups there handle 100% of field maintenance themselves.
Members roughly estimated that if 800 football players split a $13,000 fee it would work out to about $16.25 per player, comparable to the town's current per-player rate.
School custodial fees for field/facility use were estimated at around $36 to $39 an hour, separate from the field rental rate itself.

decisions.decision: Continue spending down the remaining ARPA and capital funds (heard as $97,000) to finish the Marshall Park design/engineering work, without a formal vote since prior authorization already covered it.

Do not bring the Marshall Park project back to a special town meeting in November; wait roughly a year, likely spring or later, given uncertainty from the town's broader financial issues (including a tri-board group examining town finances).
Pull/rescind the prior motion granting terms to the skate park group so the agreement/extension can be revised at the next meeting.
Do not pursue the McNall or Northfield Park master plans at this time; prioritize Fitzgerald Field resurfacing on the capital planning list instead.

Chris Ruth will send the commission a list of possible capital planning items (e.g., Fitzgerald resurfacing, Powell dugouts, fencing, kayak rack) for members to review and prioritize before the next capital planning cycle.
Leave current park user fees unchanged for now; the chair will work with Angela to redesign the field reservation forms to capture actual usage before any fee changes are considered.
Reach out again to youth baseball (and others) for a breakdown of actual field usage by field and by day/hour to inform future fee decisions.
Dog-on-leash policy enforcement at McNall Park remains unresolved pending word from town counsel via the town manager on who has authority to enforce/fine violations.

Agree to let MRPC/Massachusetts Office of Outdoor Recreation document Lunenburg's parks (McNall, Fitzgerald/Ben Norman, Town Beach, Marshall Park and Pond, Wallace Park) for a statewide outdoor recreation inventory.
Tentatively keep the August 20th meeting on the calendar in case something comes up with RDLA or the town manager, even though no new information is expected by then.

what_happened.line: The Parks Commission will not bring the Marshall Park project back to a town meeting vote this November, pushing it roughly a year out amid town-wide financial uncertainty.
The commission will keep spending remaining ARPA and capital funds to finish the Marshall Park design and engineering work.
The commission pulled its prior motion granting terms to the skate park group so the agreement can be revised at the next meeting.
Members left park user fees unchanged, deferring any change until reservation forms are redesigned to track actual field usage.
The commission dropped master-plan work for McNall and Northfield parks in favor of prioritizing Fitzgerald Field resurfacing on its capital list.

why_it_matters: Residents who expected a vote on Marshall Park at fall town meeting will not see one this cycle; the next opportunity is roughly a year out.

Park user fees, which members said cover only a fraction of maintenance and field costs, stay as they are for now, so any future increase will follow a usage review rather than happen at this meeting.
The skate park agreement returning to the table means its funding and construction terms are not yet final.

meetings.headline: Commission approved an engineering contract for North Cemetery's back-lot expansion and began a fund-spending plan.
meetings.summary: The Lunenburg Cemetery Commission approved an updated engineering scope of work for the North Cemetery back lot expansion, to be paid from capital funds, and reviewed sale-of-lots and perpetual-care trust fund balances to plan spending on headstone repair, hedge/fence replacement, and road work. No public comment was offered, and the commission approved payment for a file cabinet and scheduled August site visits to both cemeteries.
