approve payment to WB Mason for a fireproof file cabinet
adjourn the meeting at approximately 7:45 p.m.

budget_items.topic: North Cemetery engineering scope of work (Dillis and Roy)
budget_items.what_was_said: The engineering firm's updated survey/design quote for the back lot expansion would be paid out of the cemetery's capital funds. Members said the price compared favorably to other engineering firms' rates.
A member noted the total price for the engineering work, which starts with a wetlands-resources check that determines whether further filing steps are needed.
Members discussed that competitive bidding is normally required above a threshold, but engineering services are exempt from that requirement.
Old quotes from 2023 and 2013 for replacing the front hedge trees were reviewed, covering different tree sizes and counts, as a baseline for updated pricing.
A member sketched rough material costs for a granite/wood post-and-rail alternative to hedging, based on retail pricing.
A New Hampshire granite post specialist quoted a price to set posts along a stretch of frontage, excluding rails, labor and painting.

budget_items.topic: Headstone repair quote (Amanda Construction), South Cemetery front section
budget_items.what_was_said: A stonework/wall contractor quoted repairing tipped, cracked and uneven historic headstones in the oldest section, itemized by type of repair; the full quote exceeds the bidding threshold.
Members recalled a prior, higher hourly-rate quote from another provider for straightening a monument, used for comparison.

budget_items.topic: Hedge trimming quote (Bullock Brothers), North Cemetery
budget_items.what_was_said: A landscaping quote was received to trim and tie back the drooping north-cemetery hedges to prevent snow damage; no competing quote was obtained yet.
A tractor-mounted boom mower service to cut back tree branches overhanging cemetery roads was discussed as either an operational or commission expense, weighed against other planned spending.
Current balances in the sale-of-lots fund and the perpetual-care fund were reviewed as the basis for planning the year's spending, pending confirmation from the town accountant.

budget_items.topic: Interest rate assumption on trust funds
budget_items.what_was_said: An assumed interest rate was used to estimate annual interest income on the two funds, to be verified with the accountant since actual reported interest looked like an unusually high return.

Lot sales over the past five years in the south and north cemeteries were tallied at a flat per-lot price to estimate typical annual revenue, with 2025 sales so far running well below the recent average.

budget_items.topic: Average annual lot sales and revenue estimate
budget_items.what_was_said: Average yearly lot sales for each cemetery were used to project a rough annual revenue figure, which a member cautioned may not hold this year given low year-to-date sales.
Based on interest plus average annual lot-sale revenue, members discussed how much could be spent this year while preserving fund principal, and considered starting conservatively.

budget_items.topic: Capital article transfer carryover and funds currently available
budget_items.what_was_said: A prior capital article transfer left an unspent balance, which combined with perpetual-care interest gives the commission money on hand right now for planned projects.

budget_items.topic: FY spending plan across current projects
budget_items.what_was_said: Members totaled the likely near-term costs (headstone repair, cabinet, contingency) against available funds and decided to hold off drawing further reserves until a November meeting.

budget_items.topic: WB Mason fireproof file cabinet payment
budget_items.what_was_said: The commission approved paying the invoice for a fireproof file cabinet purchased from WB Mason.

meetings.headline: Sewer Commission weighed a flat ADU inspection fee and costly new NPDES mapping rules; no votes taken on either.
meetings.summary: The Lunenburg Sewer Commission reviewed completed Dana Street pump repairs and ongoing manhole rehabilitation, then turned to two bigger open items: a proposed flat fee for connecting accessory dwelling units to the sewer system, and a new MassDEP NPDES permit requiring costly annual system mapping work through engineering firm Wright-Pierce. Only routine procedural votes (minutes, adjournment) were taken; the ADU fee, easement policy for a Massachusetts Ave subdivision dispute (from which Bill Bernard will recuse), and the NPDES mapping cost questions were all left for further discussion and a planned meeting with town counsel on August 21.

votes.motion: Motion to accept the minutes from 7/8 (with a wording correction from 'effort' to 'effect' noted first)
votes.outcome: passed 3-0 (roll call: Scott D. aye, Dan Proctor aye, chair aye)

votes.motion: Motion to adjourn
votes.outcome: passed 3-0 (roll call: Scott D. aye, Dan Proctor aye, chair aye)

budget_items.what_was_said: The repair to a badly rusted coupling at the Dana Street pump station was completed using FY25 money before the fiscal year closed, narrowly avoiding a system failure.
The business manager reported all required commissioner signatures were obtained and the FY25 adjustments are ready for final approval, having been delayed by a missing signature.
The chair proposed a flat inspection fee for accessory dwelling units to cover checking the external plumbing connection from the ADU into the existing house's line.
The chair cited Leominster's practice of charging a flat per-bedroom fee when a bedroom is added to an existing house, as a possible model distinct from the ADU fee.

A commissioner recalled that Wright-Pierce's typical annual charges had run in that range in past years, well below the current bill tied to the new NPDES permit mapping requirements, and asked whether the current cost was a one-time remap or a recurring annual charge.
The business manager said billing will go out in a couple of weeks, pending Leominster, for the current year's first-quarter billing.

decisions.decision: A wording correction (from 'effort' to 'effect') was identified in the July 8 minutes and agreed to be fixed before the vote to approve them.
Bill Bernard will recuse himself from voting on the Massachusetts Avenue easement matter because he was contracted by the homeowner for the original sewer install before joining the commission.
Only one or two commissioners will attend the August 21 meeting with town counsel on ADU/easement regulations, to avoid triggering public-meeting quorum requirements.
Wright-Pierce will be asked to help fill in the gaps in the NPDES permit response, per their proposal.
Dana Street is being dropped from future agendas since the repair is complete; the manhole IFB, ADU fee discussion, easements, and NPDES permit will remain standing agenda items.
Set the next meeting dates as August 12, August 26, September 9, and September 30, 2025, alternating regular DPW hybrid meetings and Zoom-only meetings.

Only routine procedural votes (minutes, adjournment) were taken; the ADU fee, easement policy for a Massachusetts Ave subdivision dispute (from which Bill Bernard will recuse), and the NPDES mapping cost questions were all left for further discussion and a planned meeting with town counsel on August 21.

what_happened.line: The commission left a proposed flat fee for ADU sewer connections undecided, with no vote taken.
It referred a new NPDES permit's annual system-mapping requirement to engineering firm Wright-Pierce rather than setting a cost or schedule.
Only one or two commissioners plan to attend an August 21 meeting with town counsel on ADU and easement rules, to avoid triggering public-meeting quorum.
Commissioner Bill Bernard will recuse himself from a Massachusetts Avenue easement dispute because he was contracted for the original sewer install there.
The Dana Street pump station repair, completed with FY25 funds before the fiscal year closed, is being dropped from future agendas.

why_it_matters: A flat ADU sewer-connection fee, once set, would become a new cost for any homeowner adding an accessory dwelling unit tied into town sewer.
The NPDES mapping mandate could raise sewer department costs, and sewer department costs are typically recovered through sewer fees rather than the tax levy.
How the commission staffs its August 21 meeting and who recuses on the Massachusetts Ave easement case shapes how openly those decisions get made.

meetings.headline: Planning Board approved a scaled-down 260 Fula Road warehouse; continued Northfield Road driveway hearing to August.
meetings.summary: The Lunenburg Planning Board closed the hearing on 260 Fula Road and approved a modified, smaller warehouse site plan and storm water permit with peer-review conditions, while continuing the 1083 Northfield Road common-driveway/storm water hearing to August 25 amid quorum concerns. The board also voted to restructure an outdated storm water performance guarantee account for 430 Mulpus Road, heard committee updates including an ERU-based storm water enterprise fund proposal, and set a process for signing an outstanding decision (443/West Townsend Road) outside of a formal meeting.

Close (adjourn) the meeting

budget_items.topic: 430 Mulpus Road storm water performance guarantee account
budget_items.what_was_said: Restructuring an over-a-year-old performance guarantee deposit account required monetary amounts and account-holder names from the building inspector before the paperwork could be finalized, so that piece was deferred. The board proceeded anyway to vote motions to close the old account and move funds to a new one, planning to complete paperwork once figures arrive.

The storm water task force described a system based on equivalent residential units (ERU) that would charge every property, including commercial and institutional, according to its impervious area impact, intended to create a dedicated funding stream, staff and equipment for storm water work rather than relying on ad hoc DPW capacity. No dollar figures were given; the task force hopes to present something at the next town meeting.

Jasmine/Jen will correct errors in the draft minutes (attendance listings, wording) and bring them back for approval at the next meeting.

For the 443 West Townsend Road decision, Jasmine will email it to the board; members will review and, if it matches what happened at the meeting, sign it in person at the office rather than review it live at a meeting. A brief remote special meeting will be called only if a member has a concern it doesn't match.
If no public hearings or other business come in, the chair will cancel the August 11 meeting rather than hold it for minutes alone.
Because Adam has a scheduling conflict for MRPC meetings September through December, board members will split up covering those meetings among themselves.

meetings.headline: Stormwater fee rollout stalls: consultant's property data has errors and missing large parcels
meetings.summary: The task force reviewed the consultant CEI's spreadsheet of impervious-area data used to set tiered stormwater utility fees and found it missing several large properties (including Unitil and a warehouse) and questionable figures for others, so no rate structure was finalized. Members set a plan to hold extra meetings in early and late August, present to the Select Board and Finance Committee in September, and bring the fee to spring annual town meeting rather than fall, and decided to bill through the town's existing utility billing system rather than build a new one.

budget_items.topic: Funding source for stormwater fee vs. Prop 2½
budget_items.what_was_said: A resident's emailed question said the proposed funding source bypasses Proposition 2½ protections; members clarified the fee is a separate enterprise-fund charge that doesn't fall under 2½.

Members discussed whether the fee could be phased in rather than fully funding the target budget line immediately, noting quarterly billing already staggers it and that hiring/equipment can't start until money comes in.

budget_items.topic: Comparison to water and sewer rate increases
budget_items.what_was_said: Members noted sewer rates paid to Fitchburg and a per-quarter Massachusetts water-project charge have both risen over time, as an example of utility-type charges growing.
The new contract is in DocuSign awaiting signature by staff who are out; work on the task force's outstanding questions is on hold until it is executed.
A member said the town's current drainage line item is small and that a recent culvert washout cost far more than that to repair, showing the existing budget can't absorb major storm damage.

budget_items.topic: Storm water engineering line item / MS4 compliance
budget_items.what_was_said: A separate town line pays CEI for MS4 compliance engineering and reporting at a set annual amount that isn't being fully spent yet.

budget_items.topic: ERU/impervious-area tier threshold for large properties
budget_items.what_was_said: Members worked out that the consultant's tier 10 threshold is defined by an ERU or impervious-area size, and that one property likely falls well above it based on its acreage.

budget_items.topic: Fee cap represented at annual town meeting
budget_items.what_was_said: Members recalled differing figures for what was told to annual town meeting about the quarterly fee cap.

budget_items.topic: Enterprise fund target balance and spending plan
budget_items.what_was_said: Before presenting to the Select Board and Finance Committee, the task force said it still needs the DPW's finalized justification for the enterprise fund's target balance and how it will be spent.

budget_items.topic: Billing system for the stormwater fee
budget_items.what_was_said: The task force decided to add stormwater billing onto the town's existing utility billing system rather than build a separate one.

decisions.decision: Chair asked to have the resident's email forwarded so its comments can be entered into the public record, likely with the sender's name withheld.
Task force identified at least four properties missing from the consultant's large-property table and will ask him to re-check and re-run the list.
Task force will bring the fee proposal to town meeting in the spring, not the fall.
For now, keep four broad ERU tiers (0-25, 25-50, 50-100, over 100) rather than immediately expanding, revisiting in a future year.
Hold a joint posted meeting with the Select Board and Finance Committee in September to present the proposal, with the consultant possibly dialing in.
Add two extra task force meetings in August, on the 7th and 21st, to prepare for the September presentation.

The task force decided to bring the fee proposal to spring annual town meeting rather than fall.
For now the four existing ERU fee tiers stay as they are rather than being expanded.

meetings.headline: ZBA approved a garage/ADU permit and a 20-unit town-house special permit despite neighbor traffic and water worries.
meetings.summary: The Zoning Board of Appeals heard two special permit applications. It granted Matthew Glenny a special permit with a dimensional variance to build a detached garage with an accessory dwelling unit at 55 Valley Road, subject to septic upgrades being worked out with the Board of Health. It then heard and voted to approve, with added conditions on driveway width and extra parking, a special permit allowing Daniel and Rachel Brackett to build four five-unit town house buildings off a common driveway on New West Townsend Road, over objections from several neighbors about density, traffic, water supply for fire suppression, and erosion.

meetings.headline: Commissioners agreed to send residents a survey on multimillion-dollar PFAS water-treatment options.
meetings.summary: The Lunenburg Water District Commissioners approved minutes and renewed the CPA's yearly audit contract, then spent most of the meeting reworking a draft public survey on PFAS water-treatment options, debating scenarios ranging from treating the Keings well to interconnecting with Townsend or relying on Lancaster/Hickory Hills sources. They agreed to fold redundancy/interconnection costs into the treatment scenarios rather than list a standalone option, and to send the survey out largely as drafted after a couple more reviews. The board also covered new elevated PFAS results at Lancaster wells possibly triggering monthly testing, and operational items including main-replacement equipment, excavator rental, and a road saw purchase.

budget_items.what_was_said: The board discussed renewing the yearly audit contract with Mark Bueller CPA, noting the fee went up from the prior year. Members said the contract is worthwhile because there are few small firms still doing this work and the auditor knows the district's routine.
Lancaster wells came back with elevated PFAS levels, requiring another round of sampling; if results stay high the district may have to move to monthly testing of all sources.

budget_items.topic: Keings PFAS treatment vs. Townsend interconnection
budget_items.what_was_said: Commissioners compared treating the Keings well for PFAS against building a pipe interconnection with Townsend, weighing the cost difference against the cost of also needing to buy water.

A commissioner asked whether a resident had been told the district previously lost SRF principal forgiveness funding, and noted new state PFAS funding announced by the Governor may include future principal forgiveness.
The board discussed renting a 30,000lb excavator to do main replacement work themselves instead of paying an engineer and contractor, comparing rental cost to the cost of hiring engineering design.
A commissioner recalled the town had bought a 16-inch road saw for a reasonable price and suggested the district consider buying one to make main-replacement jobs easier.

decisions.decision: Board agreed scenario 7 (intermunicipal connection to Townsend) should not stand alone in the survey; its cost should instead be added as a redundancy line item to scenarios 4/5 (Keings treatment).
Board agreed to send out the treatment-options survey largely as drafted, with a request to make clearer that a cheap option still requires a second phase/redundancy cost later.
Chair will send the draft survey to a resident (Bobby Turkington) and to Nicole for review before next meeting, aiming to present a final draft then.

The board plans to send the survey largely as drafted, after review by a resident and by Nicole, with a final draft expected at the next meeting.

meetings.headline: Committee reworked master plan housing and land-use priorities; town-building specifics still deferred
meetings.summary: The Master Plan Steering Committee, meeting remotely, walked line-by-line through the consultant team's response to its earlier must-have/nice-to-have list, reworking or reclassifying items on housing (missing-middle housing, inclusionary zoning, affordable housing trust fund), land use (sewer-area density, farmland strategy), economic development, and walkability/complete streets. No formal vote was taken on any master plan recommendation itself; the committee did vote to approve the June 25 minutes with edits and to adjourn. Next steps agreed were to finalize a feedback spreadsheet for other town boards (due back around early-to-mid September) and to hold a further public meeting in October before the plan is finished.

meetings.headline: Assessors found 131 properties with undisclosed depreciation adjustments needing review
meetings.summary: The Lunenburg Board of Assessors met after extended technical/audio difficulties delayed the start. The principal assessor gave a lengthy status report covering chapter land compliance issues, a resident inquiry that uncovered dozens of undocumented property depreciation ("obsolescence") adjustments needing review, preliminary FY2026 growth figures, cyclical inspection mailings, and new billing duties added to the office; the board also discussed updating the outdated 41A tax deferral income limit, the senior tax exemption program, and scheduling for RFP review and future meetings.

budget_items.what_was_said: The principal assessor reported on chapter 61/61A/61B land counts, missing liens and applications discovered on a review, seven properties removed for non-response, and roll-back taxes issued on properties that sold without liens.

budget_items.topic: Roll-back tax invoice on a specific chapter parcel
budget_items.what_was_said: A new owner who did not receive prior correspondence was billed roll-back taxes covering multiple years after being removed from chapter land; the board discussed whether to let her back into the program if a lien and application are completed.
The roll-back invoice was sent and a response received about a month later; the board discussed a reasonable timeline for compliance.
Blue postcards were mailed to residents due for inspection this cycle; only those who received a card will be visited.
The office received a surge of resident calls about the cyclical inspection notices.

budget_items.topic: Interim adjustments contract with Vision Appraisal
budget_items.what_was_said: Vision is contracted to deliver interim value adjustments by a September deadline and has assured the office it will be on time this year, unlike the prior year.

The assessor gave preliminary FY2026 growth figures, noting personal property values are not yet complete pending appraisals from utility companies; growth is described as much lower than the prior year with no comparison figure available.

budget_items.topic: Obsolescence coding discovered on a resident inquiry
budget_items.what_was_said: A resident's property value question led staff to discover an unexplained 20% economic obsolescence code, prompting a review that found many properties with external or functional obsolescence adjustments needing justification.

The principal assessor and a board member were revising a three-year RFP scope of work with the town counsel's added insurance and compliance requirements; the board discussed doing inspections themselves rather than relying on a vendor for consistency.
The board found the income cap for the property tax deferral program has not been updated since it was set, and agreed to draft a warrant article to revise it for the next town meeting.

budget_items.topic: Senior means-tested real estate tax exemption (41D)
budget_items.what_was_said: Eligibility requires age 65+, 15 years of residency, circuit breaker credit qualification, and income/asset limits; the maximum exemption for FY2026 was stated, and applicants may also qualify for an elderly exemption in the same year.

meetings.headline: Select Board told the building committee to rescope Ritter/Town Hall, dropping ACE, before returning to voters
meetings.summary: The Select Board spent most of the meeting in a joint session with the Lunenburg Municipal Building Design Committee, giving direction after the narrow town-meeting/ballot defeat of the Ritter/Town Hall renovation: drop the ACE program from the plan, keep PAC in the building, add an Architectural Preservation District Commission representative, and lower the committee's quorum. The board also heard a legal opinion on the limited authority of the Board of Commissioners of Trust Funds, made several routine committee appointments, declared vehicles and equipment surplus, and received a town manager's report covering the Flat Hill Road bridge repair, sewer delinquency figures, and other items. No new town-meeting date or redesign budget was set.

meetings.headline: Trust Fund chair says the town manager is blocking the board's access to funds and information
meetings.summary: The chair delivered a long statement accusing the town manager of impeding the two-member Trust Fund Commission's ability to review and act on its trust funds, and outlined a vacancy dispute over filling the board's third seat. The board watched a recorded budget task force presentation by Bartholomew and Company on the new "prudent investor" law (203C), then voted to send a letter to the select board about the vacancy and approved its prior minutes.

The board watched a recorded presentation on shifting trust and stabilization funds from the state's conservative "legal list" to a "prudent investor" standard, but has not yet sent letters to the investment firm or the treasurer for more information.

why_it_matters: A dispute between an appointed board and the town manager over document access and a vacant seat can slow oversight of trust funds that fund things like scholarships.
Whether the town adopts the newer "prudent investor" investment standard, versus the more conservative rule it uses now, affects how much trust and stabilization money can grow over time.
The unfilled third seat leaves the two-member commission without a quorum cushion for future votes on these funds.

meetings.headline: Committee will ask the Select Board Tuesday whether to revive the town hall/Ritter renovation after its narrow defeat
meetings.summary: The Lunenburg Municipal Building Reuse (Design) Committee reviewed its own notes ahead of a joint meeting with the Board of Selectmen the following Tuesday, covering community outreach gaps, ADA compliance, remaining ARPA funds, and whether to broaden its charge beyond Town Hall and the Ritter building. Members debated whether to bring the roughly $23 million renovation project back to voters at a November special town meeting, discussed engaging the new town manager and new superintendent who were not involved when the plan was developed, and voted to adjourn.

meetings.headline: Commissioners revised the public PFAS/hardness treatment survey, leaning toward pricier scenarios over the cheapest one
meetings.summary: The Water District Commissioners spent most of the meeting line-editing a public engagement survey on PFAS and hardness treatment options before sending it to residents, debating scenario costs and cutting or reworking several questions. No formal vote was taken on any treatment scenario; that choice was deferred to the public survey and eventual town vote.

Much of the meeting concerned whether and how to charge new fees for accessory dwelling units and additional bedrooms, comparing neighboring towns, with a decision to draft an initial letter to the town board rather than set a fee immediately; the commission also questioned the cost of annual system mapping in its engineering contract and discussed overall system capacity.

meetings.headline: Fire chief pitched a fourth duty shift to end chronic forced overtime and thin ambulance staffing
meetings.summary: This was the first joint Select Board/School Committee/Finance Committee "tri-board" meeting, run by an outside facilitator, covering the fire department's proposed fourth shift, possible consolidation of town/school facilities, HR, legal and IT services, departmental growth pressures (special education, federal grant cuts), and financial-management controls after a revolving account ran into deficit. No consolidation, budget, or staffing item was put to a vote; the boards agreed to keep exploring facilities, HR and legal consolidation, to hold future tri-board meetings at Town Hall broadcast live, and to hold a dedicated public listening session in late October rather than public comment at every meeting.

minutes.summary: This was the first joint Select Board/School Committee/Finance Committee "tri-board" meeting, run by an outside facilitator, covering the fire department's proposed fourth shift, possible consolidation of town/school facilities, HR, legal and IT services, departmental growth pressures (special education, federal grant cuts), and financial-management controls after a revolving account ran into deficit. budget_items.what_was_said: Each new hire's uniform allowance is set by contract per year, added to the fourth-shift cost estimate.
A school committee member said the district's guaranteed legal cost last year was a certain figure, used to argue for combining town and school legal services.
A board member cited the town's flat-rate contract figure for its lawyer from the prior year, contrasted with the school's hourly labor-attorney arrangement.

budget_items.topic: Trash/recycling cost and proposed enterprise fund
budget_items.what_was_said: A member cited what the town currently pays per year for recycling and proposed shifting trash/recycling to a self-funded enterprise fund, with savings potentially redirected to fund the fire department's fourth shift.
The finance director said the town saw a premium increase from its carrier this past year and has been told to expect at least the same increase again next year.
A school committee member described the cost range of out-of-district special education placements as a reason to invest in in-district BCBA staffing instead.

The superintendent said elimination of certain federal title grants for professional development and multilingual learner education has been reported statewide, which will affect the district's budget and the governor's earmark allowances.

A member described turning a parks and recreation department in a prior town of employment from a deficit to a profit over three years as an argument for making Lunenburg's recreation director full-time.

The finance director said one school revolving account went into a significant deficit this past school year because no budget had been entered for it in the town's financial system, so overspending wasn't flagged.

decisions.decision: The boards agreed facilities-department consolidation is worth exploring as a longer-term (FY26-FY28) possibility, not part of the current budget cycle.
The group narrowed its consolidation exploration list to facilities, HR, and legal/buying-power, while treating IT consolidation as a hard no per the school side.

Rather than a public comment period at every tri-board meeting, the group agreed to hold a dedicated public listening session around the end of October and to invite email/survey input at each meeting.
The finance director and a select board member agreed to draft a prioritized list of financial best practices to bring back to the committee.
The superintendent said hiring a business manager is the district's top financial-management priority right now.
The finance committee and superintendent agreed to aim for quarterly meetings going forward to avoid budget-season surprises.
The next tri-board meeting was set for August 26th per the already-circulated draft schedule.
Future tri-board meetings will be held at Town Hall, set up without using the stage, and broadcast live, rather than at the adult activity center.

meetings.headline: Green committee will pursue a townwide Mass Save building-assessment study before its next grant push
meetings.summary: The chair recapped a Mass Save Summit he attended, walking the task force through weatherization, heat-pump, building-management and electric-lawn-equipment incentive programs, plus new "portfolio prioritization" and building-assessment studies meant to get town buildings grant-ready. The group agreed to schedule a meeting with National Grid/Mass Save and the facilities director to start the portfolio study, put the Turkey Hill project on hold until then, reviewed the town's Green Community history and open incentive programs, and closed with brief updates on a styrofoam-recycling grant, school HVAC work, committee term expirations, and a motion on prior minutes.

Projects over 20,000 square feet must meet a minimum benefit-to-cost threshold to qualify for incentives.

budget_items.what_was_said: A state incentive for switching to electric vehicles was described as too small relative to the added cost, under the Climate Leader vehicle-first requirement.

figures_as_heard: 10% of a project cost up to a million dollars

budget_items.what_was_said: A new grant would cover most of the cost of battery-powered ride-on and stand-up mowers for municipalities.
figures_as_heard: up to 75% of the total cost

The town's original Green Communities designation grant was described as a one-time award used for early energy efficiency upgrades.
Subsequent Green Communities funding moved to a competitive round with a per-grant cap, most recently used for the primary school mini-splits.

budget_items.topic: Prior primary school mini-split project cost
budget_items.what_was_said: An earlier mini-split installation at the primary school, done without the green committee's early involvement, was described as costing far more than necessary for a limited number of units.

meetings.headline: Committee authorized a replacement video-storage system after the old one failed entirely
meetings.summary: A three-member Public Access Cable Committee, down to a bare quorum with a new member just sworn in, opened its fiscal year by re-appointing its chair, vice chair and clerk/secretary, then heard the department manager's monthly report. The main substantive matter was that the committee's video-file storage system (NAS) had failed completely; the committee authorized purchase of a replacement from the maintenance budget line, discussed the Comcast cable contract renewal process, a planned studio relocation, new recordings of the trust fund commission and tri-board committee, and reviewed year-end financial and programming figures.

A reserve fund is held for a future studio project and has been placed into short-term treasury bonds under guidance from the town treasurer.

meetings.headline: A hearing was found invalid for lack of abutter notice and must be reopened from scratch
meetings.summary: The Lunenburg Conservation Commission welcomed two new commissioners, worked through a full docket of wetland hearings, and discovered mid-meeting that a hearing on a deck/sunroom project had never been properly noticed to abutters, forcing it to restart. The board also voted to split its small FY2026 timber rights fund between supplies and services, heard updates on trail grants and the pollinator habitat, got a briefing on a proposed town stormwater utility fee, and said goodbye to its departing interim administrator, Sophie.

attendees.role: presenter (wetland scientist/representative for applicant, 100 Towns and Harbor Road)

budget_items.what_was_said: The chair said the commission had to vote on dividing a spending limit for the timber rights fund between purchase of service and supplies for fiscal year 2026, using a spreadsheet supplied by the finance office.
A commissioner recommended most of the fund go to supplies rather than services since trail maintenance work is done mostly in-house.
The commission voted by roll call to allocate the fund as proposed between supplies and purchase of service.
A commissioner reported a reimbursement request had been submitted for engineering, design and permitting work at two trail sites, with the reimbursement expected to cover most of what was spent.

budget_items.topic: Eagle Scout rain barrel project funding
budget_items.what_was_said: A commissioner described an Eagle Scout project at the pollinator habitat that added a rain barrel system, funded entirely through the scout's own fundraising.
A commissioner serving on the stormwater task force said the proposed town stormwater utility fee was projected to raise this much per year from residents and businesses.

budget_items.topic: Proposed stormwater utility fee per household
budget_items.what_was_said: The same commissioner said a single-family home would likely pay a quarterly fee in this range if the utility is adopted, with larger or more paved properties paying more.
A commissioner noted the DPW's overall budget for stormwater-related equipment and infrastructure presented at town meeting, only part of which the new utility fee would offset.

decisions.decision: Because the 833 Flatville Road hearing could not proceed for lack of abutter notice, any discussion held that night would have to be repeated when the hearing is formally reopened.
The interim conservation administrator was asked to visit the 833 Flatville Road site and take notes to post in OpenGov ahead of the next hearing.
The administrator was directed to upload DEP comment emails into OpenGov going forward so all commissioners can see them.

390 Howard Street will be continued to July 16, with the office told to tell the applicant that failure to appear with an updated survey/wetland flag plan could result in the commission voting to deny for lack of action.
The chair will follow up with the office on whether the town or the original applicant should request the certificate of compliance for the 452 boulder installation, since it is now town property.

The office will be asked to correct the agenda for 167 Towns and Harbor Road, since the application appears to involve removal of about 19 trees rather than the 3 dead trees listed, which may require reclassifying it from a determination to an RDA.

meetings.headline: Select Board adopted tri-board ground rules to launch the FY27 school/town budget process, plus several appointments.
meetings.summary: The Select Board handled a full agenda of appointments (Adam Bernie to planning board, Cara McCarthy as communications/IT manager, Tiffany Warren to Cultural Council), heard a town manager report covering a state supplemental school funding award, Wallace Park damage, and staffing vacancies, and reviewed ARPA project balances nearing their spending deadline. Much of the meeting was devoted to setting FY2026 town manager and select board goals and adopting ground rules for a new joint "tri-board" process with the school committee and finance committee aimed at producing a select board recommendation on the FY27 budget, including possible cuts, level funding, or a Prop 2½ override, by around February 2026. The board closed by entering executive session for town manager contract negotiations and police union bargaining strategy.

minutes.summary: The Lunenburg Stormwater Task Force met with its consultant Nick (of CI) to work through open questions on the draft Stormwater Utility Report: how vacant, multifamily, and tax-exempt parcels are classified, whether to add tiers for the largest properties (Walmart, Unitil, storage facilities), and a pricing error discovered live where alternative fee tables did not match across tiers. The task force set a goal of presenting to the Select Board and Finance Committee in September and giving an update at the November town meeting, ahead of a planned FY2026 annual town meeting vote, and scheduled its next meeting for July 17.

budget_items.what_was_said: The consultant explained the utility fee is based on impervious area equivalent to a typical single-family residential property (one ERU), with the annual fee amount still to be decided among examples like these figures.

Board members found the per-tier prices in table 3-1 and table 3-3 for alternatives 1-4 did not match for several tiers; the consultant confirmed a drafting error and said table 3-1 has the correct numbers.

budget_items.topic: Tier 10 impervious area cap vs actual
budget_items.what_was_said: The task force compared the tier 10 threshold to the actual size of a large commercial parking lot, finding it far exceeded the cap, prompting discussion of a new higher tier.
The board discussed whether to create an additional tier above the current top tier to better capture the very largest properties.
The consultant and board reviewed the ERU ranges assigned to each tier, noting tier 9's range was unusually wide and should be narrowed by splitting tiers 9 and 10 into three tiers.
The consultant described a comparable town's flat quarterly stormwater charge applied to every user regardless of property type, cited as context for Lunenburg's fee design.

budget_items.topic: Potential large-property fee under a progressive tier structure
budget_items.what_was_said: A member raised concern that large properties could face a very large new quarterly or annual charge if tiers were weighted progressively, calling it a potential 'sticker shock.'
The board recalled that $25 a quarter had been discussed previously as roughly the upper level being considered, referencing the Amesbury comparison.
Members noted some parcels generate very small property tax bills, raising the question of how tiny utility bills would be handled and whether it costs more to mail than to collect.
The board recalled that an earlier presentation used a placeholder figure for what a typical single-family home might pay annually under the proposed utility.

budget_items.topic: CI engineering contract for next fiscal year
budget_items.what_was_said: The consultant and chair discussed needing to finalize a new contract with CI for the coming fiscal year, which starts imminently, continuing the notice-to-proceed arrangement used previously.

budget_items.topic: DPW capital equipment/project list funded by the utility
budget_items.what_was_said: The board noted the DPW director had already provided a capital equipment list of projects the stormwater utility revenue would fund, and wants more cost detail added before public presentations.

Give a more detailed update at the November town meeting, with a goal of proposing the stormwater utility at the 2026 annual town meeting.

Set the next task force meeting for July 17th, and consider adding extra meetings over the summer if needed to stay on the September/November timeline.

The task force decided against creating an exemption or waiver process for properties claiming no stormwater runoff, citing administrative overhead.

The task force set a timeline: present the draft utility to the Select Board and Finance Committee around September, then update November town meeting, ahead of a vote planned for the 2026 annual town meeting.

Members asked the consultant for lists of the parcels in the largest fee tiers and the unclassified parcels, plus a comparison of town-owned versus private impervious area, to support the case for the fee.
The next task force meeting was set for July 17, with additional summer meetings possible to stay on the September/November schedule.

why_it_matters: This is early work on a proposed stormwater utility fee that would eventually appear as a charge to property owners, sized by how much impervious surface -- driveways, parking lots, roofs -- a parcel has.

Residents will be asked to vote on adopting the utility, with the task force aiming for the 2026 annual town meeting, so how tiers, exemptions and large-property caps are set now shapes what different property owners would eventually pay.
The tier-pricing table correction and the decision not to offer runoff exemptions are still draft choices, not a finalized fee -- both remain open to public review before any vote.

meetings.headline: Water commissioners approved a Rolling Acres tie-in purchase and reworked the PFAS survey after public pushback on treatment options.
meetings.summary: The Water District commissioners approved purchasing materials for a new water main tie-in feeding Rolling Acres and spent most of the meeting revising a public survey meant to gauge community priorities on PFAS treatment, hardness, redundancy and cost. In public comment, residents pressed the board on why combining the Lancaster and Keing well sources for treatment had been ruled out, questioned treatment plant costs, and argued residents should get more cost detail before any survey goes out; the board agreed to revise the draft and bring it back in two weeks.

public_comment.topic: Questioned why the Keing-Lancaster interconnection was ruled out by engineers, gave his own comparison of PFAS, iron and manganese levels and costs between well sources, and asked for a written explanation from the engineering firm.
Said the district should not spend money until state and federal PFAS rules and the 3M/DuPont litigation are settled, and that treatment plant costs quoted by contractors are far too high.

Said the survey should focus narrowly on PFAS rather than smell/hardness/other issues, and asked why a Lancaster-only-treated plus Keing-only-treated option (no connecting pipe) was not offered, saying costs should be shown to and voted on by residents.

votes.motion: To allocate $10,388.36 for materials to install a new tee/tie-in feeding Rolling Acres, using HR Prescott as vendor
To approve the minutes of June 11, 2025
To adjourn the meeting

budget_items.what_was_said: Three vendor quotes for the parts needed to cut in a new tee and service line from Lancaster Road toward Rolling Acres were reviewed, described as all within a couple hundred dollars of each other. HR Prescott was recommended as the vendor with the best customer service among the three.
A commissioner noted gate valve prices have roughly tripled since COVID, citing prior and current prices as examples.
A commissioner noted that once a purchase reaches a certain dollar threshold, formal public procurement (bidding) rules apply, and discussed possibly setting a higher project total to plan ahead.

budget_items.topic: Hickory Hills / PFAS pilot study spending to date
budget_items.what_was_said: Commissioners said the district has already spent close to a stated amount on pilot studies, engineering and surveying for PFAS treatment options, and that another pilot study to evaluate combining Lancaster and Keings would cost roughly another stated amount.
figures_as_heard: almost threequarters of a million dollars

budget_items.what_was_said: A resident cited a capital cost figure from the district's chart and questioned whether a shorter pipe route between Lancaster and Keing would be cheaper, and compared annual operating and maintenance costs between the two scenarios.
A resident argued that water treatment plant costs quoted by contractors and engineers are excessive, comparing a plant's cost unfavorably to major infrastructure like the Brooklyn Bridge.

budget_items.topic: Full build-out cost estimate for Keing and Lancaster treatment, and Lancaster-only cost
budget_items.what_was_said: A resident argued the public should be told the cost of relying on Keing alone versus building full treatment, citing very large figures, while a commissioner noted the engineers found a Lancaster-only option too costly given its limited well capacity.

decisions.decision: Revise the PFAS public engagement survey based on today's comments and put the updated draft on the agenda for the meeting in two weeks.

meetings.headline: Committee got dire FY27–FY28 budget forecasts and agreed to push for an override or other new revenue.
meetings.summary: This meeting was largely a retirement send-off for outgoing Superintendent Dr. Kate Burnham, with extended public and staff tributes, alongside routine year-end business (transfers, surplus declarations, a scholarship gift, and a preschool/special-education compliance update). The substantive policy work was a first look at FY27 and FY28 budget projections showing large multi-million-dollar gaps, leading the committee to approve a statement for upcoming tri-board meetings committing to seek an override and/or other revenue sources (including discussion of the Community Preservation Act) rather than accept cuts alone.

budget_items.topic: Health insurance line shortfall this year

minutes.headline: Committee got dire FY27–FY28 budget forecasts and agreed to push for an override or other new revenue.
minutes.summary: This meeting was largely a retirement send-off for outgoing Superintendent Dr. Kate Burnham, with extended public and staff tributes, alongside routine year-end business (transfers, surplus declarations, a scholarship gift, and a preschool/special-education compliance update). The substantive policy work was a first look at FY27 and FY28 budget projections showing large multi-million-dollar gaps, leading the committee to approve a statement for upcoming tri-board meetings committing to seek an override and/or other revenue sources (including discussion of the Community Preservation Act) rather than accept cuts alone.

what_happened.line: The committee accepted FY27 and FY28 projections showing gaps large enough to commit to seeking an override or other new revenue rather than cuts alone.
The committee approved a joint statement for the tri-board process naming that override-or-revenue approach as its position.
The committee voted to restore fifth-grade band only as a fee-funded before/after-school club, not during the school day.
Routine year-end business also passed: FY25 transfers, an encumbrance carryover into FY26, a surplus declaration, and a scholarship gift.
The first tri-board meeting was set for July 8 at 7pm.

why_it_matters: Residents will eventually be asked to vote on an override or other new revenue source; this meeting set that as the committee's negotiating position going into the tri-board process, not a final decision.
The band restoration approach shows one program cut being addressed through a family-paid fee rather than restored school-day funding, which affects who can access it.
The FY27-FY28 gap sets the scale of what cuts or new revenue the town will be weighing in the coming budget cycle.

meetings.headline: Planning Board leans toward Tritown 'paper compliance' to meet the state's MBTA Communities housing mandate
meetings.summary: This was a public input session, not a voting meeting: the planning board chair presented the MBTA Communities zoning mandate, the four candidate sites (White Street, Tritown, Rogers Way, Leominster Shirley Road), and four possible compliance paths, then took extensive resident questions and comments. No formal vote occurred; the chair reiterated that the planning board will bring one bylaw option to a November special town meeting, and many residents and the chair himself leaned toward 'paper compliance' using Tritown's existing zoning while reserving Leominster Shirley Road for a locally designed mixed-use development.

public_comment.topic: Whether a dual/mixed-use design (retail on the ground floor, housing above) is possible under the bylaw
Support for using Leominster Shirley Road for a longer, more comprehensive mixed-use design process rather than the standard MBTA options
Disagreed that Leominster Shirley Road should be taken off the table for industrial use; asked how using existing zoning as 'paper compliance' helps solve the housing problem statewide
Argued commercial/mixed-use growth, not multifamily alone, is what raises the tax levy without burdening residents; favored a true mixed-use district at Leominster Shirley Road
Objected to the MBTA Communities law as state overreach on local zoning rights, invoking the recent ADU bylaw; open to the mixed-use counter-argument as a reason to accept some zoning

Described prior professional experience in another community choosing 'paper compliance' by zoning over a golf course; said the state monitors town meeting votes and that the legal question is largely settled after the Milton case
Raised concern that dense multi-unit housing (as seen in Harvard/Devens) brings large numbers of school-age children, citing an overcrowded school bus experience
Asked how choosing an option affects the town's affordable-housing (rental vs. ownership) requirement
Asked the presenter to address schools, sewer and water as 'the elephant in the room'
Agreed the industrial/mixed-use sites are valuable and that paper compliance is the easiest path since it does not deliver what the town actually wants (affordable housing or industrial land)
Suggested favoring affordable senior housing, arguing seniors bring tax revenue without adding school enrollment

Questioned the assumption that families won't move into mid-density housing, describing a sibling struggling to find affordable rental housing for her young family and concerns about school transportation strain
Argued the housing produced would mainly serve wealthier renters, not young families like her sister, and cited traffic/road conditions near Whalom
Favored paper compliance at Tritown to avoid state interference, while supporting a locally designed attractive development (small-scale homes, restaurants, a theater) at Leominster Shirley Road
Asked whether the neighboring town of Shirley is doing anything comparable for MBTA compliance
Pressed on whether water and sewer capacity (citing Leominster/Fitchburg constraints) is a real problem regardless of whether zoning alone is required
Noted a separate 55-and-over building built recently at Tritown and asked whether it created a compliance issue
Argued the three candidate sites serve distinct, non-interchangeable purposes and expressed concern about added traffic near Rogers Way/Mackey's
Asked why the town couldn't split zoning between Rogers Way/Tritown for compliance while reserving Leominster Shirley Road for the town's own preferred development, similar to the recommended split
Asked whether the planning board intends to zone the MBTA district as an overlay rather than rezoning outright
Asked how much land is typically needed for industrial use

budget_items.what_was_said: The presenter gave back-of-napkin figures for average home price, average rent, and average household income to argue Lunenburg residents are far outside standard affordability ratios.
The town has hired the firm Community Scale, funded with grant money, to draft the MBTA Communities compliance bylaw once a zoning option is chosen.

budget_items.topic: State grant funding tied to compliance
budget_items.what_was_said: The presenter said the state's main enforcement tool for noncompliant towns is withholding grant monies, rather than only court action.

budget_items.topic: Area Median Income threshold for affordable housing (SHI)
budget_items.what_was_said: A commenter explained the technical definition of 'affordable' housing used for the state's Subsidized Housing Inventory, including the AMI-based income threshold and the 10%/25% set-aside rules under Chapter 40B.

budget_items.topic: Lunenburg's current Subsidized Housing Inventory percentage
budget_items.what_was_said: A commenter cited Lunenburg's reported SHI percentage before and after 2020 census figures, contrasting it with another town's reported vs. 'realistic' affordable percentage.

budget_items.topic: HOA / ownership costs for multifamily units
budget_items.what_was_said: A commenter argued that townhouses, condos and duplexes are not meaningfully cheaper than single-family homes once added monthly ownership costs are included.

budget_items.topic: Value of the Whalom (Wham) Luxury Apartments development
budget_items.what_was_said: The presenter cited the development's value to argue it is not economically likely to be redeveloped even if rezoned at higher density.

budget_items.topic: Hypothetical cost to build homes at Rogers Way
budget_items.what_was_said: The presenter used a hypothetical per-home construction cost to argue that zoning capacity for many units does not mean a developer will actually build out that many homes.

budget_items.topic: Tax levy growth from commercial vs. residential development
budget_items.what_was_said: A commenter argued commercial growth, not multifamily housing, is the only way to grow the tax levy without burdening residents, favoring a mixed-use commercial/residential option.

decisions.decision: Per the town's existing agreement with consultant Community Scale, the planning board will bring exactly one zoning option to town meeting, not multiple options.
Residents were asked to submit any further questions or feedback in writing on note cards before leaving, to be passed to the planning board.
The moderator tabled further discussion of opposition to the state mandate itself in order to focus remaining time on which zoning option to recommend.

meetings.headline: APDC approved converting a barn at 936 Mass Ave into living space, no binding review required
meetings.summary: The Architectural Preservation District Commission approved a siding change at the Jones House and approved a determination of applicability for a barn-to-living-space conversion at 936 Mass Avenue after resolving that the initial submission was incomplete. The commission also discussed a shrinking town budget allocation, directing available year-end funds toward the hometown heroes banner program and mailer supplies, and heard updates on the Brooks House, a municipal building reuse project, a demolition-delay violation, a possible APDC/historical commission merger, and a dysfunctional master plan steering committee.

Members were unsure whether the current fiscal year's $5,000 could still be used or moved before the fiscal year closes in about 20 days. The chair said he would find out.
Richard said the historical commission has roughly 2850 set aside before the fiscal year ends, to be confirmed, for use toward the hometown heroes banner program.
Members discussed directing available APDC funds to the hometown heroes banner program, conditional on the town accountant confirming current fiscal year funds remain available.
A member proposed pre-purchasing envelopes and stamps for next year's mailers with any remaining year-end funds, capping spending around $50 to $100.
The historical commission voted to use its budget for historical markers and is selecting historically significant sites, including the old buttonwood tree.

decisions.decision: The committee agreed the Jones House siding replacement should be classified as maintenance, not requiring a separate Determination of Applicability form (though a motion was still made for the record).
The review clock for 936 Mass Avenue had not started because the drawings submitted through the town's permitting portal were incomplete (no site plan, exterior finish, or use information).
With complete information provided at the meeting, the review clock for 936 Mass Avenue was considered stopped/complete.
The proposed new garage at 936 Mass Ave falls primarily under the building commissioner, and possibly the zoning board of appeals or planning board, with APDC serving only in an advisory capacity.

Adam Costa will ask the town manager how a resident's letter opposing the APDC/historical commission merger affects the timeline, before the group meets again ahead of a targeted November special town meeting.
The commission agreed it needs to press the select board/committee for a concrete proposal on selling or leasing the Brooks House before drafting a warrant article for town meeting.

meetings.headline: Sewer Commission debated charging a new hookup fee for accessory dwelling units, deferring it to next meeting
meetings.summary: The Lunenburg Sewer Commission covered routine business-manager updates (Dana Street repairs, a manhole repair still under material review, and upcoming quarterly demand billing), approved a services scope with its engineering firm for NPDES and mapping work, and then spent most of the meeting discussing whether to charge a new connection fee for accessory dwelling units (in-law apartments) given new state housing rules easing their construction. No fee was set; commissioners agreed to have staff research the question and bring it back at a future meeting. Routine votes were taken to approve prior minutes and to adjourn, with no stated outcome or count in the captions.

budget_items.topic: PS engineering service agreement (Ray Pierce NPDES permit work)
budget_items.what_was_said: The chair walked through a proposed service agreement with the commission's engineering firm covering project administration, the NPDES report, collection system mapping, the O&M plan, and adaptation planning, each with hours and a dollar figure, totaling an overall contract amount. A commissioner asked whether the firm is ever put out to bid rather than just given another quote, and staff said that could be asked of Bill but the board seems comfortable with the firm's track record.

The business manager said he is waiting for the due date on supplemental billing before running quarterly demands, and noted the MUNIS system update will let the department print demand bills on proper-looking billing stock instead of the old version.
Staff reported a few recent phone calls from homeowners at end-of-life for their septic systems asking what the fee would be to hook into the public sewer system.

budget_items.topic: ADU / accessory dwelling unit connection fee
budget_items.what_was_said: Commissioners discussed whether an additional connection or hookup fee should apply when a homeowner builds an accessory dwelling unit or converts a garage, since the existing 2023 policy sets a minimum residential connection charge with an added amount per bedroom beyond three but does not address a separate unit. They floated a flat fee and agreed to bring the question to Bill and Andrew for research before the next meeting.

budget_items.topic: Standard sewer tie-in / connection charge example
budget_items.what_was_said: A commissioner described the normal process of emailing the business manager for a tie-in card and connection cost, citing an example figure as what such a connection might run.

decisions.decision: Put the question of an ADU/accessory-unit sewer connection fee on the next meeting's agenda and have Bill and Andrew research the legal and technical requirements first.
Keep Dana Street repairs and manhole repair as standing items on future agendas, and keep quarterly demands on the agenda until billing goes out.
Resume outreach/recruitment for new commission members since one member is leaving after selling his house.

meetings.headline: Select Board drafted FY26 goals built around a new tri-board process to shape the FY27 budget, override left open.
meetings.summary: The Lunenburg Select Board approved a farmers-market alcohol sampling permit for Pony Shack Cider, then spent nearly the entire meeting drafting FY26 select board and town manager goals. The dominant goal, given top priority, is overhauling the FY27 budget process through new joint 'tri-board' meetings with the finance and school committees, explicitly leaving open the possibility of a town/school Proposition 2½ override; the board also worked through goals on employee experience, transparency, municipal properties (TC Pacios, 925 Main Street, tax title parcels, Brooks House/Municipal Building Design Committee), and policy reviews, without finalizing the goals document that night.

budget_items.what_was_said: The town manager said a professional compensation/classification study, wanted by staff for years, would need outside funding, possibly sought at the fall special town meeting.
The prior SAP bylaw change created a small monetary award for a recognition program; the board discussed removing the money and using a plaque or small gift card instead.

Previously appropriated roof-repair money was designated for a different part of the TC Pacios building than now planned to remain in use; the board wants a fall special town meeting article to move those funds.
A member asked the assessed value of the 925 Main Street property being prepared for sale.
The treasurer/collector is preparing a tax title auction; one parcel's value was cited while discussing which properties boards want to retain.

budget_items.topic: Municipal building capital cost vs. free cash
budget_items.what_was_said: A member noted a project cost that would consume the town's entire free cash for a good year, illustrating why it can't be done through ordinary capital planning.

budget_items.topic: Municipal Building Design Committee project cost escalation
budget_items.what_was_said: A member recalled the committee's goal was to keep the prior building project under one figure, but it grew substantially before town meeting rejected it.
Board discussed whether state law only requires an annual report to exist, not to be printed, citing a fine for non-compliance, while considering digitizing it.

budget_items.topic: Cost of printing/mailing town meeting warrant books
budget_items.what_was_said: The town manager pulled up the cost of printing and mailing the full warrant book to look at postcard/digital alternatives.
A member asked the town manager to find out how much ARPA money remains unspent this calendar year, since unspent funds are lost after the deadline, with some possible new federal flexibility.

decisions.decision: The board agreed to skip a general Q&A on goal-setting methodology and go straight into reviewing FY25 goals.
The board agreed the FY27 budget process/timeline is the select board's top-priority goal for FY26.
The board defined a new 'tri-board' as regularly scheduled joint meetings of the select board, finance committee, and school committee to prepare the FY27 budget.
Financial policy review/adoption (from the DLS community compact grant) was moved out of the budget goal and made objective one under a separate 'review select board policies' goal instead.
The onboarding/orientation objective for the town manager was tabled for further work rather than finalized that night.
Noted (per the town manager's contract) that goals must be finalized in writing by July 15, with self-evaluation due by April 15 and a November check-in.
Added an action item to bring a fall special town meeting article moving previously appropriated TC Pacios roof-repair funds to the portion of the building that will remain in use.
Agreed the 925 Main Street sale objective will be measured by completion of sale preparation and process, not strictly a completed sale within the fiscal year.
Removed TC Pacios and 925 Main Street from the 'municipal properties' goal draft; folded TC Pacios into the Municipal Building Design Committee objective and added the Brooks House there instead.
Moved the warrant-mailing/postcard bylaw idea into the FY27 budget goal's objectives rather than treating it as a separate goal.
Directed the town manager to report back (targeted for the next meeting) on how much ARPA money remains unspent this calendar year.

meetings.headline: Planning Board chair election tied between Allison and Brener; unresolved, revisit June 23
meetings.summary: The Lunenburg Planning Board held its annual reorganization, holding town elections for chair, vice chair, clerk and committee representative roles; the vote for chair between Matt Allison and Matt Brener ended in a tie twice and was left unresolved to be revisited at the next meeting, while other roles (vice chair, clerk, and various committee reps) were filled without contention. The board also held a joint session with the Open Space Committee on chapter 61A right-of-first-refusal process and voted, along with Open Space, to recommend the town not exercise its right of first refusal on 222 West Townsend Road. Three public hearings were held: 1083 Northfield Road (continued a month pending peer review of a revised 5-lot plan), 443 West Townsend Road lot 3 (approved with three bylaw waivers for a common driveway), and 100 Townsend Harbor Road (continued to June 23rd after abutters raised stormwater/lake concerns, pending review by the incoming interim planner).

meetings.headline: Committee to seek Select Board direction after its ~$23M building plan failed at town meeting and the ballot
meetings.summary: The Lunenburg Municipal Building Design Committee, with no vote planned or taken, went around the room gathering each member's views after its major renovation/addition project failed to reach the two-thirds threshold at town meeting and lost badly at the ballot. Members largely agreed the project suffered from insufficient public outreach and scope creep, and that the committee should meet in early July, then bring the Select Board a prioritized, phased capital-projects plan (covering Town Hall/Ritter, Turkey Hill, Marshall Park, and PAC) rather than reviving the single large proposal as-is.

budget_items.what_was_said: The vice chair noted the committee's proposal was voted down and set out to gather members' views on whether a way forward exists.
The estimated construction cost covering the town meeting house restoration/renovation, the Ritter memorial renovation and the addition/site cost was reviewed from the schematic design estimate.

Tony said the project began as a small consolidated-administration addition and grew substantially by the time it went to town meeting, which he called a loss of discipline that undermined voter confidence.
Dave suggested giving PAC a fixed, limited amount of space rather than letting requirements expand further.

budget_items.topic: Cost of closing in a building (renovation vs. new construction)
budget_items.what_was_said: Tony explained that renovating an already-enclosed building like Town Hall or Ritter avoids a large share of new-construction cost compared with building new.
Dave and Tony discussed, without settling on a figure, how much of the project's cost was attributable to state prevailing-wage requirements.
Dave cited a painter's prevailing wage rate as an example of costs driving up the project price under state rules.
Tony proposed commissioning a scientific survey of residents on capital-project priorities, saying it would be inexpensive for a town Lunenburg's size.
Tony floated a future town meeting warrant article to appropriate additional money to hire an architect once project priorities are set.

budget_items.topic: 1969 capital plan for Whalom Lake park
budget_items.what_was_said: Jay recounted that a 1969 town capital plan for a beachfront park at Whalom Lake was rejected, as a cautionary historical example.

decisions.decision: The committee will go around the room to gather each member's sentiment on a path forward, to shape a framework to bring to the Board of Selectmen.
The next meeting's agenda will include approval of minutes and reorganization (replacing former member Michael Ray, adding Laura).
No formal vote would be taken at this meeting.
The committee will hold a meeting in early July to outline what it wants to present to the Select Board (projects, priorities, timeline).
Dave will contact the town manager's office (Caesar) to get the committee on the Board of Selectmen's agenda for later in July.

what_happened.line: The committee polled every member's views on next steps after its building renovation plan failed at town meeting and then lost badly at the ballot.
No vote was taken; members largely agreed the project suffered from too little public outreach and had grown in scope since it began.
The committee plans to meet in early July to draft a prioritized, phased capital plan covering Town Hall/Ritter, Turkey Hill, Marshall Park, and the PAC.
A member will contact the town manager's office to get the committee onto the Select Board's agenda later in July to present that plan.

why_it_matters: Any future building project -- Town Hall, Ritter, Turkey Hill, Marshall Park, or the PAC -- would still need to clear a two-thirds town meeting vote and a townwide ballot, so how the committee frames scope and outreach next time affects whether a plan passes.
A phased, prioritized list could mean residents see several smaller project votes over time instead of one large bundled proposal, changing what gets asked of them and when.

meetings.headline: Conservation Commission approved several wetland permits; a member publicly questioned the legality of its 30-foot no-touch buffer rule
meetings.summary: The Lunenburg Conservation Commission held hearings on several wetland permit applications (10 Sandy Cove Road, 60 Cross Road, 417 Howard Street, 221 Electric Ave), approving or issuing negative determinations for most, and continued others (1083 Northfield Road, 390 Howard Street, 31 Round Road) due to missing materials or requested delays, at one point noting the commission was near losing quorum. The meeting also covered a Chapter 61 land-sale notification the commission voted not to pursue, a Mass Trails grant reimbursement update, trail-improvement and volunteer updates, and a lengthy, unresolved debate — led by Commissioner Peter Stella — over whether the commission's 30-foot "no-touch" wetland buffer bylaw is legally enforceable.

decisions.decision: For 390 Howard Street, the commission will have the interim agent formally notify the applicant in writing that the commission is about to lose quorum for that project.

Tabled the proposal for boilerplate order-of-conditions language on large-parcel delineation, pending review by town counsel and DEP, with a preference to instead raise the issue directly with applicants at hearings.
Chair will put moving the July meeting dates to the second and fourth Wednesdays (instead of first and third) on the next agenda for discussion, to avoid a holiday-week conflict.
A commissioner's concern about apparent unpermitted land alteration at a property should be reported to the interim agent/office rather than raised first in an open meeting.
Any request to use drone footage to investigate a property should be sent privately to the chair and vice chair first, so legal advice can be obtained from town counsel before proceeding.

what_happened.line: The commission approved or issued negative determinations for wetland permits at several addresses, including Sandy Cove Road, Cross Road, Howard Street and Electric Ave.
A commissioner publicly questioned whether the commission's 30-foot no-touch wetland buffer rule has legal authority behind it, and the debate ended without resolution.
The commission voted not to exercise the town's right of first refusal on a Chapter 61 land-sale notice for a West Townsend Road property.
Hearings for three properties were continued to June 18 for missing materials or applicant delay, and the board noted it was near losing quorum on one case.

why_it_matters: A homeowner or contractor working near a wetland relies on these permits and continuances to know what conditions apply and when a decision will come.

meetings.headline: Commission leans toward a scaled-back Marshall Park plan for fall town meeting after spring's defeat
meetings.summary: The Lunenburg Parks Commission reorganized with a new chair and vice chair, then spent most of the meeting on Marshall Park: after the full renovation project failed at spring town meeting amid the town's override fight, members debated whether to bring back the full project or a smaller 'Phase 1 plus' version in the fall, weighing grant eligibility, remaining appropriated funds, and how residents would react. No final decision was made; the commission will confirm remaining funds and design costs with its consultants before choosing a direction, and also covered routine business including Wallace Park playground vandalism repairs, the beach weed-removal plan, summer programming, and scheduling.

budget_items.what_was_said: A former resident who bought two memorial benches offered to pay for new composite wood on them; the facilities director priced redoing all six benches, with the donor covering his portion and the rest needing select board approval to accept the donation.

budget_items.topic: Wallace Park playground repair (merry-go-round and accessible swing)
budget_items.what_was_said: The facilities director located the manufacturer and priced replacing the stolen/damaged merry-go-round handles and the missing accessible swing, funded from the revolving account, with pricing rising July 1st.

The prior resurfacing was done incorrectly and is peeling, creating a tripping hazard; a new contractor is not correctly on state contract and must be posted for three weeks, pushing the work to September, but the project is reported under budget, funded through capital.

budget_items.topic: Town beach weed removal — hydro-rake permitting
budget_items.what_was_said: Estimates for an Army Corps-level permit for hydro-raking, which would only be good for one year, were cited as a reason to move to diver-assisted suction harvesting instead.
Last year the beach offered a town-employee discount rate at the request of someone at DPW; the recreation director recalled the family rate and said pricing will stay the same this year.

budget_items.topic: Marshall Park septic/design funds — Board of Health appropriation
budget_items.what_was_said: The original Board of Health money was designated for septic work only; the new Board of Health is reportedly more open to using it for a sewer connection instead.

The chair got a current balance from the finance director and subtracted an in-process invoice to estimate remaining appropriated design funds, before further invoices from both consultants were accounted for.
An additional consultant invoice was approved at this meeting, further reducing the remaining Marshall Park design balance, with one more invoice still expected from the other consultant.
After all known invoices, consultants estimated the remaining appropriated Marshall Park money was enough to fund an updated design for the smaller ('Phase 1 plus') project.

budget_items.topic: Marshall Park grant eligibility — smaller vs. full project
budget_items.what_was_said: Building only the smaller phase would disqualify the project from a larger state park grant it currently qualifies for under the full design, dropping it to a much smaller grant.
A commissioner did not want the town to look like it was returning a large previously awarded grant if the project were scaled back.

budget_items.topic: Debt exclusion / tax impact confusion at town meeting
budget_items.what_was_said: A commissioner said residents at town meeting did not understand that other debt exclusions (primary school, library, public safety building) were coming off their tax bills at the same time new debt would be added, and reacted only to a tax increase figure.

The chair and recreation director said the department spends a large amount on facilities and brings in relatively little revenue from a small user base, and want to revisit user fees with the town manager and finance director before the fall.

decisions.decision: Leave the clerk position vacant for now since minutes are being handled by a separate recording secretary; can revisit later if needed.
Route the resident's donation for bench materials to the select board for formal acceptance, as has been done before for similar donations.
Karen Manard will follow up with the design consultants (Tom Doolittle and Ray) to confirm remaining Marshall Park funds and continue design work while the commission decides on project scope.
Anita Shapers and Karen Manard will step back from regularly attending the Marshall Park design team's virtual meetings; the new chair may take over, with Marian not yet ready to lead that piece.
Invite the skate park group to a future meeting to present their 3D model, date to be confirmed.
Invite the town manager to a future meeting to review the recreation/facilities financial picture.
Aim to review and possibly change recreation user fees around August–September, before user groups advertise for the next season, with input from the finance director and town manager.
Next meetings set for July 30th and August 20th.
