meetings.headline: FinCom reviewed the full FY26 town/school budget and a ~$2M citizen override petition for schools; no votes taken.
meetings.summary: The Finance Committee heard the Town Manager's complete FY26 budget presentation department by department, including a restructured chart of accounts, a proposed $500,000 free-cash transfer to the schools, restored pavement funding, and a 14.84% health insurance increase. It also heard a citizen's Proposition 2½ override petition (roughly $2 million) to restore school cuts, and a member's presentation finding unreconciled figures in the school budget, prompting agreed-upon follow-up data requests. No substantive votes were taken; the board plans to vote on all warrant articles and finalize its annual report the following week.

public_comment.topic: Asked whether public comment on each budget section can be made now or must wait for next week's formal public hearing.

Criticized the town manager's proposal to cut the grant writer/manager position and use $50,000 for a pavement pilot instead, and questioned cemetery- and pavement-related capital requests as lacking a plan.
Explained how a Worcester Regional Retirement COLA would translate into a small monthly pension increase, and noted the impact of health-insurance costs on retirees on fixed incomes.
Urged the committee to scrutinize the core school budget itself (teacher cuts, salary lines, transportation increases), separate from the override question.
Suggested putting a QR code or link on the printed Finance Committee report so voters can access more information before town meeting.
Explained the financial-approval language in the cemetery citizen petition article and proposed spending $50,000 on cemetery electrical/lighting instead of pavement crack-sealing.
Listed a range of unresolved town financial pressures (storm water utility, sewer commission default rate, PFAS remediation costs, trash pickup funding) for the committee to weigh.

votes.motion: Motion to adjourn.

budget_items.what_was_said: The overlay reserve was originally budgeted at $250,000 but has been reduced by the assessors to $175,000.
A transfer of certified free cash to the Lunenburg Public Schools' FY26 operating budget was proposed as a stop-gap ahead of a possible FY27 override.
The planned $100,000 transfer to the general stabilization account was reduced to zero to help fund the school transfer.
The planned transfer to special-purpose stabilization funds was eliminated entirely.
Three special projects were proposed totaling $152,500: TCP decommissioning, an assessors' DOR directive, and Cemetery Road network repairs.
FY25 transfers total $465,000 in the warrant, though the snow-and-ice deficit portion may come in below the printed figure.
An additional $50,000 was requested to cover unanticipated special-education student move-ins in FY25, on top of $150,000 already absorbed.
A $36,250 grant reimbursement transfer was removed pending research into whether it must be repaid.
The FY26 capital program totals $655,000, partly funded by shifting unused FY23 capital funds.
A new one-time $10,000 fund was proposed to cover payouts for employees separating from service.
After all proposed FY26 appropriations, free cash would fall from about $2.2 million currently certified to roughly $219,524.
The consolidated FY26 general government budget, now including several relocated departments, totals about $2,962,263.
Legal expenses were increased $10,000 despite what officials called a favorable flat-fee contract.
The unfilled $50,000 grant manager/writer position was proposed for elimination to help restore pavement management; a member pushed back and floated a free-cash-funded pilot instead.
The FinCom reserve fund line was reduced from $200,000 toward $185,000 for FY26, called still a healthy level.
A $210,000 salary reserve fund was proposed to cover upcoming police and DPW/Teamsters bargaining increases and non-union COLAs.
The proposed non-union COLA was raised from 2.5% to 3% (about $7,000 more) after pushback, well short of the roughly $40,000 cost of matching the clerical union's 5%.
IT/communications staff hours were made permanent at an increased level, adding $14,800.
IT department expenses overall increased by $166,000.
The internal network IT administrator position was eliminated, a $79,000 salary decrease, as support shifts further to an outsourced contractor.
The outsourced IT contract line grew from a $25,000 (revised $66,203) budget to a new $159,285 contract for FY26, partly offset by ARPA funds only this current year.
The FY26 police budget totals about $2,434,772; it appears reduced only because negotiated raises sit in the salary reserve, not the department line.
The police motorcycle lease, expiring in October and already paid through then, was eliminated to help fund pavement management.
The FY26 fire budget totals about $1,744,588 and excludes a proposed fourth shift/42-hour work week expected as an FY27 override item.
A new benefit allowing holiday pay for call firefighters was estimated to cost up to about $7,000.
The consolidated 'other protection' category totals $368,900; regional dispatch stayed flat after Hudson joined the agreement.

Several school budget totals were given, including a town-manager-recommended figure, a prior override amount, a special town meeting transfer, and a net increase described as $94,900 (3.64%); captions rendered these inconsistently.
The Monty Tech assessment was described as rising substantially, with the percentage and dollar amount rendered inconsistently.
The FY26 DPW budget totals about $2,476,195, not reflecting still-unresolved union salary adjustments.
Pavement management, once cut to zero, was restored to $279,000 rather than the prior $550,000 target.
Chapter 90 state road aid is expected near $69,900 (later given as $69,700), down from about $418,000 the prior year, pending a state bond bill.
Facilities totals about $1,673,196, including roughly $155,000 more in utilities/maintenance and a $27,000 internal offset for lost TCP rental revenue as schools vacate.
The Council on Aging budget rises $31,500 as formula grants move into the operating budget, plus $33,000 more for programs, while a 10-hour outreach position is eliminated by mutual agreement.
The veteran services (Chapter 115) benefits line was reduced, said to still leave room for new qualifying residents; the figure was truncated in captions.
The new culture-and-recreation category totals about $639,036.70 and funds 100 extra floating library-director hours but not a proposed $18,000/year teen-room position.
Debt service decreases $393,100; total FY26 principal and interest is about $2.5 million across excluded and non-excluded debt.
Now folded into the omnibus budget, the retirement assessment rises $264,700 (12.4%) to about $2,392,572, partly from a state-mandated retiree COLA repaid over years.
Although the actual increase is 14.84%, the town-side line rises only about 7%, using a previously built-in budget cushion.
The line was built from actuals plus 14.84% and an estimate of five additional family plans, flagged as needing closer tracking for FY27.
The number of employees, including school, on town health plans ranged from about 531 to 540 month to month.
The FY26 sewer enterprise budget totals about $1,886,152.
Proposed transfers include $19,124 to a sewer stabilization fund and a smaller amount to a sewer reserve capacity stabilization fund.
Pay-as-you-throw revenue of $500,000 funds trash, with total trash-and-recycling costs (including tax-supported recycling) around $1 million; a comparison town subsidizes recycling far less.
A $45,000 item appears under the water enterprise budget.
Declining cable-provider revenue means the PEG (public access) program is drawing down its own retained earnings to stay funded.
A citizen filed an override petition equal to the gap between the school committee's approved (cut) budget and its level-service budget, meant to let voters restore school cuts directly.
A committee member questioned how much of the school increase is attributable to special education/out-of-district tuition, citing inconsistent public figures.
The DPW director position was proposed to be regraded from A16 to A17 for competitive-salary alignment.
A $22,500 transfer to the OPEB trust fund was proposed per town financial policy.
A previously voted $300,000 TCP roof repair may need to be re-voted because the original vote specified a location on the portion of the building now slated to close.
A roughly $100,000 school-requested article to fix a bulging wall and drainage has no identified funding source and may be withdrawn or passed over.
A pending reserve-fund transfer request from the fire chief for vehicle maintenance, roughly $10,000-11,000, awaits committee action.

reconciliation.what: Our minutes against the minutes the town published. caption_error = the same fact the captions rendered badly, resolved by the official reading shown beside the as-heard one; discrepancy = a substantive difference, flagged and not resolved. Neither record is treated as the referee.
reconciliation.summary: The two records agree on most budget figures and differ mainly in what each chose to record. why_it_matters: Residents will be asked to vote on the full FY26 town and school budget and the override petition at town meeting next week.

meetings.headline: Cemetery Commission voted to back the North Cemetery expansion design and a separate cemetery road repair request.
meetings.summary: The DPW director briefed the commission on spring cleanup, a compact backhoe, North Cemetery expansion design and cemetery road repairs. The commission discussed remaining plot counts in the North and South cemeteries, and why the Rainmaker software count differs from what is actually available. It voted twice to move forward on the expansion design and the road repair request. A resident objected during public comment, and the exchange ended heatedly before adjournment.

meetings.headline: Finance Committee reviewed the FY26 town/school budget and a citizen-petitioned $2M+ override; no votes were taken.
meetings.summary: The Finance Committee heard the town manager's final FY26 budget presentation department by department, including a $500,000 free-cash transfer to schools, restoration of the pavement management line by cutting a grant writer position, and a 14.84% town health insurance increase. It also received a citizen's petition for a Proposition 2½ override of over $2 million to restore school cuts, heard a detailed member critique of unreconciled school budget figures, and reviewed the full town meeting warrant; all votes and the annual report were deferred to next week.

minutes.headline: Finance Committee reviewed the FY26 town/school budget and a citizen-petitioned $2M+ override; no votes were taken.
minutes.summary: The Finance Committee heard the town manager's final FY26 budget presentation department by department, including a $500,000 free-cash transfer to schools, restoration of the pavement management line by cutting a grant writer position, and a 14.84% town health insurance increase. what_happened.line: The Water District board took no vote on a rate-forecasting software subscription; members favored a one-year trial and asked for reference checks first.
The board heard that the Keyes PFAS pilot test showed good breakthrough results, with PFAS in the backwash and plugging of the filter media.
The district's water efficiency grant application was not funded, and the board said it will hold the meter on a delinquent Butterfly Lane account pending a payment arrangement.
Readers were assigned for the annual meeting articles, and the Woodlands zone one letter was received with no further response.
The only formal motions were on minutes and adjournment.

why_it_matters: The software subscription is not in the budget and would be paid from the system upgrades line, so it competes with infrastructure money that ratepayers fund through water bills.
The Keyes PFAS results and the wells being offline bear on water quality and on what treatment may cost, which is a likely driver of future rates.
The annual meeting articles are what residents will be asked to vote on at Saturday's meeting.

what_happened.line: The only votes were to approve two sets of minutes and to adjourn; no vote was taken on the FY26 capital list.
The committee went through the draft warrant article's FY26 capital list with the new town manager, who questioned the teen center flooring and Marshall Pond weed treatment.

A track and field warrant article and a special projects article (TC Passos decommissioning, cemetery roads) sit outside the capital plan; the special projects item ended with no resolution.

why_it_matters: The capital list that goes to town meeting is shaped partly by items this committee did not rank, such as the track and field and special projects articles, so what residents vote on can differ from the committee's own ranking.

Because the plan is described as funded by reappropriated prior-year items and a debt service reduction, the projects in it may not require new money, while the articles outside it are where new spending questions fall.

meetings.headline: FinCom sharply challenged school-run summer athletic camps as redundant with the Rec Department; no vote taken
meetings.summary: The Lunenburg Finance Committee received an update from the superintendent on changes to the school department's FY26 budget since a March 6th presentation, covering transportation, staffing restructurings, health insurance, and a new bus fee. Much of the meeting was consumed by a contentious debate over the athletic department's proposal to run fee-based summer camps, which one member strongly opposed as redundant with the town's Recreation Department; no vote was taken on the camps issue. The meeting closed with members raising concerns about next year's budget outlook, state aid, and school choice, then adjourned by roll call vote.

budget_items.what_was_said: The superintendent said the legal expense line was increased to cover additional HR-related legal needs.

budget_items.topic: Band transportation, middle and high school
budget_items.what_was_said: Funding was restored to middle school and high school band transportation lines.

budget_items.topic: General education transportation / new bus fee
budget_items.what_was_said: The general education transportation line was cut in anticipation of new bus fee revenue after the school committee adopted a per-day fee with a family cap and waivers for free/reduced lunch students.

A proposed cut to the co-op ski team, which would have freed money into the athletics revolving account, was tabled by the school committee; officials expect the transportation fee to recoup a similar amount instead.
The athletic transportation line was reduced in the budget in anticipation of new revenue from advertising, sponsorships and summer camps.

The athletic department proposed several summer camps intended to be self-sustaining, covering coach pay and a coordinator, with revenue to help offset the athletic transportation cut; a finance committee member strongly opposed it as redundant with the Recreation Department.
A member found the printed total salaries figure did not match the sum of the salaries column and asked the superintendent to check it.

The health insurance budget line changed due to shifting positions and enrollment; the superintendent said the district does not budget health insurance for every position, unlike a prior town manager's practice.
The director of finance and administration position was restructured into a business manager/accountant role, moving the HR salary line to zero.

budget_items.topic: Elementary school teachers line / grant offset
budget_items.what_was_said: The elementary teachers line was adjusted after the elimination of a grant-funded specialist coach position, with Title I grant money applied to offset an intervention teacher instead.
Some paraprofessional positions are carried in the budget with federal special education grant money applied as an offset, reducing the net budget line.
The school committee restored a social worker position by instead cutting one athletic coach position.

budget_items.topic: Athletic director and athletic trainer lines
budget_items.what_was_said: The athletic director's budgeted salary line went down due to a revolving-account offset from an eliminated part-time secretary position, while the athletic trainer's line went up due to a contract increase.
The superintendent said the combined local-budget and revolving-account cost of all athletics last year was a specific total.
figures_as_heard: a little bit over a half million

budget_items.what_was_said: The presentation listed all cut positions and expense lines; the superintendent said the cuts total a certain number of FTEs across a larger number of individuals.
The district is in the first year of a new multi-year bus contract that is already settled.
A member noted Chapter 70 aid rose only slightly while it covers a large share of the operating budget, and asked for a fuller revenue picture in future budget presentations.
A member compared Lunenburg's school choice and charter revenue as a share of the operating budget against several comparison towns, noting Lunenburg's share was highest among most of them.
A member noted that after the proposed FY26 cuts, the number of full-time teachers would return to roughly the level reported for FY19.

decisions.decision: The superintendent agreed to email the committee chair a five-year history of position changes back to FY21.
The superintendent agreed to check and report back on the $42,567 discrepancy in the salaries total line.
The superintendent agreed to verify and report back the exact percentage of positions budgeted with health insurance.
The chair decided not to open the floor for public comment tonight due to the time limit before the capital planning committee meeting.

why_it_matters: Peer review is paid for by the applicant under the bylaw, so more frequent use shifts review costs from the town to project applicants and could lengthen timelines for projects near wetlands.

Much of the discussion centered on a citizen-petitioned override on the ballot, frustration over repeated town budget presentations, and the superintendent search timeline, with no vote taken on the override itself.</summary>

meetings.headline: School Committee passed a deeply-cut FY26 budget and created Lunenburg's first student transportation fee.
meetings.summary:
The School Committee worked through the superintendent's FY26 recommended budget line by line, confirming a Director of Finance restructuring, a cut to one of two curriculum coaches, and rejecting a proposed librarian cut, while extensive public comment focused on athletic and band cuts, the co-op ski program's cost, and equity between academics and extracurriculars. The committee voted to table a ski program cut pending renegotiation with partner schools, adopted a new student bus fee (with rates and a waiver policy sent to the policy subcommittee) to help offset transportation costs, and ultimately passed the FY26 budget unanimously with the ski program retained and funded by projected bus fee revenue; members also confirmed they will not pursue a school override this year in favor of a possible townwide override next year.</summary>
</invoke>

meetings.headline: Committee raised athletic and facility fees to help close a deep FY26 budget gap forcing likely staff cuts.
meetings.summary: The Lunenburg School Committee spent most of a long meeting confronting a severe FY26 budget shortfall driven by inflation, rising special education and transportation costs, and state Chapter 70 aid not keeping pace, with public and committee comment repeatedly blaming inadequate state funding and past reluctance to override. The committee voted to raise athletic fees and facility rental rates, tabled proposed transportation and student-activity fee changes, walked through a long menu of possible administrative, staffing and program cuts, and took public budget questions; a member also announced he will resign in May.

attendees.role: school committee member (announced resignation effective May 16)

attendees.name_as_heard: Mr. Skulbrini (heard variously as "Scho brini"/"Scholbrini", called "Tony" by colleagues)

budget_items.what_was_said: The chair read the total warrant amount for the period covering line-item transfers.

budget_items.topic: Vehicle maintenance to contractor services transfer
budget_items.what_was_said: Dr. Gilson requested a transfer to cover HVAC unit repairs on the roof, after a committee member asked for more detail on what was being fixed.
A second transfer moving money from general supplies, ELL, ACE and mileage reimbursement lines into a contracted evaluation special education line was described but not voted this meeting.
The superintendent's report noted an unbudgeted cost presented to the finance committee for 911 compliance upgrades at Turkey Hill Elementary, now complete districtwide.
Dr. Gilson said current athletic fees offset only a portion of athletic expenses under FY24 numbers, and that the fund faces a growing deficit without a fee increase.
The committee voted to raise athletic fees for the first student, with a sibling discount, a reduced/waiver rate, and a family cap.
The athletic director's cost breakdown by season was read into the record for fall, winter and spring sports.
A per-sport cost figure for football was given, though the figure stated moments later was inconsistent with it.
A proposal to replace the flat activity fee with a lower base fee plus a special-interest club fee was presented for feedback, not a vote, citing a growing deficit in the activity account.
A proposal to charge a K-6 transportation fee (not legally required) at several possible daily rates was presented and tabled pending a parent survey.
The committee voted to raise custodian, kitchen and field monitor labor rates and increase facility rental fees roughly across the board.

budget_items.topic: FY26 budget gap and town manager's revised number
budget_items.what_was_said: The town manager's revised budget figure was described as higher than originally expected but largely absorbed by a higher-than-budgeted health insurance increase, leaving a personnel-cut gap.
Administration compared annual Chapter 70 increases to inflation for three prior years to argue state aid is not keeping pace.

budget_items.topic: North Middlesex central office consolidation option
budget_items.what_was_said: A proposal to eliminate central office administrators and pay North Middlesex for shared time was estimated to produce savings, though not adopted.
A proposal to eliminate the director of finance and administration position and add an accountant plus contracted HR support was discussed and tabled over continuity concerns.

budget_items.topic: Money available to restore cut positions
budget_items.what_was_said: Administration walked through cumulative dollars becoming available toward restoring positions, including expense cuts, a lower out-of-district tuition need, and the possible transportation fee.

Costs of educating certain out-of-district-eligible students in-district versus at Keystone Collaborative or North Middlesex were compared; staying in-district was said to be cheapest and best for students.

budget_items.topic: Federal special education and title grants
budget_items.what_was_said: Staff described how IDEA and Title I/IIA/IVA grant funds are targeted, mostly paying for paraprofessionals and coaching/mentoring rather than covering the deficit.

decisions.decision: Tabled the bus transportation fee proposal for further discussion, pending a parent survey and more data.
Tabled the student activity fee restructuring proposal and agreed to seek student council feedback before acting.
Tabled cuts to middle school/freshman athletic coaches and uniform replacement, pending a recommendation from the athletic director on which sports could be cut.
Tabled the proposal to eliminate the director of finance and administration position, citing continuity-of-operations concerns with an incoming new superintendent.
Gave direction to proceed with hiring the previously interviewed candidate for facilities/grounds director rather than leaving it vacant or merging with the town.
Agreed to pursue a joint meeting with the select board tentatively on March 11.
Agreed to proceed with the MASC-recommended superintendent search timeline, with the possibility of the search committee proceeding with 11 rather than 12 members due to a scheduling conflict.
Mr. Beardmore announced he will resign from the school committee effective May 16, creating a third vacancy on the ballot.
Set March 11 as the date for a joint meeting with the select board given the March 17 warrant deadline.

meetings.headline: Water commissioners declined to abate a resident's disputed high water bill, offering only a year of zero interest on the balance.
meetings.summary: Most of the meeting was a resident's appeal of high water bills at her home. The board held that water passing the meter is the customer's responsibility. It offered to waive interest for a year on the past-due balance and to test the meter, at the customer's cost if the meter proves accurate. The board also approved the annual meeting warrant with an added radio communications article, and heard the superintendent's report on a road repair, paving and PFAS pilot testing.

The board held that water passing the meter is the customer's responsibility, and offered a meter test, paid by the customer if the meter proves accurate.

The radio article would draw on the cellular account and split costs among three departments, and the budget and warrant articles go to a vote at the annual meeting, where residents vote on them.

what_happened.line: The Sewer Commission voted to accept the final FY26 budget for presentation to the Finance Committee.
The commission voted to accept the third quarter FY2025 commitment letter after commissioners reviewed and signed the commitment numbers.
Staff said demand notices could not be printed after the MUNIS upgrade, and a legal question is open on whether an unsent demand fee can be charged.
The town director is to present the FY26 budget to the Finance Committee on Thursday at 7 PM; commissioners may attend.
Commissioners discussed recruiting more commissioners; one is to draft a social media post, and another is to check parameters with the town.

why_it_matters: The FY26 sewer budget draws on retained earnings, and staff said unpaid customer bills drive that draw, so collection affects how much reserve is used.
Demand notices that could not be printed since the MUNIS upgrade mean late-payment collection was disrupted, and the legal opinion on the demand fee is still pending.
The sewer budget now goes to the Finance Committee, the next public step before it reaches a town vote.

meetings.headline: Finance Committee heard police, fire and land use budget briefings; fire chief floated a fourth shift, no votes except adjournment.

public_comment.topic: Chair asked for public comment at the start; none on Zoom.
Asked why the police switched from a patrol K9 to a drug-sniffing dog and suggested one multi-purpose dog rather than separate comfort and K9 dogs.
Praised both chiefs, urged the town manager to make the fire fourth-shift proposal happen, and said he does not support the new town hall proposal.
Commended the fire chief's honest answer that a fourth shift would not simply save overtime.

votes.motion: Motion to adjourn; all in favor, chair said it passes.

budget_items.what_was_said: The police secured ARPA funds for 30 body cameras to replace failing four-year-old units. The chief said future replacement will likely need a capital plan as grants run out.
A state earmark funded a virtual use-of-force training simulator now in service.

budget_items.topic: Police FY25 spending to date and prior-year spending
budget_items.what_was_said: The police budget is partway through the year with some lines trending high; prior years were mostly expended with surpluses from vacancies.

budget_items.topic: K9 stipend for comfort dog handler
budget_items.what_was_said: Chief requested an incentive increase so the comfort dog handler receives the same K9 care stipend as the patrol K9 handler.
The lease increased and now covers maintenance.
Insurance on the patrol K9 is cheaper than potential vet bills.
Lockup level funded and much lower than before the Sheriff's safekeep program.
The town's assessment for regional dispatch could change as other towns' allocations shift.
Increase without dispatch and including dispatch were stated, about a 1.2 increase; dispatch figures may change.
No salary reserve in the police budget; any settlement would come from the town-level salary reserve.
Grant funding was pulled back by the state and the position could not be filled at the offered pay.

budget_items.topic: Fire FY25 salaries and EMS expense
budget_items.what_was_said: Salaries are on target but extra was spent on open per diem shifts; EMS expense continues to run over.
Contractual increase in salaries and a requested increase in overtime.
Rates were raised in September but most patients are on government insurance so revenue gain is limited.
Estimated cost of adding a fourth shift in one year, which could be phased over up to three years.
Training four call staff cost the town roughly this amount, with buyback agreements.
Requested additional funds for advanced life support supplies.
Requested additional funds for department software.
Requested increase to a line unchanged since before 2010; radios cost several thousand each.
Proposed FY26 capital replacement of the 10-year-old prevention vehicle.
ARPA covered an ambulance and equipment for the fire department.
A state grant funded protective clothing dryer, thermal cameras and gear.

budget_items.topic: Federal AFG grant for brush truck
budget_items.what_was_said: A federal grant application for a brush truck would need a small town match; outcome unknown.
State grants for fire education each year.
Ambulance receipts go to the general fund and flow into free cash; the estimated yearly amount and rate increase were stated.
Chief stated the overall fire budget increase percent.
A member asked for the sources of last year's certified free cash; the town manager will provide it and said free cash should not fund operations.

decisions.decision: Ambulance receipts, revolving/enterprise fund options to be reviewed, with the town manager to provide detail and the topic kept for a later meeting after budget season.
Town manager agreed to provide a breakdown of sources of certified free cash within about a week.
Police staffing plan to be reassessed by the chief and new town manager.
Committee will need further discussion and targeting on the fire fourth-shift proposal once the preliminary budget is presented.

The fire chief proposed a fourth shift, and the committee said it will need further discussion once the preliminary budget is presented.
Members discussed ambulance receipts and whether a revolving or enterprise fund is possible; the town manager is to provide detail, with the topic held until after budget season.

why_it_matters: A fourth fire shift and any change to how ambulance receipts are held would affect the fire budget and the town's reliance on free cash, and so could shape what residents are asked to approve at town meeting.
Grant and earmark money paying for police equipment, such as body cameras, is running out, so replacement costs may move into the regular budget or a capital plan.

meetings.headline: Planning Board endorsed an ANR, approved two Conservation parking site plans and a Pleasant Street addition, and continued 494 Electric Ave to March 10.
meetings.summary: The board endorsed an ANR for 589 Flat Hill Road and approved a site plan for 110 Pleasant Street, then held hearings on three Conservation Commission and contractor site plans. The 494 Electric Avenue hearing took most of the night. The board split on the Pierce Avenue entrance and crosswalk, and the legal status of Pierce Avenue is still with Town Counsel. The board declined to sign two stormwater decisions over unclear wording, signed the common driveway decision, and discussed committee reports and its schedule.

public_comment.topic: Opening public comment: none.

Mr McDonald (by Zoom) supported helping the Il Forno business succeed, asked whether the owner's preferred entrance was known, and suggested conditions to re-evaluate when the land across the street is developed.

Bob Pierce (11 Wintergreen Court) urged the board to take straw polls of members on difficult applications. He said the 494 Electric Ave project should have applied as a shopping center, and he objected to the withdrawal request.
A resident of 914 Northfield Road asked where the parking would go and whether it was near Stage Coach Road; she was told it is a separate hearing.
Bob Pierce described the planned loop trails and the connection to Parks and Rec land and Table Rock, in support of the 801 Northfield Road lot.
Michelle Matthew asked about parking near her property and Stage Coach Road, and was told the lot is about 200 feet away with access off Northfield Road.
Owner of Settlers Crossing Golf Course raised concerns about golf balls hitting cars, trespass onto the course, wetlands and runoff, and policing of the new lot.
Bob Pierce responded on behalf of the Conservation Commission: the lot avoids Stage Coach Road, and a similar lot on Holman Street has had few problems.
Michelle Matthew asked how people would reach the other parking area (801 Northfield Road).
Bob Pierce said he saw no golf balls and has flagged the trail route up to Table Rock.
Bob Pierce asked the board to again assign its MRPC GIS hours to the Conservation Commission for trail mapping.

Continue the 494 Electric Avenue site plan and stormwater permit hearing to March 10 at 6:05 p.m.
Close the public hearing for 801 Northfield Road.
Approve the site plan for 801 Northfield Road with standard conditions.
Continue the 994 Northfield Road public hearing to March 10 at 6:05 p.m.
Close the public hearing for 110 Pleasant Street.
Approve the site plan for 110 Pleasant Street with standard conditions.
Authorize the land use director to assign the MRPC GIS contribution to the Conservation Commission for trail mapping.
Approve the minutes of the February 10, 2025 meeting.
Adjourn.

budget_items.what_was_said: Town Counsel is to give a cost estimate for the deep-dive legal review, which the applicant would pay, likely into escrow like a peer review. The estimate was not yet available.

decisions.decision: For 494 Electric Ave, the board will leave the Pierce Avenue entrance as designed for now and wait for Town Counsel's review of the road status; the applicant will return March 10.
The applicant will take the canopy to the land use director as a possible de minimis change to the prior approval, to be considered at the next meeting.
The March 10 meeting will go ahead despite overlapping the Citizens Caucus. Applicants are advised against scheduling special permits that night because of quorum risk.
The board did not sign the 255 Sunny Hill Road and 560 Goodrich Street stormwater decisions because the deed-recording wording and a special condition were unclear.

Community notices from neighboring towns will be emailed to the board as they arrive rather than read at meetings.
The Master Plan Steering Committee will keep its two vacant seats for now; the chair will ask the Select Board whether it wants to fill its seat.
The Open Space Committee review of the 100 Townsend Harbor Road property will go on the next agenda so the board can vote on a recommendation to the Select Board.
Review of standard operating procedures is deferred until the land use director is present.
The two zoning workshops were deferred because there was no guest and no land use director.

meetings.headline: Stormwater task force found the consultant's draft fee tiers unclear and will seek clarification before the next meeting.
meetings.summary: The task force went through the consultant's first-draft stormwater utility rate structure. Members could not tell where multifamily, apartment, condo and commercial properties fall in the tiers, and thought too few large properties were counted. They worked backwards from a revenue target using the fee alternatives and Chapter 90, and discussed offsetting existing town budget lines, tax-exempt properties, billing and delinquency, and a public message for Town Meeting. The only votes were approving the January 23rd minutes and adjourning.

budget_items.what_was_said: The consultant's draft offers fee alternatives with differing values per equivalent residential unit, plus a tier structure.
A member's preliminary budget shows personnel alone consuming much of the needed revenue, and one-time equipment purchases were noted.
Members noted Chapter 90 is state money for specific projects, not salaries, and one member listed expected yearly amounts.

budget_items.topic: Existing town budget stormwater lines offset
budget_items.what_was_said: A member argued the existing town drainage and stormwater budget lines should be subtracted from what residents are shown as the new cost; others noted the money would be reallocated, not removed.
Using the commercial alternative and the single/multi-family alternative gives a total that, with Chapter 90, comes near the consultant's original ask.
Members leaned toward adding the charge to the property tax bill to keep overhead down, and cited a monthly household amount.
Sewer delinquency is handled with a demand fee and daily interest and a lien after a year; the delinquency rate was cited, and the sewer minimum bill was compared to the stormwater charge.
Members favored keeping residents near the lowest tier and weighting commercial tiers higher.
A member estimated the added yearly cost to a large commercial site.

decisions.decision: The chair will get clarification from the consultant on the tier structure by the next meeting and email it to members.

Questions recorded for the consultant: where properties like the apartment complex fit, what to do about tax-exempt properties and churches, and a rewrite of the unclear section three paragraph; Jen asked for a breakdown of properties in each category.
Members will decide the public message for the Town Meeting update at the March and April meetings, avoiding dollar figures for now.
The Town Meeting warrant article to allow a report will be taken at the spring town meeting as a formality, with a PR campaign to follow.

what_happened.line: The task force found the consultant's first-draft stormwater fee tiers unclear and will get clarification from the consultant before the next meeting.
Members could not tell where multifamily, apartment, condo and commercial properties fall in the tiers, and thought too few large properties were counted.
Working backwards from a revenue target, members found the fee alternatives plus Chapter 90 come near the consultant's original ask; no resolution was reached.
Members leaned toward putting the charge on the property tax bill and weighting commercial tiers higher, keeping residents near the lowest tier.
The only votes were approving the January 23rd minutes and adjourning; the Town Meeting warrant article to allow a report is planned as a formality.

why_it_matters: A stormwater utility fee would be a new charge, and which tier a home, condo, apartment complex or business lands in decides what it pays, so the unclear tiers are the open question for any resident or owner.
Whether existing town drainage budget lines are netted against the new fee, and whether the charge rides on the tax bill, changes what residents are shown as the new cost and how it is collected.

budget_items.what_was_said: The finance director asked for a vote on the budget amount for the revolving fund, which sets the ins and outs in the accounting system. It can still be amended by a committee vote.

Two cost estimators reconciled their 60% design estimates, narrowing the gap between them. The estimate is broken out by phase and includes general conditions, design contingency, overhead and profit, bonds and escalation.

budget_items.topic: Marshall Park total for the vote
budget_items.what_was_said: The two estimating firms came in close together; the chair suggested using the higher number, plus OPM costs still to be confirmed.
A bathroom is estimated at a quarter million. Board of Health septic repair money cannot currently be used to connect to sewer.
The Select Board indicated the project would be a debt exclusion needing a Town Meeting vote and a ballot vote. Members discussed explaining the tax impact to voters.
An invoice for January design development costs was reviewed by the OPM, which recommended approval.
The commission is collecting comparable-community data on user fees and will likely hold a workshop in March or April; no fee changes are planned for the coming year.
The design adds roughly 130 spaces; a grant requires staying above a minimum space count.

decisions.decision: The commission agreed in principle to let the school use the outfield of the 90-foot diamond, so long as the dimensions work; the chair will have the contact connect with the facilities director.
Consensus to put the full Marshall Park project (phases 1, 2A, 2B) before Town Meeting, with the option to amend the article down to phase one if support is lacking.
The higher cost estimate will be used, conditional on the chair confirming extra owner's project manager costs with the OPM the next day.
No fee changes this year; a user fee workshop will be set for March or April if data comes in, possibly folded into a light April agenda.
The next regular meeting is aimed at March 19, and the chair will ask the clerk's office for the room.
Plan for two public information sessions on Marshall Park in April; the chair will email details.
Beach staffing will be put on the March agenda because of low lifeguard interest.

what_happened.line: The Parks Commission voted to take Marshall Park phases 1, 2A and 2B to Town Meeting, with added owner's project manager costs still to be confirmed.
The commission agreed to use the higher of two reconciled cost estimates for the vote, conditional on the chair confirming extra project manager costs the next day.
The Select Board indicated the project would be a debt exclusion, which needs both a Town Meeting vote and a ballot vote.
The commission reached consensus to put the full project forward, with the option to amend the article down to phase one if support is lacking.
Members conditionally approved school use of the 90-foot diamond outfield, approved a revolving fund budget and approved a January design invoice; vote counts were not audible.

why_it_matters: A debt exclusion raises property taxes above the levy cap for the life of the debt, so residents would be asked to vote at Town Meeting and again at the ballot on Marshall Park.
The final amount is not fixed: the estimate is still at the 60% design stage and owner's project manager costs are still to be added, so the figure voters see may differ from the one discussed.

what_happened.line: The Sewer Commission voted by roll call to accept its FY2024 annual report, on condition that highlighted figures are finalized and initialed before Friday's deadline.
Some figures highlighted in the report come from past years, and staff must update them before the report is submitted.
A file upload into MUNIS doubled some bills in the latest quarterly billing; customers who called in had their bills corrected.
MUNIS still cannot send demand letters on late accounts, a problem more than a year old.
Hiring for the assistant business manager waits on a second interview and HR reference checks, and a manhole repair meeting waits for the frost to leave.

why_it_matters: Sewer bills come from this commission's billing system, and a doubled bill or a late account that gets no demand letter is a billing problem that lands on ratepayers or on collections.
The annual report was accepted before its numbers were final, so what the town files depends on staff corrections that the minutes show only as a condition, not as a completed check.
watch_next: The Friday submission deadline for the FY2024 annual report, with the highlighted figures finalized and initialed.
The next agenda: a billing update, the assistant business manager position, and the manhole repair.

meetings.headline: Athletic Advisory Council discussed a proposed athletic fee increase (first-student fee proposed at $325 per season); no vote taken.
meetings.summary: The virtual Athletic Advisory Council meeting centered on the administration's proposal to raise athletic user fees because of rising transportation, coaching stipend and official costs against a tight budget. Dr. Gilson presented the fee proposal, and residents and parents raised concerns about equity, the effect on middle-income families, participation data and revenue alternatives. No votes were taken; comments will be passed to the school committee and administration, and the meeting adjourned.

public_comment.topic: Asked whether fee increases will be repeated yearly with expenses or whether there is a long-term plan; also remarked that academics was named priority one and athletics second.

Asked about a per-sport cost breakdown requested last week; argued a roughly 30% jump hurts middle-income families who don't qualify for reduced lunch or waivers and may reduce participation and fund revenue.
Asked what participation data will be released (baseline from prior years) and what other mechanisms could help close the equity gap, including for families who don't fill out low-income forms.
Asked about participation counts, enrollment, and how many participations are unique students versus counted per season; suggested granular data on families dropping from three sports to two.
Asked what happens if fees are not raised; raised the town's limited levers for revenue generation, and noted Parks is considering fee increases for youth baseball/softball.

votes.motion: Adjourn the meeting

budget_items.topic: Athletic user fees share of program funding
budget_items.what_was_said: Parents through user fees fund about a quarter of the total athletic program, later described as about 26%.
A neighboring town charges a per-sport per-season fee with a high school family cap; Brookfield offers only three sports.
Transportation, coaching stipends and MIAA official fees are rising; stipends rose this year and will rise again next year.

budget_items.topic: Proposed athletic fee for first student
budget_items.what_was_said: Proposed fee for the first student in the family per season with sibling discounts and a family cap extending grades six through twelve; still open to discussion.
Revolving account revenue is not matching expenses; goal is to zero the account down each year rather than stockpile.
A participant compared potential full-pay fee revenue to what FY24 combined fees brought in; participation counts are student-seasons, not unique students.

budget_items.topic: Town manager's budget guidance for schools
budget_items.what_was_said: The district must fit its budget within a projected increase over last year, which does not keep pace with costs; painful cuts to be proposed the next night.
Uncertainty about federal grant funding could reduce district funding.
Chair said turf and track complex project costs might be offset through cell towers and solar, and a sponsorship policy might be opened.
A commenter described the proposed increase as a large jump for middle-income families.

decisions.decision: Per-sport cost breakdown was not released at this meeting; release would require action by the superintendent or school committee, and the chair noted reservations.
Commentary from the meeting will be brought back to the school committee and administration for further consideration.
Council will hold an annual meeting at the end of summer rather than meeting every season (stated as earlier agreed).
Athletic director to try to obtain the unique-student participation count and share it if found.

Residents said the proposed jump would fall hardest on middle-income families who do not qualify for waivers, and asked about the effect on participation.

what_happened.line: The Municipal Building Design Committee previewed the Town Hall, Ritter and Meeting House plan and a newly finalized cost estimate ahead of the next night's Select Board presentation.
The committee set March 17 to confirm the wording of a borrowing warrant article and to come prepared on which of four price options to pursue.

why_it_matters: This committee will screen candidates for superintendent, a hire that shapes district leadership and, ultimately, budget and program decisions for years.

The planned listening sessions are a specific opportunity for residents to influence the criteria used to pick the next superintendent.

meetings.headline: Committee tabled the screening-committee vote to Saturday and spent the workshop setting superintendent search criteria.
meetings.summary: This was a School Committee workshop devoted almost entirely to the superintendent search: shaping a short list of desired superintendent characteristics, planning staff and public listening sessions, and reviewing the internal hiring process, screening-committee makeup, and legal/HR considerations including possibly engaging MASC if the search goes external. The committee voted to table the screening-committee membership appointment to a Saturday meeting because an earlier notice had listed an incorrect application deadline, and closed with public comment thanking the chair and a colleague for the effort.

budget_items.what_was_said: A member said the district had repeated elevator breakdowns last year because there was not enough money to fix or maintain it properly. It was cited as an example of a money problem that also became an operational problem because it was not planned for.

A member said the federal government's abrupt stopping and restarting of funding streams had created a serious problem for educational institutions nationally. They said it could have a direct impact on the district if fully implemented.

Asked for a better breakdown of the costs of each sport to understand equity, supported paying coaches and referees better, and noted the bus company's monopoly.
Asked to see what each sport costs and why other places seem to get grants and funding so students do not pay fees.
Asked about youth sports and field rental fees, the local budget contribution to athletics, and what the fee increase avoids; did back-of-napkin math on net revenue after assumed participation loss.
Asked whether adding more teams would bring in more fees and said information about middle school sports and sign-ups is hard to find.
Asked about gate receipts collected at games and whether cell tower lease money is used for field maintenance.
Asked whether the district talks to neighboring towns without fees, and noted that booster parents are the same parents paying fees.

meetings.headline: Superintendent previewed a much larger FY26 budget need as grants and revolving funds dry up, likely forcing staff cuts
meetings.summary: The School Committee heard a lengthy FY26 budget preview showing many previously offset costs (athletics, stipends, transportation, health insurance) now landing on the local budget as revolving accounts and grant money disappear, with no decisions made but clear signals that staff cuts and fee increases are likely. The meeting also covered a PE curriculum standards update with no waiver recommended, a new post-MCAS competency determination for graduation, a PowerSchool data breach response, superintendent search committee planning, and the planned move of central offices out of the TCP building into Turkey Hill Elementary.

Adjourn the meeting at 9:39 p.m.

budget_items.what_was_said: Warrants for the period were presented for review with no additional questions raised.
Leasing three portable trailers for central offices and the Ace program was estimated to cost this much per year, after no suitable properties were found in town.
A 4% tuition increase for FY26 was proposed, consistent with the historical annual increase, and approved.
The Governor's proposed FY26 local aid distribution for Chapter 70 funding to Lunenburg was cited from the newly released state budget.
The Governor's budget figure for UGGA was cited alongside the Chapter 70 number.

budget_items.topic: Inflation and pupil minimum in state aid formula
budget_items.what_was_said: The inflation rate used in the Student Opportunity Act formula and a new per-pupil minimum increase were described, the latter differing from last year's figure.
The FY25 total budget, including the override and additional Chapter 70 money granted at town meeting, was shown as the baseline against which FY26 percentages are calculated.
The FY26 budget draft includes a 12% health insurance increase, built into all the driver figures shown.
The transportation budget line rose partly because three additional special education vans are needed for projected students next year.

The athletics transportation line has historically been underfunded at $40,000 from the town budget with the rest covered by a revolving account; fully funding it would add substantially more to the local budget.
The draft budget includes a projected increase in out-of-district tuition costs.
A member asked how likely the 12% health insurance estimate is, noting last year's estimate of 10% came in at 6%; staff said 12% may now be closer to a floor rather than a worst case.
Based on current enrollment and a 12% increase, the health insurance line alone was estimated at this amount.

budget_items.topic: Governor's per-pupil minimum aid increase for Lunenburg
budget_items.what_was_said: The Governor's proposed statewide per-pupil minimum increase was translated into an estimated dollar impact for Lunenburg specifically, though enrollment figures used were questioned as inconsistent.
A proposed increase to athletic fees per sport is being floated for community feedback ahead of budget decisions.
A member noted it would be hard to justify to parents that athletics transportation costs are rising by this amount per student.
Engaging MASC for a superintendent search, if no qualified internal candidate is found, was estimated to cost this amount, described as low relative to the value of finding the right candidate.
The prior town manager search using Community Dynamics was cited as a cost comparison, funded by ARPA money, though the figure was stated two different ways in the discussion.
Plumbing-related work to prepare space at Turkey Hill Elementary for the Ace Program to move in was estimated to cost under this amount.

budget_items.topic: Ledger advertisement for search committee posting
budget_items.what_was_said: Posting the superintendent screening committee notice in the Lunenburg Ledger carries this cost, to be paid from the advertisement budget line.

decisions.decision: Central office relocation will move forward with the option of occupying space at Turkey Hill Elementary rather than leasing trailers or other properties.
The committee will target holding the required public budget hearing on March 5th, ahead of the March 6th finance committee presentation, understanding more public input may follow.
The decision on school choice participation for next year will be delayed until after the extent of budget cuts is known, rather than being decided at the next meeting.

Rather than the full committee discussing individual superintendent screening committee applicants publicly, the chair and vice chair (Carol) will compile member feedback and bring forward a joint recommendation.
A workshop-style meeting will be held on January 29th at 6 p.m. to discuss superintendent search committee membership, listening sessions, and guidance for the screening committee.
The school committee affirmed its intent to fully vacate the TCP building space, likely by July, without a formal vote, to relay to the interim town manager.

what_happened.line: The superintendent previewed a much larger FY26 budget need as revolving funds and grants covering athletics, stipends, transportation and health costs run out, pointing toward staff cuts and fee increases.
The committee voted unanimously to raise preschool tuition for FY26.
The committee targeted March 5 for the required public budget hearing, a day ahead of the finance committee's presentation.
A decision on school choice participation next year was put off until the scope of budget cuts is known.
The committee affirmed plans to fully vacate the TCP building, likely by July, favoring space at Turkey Hill Elementary over leased trailers.

why_it_matters: Costs the town budget has not carried before -- athletics transportation, stipends, added special-education vans -- are shifting onto the local school budget as outside funding lapses, which is the mechanism behind any staff-cut or fee proposal that follows.
Preschool families face a tuition increase for FY26, and the public budget hearing set for March 5 is where residents can weigh in before the finance committee sees the numbers on March 6.
Whether the district takes school choice students next year, which affects both enrollment and revenue, will not be decided until the size of the budget gap is clearer.

meetings.headline: Design committee reviewed revised Town Hall/Ritter plans with a PAC basement; only vote was adjournment, cost estimates due Feb 3.
meetings.summary: Taylor and Burns presented updated site, floor and exterior plans for a new Town Hall, a Ritter renovation for school offices and an Old Town Hall meeting house. The PAC studio moved into a 12-foot-deep basement under the new Town Hall. Members and the public commented on basement and ledge cost risk, slope walkway safety, and school/town co-location; an update on mothballing a building with asbestos was given, and the meeting adjourned by roll call as quorum was about to be lost.

what_happened.line: The Board of Assessors agreed to set up a subcommittee to work out the process for the new senior means-tested tax exemption, with a target of two months or less.
Members agreed to review neighborhood and site-index values in house, starting with the lake properties, and to implement nothing until the review is done.
Most of the meeting went to editing a public presentation on senior exemptions and deferrals; the senior circuit breaker pages were pulled out and a HERO Act bullet added.
Members said the new senior exemption would probably be paid for from the overlay, possibly raising it, and deferred that question to February 5th.
The principal assessor will draft a placeholder warrant article on exemption income and asset limits for the next meeting. No formal votes were audible.

why_it_matters: A new senior means-tested exemption is likely to be paid for from the overlay, the reserve for abatements and exemptions, so the cost could be spread across other taxpayers' bills rather than appearing as a separate line.
A review of site-index values for lake properties could change how those homes are assessed, though the board said nothing will take effect until the review is finished.
Updated exemption income and asset limits would likely need a warrant article, which is a vote residents may be asked to take at town meeting.

what_happened.line: The Sewer Commission voted 3-0 by roll call to accept the fiscal year 2026 budget, with the capital line raised above the staff proposal.
Before the vote, the commission agreed by consensus to add a cushion to the capital line against failed pump-station cut-off valves; unused money returns to retained earnings.
No rate increase is proposed; projected user revenue is reduced for a high delinquency rate, and the shortfall is drawn from retained earnings.
The commission assessed a privilege fee and betterment, with a lien recorded at the registry of deeds, on 12 Kimble Street by a 3-0 roll call.
Staff reported that second-quarter demand billing is blocked by a software problem in the town's billing system, with no resolution at the meeting.

why_it_matters: The budget sets the sewer user rate residents are billed, and holding it flat while revenue is projected short means the gap is covered from retained earnings rather than from bills.
Fitchburg and Leominster, which treat the town's wastewater, raise their rates in coming years, so the flat rate depends on retained earnings or later user charges absorbing those increases.
Delayed demand billing from the software problem affects when residents receive second-quarter sewer bills.
watch_next: Future agendas will carry manhole repairs, second-quarter billing, the assistant to the business manager, and Kimble Street.
Any capital funds beyond the town-meeting appropriation would need the November special town meeting.

meetings.headline: School Committee approved an internal superintendent job posting and a 12-person screening committee to begin the search.
meetings.summary: This special meeting, held mostly to act on the superintendent search following Dr. Burnham's planned retirement, opened and closed public comment with none offered, then went into a roughly half-hour executive session on non-union personnel matters. After returning, the committee reviewed draft timelines for an internal-first, external-if-needed search process, and voted to approve the internal job posting and to authorize a call for a diverse 12-person screening committee, with search timeline dates left flexible.

Committee discussed holding a special meeting around January 29th to appoint the screening committee sooner, allowing subcommittee work to start the first week of February.
Committee agreed to decide later, after the internal search concludes, whether to seek MASC assistance for an external superintendent search.

Committee agreed not to specify particular seats (e.g. Select Board, Council on Aging) in the screening-committee call itself, and instead to build a diverse candidate pool together as a full school committee once applications are in.

meetings.headline: Commissioners heard a clean FY24 audit, eased one resident's leak-inflated bill, and got no bids for the cell-tower lease.
meetings.summary: The auditor reported an unmodified opinion on the June 30, 2024 financials and walked through the main variances; commissioners said expenses looked well controlled, and a resident asked about categories, receivables and pension. A resident asked for relief on a bill that jumped after a leak, and the board agreed to charge the usage at the first-tier rate. The board also discussed the cellular equipment RFP that drew no bids, pilot testing, the water management permit, and a sewer betterment it disputes, which it put off.

minutes.headline: Commissioners heard a clean FY24 audit, eased one resident's leak-inflated bill, and got no bids for the cell-tower lease.
minutes.summary: The auditor reported an unmodified opinion on the June 30, 2024 financials and walked through the main variances; commissioners said expenses looked well controlled, and a resident asked about categories, receivables and pension. A resident asked for relief on a bill that jumped after a leak, and the board agreed to charge the usage at the first-tier rate. The board also discussed the cellular equipment RFP that drew no bids, pilot testing, the water management permit, and a sewer betterment it disputes, which it put off.

public_comment.topic: Resident asked the auditor whether expense categories are the same year to year and whether deviations could be missed, then asked about the rise in accounts receivable and about county retirement returns.
Resident questioned a water bill that jumped from about 1100 to 5900 cubic feet, asked whether meters can be wrong, and asked for an adjustment and a payment arrangement.
Resident asked whether changing the meter would help; staff explained testing and calibration.

votes.motion: Motion to adjourn, moved and apparently seconded; captions cut off.

budget_items.what_was_said: The auditor said the district received an unmodified opinion on the June 30, 2024 financials.
Cash rose at year end and short-term borrowing for the water main project rose by a similar amount; the district earned interest on the cash.
Water revenue rose, attributed mainly to the new rate system, even though fewer gallons were pumped.
Receivables rose, which the auditor called unsurprising given larger bills.
Wage lines rose slightly more than the budgeted base-salary increase because of on-call, emergency and overtime pay.
Reported pension expense is an actuarial amount and differs from the required cash contribution.
Operating expense rose, driven mostly by pilot studies; supplies and corrosion control were up.
A board member said the cost of a system-wide meter replacement would be weighed against added revenue from more accurate readings.
The RFP drew no bids; the board will rebid and may add the Sunny Hill Road tank.
Replacement wells would yield less than the original well, making a large spend poor value.
The district keeps being billed a betterment for a sewer line it says does not pass its property, and the board debated paying it off.
The bill will be recomputed at the first-tier rate after a leak stopped, with payment options to be discussed.

decisions.decision: The board will charge the resident's high usage at the flat tier one rate and staff will recalculate the bill the next day.
Staff will redo the cellular equipment RFP, possibly adding the Sunny Hill Road tank.
The board deferred a decision on paying off the sewer betterment and will research it further.
The engineers will come to the next meeting on the 22nd to present the final pilot testing report.

budget_items.topic: New town hall footprint and cost
budget_items.what_was_said: The architect said the new town hall is about 20% larger than the last version and he is concerned about how that will show up in the budget.
The chair recalled that renovating the previous building would have committed roughly $30 million, which led to widening the charge to all municipal buildings.

budget_items.topic: Cost of treatment at the Ritter front
budget_items.what_was_said: A member warned that extras such as a terrace add cost and that a high number could be rejected by the town. Another suggested showing a green space as an add alternate.
The chair estimated the cost of an elevator shaft and the architect guessed lower. The committee asked for cost analysis of a lift versus a full elevator.
The architect referred to a figure of roughly $15 million for the project.

decisions.decision: The chair noted Dave's three points (stairs at the Ritter front, the superintendent window, prominence of the School Street entrance) to carry into the group discussion.
Straw poll: no committee interest in creating an actual entrance at the historic Ritter front. Members want something done there, not an entrance.
Architects are to return with several options for treating the former Ritter stair location (pseudo-stairs, plantings, landscaping, seating). The committee agreed.
The majority wants a prominent facade facing Mass Ave, preferring the arch design without the wraparound porch.
The committee is split on the superintendent window, and it will get staff input. The majority favors replacement, with the architect offering aesthetic options.
The architects will analyze the cost of a lift versus a full elevator in the Ritter building.
The chair and members agreed the crosswalk should stay in its existing location.
The next meeting is Wednesday, January 22, at 5:30 pm. Renderings are due February 3 and go to the select board on February 4.

what_happened.line: The Finance Committee heard the Budget Task Force present its 20 recommendations, from an investment policy and a targeted audit to a split tax rate.
Members agreed in discussion that the task force recommendations should be tracked with actions through to conclusion; no budget votes were taken.
The chair asked for four meetings after the public hearing, planned back from a 25-day warrant deadline before the May 2nd town meeting.
Members heard that Lunenburg receives the minimum per-pupil Chapter 70 increase while other communities receive larger percentage increases.
The chair will put the budget season schedule on the January 9th agenda and check the preliminary budget timing with the town manager.

why_it_matters: The task force list touches the tax bill and town services (trash and recycling costs, health insurance, snow removal, a split tax rate), but nothing was decided; each item is still a proposal that would need later votes.
Chapter 70 state aid is a large part of school funding and, as discussed, grows more slowly than expenses, so the FY26 budget gap depends on a figure the town does not set.

meetings.headline: Committee debated raising or restructuring student activity fees as costs outpace revenue; no fee change voted.
meetings.summary: The school committee handled routine business (minutes, warrants/donations, a line-item transfer, a food service administrative review, the FY24 end-of-year report, and the secretaries' union MOU, all approved by roll call) before a long discussion of LMHS and middle school student activity fees, where members debated whether flat per-student fees are fair versus tiered or club-specific fees, without reaching a decision. Reports covered MSBA updates, the town manager search narrowing to three finalists, a capital plan list likely to be well-funded due to extra free cash and ARPA offsets, and the concluded budget task force's presentation to the select board, including support for pursuing the Community Preservation Act.

An error found in the free cash calculation raised the certified free cash figure, which is expected to increase the amount available for the FY26 capital plan beyond the level previously estimated.

A member asked whether an updated cost quote had come in for the primary school generator project; the chair said a quote came in north of the prior estimate, though he initially confused it with a separate fire-suppression overrun.

Commissioners said they want permanent pins, rebar or steel, rather than stakes, to mark the well radius.
Commissioners agreed to proceed with the InvoiceCloud payment change even though it takes effect at the end of January rather than January 1.

why_it_matters: Marking the protective radius around the Hickory Hills well is a step toward the district formally claiming control of the land around the well, which bears on keeping that water source protected.
The InvoiceCloud change alters how water bills can be paid, and its delay to the end of January means customers get the new payment options later than first planned.
The loader purchase and the radio installation are district spending that residents may see raised again, since the loader drew a public question and installation may have to go out to bid.
watch_next: The surveyor's marking of the well radius at Hickory Hills, and whether the district then moves to claim the area around the well.

what_happened.line: The Board of Assessors voted by roll call to approve State Tax Form 54 and the FY2025 commitment, contingent on corrections to the form.
A motion to buy newspaper space announcing the abatement deadline failed, with two of the three members voting no.
After a resident couple described a steep condo assessment increase, the board said it would pursue a state remedy and give them an abatement application.
A motion to invite the whole assessor's office staff to the senior center conference failed.
Meetings were set for January 8 and 22, with first and third Wednesdays proposed for February through April.

why_it_matters: Form 54 is the filing behind the FY2025 tax bills, and the board's vote on the public-notice motion leaves the abatement deadline to be learned by word of mouth or the town's existing postings.

A resident who believes an assessment is wrong must file an abatement application before the deadline, so the failed outreach motion and the couple's case show the cost of missing it: escrow-backed payments rise whether or not the assessment is later corrected.

The board voted unanimously to entrust the remaining ARPA funds to the interim town manager, pending the school bid opening, with a report back.
The Budget Task Force gave a long joint presentation of recommendations on revenue and savings, including CPA and overrides; it was informational and no vote was taken.
The board heard the unaudited FY24 year-end financials, in which revenue came in above projection and free cash above the earlier estimate.
Town manager finalist interviews were set for January 14, with January 15 as backup, and the public may send candidate questions to the chair.

why_it_matters: The ARPA delegation means the last of the federal relief money can be committed by the interim town manager without a further board vote, with only a report back required.

The Budget Task Force's ideas on CPA and overrides are the kind of revenue options that would eventually reach residents as tax-bill changes or ballot questions, but nothing was decided at this meeting.
Foreclosure on the tax-title parcel moves it toward sale, and the choice of a permanent town manager will shape the next budget cycle.
watch_next: Town manager finalist interviews on January 14, with January 15 as backup.
The comparison communities list returning with an added wealth/affordability factor, followed by a formal vote.

what_happened.line: The Budget Task Force ranked its recommendations for its executive summary, putting consolidation of town accounts first and the split tax rate last.
A targeted diagnostic audit, the prudent investor rule and a review of the Community Preservation Act (CPA) were set second through fourth.
The final order of 20 recommendations was read out, with HVAC grants fifth and school and landfill solar sixth and seventh.
The CPA was kept on the list of potential recommendations in the report, after members discussed its likely yield.
The executive summary is due before noon the next day, to be presented to the Select Board and Finance Committee, with the task force's documents and slides to be posted online.

why_it_matters: The ranking sets the order in which the Select Board and Finance Committee will see the task force's proposals, so it shapes which ideas for the town and school budgets get attention first.
A targeted diagnostic audit and the CPA review could each reach a future Town Meeting vote, and the CPA would add a local surcharge to tax bills if adopted.

what_happened.line: Members gave the architects direction that school offices belong mainly on the Ritter second floor, with the town manager closer to the new town hall.
By a slim majority, members favored an entrance facing Mass Ave on the right side of the building, with a side entrance on School Street.
The chair said the performing arts center's space will be priced separately, as a standalone building or annex, so it can be voted on separately.

The Brooks House request was deferred to the next agenda; architects will return with revised renderings in mid-January, and the next meeting is January 6.

The board voted unanimously to vacate a tax-lien foreclosure judgment on one Sunset Avenue property, subject to full redemption payment within 14 days.

meetings.headline: PACC was told its studio has no place in the planned town hall annex, and the current building's boiler may fail this winter.
meetings.summary: A special PACC meeting heard the municipal building design committee's representative explain why the cable studio does not fit the planned new town hall, and that the current building's leaking boiler may not last the winter. PACC presented a reduced space plan and rough standalone-building costs. The representative agreed to send the floor plan to the architects and ask for standalone and add-on options. No formal votes were captured.

budget_items.topic: Previously approved capital funds for roof
budget_items.what_was_said: Funds approved earlier for replacing a roof section in the middle of the building are being considered for reprogramming to the front portion that would be preserved.
The leaking boiler needs an expensive repair or a replacement, and neither is in the budget.
A PACC member roughly guessed the cost of an empty standalone building to equip.
figures_as_heard: one and a half or two million

budget_items.what_was_said: An earlier study of a steel building like one in another town put the shell at a little over a million, with no money to run it. Another speaker cited a per-square-foot cost for a similar building.
figures_as_heard: just a little over a million

budget_items.topic: Cost of rehabilitating the old primary school
budget_items.what_was_said: Reusing the whole old primary school building was described as a price tag nearing a level the town would not accept.
The school committee has put out to bid a specialist to assess Turkey Hill building systems and has money ready for it.
The food pantry pays no rent. PACC was said to make a small transfer toward maintenance.
Some residents oppose tax dollars for studio space and want PACC's accumulated funds spent on any project.
The design committee has a self-imposed cap on the building project, with PACC seen as an add and a capital plan change adding more.

decisions.decision: The design committee representative will take PACC's floor plan, if emailed, to the architect and ask for standalone and add-on options for a PACC studio near the Ritter lot.
PACC members will not need to attend the design committee's meetings. They will be kept in the loop by the representative, who will ask the architects for alternatives.
The architects will work from the earlier 2300 square foot figure rather than the 2700 request, though PACC says its 1425 minimum is what it needs.

meetings.headline: Green Communities group heard a grant update and summit report, and set a January 6 virtual meeting.
