what_happened.line: The Select Board voted unanimously to adopt a single tax rate and not adopt any available exemptions, following the assessors' recommendation.
After a public hearing with comment for and against a split rate, the board held no further delay; one speaker had asked for a one-week hold.
The board voted to change the Marshall Park ARPA allocation to the remaining amount, then committed ARPA funds to Boys and Girls Club equipment, Historical Society items and fencing.
The board approved t-ball use of the old primary school property, a skate park grant support letter, an Agricultural Commission appointment, and a purchasing card policy.
The interim town manager reported a two-year property insurance renewal and said health insurance renewals are expected in mid-January with a high trend rate.

why_it_matters: The single-rate vote means residential and commercial property are taxed at the same rate in the FY2025 tax bills, so no shift of the levy onto commercial property is built into the average single-family bill.
The ARPA votes reallocate a fixed, one-time pool of federal money, so each dollar committed to a small request is no longer available for other projects.
Health insurance is a large, recurring cost in the town budget, and a high renewal trend would press on the FY2026 budget the board will be asked to set.
watch_next: Health insurance renewal figures, expected in mid-January.
The skate park support letter, due back at the next meeting with a December 31 grant deadline; the climate survey policy and goal-setting are postponed to December.

meetings.headline: Water commissioners directed the clerk-treasurer to go for the final 20-year bond in February for the Massapoag main project.
meetings.summary: Commissioners reviewed the near-complete water main replacement and choices for financing it (another temporary note versus going to bond now, 20 versus 27 years). They moved to charge the clerk-treasurer to pursue the final 20-year bond in February. They also heard worsening PFAS results at Lancaster Ave wells, discussed fixing the old dump truck and pricing a wheeled excavator, and approved prior minutes.

public_comment.topic: A resident asked about the rubber-tire excavator replacing the backhoe, the Kings pilot/treatment process and disposal of PFAS-contaminated hardness waste, in-house digging, the Rolling Acres phasing, and why own funds rather than borrowed money would cover overruns.
A resident asked about borrowing costs and rates for the short-term and long-term options, whether there is a prepayment penalty, and whether interest rates will drop.

budget_items.topic: Temporary borrowing for water main project
budget_items.what_was_said: Temporary borrowing comes due in February; options were another temporary round until July or going to final bond now.
Total repayment over 20 years was presented, with the per-quarter customer charge; 27 years would cost much more in total but only slightly less per customer.
The current charge brings in more per year than the loan needs, giving some cushion; the charge is dedicated to this project.
Project is roughly on budget with some spring work to come; modest overruns could be covered from existing funds.
Amounts under a threshold can be reallocated by the chair to a similar water project; larger amounts need a special meeting.
Possible Mass DOT paving requirement estimated as a modest extra cost that could be paid from existing funds.
A new dump body was priced far above the repair option; board favored repairing the truck from the maintenance/special line or truck account.
State-bid prices were obtained for wheeled excavators to replace the old backhoe; no purchase decided.
Pilot delayed for lack of well run time; the well will run continuously, costing only electricity.
Estimated rates were discussed for 20 and 27 years, with total interest over the term noted.

decisions.decision: Board consensus to go to bond now rather than another temporary round, and to use 20 years rather than 27, so rating work with S&P Global can start.
Agreed to repair the dump truck's body using the maintenance/special line and truck account rather than buy a new truck.
Agreed a workshop and cost comparison of in-house versus contracted water main work (e.g. Rolling Acres) is needed before buying equipment.

meetings.headline: Town meeting narrowly passed sweeping town-employee benefit/hiring changes over a select board member's objection.
meetings.summary: This was Lunenburg's fall 2024 special town meeting, covering fifteen warrant articles: budget transfers, an elderly tax exemption COLA, a rewritten water supply protection bylaw, several revolving funds, a request to explore selling or leasing the Brooks House, and two lengthy, contested articles amending the town's salary administration plan to add sick banks, holiday pay, merit awards and employment contracts aimed at staff recruitment and retention. The salary plan articles drew extended public debate over the lack of a seated Personnel Committee and process speed but passed; a Marshall Park renovation appropriation and a citizen petition article were both passed over without action.

minutes.headline: Town meeting narrowly passed sweeping town-employee benefit/hiring changes over a select board member's objection.
minutes.summary: This was Lunenburg's fall 2024 special town meeting, covering fifteen warrant articles: budget transfers, an elderly tax exemption COLA, a rewritten water supply protection bylaw, several revolving funds, a request to explore selling or leasing the Brooks House, and two lengthy, contested articles amending the town's salary administration plan to add sick banks, holiday pay, merit awards and employment contracts aimed at staff recruitment and retention. The salary plan articles drew extended public debate over the lack of a seated Personnel Committee and process speed but passed; a Marshall Park renovation appropriation and a citizen petition article were both passed over without action.

what_happened.line: Voters passed sweeping changes to town-employee pay and benefits, despite objections over the empty Personnel Committee seat.
A rewrite of the water supply protection bylaw passed, after residents raised concerns about lake water withdrawal and which map applied.
Voters asked the select board to study selling or leasing the Brooks House, without authorizing any sale.
A Marshall Park renovation appropriation was passed over after cost estimates came in far higher than expected.
Voters approved additional funds for the FY25 school operating budget and for current-year salary and health insurance lines.

why_it_matters: The salary plan changes touch pay, sick time, holidays and hiring contracts for every town employee, and were adopted without a seated Personnel Committee to vet them.
The water bylaw rewrite governs protections around the town's water supply and the lakes near Hickory Hills, an area several residents spoke about directly.
Residents should expect a revised Marshall Park proposal at spring town meeting, and a select-board report on the Brooks House's future.

Select board report on selling or leasing the Brooks House

what_happened.line: Committee ratified a new three-year contract with the teachers' union by unanimous roll call, setting cost-of-living raises for three years.
Committee voted unanimously to recommend a study on selling or long-term leasing the Brooks House at the November 12 special town meeting.
Committee also voted to recommend the Chapter 70 funding article at the same special town meeting.
Several facility projects -- 911 compliance cabling, the primary school generator, and a fire alarm upgrade -- came in over their budgeted allocations.
Committee agreed no budget update for next year will be given until January.

why_it_matters: The new teachers' contract sets pay increases across three years that will show up in future school budgets and, in turn, the town's tax bill.
The Brooks House study, if the special town meeting approves it, could lead toward a future vote on selling or leasing a town-owned property.

The facility cost overruns on 911 cabling, the generator and the fire alarm mean the capital plan may need more money than was budgeted, a gap the committee discussed covering with leftover ARPA funds.

January budget update for next fiscal year

meetings.headline: Parks Commission voted to take a rephased Marshall Park plan to spring town meeting and let the skate park build through October 1, 2025.
meetings.summary: The commission, meeting in person in a small room without Zoom, spent most of the night on Marshall Park. It heard the interim Town Manager on ARPA deadlines, voted to proceed with a rephased plan, and held a long discussion with youth baseball and softball representatives about user fees and field maintenance. It also approved an RDLA invoice, the skate park access timeline, a May all-vendor fair date and four sets of minutes. User fees were put on the December agenda with no decision.

minutes.headline: Parks Commission voted to take a rephased Marshall Park plan to spring town meeting and let the skate park build through October 1, 2025.
minutes.summary: The commission, meeting in person in a small room without Zoom, spent most of the night on Marshall Park. It heard the interim Town Manager on ARPA deadlines, voted to proceed with a rephased plan, and held a long discussion with youth baseball and softball representatives about user fees and field maintenance. It also approved an RDLA invoice, the skate park access timeline, a May all-vendor fair date and four sets of minutes. User fees were put on the December agenda with no decision.

public_comment.speaker_as_heard: Greg Le frer, 15 Park Street Terrace
public_comment.topic: Asked where the projected 5-10 year maintenance plan for Marshall Park is, and who will maintain what once phases are complete. Youth baseball and softball have carried that burden so far.
Linked user fees to the cost of maintaining new facilities, which will cost more than the old fields to maintain.
Said youth baseball and softball brings over 5,000 visitors to the parks and asked for consideration and communication.
Said the user fee conversation came up when the field-use notification was voted on. Argued the commission should analyze maintenance across all parks, and asked about capital plans for other parks.
Said youth sports feel pushed out in town, with football, baseball and softball all affected. Asked for understanding of recreational sports.
Asked when field maintenance allocations will be known. Questioned whether Parks is responsible only for big design projects and who handles repairs.
Asked whether the schools pay to use the ball fields, whether pickleball users would be charged, and who handles toilets and trash.
Said the fields are already degraded and asked what backend plan accompanies any user fee increase. Questioned whether punch lists should go through Parks or the facilities director.
Asked that the town consider long-standing cultural groups such as youth baseball and softball, which bring many visitors. Said they feel brushed aside.
Asked why ARPA money is being returned to the town while the parks have many needs. The chair explained the funds were granted for this purpose and must be under contract by year end.

votes.motion: Authorize the recreation director to proceed with planning the all-vendor fair on May 10, 2025.
Move forward with the updated, rephased Marshall Park plan and a new request at town meeting in May.
Approve the RDLA invoice dated October 31.
Allow the skate park group to proceed with construction through October 1, 2025, without interrupting ball field use.
Approve the minutes of the four prior meetings as a group, with edits.
Adjourn at 8:33 p.m.

budget_items.what_was_said: The new estimate is far above the original anticipated cost and applies to phase one and the remaining work. There is not enough money for phase one now, so the fall special town meeting borrowing article was not pursued.
The design team estimates a range of funds is needed to bring phases 1 and 2 to permitting design with updated cost estimates before spring town meeting.

budget_items.topic: ARPA funds and amount to return to the town
budget_items.what_was_said: The commission holds ARPA funds. Using only part for design would leave a balance to return to the town for other departments before the calendar-year-end deadline.

The Town Manager said funds must be under contract or spent by December 31, so contingency estimates will not work. He said interest has accumulated on the funds and asked that firms submit bills by Tuesday to clear the account.

budget_items.topic: Public presentation and test pit observation costs
budget_items.what_was_said: The Town Manager said the proposals appear to omit in-person public meetings and observation of test pits. He estimated each meeting at a few thousand dollars.
The existing Skanska contract has enough authorized funds for the proposed work. The RDLA design contract will need to be amended.
The invoice covers design development, permitting and construction documents, and was approved for payment by motion.
The chair presented the current grounds maintenance contract by park. The facilities director thinks 17 mowings a year may be low.
Per-player fees were stated for in-town and non-resident players. Youth baseball paid a season total for its players, and the Phillies paid a smaller amount for out-of-town players.

budget_items.topic: School field fees paid by another league
budget_items.what_was_said: A speaker said a league pays a yearly sum to use school fields.

what_happened.line: The Sewer Commission voted to allow a change of use at 1335 Massachusetts Avenue from theater to retail shop, with expected sewer flow estimated to drop.
The commission voted to waive interest that was missed on the final sewer bill for 165 Massachusetts Avenue.
Staff reported two manhole repair bids above the office estimate; members leaned toward the lower bidder, and no vote was taken.
Staff described difficulty hiring a business manager and an assistant, and the board agreed to put recruitment on a future agenda.
The board set its next meetings for Nov 19 (Zoom), Dec 10 and Jan 14, skipping Dec 24.

why_it_matters: Sewer bills depend on billed flow, so a change of use that lowers expected flow, and a waived interest charge, affect what individual accounts pay.
The manhole repair bids exceed the estimate, with the gap to come from grant and capital funds, so other planned sewer capital work could be delayed.
Trouble filling the business manager and assistant posts bears on how reliably quarterly bills go out, which is currently done with outside help.
watch_next: Nov 19 meeting (Zoom): an update on the assistant interviews and the recruitment discussion the board agreed to schedule.
A formal vote awarding the manhole repair contract, which had not been taken.

meetings.headline: Budget Task Force heard assessors say a split tax rate would raise commercial bills sharply for small resident savings; not recommended.
meetings.summary: The assessors presented the residential exemption and a split tax rate using estimated numbers. They concluded neither fits Lunenburg: the town is mostly residential, so the shifts save homeowners little and raise commercial bills a lot. The group also discussed the Community Preservation Act and the stormwater utility, reviewed plans for the special town meeting presentation, and approved seven sets of prior minutes by roll call.

what_happened.line: The board voted to fund an outside peer review for the 494 Electric Avenue parking and commercial building project, paid by the applicant.
All four hearings, 494 Electric Avenue, 791 and 795 Lemonster Road and 70 Kilburn Street, were continued to November 25 pending peer review.
For the three storm water hearings on Lemonster Road and Kilburn Street, the board required peer review, with an applicant deposit to the town's 53G account.
The board approved the 1260 Reservoir Road site plan with standard conditions and did not require peer review.
The board approved a certificate of completion for the 319 Highland Street storm water permit and signed two decisions.

why_it_matters: Neighbors of 494 Electric Avenue raised flooding, traffic, lighting and noise, and the independent engineering review that now follows is meant to test the drainage before the board decides.

The town has no money of its own to pay peer reviewers, so applicant deposits to the 53G account decide whether a storm water review happens, and a fee schedule revision is meant to make applicant fees cover the department's budget.

what_happened.line: The Finance Committee voted a recommendation on each article of the special town meeting warrant, mostly approval or no financial impact.
The committee recommended deferral on Article 1, the FY25 budget amendment, and on Articles 14 and 15, which are to be passed over.
Salary administration plan amendments one and two (Articles 11 and 12) were recommended 4-1; the committee recommended approval of Articles 2 through 6 and Article 9.
The Parks Commission said the new Marshall Park cost estimate is far above earlier ones, so existing money cannot fund phase one and it will seek to pass over its borrowing article.
The committee held its public hearing on the warrant, then assigned liaison roles and set no November meeting; the next regular meeting is in the second week of December.

why_it_matters: The recommendations shape how residents are likely to be asked to vote at special town meeting on the FY25 budget amendment, school aid, the salary plan and new revolving funds.
Part-time holiday pay and prorated leave would be paid mostly from existing budgets, which reduces free cash rather than adding a new appropriation.
Marshall Park's phase one is not funded by existing money, so the project's cost and timing remain open.
watch_next: The special town meeting vote on the 15 warrant articles, including whether Article 1 and the Marshall Park borrowing article are passed over.
The next regular Finance Committee meeting in the second week of December.

budget_items.what_was_said: The chair asked for regular updates on budget accounts, with a walk-through at the first one. The commission settled on quarterly, with a June one before year end.

The recreation director asked whether the commission wants a set contribution to the fair, noting costs like tents, chairs, portable toilets and trash. The chair said she should bring a figure after getting quotes.

budget_items.topic: Marshall Park cost estimates and funding plan
budget_items.what_was_said: Estimates rose from the conceptual figure to a later one and then a newest one. The commission planned to request money at town meeting to match the Land and Water Conservation grant.
A per-square-foot estimate for poured rubber surfacing differed greatly between January 2024 and the latest estimate. The speaker said the market rate has been in the low 30s for years.
Phase one was originally thought to be fully funded, but after paid invoices less is available. Value engineering would cut grant-required components and risk the grant contract.

budget_items.topic: Park grant and Land and Water Conservation grant
budget_items.what_was_said: The state said that skipping grant components makes the contract null and void with no reimbursement. The LWCF grant was based on the second estimate, which now looks underestimated.

budget_items.topic: Remaining Marshall Park money including ARPA
budget_items.what_was_said: Remaining funds are a small amount of prior warrant article money plus a million dollars of ARPA. The commission must decide quickly so ARPA money is committed by year end and not lost.
Prior town meeting design appropriations were recited and a remaining balance given.
Commitments for phase one were stated for the OPM firm and the design firm, not all expended. Combined ARPA and design funds remaining were roughly stated.
A member asked what a roughly 15 million dollar project would mean for taxes. The chair said the town accountant could model it by interest rate, term and average tax bill.
A member wants user fees on the November or December agenda because field maintenance costs seem to serve mainly one youth organization.
An invoice for OPM services was approved, in addition to two earlier ones.
An RDLA invoice for September design development labor was approved.

budget_items.topic: Revolving fund article (53D to 53E and a half)
budget_items.what_was_said: The 53D revolving account can hold a limited balance at year end, but the commission has carried more. The article would move the balance to a 53E 1/2 account, and the Attorney General may approve less.

budget_items.topic: Grants and ARPA share of the project
budget_items.what_was_said: A member noted grants secured plus ARPA made up a significant share of the project, and the commission would potentially walk away from grant money.

transfers.description: Proposed transfer of the existing balance in the 53D revolving account into a new 53E 1/2 account via the town meeting article; the AG may allow only a limited amount.

decisions.decision: Chris (town finance staff) will be asked to present the first quarterly budget report, with a walk-through, at the next meeting covering the first quarter of FY25.
The recreation director will bring dates and a money figure for the spring vendor fair to the next meeting; May 10 is the preferred date.
The Boys and Girls Club Polar Plunge goes on the next agenda; the Polar Plunge date is November 30, noon to 2, and the club will check with the fire chief on lifeguard needs.
The commission leans toward continuing and completing the design during the pause, to bring an updated cost estimate to the spring town meeting.
User fees will be added to the November agenda; a beach and staffing item is targeted for December.
A special meeting will be held on November 6 to vote on extending consultant design work; the chair will gather fee information beforehand.
The chair will notify sports users, the schools superintendent and the sports director, and the park grant and LWCF grant contacts.
The commission has no interest in any of the tax-taking list properties; the chair will email back no interest. No vote was taken.

Commissioners left the replacement dump truck undecided; the superintendent will send them state-bid quote information for a Ford and a Dodge to consider.

why_it_matters: PFAS grant money, if awarded, would bear on how much of the cost of testing and treatment lands on water bills, and no decision on it is expected until the state responds.

The cell tower RFP and the truck purchase are the district's near-term spending choices; both are still open and neither has a recorded vote.
watch_next: The PFAS grant decision from the state, for which no timeline was given.

minutes.headline: Budget Task Force backed a narrowly scoped audit and health insurance opt-out research ahead of special town meeting.
minutes.summary: The task force discussed a Finance Committee idea for a deep-dive audit of town records, with the scope to be kept narrow. Most of the meeting covered town health insurance: the opt-out incentive and its rules, a high deductible plan, and retiree contribution rates. The group reviewed a one-page list of recommendations for special town meeting, dropped the Proposition 2.5 explanation from it, and no formal votes were audible.

budget_items.what_was_said: A member said a vaguely described miscellaneous non-recurring line that disappeared is why a deeper audit is wanted before asking voters for more money.
The current incentive is paid only to people who first took town insurance and then dropped it, and was said to be weak against rising costs. Other communities were said to range widely.
The policy requires two years on the insurance before opting out, with individual and family amounts differing. The payout comes from the town, not the school budget, and is paid at fiscal year end.
Last year's preliminary increase was feared to be double digit but the final was lower. Trend numbers come mid to late December and real numbers in January.
Examples were given of emergency room co-pay changes with surplus paid back to employees, and gradual retiree contribution rate increases. Examples were illustrative, not proposals.
DLS data shows fees already rose significantly, so wording was shifted toward periodic fee review.
Accepting town roads that are maintained but lack documented acceptance could raise Chapter 90 funding.
The advisor suggested a top-to-bottom review of trash disposal, with possible considerable savings. Bag and cart costs were discussed.
Heating and cooling grant applications were discussed, including a phase 2 application submitted Friday.

decisions.decision: The advisor agreed to research opt-out practices and incentive levels in peer towns, expected to take about two weeks.
The advisor will raise a high deductible plan with the insurance association reps next week and ask them to cost it out.
The Proposition 2.5 and override explanation was dropped from the talking points to keep the document simple.
Next meeting set for the 4th, before special town meeting, with assessors invited and health insurance follow-up on the agenda.

meetings.headline: Assessors backed a policy requiring written requests from other departments; website table of contents split the board.
meetings.summary: The Board of Assessors heard the principal assessor's report on abatements, motor vehicle commitments, and preliminary interim LA-4 figures from Vision, signed an invoice and abatement paperwork, and argued at length over the town website layout and a table of contents. They also reviewed the cost-of-living exemption warrant article and a neighborhood review working group's work on site-index zero properties, and adopted a new written-request policy by voice vote.

what_happened.line: The Board of Assessors adopted by voice vote a policy that any action by another town department needing assessors to act or vote must come with a written request and explanation.
The board passed a compromise on the assessors website table of contents, with two yes votes and one abstention, after a long dispute; key forms go up front and a table of contents below.

The board heard the principal assessor's report: three abatements processed with no appeals outstanding, a supplemental bill for an omitted building, and preliminary interim LA-4 figures from Vision.
The board signed a partial Vision invoice and a fifth motor vehicle commitment, and postponed the September 4 and October 2 minutes to the next meeting.

why_it_matters: The written-request policy sets how other town departments bring matters to the board that sets property valuations and exemptions, which affects how those requests are documented.

The exemption warrant article for town meeting, with a one-page summary and a handout still to be drafted, is a vote residents will be asked to take, and the cost-of-living exemption terms bear on who qualifies for a tax reduction.

The commission agreed to submit that figure to the town manager by the 15th, keeping the option to amend or pass over the article later.
Updated Phase One cost estimates came in well above the funds available, so value engineering continues and some items move to Phase Two.
Members discussed a risk that two reimbursement grants could be lost if the project scope is cut.
The chair will contact the park grant administrators and email members, and will poll them for an extra meeting before the Nov 12 special town meeting.

why_it_matters: The borrowing figure is expected to go to voters at the Nov 12 special town meeting, so residents may be asked to authorize debt for a park whose Phase One cost still exceeds the money in hand.

The interim town manager's advice, as the minutes record it, was that the borrowing would sit within the operating budget and replace retiring debt rather than be a debt exclusion, so it would not be a separate vote to raise taxes above the levy limit.
Cutting scope to close the gap could put the grant reimbursements at risk, which is a mechanism that could leave more of the cost to the town.

what_happened.line: The Town Manager Screening Committee approved the town manager position profile by voice vote, with small wording edits and no opposition heard.
Interviews with candidates were set for December 11 and 12 at 6 pm at an off-site location, with the consultant to email about booking.
The meeting to choose which candidates to interview was set for Monday, November 18, at 7, in executive session.
Candidate discussions will be confidential: minutes will refer to candidates by number and only finalists will be named publicly.
The return date originally set for October 31 moved to November 8, and candidates will be asked to bring a document they authored and speak to it.

why_it_matters: The profile sets the criteria the committee will use to screen candidates for town manager, so residents who want a say in what the job requires have the least time to give it before interviews begin.
Because candidate discussions are confidential and minutes use numbers, the public will see names only at the finalist stage, so that is the point at which public input becomes possible.
watch_next: Monday, November 18 at 7: executive session to choose which candidates to interview.
December 11 and 12 at 6 pm: candidate interviews at an off-site location still to be booked.

meetings.headline: Committee moved to work toward vacating the aging, ill-suited TC Pasos office building.
meetings.summary: The board heard a presentation on the new second school resource officer and comfort-dog Hank, then spent most of the meeting on facilities and money: the TC Pasos building's deficit and poor condition, FY26 budget priorities including whether to move health insurance out of the school budget, and school committee goals emphasizing facilities and financial stability. Several routine votes passed (minutes, a LEAF nomination, a one-day Spain-trip date change, facilities report, a batch of third-read policies) and the meeting closed by moving into executive session for non-union personnel/collective-bargaining matters.

what_happened.line: Committee directed the superintendent to explore moving central administration out of the TC Pasos building, citing its condition and an account deficit.
Superintendent will bring two or three FY26 budget scenarios to the committee no later than the first December meeting.
Committee said it will not cut the district's two BCBA positions in FY26 budget planning.
A proposal to move the health insurance line out of the school budget and into the town's municipal pool was tabled for the FY26 budget discussion.
Members narrowed a proposed facilities goal to TC Pasos, Turkey Hill, and the turf field and dropped another goal, without formally adopting FY26 goals.

why_it_matters: Where central administration is housed touches a building account residents' taxes cover, and any move to Turkey Hill or leased space would run through the FY26 budget or a future capital request.
Whether health insurance stays in the school budget or moves to the town's pool changes what a resident sees when the school budget comes up for a vote, without changing what the insurance costs.
The board's commitment to keep both BCBA positions is a signal about which special-education services it intends to protect as it builds FY26 budget scenarios.
watch_next: FY26 budget scenarios, due to the committee no later than the first School Committee meeting in December 2024
Formal adoption of the FY26 school committee goals, once goal three's wording is finalized

what_happened.line: The Finance Committee voted 4-0 by roll call to approve an edited department budget presentation template and have the chair send it to the interim town manager.
The template was the main business of the night; it was built on town manager target budgets plus any above-target requests from departments.
The committee heard a split tax rate presentation showing amounts shifted from residential to commercial at different shift factors, with no vote taken.
The Mart taxi and livery grant program has ended, yet the town keeps subsidizing it, and a source of funds must be found for the rest of the fiscal year.
The chair will call the grant writing firm again and reach out to the interim town manager, amid concern the appropriated line may go unused.

why_it_matters: The template sets how each department presents its FY26 request, so residents will see requests above the town manager's target shown separately from the baseline.
The split tax rate discussion bears on how the tax burden is divided between homeowners and commercial property, a choice that ends up on a resident's tax bill.
The Mart taxi subsidy and the unused grant writing line show how a budget line can continue or be absorbed elsewhere without a separate vote.
watch_next: A possible Finance Committee meeting on Oct 17 to finalize warrant votes, which may replace the Oct 24 meeting.
The chair's follow-up on a redline version of the DLS financial policy manual.

budget_items.what_was_said: Presenter showed local receipts were consistently underestimated versus actuals, with multi-year averages in the hundreds of thousands. He asked whether estimates should be less conservative.
The unlevied amount plus underestimated receipts was compared to the size of the recent override.
A finance official described a five-year average dropping the high and low, adjusted for market trend. Members noted no estimating methodology appears in the financial policy.
Discussion of free cash as a share of levy or general fund, with a rule of thumb given by a participant.
The former town manager's presentation showed local receipts estimates and an increase added to school department funding.
Free cash was transferred to the overlay account to cover abatements; the assessors can raise overlay to absorb unlevied room.
Presenter modelled Maynard's levy split on Lunenburg's FY24 levy; residential savings are a shift of burden, not new revenue.

budget_items.topic: Split rate impact on house vs business
budget_items.what_was_said: Carter illustrated a 1.1 shift saving a $500,000 house a small amount while a $500,000 business pays much more.
Recent override tax-rate impact was compared to the split rate savings.

budget_items.topic: Local receipts and free cash link
budget_items.what_was_said: Carter explained raising local receipts estimates reduces free cash available for capital and snow and ice.
CPA is a surcharge with state matching that has fallen over time, restricted to three spending categories.
A citizens petition for Marshall Park bonding was noted, with a project total and ARPA contribution mentioned.
Participants estimated annual debt service on a 20-year borrowing at an assumed rate.

meetings.headline: Water commissioners heard public pushback on a master-plan proposal from Tighe & Bond and deferred decisions a month pending the grant.
meetings.summary: The commissioners reviewed an updated Tighe & Bond proposal for the PFAS master plan, built from public feedback, and residents debated whether intermunicipal connection studies, redundancy studies and O&M cost work justify the spending. public_comment.topic: Chair asked for public comment at the start; none was offered.
Asked what happens to the town clerk's second office and storage planned for TCP. Said she does not favor spending money on TCP and wants the plan run past the select board and the public.
Asked where money would come from to relocate Ritter offices into TCP before renovation. Said TCP is only partly occupied and has a damaged hallway roof. Said the RFP does not budget for the moves.

budget_items.what_was_said: The committee has an ARPA allocation for the design work. A rule change over the summer requires the funds to be under contract by year end, so the select board wants contracts by October.
The figure came from an architectural team's estimate, with an escalator added for wiggle room. It was not set by the committee as a group.

budget_items.topic: Estimated construction cost in the RFP
budget_items.what_was_said: The draft states one construction estimate. The chair thinks the real figure is lower, and the town manager wants costs kept down.
The RFP notes the Ritter building was built for book storage, which affects pricing because floor loading is higher than for an office.
Evening meetings drive up a design contract's price. Members discussed reducing the meeting count or letting the bidder price it.
Soil borings could use up a large share of the design money, though an exotic foundation could add major cost. Members agreed to drop them from this phase.
A member said the RFP's required experience range is too low given the project size and should be raised.
A resident cited the earlier TCP estimate. She said she opposes putting money into TCP.
A speaker said the cost of moving offices into TCP is not in the RFP request.

decisions.decision: Reduce the number of paper copies required to three and add a requirement for a digital copy.
Remove the soil borings and subsurface investigation requirement from this phase's deliverables, with the committee in agreement.
TCP stays the voting location and holds the town clerk's voting equipment for now. The chair will make a note on town clerk storage.
The chair will email the RFP with the notes so far and ask members to review the quality requirements section before the next meeting.
The meeting adjourned without a motion because it had lost its quorum.

what_happened.line: The Commission voted to issue a per-day violation notice at 390 Howard Street until erosion controls are restored and approved by the office.
The 160 Sunset Lane tree removal determination was continued to September 18, pending a more detailed erosion control and replanting plan.
The 390 Howard Street abbreviated notice of resource area delineation hearing was continued to October 2.
Three certificates of compliance were approved, along with a negative determination for a driveway and sewer connection and a notice of project change at 10 Sunset Ave.
The Commission allowed use of the town purchase order for bridge repairs at Larkin Town Forest and asked the planning board to release 2024 GIS hours for trail maps.

why_it_matters: Erosion at 390 Howard Street is the kind of unresolved site problem that can drain into nearby waterways, and the Commission is now using fines and agency escalation, not further hearings, to force a fix.

The Commission's enforcement relies on a bylaw cap and a notice written and mailed each day, and the agent's workload and a part-time hire with reduced hours affect how quickly violation letters and decisions get out.
watch_next: September 18: the 160 Sunset Lane hearing resumes with a native planting and erosion control plan.
October 2: the continued 390 Howard Street delineation hearing, where the Commission said the application could be denied for lack of information if it keeps being continued.

Commissioners discussed how to function with only three members and no quorum; the Town Manager and possibly the Select Board will be asked about an interim appointment.
The commission voted to accept an estimate for repairing the Mass One suction lines, plus an allowance for pumping, with the estimate above what was budgeted for the year.
The commission authorized the business manager to request line-item budget transfers, and voted to impose a fine on the one grease trap establishment found non-compliant.
Two votes aimed at filling commission vacancies passed: a letter to the editor, and a recruitment letter to sewer customers sent from the Town Manager's office.

why_it_matters: A sewer commission without a quorum cannot vote on rates, repairs or budget transfers, so sewer service decisions depend on the vacancies being filled.
Sewer customers may be asked to vote on the placeholder articles at a special town meeting, and the repair, mailing and transfers are paid from the sewer budget rather than general tax revenue.

meetings.headline: Select Board reprogrammed ARPA funds and allocated about $353,000 to requests using median rankings; vice chair recall pressure aired.
meetings.summary: The board heard extensive public comment about the vice chair and a possible recall, then took up ARPA funds. It voted to redirect two ARPA lines, chose the median over the average for ranking requests, and voted to commit the final allocation list. Other business: St. Bonifice Oktoberfest license, interim town manager report, Chapter 70 letter from the school committee, flat hill speed limit discussion, and a request for an HR state-of-the-organization report.

public_comment.topic: Resident urged the vice chair to resign, citing rule violations and the effect on recruiting a town manager; said she would support a recall otherwise.
School committee member speaking for himself asked the board to reconsider the $10,000 request to finish the track and field drainage assessment, saying the turf field is at end of life.
Library trustees chair praised the vice chair as board liaison to the library and lamented strife on the board.
Resident urged civility, lamented vacancies and board dysfunction, and thanked the interim town manager for attention to the Council on Aging.
Resident defended the vice chair, said there is no groundswell for removal, and urged people not to sign the recall petition.
Resident said he is researching a charter review committee under Chapter 43B and a petition requiring 15% of registered voters.
Council on Aging director disagreed with the earlier comparison of the interim manager to the former manager and said the former manager supported the COA.

votes.motion: Approve special event license and one-day wine and beer license for St. Bonifice parish Oktoberfest on September 21, 2024, rain date September 22.
Redirect ARPA consultant line to ARPA Administration and IT staffing challenges, and FY23 tax assessment support line to FY24/FY25 valuation services.
Approve minutes of the August 6, 2024 meeting.
Commit the ARPA funds as stated by the chair in the final updated median allocation.
Adjourn.

budget_items.what_was_said: The school committee asked that the added Chapter 70 over the governor's proposal be appropriated to the school department at the November special town meeting; the board agreed to forward it to the interim town manager for inclusion.
A resident said last year's appropriation did not cover drainage beneath the track and turf, and an added amount would complete the assessment.
The interim manager reviewed the status of each ARPA line, noting which are fully expended and which are lagging, and stated the unallocated amount available.
Delaying implementation to January 1 reduces the first-year cost; later years are an annual subscription, and the finance director's plan to phase in funding was questioned.

budget_items.topic: Final ARPA allocation list by median
budget_items.what_was_said: The chair read the funded items, including a full-amount weekend food kit program, DPW garage floor and roof repairs, and the flat hill detention basin contribution; the total came to roughly $353,500 with a small remainder.
A member noted $125,000 was pulled from the capital plan and several requests, including the school committee's, did not make the list.
The interim manager said unpaid FY24 assessing bills and interim valuation services could be paid from reprogrammed ARPA rather than appropriating new money at fall town meeting.

what_happened.line: The Select Board voted unanimously to redirect two ARPA lines, one to ARPA administration and IT staffing and one to FY24/FY25 valuation services.
The board chose the median tab over the average to rank ARPA requests.
The board voted unanimously to commit the final ARPA allocation list as read by the chair; the weekend food kit program was funded in full.

budget_items.what_was_said: Per capita spending rose FY19 to FY23; education is about half the budget; Lunenburg compared to 29 other towns.

Debt service is a little over a tenth of expenditures in FY23; officials said paid-off debt has been absorbed elsewhere so there is no source to cover new non-excluded debt.

Only one company bids on busing; a bill would require competitive bidding; a fee for non-required riders was judged not worthwhile.
A member estimated a multi-million gap in total spending and guessed Chapter 70 as a possible source.
Presenter said Lunenburg's schedule is the lowest in the comparison range, hurting hiring and retention.

what_happened.line: The task force took no votes; its only motion was to adjourn.
Two investment advisers explained a new prudent-investor law that would let trust funds be invested beyond the legal list, with town meeting approval; stabilization and CPA funds are excluded.
Members asked about earning more on cash held in bank and liquid accounts, and an adviser agreed some could be moved to laddered treasuries.
Members presented state (DLS) spending comparisons with other towns, covering health insurance, debt service, recycling, busing, special education and teacher pay.

why_it_matters: Investing trust-fund money more broadly would need a town meeting vote, so residents may be asked to approve a change in how the town's affordable housing and similar trust funds are invested.
The comparison work on health insurance, debt service and school costs bears on how large the gap between spending and the levy cap looks, and so on what the next budget asks of taxpayers.

public_comment.topic: Supported replacing special permit with site plan review in Zone 1 and 2. Recommended adding the 310 CMR 22 permitted-use language. Explained that the AG reviews a bylaw only after town meeting.

budget_items.topic: Two-way radio replacement and joint system with fire and police
budget_items.what_was_said: The district's radios are 14-15 years old and failing. The superintendent suggested joining the fire and police upgrade with a combiner antenna, which would split the cost across three departments and help with bidding-law limits.

budget_items.topic: Townsend offer to sell water to Lunenburg Water District
budget_items.what_was_said: The board discussed buying or selling water. Past experience was that buying from an outside entity cost more than the loan payment for own supply.
The investment comes due on the 22nd. The money was allocated for the tank. Six- and 12-month rates were offered, and the board favored 12 months given falling rates.

decisions.decision: Commissioners want the special permit requirement removed from Zone 1 and Zone 2 uses, and the H6 item under permitted uses removed.
Instead of deleting the section, the draft will say uses require site plan review where it now says special permit. The Planning Board can accept or not.
The clerk will add the 310 CMR 22 permitted-use language to the draft, highlight the requested changes, and send it back to the Planning Board before its meeting on the 26th.
Once the Planning Board's final version exists, the commissioners will consider forwarding it to DEP for review.
The commissioners favor reinvesting the maturing investment for one year, and the clerk will contact the broker.
The board will post a visit to Townsend's new treatment plant as a full-board meeting after it comes online in mid-September.
The clerk will share the Lancaster Rd past test data with the resident.

meetings.headline: Committee publicly grappled with backlash after a new hire withdrew amid a social-media firestorm over race and curriculum
meetings.summary: The meeting opened with public comment and extended committee reflection on a weekend social-media controversy after a newly selected hire withdrew amid online attacks referencing race, religion and curriculum rumors; members debated communications policy and hiring-policy gaps without taking a vote. A finance consulting firm (TMS) gave a long best-practices presentation on budget development, MUNIS use, personnel control ledgers and purchase-order controls, and the committee worked through an early draft of the FY26-FY35 capital plan, including the failing turf field drainage, a primary school generator, and Turkey Hill facility needs. The committee approved a letter asking the town to allocate an additional round of Chapter 70 funding to the school budget and approved minutes and warrants before adjourning.

meetings.headline: Budget Task Force reviewed town and school revenue data and flagged investment income and a vanished revenue line to pursue.
meetings.summary: The task force heard a master revenue presentation covering state aid versus tax levy, local receipts, fees, new growth and comparison towns, followed by school-side revenue streams. Members focused on poorly invested town accounts, an unexplained drop in a miscellaneous non-recurring line, and Medicaid reimbursement. No formal votes were recorded; the next meeting will look at expenses and the treasurer may be invited.

public_comment.topic: Mr pasos was invited first; the captions do not make clear what he said, and an observer said he was only there to observe.

Dave pasio (56 wedding Street) praised the task force, said the CPA attempt never got past the select board, urged contacting the library trustees about raising investment returns, and proposed seeking a state empowerment act for a local income tax.

budget_items.what_was_said: Presenter observed an inverse relationship between tax levy and state aid shares across towns. Another member said this is the expected net effect of the state formulas, not causal.
This local receipts line dropped sharply around FY16 and stayed down, and nobody knows what it contained. Carter will dig through records.
Revenue from the fees line rose over five years, more steadily than in other towns.
Reimbursement program for DPW road work, funds accumulate and stay available; a plan was presented to the selectboard.
First funded in FY24, restricted to roads and bridges, in addition to Chapter 90. School-related portion covers free lunches; schools not eligible for a grant.
Town-side line dropped away; school-based Medicaid is a school claim and is believed to bring in a steady amount, but where it is recorded is unclear.
Town earns little compared with peers, with many accounts at very low rates and millions sitting idle. Consolidation and better returns were called a quick win.
A member estimated that restoring the vanished revenue streams and fixing investments could find a large sum.
CPA would add a surcharge with a partial state match, restricted to open space, recreation and housing, not operating revenue.

budget_items.topic: School revenue streams: Chapter 70, circuit breaker, grants
budget_items.what_was_said: Chapter 70 is steadily increasing; circuit breaker reimburses a share of high-need special education; entitlement and competitive grants described.
Tuition is variable and depends on committee decisions; the committee chose not to expand slots, so no increase is projected.
Fees have not risen in six years while costs have, and fees do not cover athletics costs. Fee relief tied to lunch status and sibling discounts.
Cell tower rent goes to the town, possibly the turf revolving account or the fees line, not through the school district.
School side is trying to untangle solar agreements and credit rates; buying out leases was suggested.

decisions.decision: Invite the treasurer to a task force meeting to discuss investment strategy and the FY24 figures.
Raise a review of trust fund and investment accounts with the finance team this week, possibly asking Bartholomew.
A member will contact an expert on another board for names of people who can advise on investment consolidation.
Next meeting will look at expenses, focusing on unavoidable contractual and statutory costs, and try to identify the miscellaneous non-recurring revenue.
Next meeting set for two weeks out, the 29th.
Town will ask the assessor to preview the classification hearing material and make it more informative.

what_happened.line: The Budget Task Force heard a master presentation on town revenue, then school revenue streams, and recorded no formal votes.
Members flagged town investment income as a possible quick win, citing many accounts at very low rates and idle balances.
A local receipts line for miscellaneous non-recurring revenue dropped sharply around FY16 and stayed down; nobody present knew what it held, and Carter will search records.
The task force agreed to invite the treasurer to discuss investment strategy and the FY24 figures.
The next meeting, set for the 29th, will look at expenses, mainly contractual and statutory costs, and try to identify the vanished revenue line.

why_it_matters: Interest earned on town cash and trust accounts, and any revenue line that disappeared, can reduce how much must be raised through the tax levy, so these are the places the task force is looking for money before asking residents for more.
The school-side discussion showed that state aid and fees, not the levy alone, carry much of the school budget, and athletics fees have stayed flat while costs rose.
watch_next: Task force meeting on the 29th, which will cover expenses and try to identify the miscellaneous non-recurring revenue line.
A treasurer appearance on investment strategy and FY24 figures, which the task force agreed to request.

what_happened.line: The Open Space Committee voted by roll call, all ayes, to recommend that the town waive its right of first refusal on three Chapter 61 lots.
The same motion asked the planning board to forward Chapter 61 withdrawal notices to the committee and to confirm with the assessor that subdivided parcels over five acres are not enrolled.
Members discussed the value of the right of first refusal, the reduced taxes owners pay under Chapter 61B, short statutory timelines and the lack of notice.

why_it_matters: Chapter 61 land taken out of that program can be bought by the town first, and a recommendation to waive means the committee is not advising the town to buy these lots.

meetings.headline: Committee skipped a vote, told the superintendent to submit turf-field drainage study and auditorium upgrades as its top ARPA asks
meetings.summary: The school committee spent most of this meeting deciding what to request from the town's remaining ARPA funds, reviewing a superintendent-prepared list of capital-type projects including a primary school generator, AC phase two, concession stand keycard access, auditorium booth upgrades, and a track/turf drainage study. Rather than vote, the committee reached consensus to prioritize the turf drainage study and the auditorium booth upgrades, drop the AC project from the list, and let the superintendent compile and submit the remainder for the select board's consideration. The committee also approved June 5 minutes, tabled two other sets of minutes pending corrections, and agreed to schedule an August meeting to act on the capital plan.

budget_items.what_was_said: The town notified the school committee of a new round of remaining ARPA funds available, with submissions due by the end of the month, prompting this meeting.

The original vendor quoted the whole building on backup power, but the district only needs the boiler room and kitchen covered; the original site visitor has since retired and a new site visit was requested, with a rough estimate given.

budget_items.topic: Primary school AC project phase two
budget_items.what_was_said: Beardmore said the select board is unlikely to fund the full ask given questions about green-communities rebate eligibility, but any partial funding for two more classrooms would help.

The original study only covered the hill down to the track, not drainage under the turf itself; the committee wants enough additional money to complete the assessment before committing to new turf, but does not yet have a firm number.
A vehicle request has been turned down two years running and Beardmore suggested it be raised again in next month's capital plan discussion.

budget_items.topic: Primary school driveway phase one assessment
budget_items.what_was_said: Last year's capital request for a driveway-expansion phase-one assessment came in below the funding threshold that would normally get select-board attention.
This was already funded using school lunch program funds rather than needing capital or ARPA money.

A hearing-aid-compatible audio loop for the library's community room, previously requested in capital planning, was recalled at roughly this cost and the committee asked to have it added to the auditorium booth quote.

meetings.headline: Select Board interviewed two interim Town Manager candidates and chose Mr. terenzini first, Blanchard second, unanimously.
meetings.summary: The board interviewed two candidates for interim Town Manager, Charlie Blanchard and Carter terenzini, asking the same questions about availability, budgets, town meeting, hiring and management style. In discussion, members agreed both were qualified, and all leaned to terenzini partly because he has no stated hour limit. They split up reference checks, asked the Town Council-side staff to draft an agreement and get salary ranges, and voted a first and second choice before adjourning.

meetings.headline: Select Board adopted a public communications policy 3-2 after one night's notice, and took no action on the Flat Hill Road petition.
meetings.summary: After a long executive session, the board appointed a Parks Commission member, approved a skate park toll booth fundraiser and new police sex offender policies, and heard a petition from Flat Hill Road residents seeking a lower speed limit. what_happened.line: The Conservation Commission approved the 2024 treatment plans for Lake Shirley and Hickory Hills Lake, each by unanimous roll call.
Two 60 Crossroad notices of intent were continued to August 7, pending test pits, staking of the house and buffers, and a draft subdivision sketch.
Seven previously continued hearings were not opened because no agenda had been posted for them; they move to the next regular meeting.
The commission voted to write to the town requesting ARPA money for the matching portion of a grant project, and authorized a not-to-exceed purchase of a replacement riding mower.
The commission voted to recommend the town not pursue the 20 Kilburn Street parcel; reorganization is the first item next meeting, with no one yet willing to be chair.

why_it_matters: The ARPA request and the mower authorization draw on town money, and the commission described the harvest income that offsets such costs as uncertain.
The Crossroad filings, including a new house and a subdivision sketch, stay open near wetland buffers until August 7, and the seven unheard hearings wait on a properly posted agenda.
The commission has no chair willing to serve, which affects who runs its hearings and signs its decisions.
watch_next: August 7: continued hearings on the two 60 Crossroad notices of intent.
Next meeting: reorganization of the commission, including who will serve as chair, and the seven unheard hearings.

Public comment from John Fortune turned into a heated exchange, and the meeting adjourned.

minutes.headline: Water commissioners favored a six-month temporary loan, heard a Planning Board bylaw debate, and a public comment turned hostile.
minutes.summary: Commissioners got updates on temporary water lines and on short-term borrowing, where the financial advisor recommends a six-month note with bids due next meeting. They compared the Ayer PFAS plant's cost to their own estimates and discussed the Planning Board's draft zoning bylaw, favoring a site plan review or a special permit but deciding nothing. public_comment.topic: Thanked the commissioners for investigating the Ayer treatment plant, asked about cost escalation and the timeline, and urged them to keep raising PFAS treatment at every meeting.

Read a letter on behalf of several citizen groups asking for cooperation, accurate cost information, water-use data, and an emergency water plan, and set out the groups' positions. The commissioners responded angrily.

votes.motion: Motion to accept the minutes of July 10th (actually the July 8th minutes) was raised, then withdrawn on a motion to pass over the minutes.
Motion to pass over the June 26 and July 8 minutes, seconded.
Motion to adjourn, seconded.

budget_items.what_was_said: The financial advisor recommends a six-month temporary note rather than four months, citing timing and election-related rate uncertainty. Commissioners asked what the cost difference would be, and the superintendent said it won't be known until bids come in.

budget_items.topic: Existing temporary borrowing due date and bid timing
budget_items.what_was_said: The current temporary note comes due in early August and the new borrowing goes out to bid next week. Bid numbers will be presented at the July 24 meeting so the board can sign before the deadline.

budget_items.topic: Ayer PFAS treatment plant cost comparison
budget_items.what_was_said: Ayer's plant cost about $7 million, and engineers said today's cost would be roughly 20% higher and more than double with iron and manganese removal. The Lunenburg Hickory Hill estimate is comparable to or higher than that.

The article at the last meeting sought a financing figure with cushion, whereas the actual construction estimate was lower and included water main across town. Approval does not mean the full amount is spent.

budget_items.topic: Rising bid prices and loss of infrastructure grants
budget_items.what_was_said: Commissioners said bids are coming in much higher than estimates and that the federal infrastructure funding is gone. They expect costs to be higher than previously planned.

budget_items.topic: ARPA funding for pilot testing at Keyes well
budget_items.what_was_said: Commissioners discussed asking the Select Board for ARPA money to complete pilot testing and noted a possible reimbursement through a grant. They said a clock is ticking to put funds under contract by the end of 2024.
A pressure relief device on a hydrant might cost a thousand or two to install.
A commissioner said the town has already invested in the well and will not throw that money away.

decisions.decision: The commissioners will see the bid numbers for the temporary loan at the next meeting on the 24th and sign the note before the August deadline; the advisor's six-month recommendation was accepted in principle.
The Planning Board's zoning bylaw (special permit versus site plan review) will be put on the agenda for the next meeting, with no decision tonight.
Mr. Fortune's letter will be discussed at the next meeting.

what_happened.line: Water commissioners took no votes; the financial advisor's recommendation of a six-month temporary note was accepted in principle, with bids to come back at the next meeting.
The current temporary note comes due in early August, so the board plans to see the bid numbers on July 24 and sign before the deadline.
Commissioners compared the Ayer PFAS plant's cost with their own Hickory Hill estimate and said bids are running above estimates now that federal infrastructure funding is gone.
The Planning Board chair presented a water supply protection bylaw, with site plan review set against a special permit; no decision was made and it goes on the next agenda.
Public comment by John Fortune became a heated exchange, and his letter will be discussed at the next meeting.

why_it_matters: The temporary note is short-term borrowing for the PFAS treatment project, and its term and interest cost come from bids not yet received, so the cost of carrying the project is still open.

The commissioners say construction bids are above estimates and that federal infrastructure money is gone, so the project's final cost, and what water users and taxpayers are later asked to pay for it, may be higher than first planned.

meetings.headline: Planning Board backed pursuing state technical-assistance funding for MBTA zoning, heard water bylaw compromise talks, kept the pledge.
meetings.summary: The board heard a Montachusett Regional Planning Commission presentation on MBTA Communities multifamily zoning for Lunenburg and agreed to pursue Mass Housing Partnership technical assistance funding. It held a long joint discussion with the Water Commissioners on the water supply protection district bylaw (Zone 1, 2 and 3 uses, special permit versus site plan approval), with no decision. It continued the Sunny Hill Road stormwater hearing, cancelled the Lancaster signage hearing, granted a certificate of completion for 321 Sunny Hill Road, and voted by show of hands to keep saying the Pledge.

minutes.headline: Planning Board backed pursuing state technical-assistance funding for MBTA zoning, heard water bylaw compromise talks, kept the pledge.
minutes.summary: The board heard a Montachusett Regional Planning Commission presentation on MBTA Communities multifamily zoning for Lunenburg and agreed to pursue Mass Housing Partnership technical assistance funding. It held a long joint discussion with the Water Commissioners on the water supply protection district bylaw (Zone 1, 2 and 3 uses, special permit versus site plan approval), with no decision. It continued the Sunny Hill Road stormwater hearing, cancelled the Lancaster signage hearing, granted a certificate of completion for 321 Sunny Hill Road, and voted by show of hands to keep saying the Pledge.

public_comment.topic: Chair opened public comment at the start of the meeting; none offered.
Joan P., Winter Green Court, said residents have no objection to removing section E (farming, gardening) from Zone 1 uses.

Joan P. said residents are not opposed to treatment plants but want a special permit for new ones in Zones 2 and 3 so neighbors can have input on screening and placement; said the bylaw failed at town meeting before.
Asked whether industrial versus residential areas are treated differently and who looks out for the neighborhood.
Argued only water district voters vote before a project reaches the board, so a special permit should stay in the board's back pocket.
Said voters want the most stringent regulation and a special permit is the way to get two-thirds at town meeting.
Proposed compromise: no treatment plant in Zone 1 within 400 feet of a lake shore; later proposed special permit for any new construction in Zones 1 and 2.
Remote member of the public asked why saying the Pledge is so important to those who want it.
Thanked the board for the pledge vote and criticized chair comments about attracting attendance.

Options are another planning assistance grant, the District Local Technical Assistance next January, or Mass Housing Partnership funding with a 4 to 8 month timeframe.
Grants vary in amount.
Noncompliance with MBTA zoning could make the town ineligible for Housing Choice, Green Communities, MassWorks and other grants.
A guarantee covers 317 and 321 Sunny Hill and remains if the certificate is issued.
Water district said treatment plants are very costly and forcing them out of the protection zones would add millions.

what_happened.line: The Planning Board voted to pursue Mass Housing Partnership technical assistance funding to evaluate MBTA Communities zoning compliance.
A long joint session with the Water Commissioners on the water supply protection district bylaw ended with no decision; a redraft is due for August 26th.
The board and the water district agreed to remove farming and gardening (section E) from the Zone 1 permitted uses.
The Sunny Hill Road stormwater hearing was continued to July 22nd, and a certificate of completion was granted for 321 Sunny Hill Road.
The Lancaster signage hearing was cancelled so the applicant can withdraw and resubmit, and a show of hands favored keeping the Pledge of Allegiance.

why_it_matters: Noncompliance with MBTA zoning could make the town ineligible for grants such as Housing Choice, Green Communities and MassWorks, so the technical-assistance application bears on future town funding and on a zoning article residents may be asked to vote on.

The water bylaw failed at town meeting before, and whether new treatment plants in the protection zones need a special permit is still open, so the final wording will decide what residents are asked to approve.
watch_next: July 22nd: the Mass Housing Partnership application and support letter are due, and the Sunny Hill Road stormwater hearing resumes at 6:05 p.m.
August 26th: the revised water bylaw draft, with the special permit option for Zones 1 and 2, returns for discussion; a public hearing is tentatively aimed at September 23rd.

meetings.summary: This remote School Committee meeting closed out FY24 business: a $41,675 salary-to-expense line item transfer, approval of the FY24 encumbrance/open-PO list, and updates on the messy year caused by long-vacant town accountant and finance director positions. The committee also heard a lengthy concussion-protocol discussion with a guest sports-medicine physician, approved joining the Community Eligibility Provision for free meals at Turkey Hill, appointed a member (with backup) to a new town budget task force, and reviewed a personnel report describing many more staff separations than new hires, attributed largely to pay concerns following the district's recent budget-cut scare.

public_comment.topic: Asked about the new finance director's hiring, cost and start; questioned the chair's union membership given his teaching role; asked how long the outside finance consultants (Livingston/Deo, TMS) would remain and what they cost.

Appoint Anthony Scolbrini to the town budget task force, with Laura Brazowski as designated backup.
Table the class accounts discussion until a later date.
Adjourn to executive session and, following executive session, adjourn.

budget_items.what_was_said: The finance consultant recommended transferring available salary-line funds to expense lines to reclassify grant money that should have paid salaries, ahead of the FY24 closeout. This was necessitated by the town accountant and finance director positions being vacant for months.
The finance office reported the total of the warrants already signed for information only; no committee action was needed.

About this amount sits between items truly on the encumbrance list and those simply being held pending review, some funded by grants or the school lunch revolving account rather than the general budget.
The finance consultant cited a small shipping-cost PO adjustment as an example of how many back-and-forth steps with the town are currently required for even minor changes.

budget_items.what_was_said: CEP would let Turkey Hill serve free meals to all students without meal-benefit applications, reimbursed by formula rather than by processing applications; the food services director said funding could be the same or slightly enhanced but did not give a figure.

The superintendent said the district awarded a contract to TMS (Livingston and Deo) for finance support from February 1 through June 30 at roughly this amount, with a possible extension into the transition period.
The incoming finance director begins July 1 on a three-year contract; her first-year salary was stated at this figure.

what_happened.line: A personnel report showed far more staff departures than new hires, attributed largely to pay concerns after the district's recent budget-cut scare.
The committee approved a transfer from salary lines to expense lines to close out the FY24 budget, made necessary by town accountant and finance director positions sitting vacant for months.
The committee approved the FY24 encumbrance list, holding a number of purchase orders open, some funded by grants or the school lunch revolving account rather than the general budget.
The committee voted to join the Community Eligibility Provision at Turkey Hill Elementary, which would let the school serve free meals to all students without meal-benefit applications.
A member was appointed, with a backup, to a newly formed town budget task force.

why_it_matters: Staff leaving over pay, even described only as a pattern here, touches classroom continuity and who is teaching students next year.
The salary-to-expense transfer and the vacant town finance positions behind it affect how reliably the district's books close each year, which residents rely on when judging the budget.
Joining the Community Eligibility Provision would change how families at Turkey Hill Elementary access school meals, regardless of income.

Student cell phone use, added as a future agenda topic

meetings.headline: Water commissioners offered a resident a reduced high-usage bill and meter swap; borrowing and bylaw decisions deferred.
meetings.summary: The Lunenburg Water District commissioners heard a resident contest a high-usage bill and offered to recalculate it at the first block rate and swap his meter. They discussed the Hickory Hills security camera, the Mass Ave main replacement and its temporary borrowing, and approved updated rules and regulations. They objected strongly to the Planning Board's draft water protection bylaw, and public comment centered on that bylaw and PFAS treatment costs.

The budget was reported in deficit for now, with late Q4 bills, Q1/Q2 delinquencies and slow betterments still to come in; the captions give two different deficit figures.

why_it_matters: Sewer is an enterprise fund paid by user bills rather than the general tax levy, so a late or unwaived payment from the schools, and the fund's cash flow, bear on what sewer users are billed.
Manhole repairs must go to formal bid and clogs from flushed items are being tied to bills, so both bear on future sewer costs, and the commission still has only three members.
watch_next: Next meetings are July 9th and 23rd; the commission hopes to have a fourth and fifth member by the ninth.
An invitation for bids for manhole repairs is due to be drafted over about the next month.

meetings.headline: Commission voted to name the beach house for longtime beach manager Genevie Nass and authorized the chair to sign the skate park right-of-entry agreement.
meetings.summary: The Parks Commission heard facilities updates, named the town beach house in memory of a longtime beach employee, and authorized signing the skate park right-of-entry license agreement. what_happened.line: The Parks Commission voted to name the town beach house in memory of a longtime beach employee; the minutes do not record the vote count.
The commission voted to authorize the chair to sign the right-of-entry license agreement for the skate park.
The commission rescinded its May 2023 vote setting a skate park construction end date, and will revisit the time period by October.
Three grant applications were reported: the trails grant and the dredging grant were not awarded, and an ADA grant decision is expected in the fall.
A fully remote special meeting was set for Monday July 1 to vote on a municipal employee rate for the town beach.

why_it_matters: Signing the license agreement and dropping the old end date clear the way for skate park construction at Marshall Park, but with no replacement deadline until the commission sets one.

A rate set for town employees at the beach would change what some residents pay for beach access.
watch_next: Remote special meeting Monday July 1 at 2:30 to vote on the municipal employee beach rate.
Special meeting aimed for July 16 on volunteers for the vacancy, then the regular meeting July 31, and a revisited skate park construction time period by October.

TMS consultant Paul Livingston explained a transfer moving money from psychologist salaries, fire safety and furniture repair lines to dues and fees, transportation, computer purchase/lease, and water charges, because psychologist positions could not be filled and a contracted service was used instead.
A one-year, 2.5% increase was proposed for unaffiliated staff, mostly extended-day program employees paid from a revolving account, with minimal budget impact.

All high school students pay a mandatory annual activity fee funding guest speakers, advisor stipends, Science Olympiad, graduation/homecoming supplies and some field trip bus costs; students who don't pay cannot graduate. The board discussed whether it is fair as a mandatory, non-optional fee.
Middle school clubs such as ski club and Science Olympiad charge a per-club fee covering supplies, registration and some transportation.
Turkey Hill charges a fee for after-school activities, funding teacher stipends and materials for a roughly five-week session.
The primary school charges a similar fee for its after-school activity sessions, funding stipends and materials.

The committee discussed returning ARPA funds to the town for reappropriation by the select board, consistent with what was represented at town meeting, and asked to be part of future discussions on how the money is reused.

budget_items.topic: Maintenance of buildings contracted services line
budget_items.what_was_said: This line was discussed relative to the prior year's figure and the current budget figure after removing E911 compliance costs intended to be funded through ARPA.
A one-time E911 compliance cost was discussed as possibly funded through ARPA or state earmark funds; there was uncertainty whether an earmark would come through.
A public safety training system fell just below the funding line on the capital plan; a member expressed support for finding a way to fund it.
The out-of-district/private special education tuition line was funded at a stated amount, adjusted based on newly known student needs.
This line was adjusted due to a transition between IEP software systems.
The curriculum adoption line was reduced as part of budget line adjustments.

budget_items.topic: Primary school math supplies / library books
budget_items.what_was_said: These lines were reduced after principals were told they could spend down current-year budget lines that had been frozen.
The special education transportation line was increased to reflect newly known added students requiring transportation.

The committee voted to approve the total budget reflecting the override, adjusted from the earlier 'pink' budget for updated salaries and grant offsets, with one member abstaining due to insufficient review time.

The chair reported Chapter 70 came in higher than expected for Lunenburg and said she needed to ask the state representative where the additional amount came from, given the district is not a hold-harmless district.

budget_items.topic: Town payroll timing change / overtime pay
budget_items.what_was_said: Members objected to a planned change in town payroll timing that could cause employees, including lower-wage workers, to miss a paycheck by about a week; they asked for cost details on mitigation options such as a special check.

transfers.description: From psychologist salaries, fire safety, and furniture repair lines to dues and fees, regular transportation, computer purchase and lease, and water charges
