decisions.decision: The chair will reply to the state representative's office that someone from the committee will attend the DESE regional meeting regardless of who holds the chair role at that time.
The superintendent's office will develop the requested overview/talking points about the district for DESE.
Discussion of TMS's suggested best practices for financial operations will be held for a summer workshop rather than at this meeting.

The LHS activity fee and related fee structure will be revisited as a fall agenda item before the FY26 budget process begins, with the superintendent researching how other districts handle similar fees.
The committee will work to schedule the legislative delegation meeting for the fall rather than immediately, given the state budget process has largely concluded for this cycle.
The June 26th meeting will be held remotely via Zoom given member availability.

Members approved a line-item transfer moving funds out of unfilled psychologist salary lines into other accounts.
A consultant reported ongoing MUNIS accounting delays at Town Hall affecting the district's financial operations.

why_it_matters: This vote finalizes the school budget funded by the property tax override residents approved, setting spending for the coming year.
The high school's mandatory activity fee -- required for graduation -- will be revisited before next year's budget is built, which could change what students and families pay.
A town-wide payroll timing change under discussion could affect when school district employees receive a paycheck.

meetings.summary: This School Committee meeting was largely a post-override celebration and reporting session: public comment and the chair's report thanked voters, staff, and advocates for the town's successful override vote, which will level-fund schools (offsetting expiring ESSER money) without expanding programs. The committee voted to reject a proposed rainwater retention/stormwater demonstration project at the middle-high school after learning it was sited without consulting the district and had already cost several thousand dollars in engineering, and voted not to increase school choice seats to protect small class sizes; it also received presentations on a new family-school partnership compact, the state's new IEP form, and facilities project updates.

what_happened.line: The town's override passed, which will level-fund the schools by offsetting expiring ESSER money rather than add programs.
The committee voted to reject a rainwater retention project proposed for the middle-high school after learning it was sited without district input and had already run up engineering costs.

Holding school choice seats flat affects class sizes and the revenue those seats would otherwise bring the district.

The yes count is unreadable in the captions, so the official record of the vote is the only reliable source for the outcome.

meetings.headline: Town meeting passed the FY26 school and town budget with deep staff cuts and voted on a $948,000 school override.
meetings.summary: Annual Town Meeting worked through the full warrant: consent-calendar articles, a Wetlands revolving fund, prior-year bills, reserve-fund transfers, a contested capital plan, the $44M-plus Omnibus budget (which includes deep school staffing cuts as one-time ESSER and ARPA funds expire), a $948,000 Proposition 2½ override for the schools that still needs town-election approval, salary and leave-policy changes for non-union employees, the sewer enterprise budget, a cemetery-lots appropriation, a lowered senior property-tax exemption age, re-adoption of the OPEB trust statute, a historical commission bylaw codification, and a new battery-storage/solar zoning bylaw. Numerous floor amendments were proposed on the capital plan, the cemetery appropriation, and the parental-leave article, with mixed results, and the override's final town-meeting vote tally was not clearly announced in the captions.

what_happened.line: Town meeting approved the town/school Omnibus budget 309-37, which includes deep school staffing cuts as one-time COVID relief funds run out.
Town meeting also acted on a Proposition 2½ override for the schools, an amount heard as roughly an amount as heard but the final tally was not clearly announced in the recording.
The override still needs separate approval at a town election before it can take effect.
The FY25 capital plan passed 320-31 after floor amendments to cut Turkey Hill safety-film and Wallace Park court funding both failed.
Town meeting changed the parental sick-leave policy for non-union employees, passing it as amended 123-13.

why_it_matters: The Omnibus budget sets what schools and town departments can spend this year, and the staffing cuts tied to it follow the expiration of temporary federal pandemic aid, not a new decision to cut on its own.
The override next goes to a town-election ballot; if approved there, it would raise the tax levy above the state's normal cap specifically to fund schools.
The capital plan funds building and site work, including two disputed projects, at Turkey Hill and Wallace Park, that residents will see this year.

what_happened.line: The commission approved a beaver-flow device at the Cranberry area and sent the 255 Sunny Hill Road wetland review to third-party review, then continued that hearing to May 15.
It accepted a quote for third-party wetland delineation review only at 255 Sunny Hill Road, a narrower scope than the full-scope quote the applicant had objected to.
It approved wetland filings: a beach sand RDA at Hickory Hills, a tree-removal RDA at 189 Hemlock Drive, and an order of conditions amendment at 386 Sunset Lane.
A motion to issue a notice of non-compliance at 205 Sunset Lane was not audible in the record, and staff were assigned to research the order's timing first.
The commission moved title search spending from the Kelly Fund to the timber rights fund, and approved several small purchases and a building repainting.

why_it_matters: The Kelly Fund is being kept for major land acquisitions, so routine title-search costs now come from the timber rights fund instead.
Third-party wetland review at 255 Sunny Hill Road adds a consultant step before the commission rules, and the applicant pays a deposit for it.
The commission is considering an earlier meeting end time because the administrator cannot support meetings past 10 pm, which could affect how long hearings can run.
watch_next: Continued hearings at 390 Howard Street, 171 Arbor Street, 141 Hemlock Drive and 255 Sunny Hill Road return on May 15.
The 205 Sunset Lane non-compliance question and the 950 Chase Road drone photos are due for review at the next meeting.

meetings.headline: Committee rehearsed its override pitch for town meeting, warning of deep staff and program cuts if it fails.
meetings.summary: This meeting was largely preparation for Saturday's annual town meeting and the May 18th override vote: a full rehearsal of the override presentation (budget history, what it would fund, and estimated tax impact), plus logistics for food, overflow seating, and voting clickers at town meeting. The committee also heard a stormwater rain-garden project proposal (deferred to May 22nd), approved extended-day/ELC handbooks, discussed but took no action on new fees, reviewed school choice options and athletic program funding, and voted to enter executive session at the close.

All high school students are charged this fee whether or not they participate in an activity; a member recalled it being lower in past years.

The town received a rural roads allotment that is added to its Chapter 90 amount.
An appropriation from town meeting covers removal of old farm debris on a town-owned property.
A member suggested not spending the roof money and instead directing it to schools and a demolition plan.
A small free cash payment of a prior-year expense requires a four-fifths vote at annual town meeting, prompting its removal from the consent calendar.
A member recalled a much larger figure for the line; it was explained as a pass-through of Fitchburg water billing for a handful of users.
The report shows estimated tax bills with and without the override, using an average valuation, and an asterisk was to be added.

The DPW director described Chapter 90 road funds, a large unspent balance, and a request for milling and paving on several roads.

why_it_matters: Writing off ambulance receivables removes old billed amounts the town was carrying as owed, so it bears on how much ambulance revenue the town can count on collecting.
The consent calendar covers stabilization transfers, OPEB, enterprise budgets and prior-year bills, which residents will be asked to vote on together at town meeting unless an article is pulled.
The revenue turnover policy, which sets how revenue is handled, is still undecided, and other boards will see it before the Select Board votes.
watch_next: The revenue turnover policy returns at the Select Board's next meeting, one week out.
The town meeting consent calendar, as drafted, goes to the floor with no articles pulled.

budget_items.what_was_said: State permit requirements not in the contract produced massive added costs; the district will try to renegotiate with the contractor.
Contractor price for filling old pipe under roadway was very high, exceeding available contingency.
The district borrowed for the job and the contract came in a little over a lower figure, leaving small contingency.
Restricted state permit work hours produced a change order that may be eliminated if a town support letter lets hours be extended.
A commissioner said a special meeting would be needed to appropriate more money for the roughly four thousand feet of pipe.
The job is funded entirely by borrowing with no outside funding; terminating would still incur contractor costs.
New EPA limits apply to all sources, requiring treatment; three years to decide and meet the rule by year five.
Policy references last year's voted buyback program and requires proof of alternate coverage if an employee declines district insurance.

meetings.headline: Sewer Commission raised the minimum connection charge and let ReBoot's overdue sewer bill ride on a $2,000 good-faith payment.
meetings.summary: After a public hearing, the commission voted to raise the minimum residential connection charge to match a Leominster increase. It then took up ReBoot restaurant's non-compliance with its sewer payment agreement, with a liquor-license review pending on May 21. A member announced he is resigning, and the business manager reported on Munis software problems and delinquent bills.

what_happened.line: The Sewer Commission voted to raise the minimum residential connection charge as written, after a public hearing.
The commission took no vote on ReBoot's non-compliance with its sewer payment agreement and continued the matter to the end of the month.
A an amount as heard good-faith payment from ReBoot was expected the next day, with updates set for the April 30 and May 14 agendas.
The commission accepted the third quarter commitment, and a member announced he is resigning, staying through May as needed.
Commissioners agreed to a public notice campaign on clogs from wipes, and Wright-Pierce's engineering proposals were held for the next meeting.

why_it_matters: The higher minimum connection charge is a one-time cost for new sewer connections, and the minutes tie it to a Leominster increase in the new intermunicipal agreement.
An unpaid commercial sewer balance and many unpaid third quarter bills affect the revenue the commission collects, and the minutes say missing demands on bills cost it revenue.
Engineering proposals that commissioners found costly, and a grant-dependent pump replacement, bear on future sewer rates and capital costs.
watch_next: April 30 and May 14 Sewer Commission agendas, where ReBoot updates are scheduled.
May 21 liquor-license review for ReBoot, which the commission's handling of the payment agreement bears on.

minutes.headline: Committee voted that ARPA/Esser funds now in the budget must revert to the town if the property-tax override passes
minutes.summary: This was a long, wide-ranging remote School Committee meeting: routine business (minutes, warrants, a surplus truck, staff-appreciation resolutions, an eclipse-glasses donation) alongside substantive discussion of the pending override and the superintendent's evaluation timeline. The committee voted 5-0 that if the override passes, one-time ARPA/Esser funds currently built into the level-service budget should revert to the select board rather than be kept by the schools, while agreeing to ask for some of it back for facilities needs like HVAC repairs; members also discussed an AT&T cell tower revenue opportunity and committed to building a public communication explaining what the override is (and is not) for.

what_happened.line: The Select Board recommended approval of the school override ballot question, article H, by a 3-2 vote.
A roll call vote to put the override question on the May 18 ballot was taken, but the result is not audible in the recording.
The board recommended the FY25 capital plan borrowing and the FY25 omnibus budget, each 5-0, and deferred the prior-year expenses and FY24 budget amendment articles.
The sick-leave article for new parents was deferred pending information on financial impact and union equity.
The board approved a change of manager for Hannaford's alcohol license, contingent on proof of sewer bill payment, and continued the hearing a week.

why_it_matters: The override question is the one that will change a tax bill if voters approve it, so the 3-2 recommendation is the board's signal ahead of the ballot, though the recording does not capture the final ballot vote.

Deferred and removed articles, including prior-year expenses, sick leave for new parents and additional real estate exemptions, will come back at a later town meeting, so what residents vote on this spring is narrower than the original warrant.
watch_next: The Select Board meets April 9, where the continued Hannaford hearing should confirm whether the sewer bill was paid.
The deferred sick-leave article and the exemptions article, which was sent to the November special town meeting.

budget_items.what_was_said: Heavy programming and long meetings have nearly depleted the payroll line for videographers, so the manager asked for a line item transfer.
The videography budget was increased for next year but cannot be changed now since it has been through the finance committee and goes to town meeting in May.
Capital is the only line with enough money, but it covers catastrophic failure such as the TriCaster; some was already moved to equipment maintenance and supplies.
Members discussed moving in smaller monthly amounts versus one transfer; the town accountant prefers one transfer. A compromise of a first tranche was settled with a review in June.
A member asked whether the manager's own salary line has leftover money that could cover part of the need; the manager said some remains for three months and it will be revisited.
A resident noted a spreadsheet discrepancy; the chair said the presentation total, operations plus capital, is the correct one.
The ending balance is off by an amount that the finance director could not explain yet; the manager keeps looking.
Return of indirect costs taken in FY23 remains unresolved, so reported balances are lower than they should be.

The quarterly Enterprise fund statement is not yet received; no interest has been received since December and a portion is uninvested. Interest and franchise fees are operating income; bond interest is held for the new studio.
The cost of an Owl video conferencing device was discussed and the manager was asked to look into feasibility of using the town's existing one.
A resident described a telethon that raised money for scholarships as a model for a small start-up call-in program.

what_happened.line: The Public Access Cable Committee voted unanimously to request a line item transfer from new equipment capital to videographer payroll, pending Town Manager approval.
The manager reported that heavy programming and long meetings had nearly used up the videographer payroll line, which prompted the request.
Members settled on a first tranche now, with the need for more to be reviewed at the June meeting, rather than one full transfer.
The manager was asked to look into getting or taking over an Owl camera for recording town committee meetings; no purchase was decided.
The committee agreed a letter supporting H74 will be finished and sent to the legislator by the April 8 deadline.

why_it_matters: Cable access budgets are small, and capital set aside for equipment failure was drawn on to keep videographers paid for meeting coverage that residents watch.
The videography budget was raised for next year but is already past the Finance Committee, so it goes to Town Meeting in May as is; the current-year gap was handled by a transfer instead.
watch_next: Town Manager approval of the requested transfer, and the June review of whether more is needed.
Next committee meeting on May 6; the H74 letter is due by April 8.

Voters unanimously authorized the treasurer to borrow in anticipation of revenue and renew notes; no dollar cap was stated, only what is needed to fund the budget.
Voters unanimously approved two further appropriations: one from the water enhancement account for repair of water services, one from surplus revenue for a replacement vehicle.
Article One, the election, was postponed until the ballots were counted; after a recess the results were announced, with Mark Burch winning, and the meeting adjourned.

why_it_matters: Water district customers pay for the operating budget through district income, so the Article Three vote sets the spending behind the district's rates for the year starting July 1, 2024.
Short-term borrowing was authorized with no stated limit, so the size of any notes depends on cash needs during the year rather than on a figure voters approved.

budget_items.what_was_said: Chapter 90 is state money for town roads and drainage, paid as reimbursement. A five-year spending plan was prepared at the town manager's request, including equipment.
A reimbursement request was submitted for the first four projects, including mill and paving.
The sidewalk engineering would not all be spent in FY24, with most in FY25.
Chapter 90 is described as not enough for all needed projects.
The plan's balance rises each year because the state adds funding annually, unadjusted for inflation.
A dump truck was hoped for through capital funding, and a mini excavator with trailer is planned in FY26, mostly for stormwater use.
A member asked why the excavator isn't moved earlier given the remaining balance. There is no limit on how much can be used, but it must be paid and then reimbursed.
Draft assumes one big project and two small ones.
Rough first-year estimate includes equipment, with ongoing annual costs lower afterwards.
Projections would apply an annual inflation multiplier.
CI consulting is included in the utility budget with an engineering and audits line.
Earlier estimate per resident was about 60 dollars; with the larger budget it might be around double. Unclear whether it included businesses.

budget_items.topic: Current DPW drainage and stormwater lines
budget_items.what_was_said: Drainage line is nearly spent; stormwater line includes rolled-over funds and is mostly spent.
Stormwater labor in FY23 was estimated, and existing town budget amounts could shift to the utility.
After offsetting existing town budget amounts, net need is lower. Per-household figures were discussed and described as override territory.
Members want Chapter 90 on top of the utility for big projects such as Flat Hill/Page Street.
Nonprofits pay no property tax; the group discussed charging them stormwater fees, with a figure floated.
The labor figure given will be used in outreach budget material.

decisions.decision: Appointment of a vice chair was deferred until all members are present.
Target start for a stormwater utility is FY26; a special town meeting that soon was judged too quick.
Next steps: have CI estimate business footprints/impervious area, then combine with the residential figure, then draft bylaws and specs.
The outreach outline will be emailed to members for comments, with follow-up in about a week.
Next meeting moved to April 18 (third Thursday) because of vacation week.

what_happened.line: The Select Board amended the school override article, article H, to carry a stated dollar amount and placed it on the town meeting warrant.
The board placed articles A through Z on the warrant, then recommended approval of articles A, B, C, I, L, M, N, P, T and W, each 5-0.
The board deferred its recommendation on articles Y and Z to town meeting, and put articles still lacking numbers over to next week.
The town manager reported that new positions were pulled from the budget to cover a possible trash contract increase and wage impacts, with the final gap closed by raising local receipts estimates.
The school committee will send its final override number after its Wednesday meeting so the board can modify article H next week.

why_it_matters: The school override is headed to a ballot question, so residents will be asked to vote on a Proposition 2 1/2 amount that is still open to change next week.

The trash contract, which the hauler indicated would rise sharply to extend, and the removal of new positions bear on town services and on how much of the budget gap is met by estimates rather than cuts.
watch_next: Next week's Select Board meeting: the final override number from the school committee, the override ballot wording and recommendation, and a public hearing on early voting by mail.
The deferred warrant articles that still have no numbers, and the board's decision on adding to article V after hearing from the board of assessors.

what_happened.line: The Planning Board continued the water supply protection and battery energy storage bylaw hearings to April 8th, with no vote on either bylaw's text.
The board agreed to consider restoring Zone 1 protections in the water bylaw and dropping special permit requirements, pending easement documents from residents.
The board voted to send the Select Board a message that it has no recommendation on the right of first refusal for 100 Howard Street.
The board voted to issue certificates of completion and release the performance guarantee for 147 and 159 Homan Street.
The board approved a member-at-large application to the master plan steering committee and continued the 255 Sunny Hill Road hearing to April 22nd.

why_it_matters: The water bylaw decides what can be built or done in protected zones around the town's water supply, and residents near Hickory Hills spoke against losing Zone 1 protections before any final text exists.

The Planning Board gave the Select Board no recommendation on 100 Howard Street, so any decision on exercising the town's right of first refusal, a possible spending question, rests without that board's advice.
The battery storage bylaw sets noise, surety and definition rules for future installations, and its wording is still being revised.
watch_next: Planning Board hearings on the water supply protection and battery storage bylaws resume April 8th at 6:05 p.m.
The 255 Sunny Hill Road hearing resumes April 22nd at 6:05.

why_it_matters: Moving one-time ARPA money and paving funds to the school budget narrows the gap without a tax increase, but does not close it, so residents may still be asked to vote on an override.
The trash contract will be rebid after the 90-day extension, and the larger price at the new contract could change what the town spends on solid waste and recycling next year.

what_happened.line: Water commissioners heard a consultant present a draft master plan recommending one PFAS treatment plant at Lancaster Ave for the Lancaster and Hickory Hills supplies, plus a separate Keating plant.
No plan was adopted and no votes were taken other than adjournment.
The consultant described a combined plant with a cross-town transmission main and a standalone Keating plant, each with a budget estimate given as a figure in the recording.
The district has applied for state revolving fund financing, which offers zero percent loans and possible principal forgiveness, but first-year funding is capped, so a borrowing vote would be needed.
The consultant advised sending a letter to the SRF program once its project list is final, asking that the changed scope and amount be treated as a carryover project.

Because first-year SRF funding is capped, district voters would likely be asked to approve borrowing for the remainder of the project.

meetings.headline: Town meeting rejected a $986,000 ARPA-vs-stabilization-fund transfer for a new ambulance and dump trucks.
meetings.summary: This special town meeting acted on sixteen warrant articles: it approved FY24 budget adjustments including a town-clerk raise (despite objections over an executive-session vote), funded a clerical union contract and a police opioid co-response program, funded primary-school air conditioning after rejecting amendments tying it to a grant, and passed a roof repair, a Marshall Park grant-qualifying article, and several zoning bylaw changes (water supply protection map rewrite passed over, farm definition, common driveways, solar parking canopies). minutes.summary: This special town meeting acted on sixteen warrant articles: it approved FY24 budget adjustments including a town-clerk raise (despite objections over an executive-session vote), funded a clerical union contract and a police opioid co-response program, funded primary-school air conditioning after rejecting amendments tying it to a grant, and passed a roof repair, a Marshall Park grant-qualifying article, and several zoning bylaw changes (water supply protection map rewrite passed over, farm definition, common driveways, solar parking canopies). what_happened.line: Town meeting voted down a transfer from the special purpose stabilization fund meant to reimburse ARPA-funded purchases of an ambulance and two dump trucks, 29-92.
Town meeting approved FY24 budget adjustments, including a town clerk salary increase, 126-13, after residents objected that the raise had been discussed in executive session.
Town meeting funded the first year of the clerical union contract, 132-11, after public comment that clerical wages lag comparable towns.
Town meeting approved a transfer for ductless mini-split air conditioning at the primary school after voting down two amendments that would have tied the funding to a Green Communities grant.
Several zoning bylaw changes passed by the required two-thirds margin, including a farm-definition update, common-driveway provisions, and solar parking canopy rules.

why_it_matters: The rejected transfer leaves the ambulance and dump-truck purchases without an approved funding source and keeps the special purpose stabilization fund at its current balance rather than drawing it down.
The town clerk raise and the clerical union contract affect town payroll costs and, indirectly, what the town needs to raise going forward.
The air-conditioning vote and the failed grant-first amendments determine whether primary-school cooling work proceeds now or waits on a separate grant application.

meetings.headline: Town Meeting passed the FY24 town and school budget and created a new senior property tax exemption program
meetings.summary: Lunenburg's Annual Town Meeting worked through 22 warrant articles: a consent calendar of routine transfers, the FY24 town and school operating budget, a large transfer to the overlay account to cover FY23 tax abatements, the FY24 capital plan, union and salary-plan wage increases, new special-purpose, OPEB and opioid-settlement stabilization funds, the sewer enterprise budget, a new means-tested senior property tax exemption requiring state special legislation, and a zoning bylaw change to allow self-storage by special permit. Finance Director Karen Brochu was honored on her last town meeting before retiring after 38 years.

minutes.headline: Town Meeting rejected new authority to amend the capital plan, but approved Marshall Park engineering funding.
minutes.summary: This special town meeting acted on 15 warrant articles: it approved FY23 budget adjustments, a police union contract's first-year funding, $184,000 for Marshall Park engineering (to support up to $2 million in outside grants), a firefighter/reserve-officer retirement buyback provision, and a motel zoning change and a citizen-petitioned rezoning. what_happened.line: Town Meeting rejected giving itself authority to amend individual line items in the capital plan.
It approved a transfer for final engineering and design at Marshall Park, meant to support outside grant applications.
It approved FY23 budget adjustments to town management, assessors, planning board and facilities and grounds lines.
It approved year-one funding for the new police officers' collective bargaining agreement.
It rejected overriding the APDC's denial of Ritter Library window replacement and rejected changing the APDC's own review bylaw.

why_it_matters: The capital plan vote leaves individual project funding outside town meeting's amending power unless a future warrant article changes the bylaw again.
Marshall Park funding lets the town move ahead on grant applications that the project depends on to cover a large share of its cost.
The Ritter Library and APDC bylaw votes leave the historic commission's review process and the library's window question unresolved.

meetings.headline: Town Meeting passed the FY23 town/school budget and capital plan, and cut back old primary school park funding by floor amendment.
meetings.summary: This was Lunenburg's annual Town Meeting, working through a full warrant covering the FY23 town and school operating budget, the capital plan, a new facilities director position, and numerous bylaw and building articles including the Woodruff property cleanup, old primary school demolition, sewer bylaw waivers, a marijuana licensing fix, and the water supply protection district. Nearly every article passed, though residents amended the old primary school demolition article down from its original funding level after a lengthy, twice-redone floor debate, and repeatedly pushed back on whether the capital plan should have allowed item-by-item votes. The meeting also passed over a citizen petition to expand the sewer service area and took up a resolution supporting a new state flag, with the final tallies on the water-district and flag articles not clearly captured.

minutes.headline: Town Meeting passed the FY23 town/school budget and capital plan, and cut back old primary school park funding by floor amendment.
minutes.summary: This was Lunenburg's annual Town Meeting, working through a full warrant covering the FY23 town and school operating budget, the capital plan, a new facilities director position, and numerous bylaw and building articles including the Woodruff property cleanup, old primary school demolition, sewer bylaw waivers, a marijuana licensing fix, and the water supply protection district. Nearly every article passed, though residents amended the old primary school demolition article down from its original funding level after a lengthy, twice-redone floor debate, and repeatedly pushed back on whether the capital plan should have allowed item-by-item votes. The meeting also passed over a citizen petition to expand the sewer service area and took up a resolution supporting a new state flag, with the final tallies on the water-district and flag articles not clearly captured.

what_happened.line: Town Meeting passed the FY23 town and school operating budget as one omnibus article, funded without drawing on free cash or stabilization.
The FY23 capital plan passed as a single up-or-down total after the moderator ruled, on town counsel's advice, that individual projects could not be voted or amended separately.
After a floor debate redone once for a procedural flaw, voters cut back the old primary school article to cover demolition and design only, not the fuller park funding first proposed.
A new facilities director position was created, and free cash was approved to clean up illegally dumped waste on the town-owned Woodruff property.
Votes on the water supply protection district bylaw and a resolution on the state flag were not clearly captured on the recording.

why_it_matters: The operating budget vote sets what residents' tax bill funds for town and school services in FY23, including new police, fire and school staff positions described by the town manager and superintendent.

Because the capital plan can only be voted as one total, residents cannot currently approve or reject individual projects like the senior center HVAC or the primary school classroom AC separately — a process several people at the meeting pushed back on.
The old primary school site now has money for demolition and design, but not for a built-out park, so what that land becomes is still an open question for a future town meeting or town decision.
watch_next: Whether the primary school AC project comes back to a future town meeting as a capital request if it exceeds what the school's operating budget can absorb.
A future decision on the final design or use — park versus open space — of the old primary school lot.

minutes.headline: Parks Commission chose Wolla to design the Marshall Park overhaul and authorized skatepark land for preliminary design.
minutes.summary: The Parks Commission voted to grant the Lunenburg Skatepark project space at Marshall Park (up to 8,000 sq ft) to proceed with a preliminary design, after lengthy discussion of siting, parking, maintenance costs, and fundraising progress. It also voted to hire Wolla as the landscape architecture/engineering firm for the broader Marshall Park redesign, over three competing firms, and set December 2nd as the next meeting, doubling as a public forum on the park's future.

what_happened.line: The commission voted to let the Lunenburg Skatepark project use a defined area of Marshall Park to develop a preliminary design.
It also voted to hire Wolla as the landscape architecture and engineering firm for the full Marshall Park redesign, chosen over three competing firms.
The skatepark group reported fundraising progress but said an amount was still needed before construction could start.
The next meeting, December 2nd, was set to double as a public forum on the Marshall Park redesign with the design firm.
Commissioners were asked to propose how to spend an Open Space Committee donation ahead of a December meeting of that committee.

why_it_matters: Marshall Park's redesign now has a hired design firm and a defined skatepark footprint, moving the project from concept toward a plan residents will see at the December forum.

The skatepark's construction is expected to be funded by the group's own fundraising rather than town appropriation, so how much it still needs to raise affects whether the project breaks ground on the timeline discussed.
A separate donation held by the Open Space Committee is still unassigned, and the Parks Commission may propose a project for part of it before that committee's December meeting.
